paper_title: The formation and evolution of early-type galaxies : solid results and open questions
context_brief: Size evolution of compact high-redshift early-type galaxies
original_question: What explains the compact sizes of early-type galaxies at redshift z > 1, and how do these superdense galaxies increase their sizes enough to match the local Kormendy relation by redshift z approximately 0? The problem concerns early-type galaxies with effective radii Re ≤ 1 kpc, sizes about 2--3 times smaller than present-day early-type galaxies, stellar mass surface densities up to about 10 times local values, and stellar volume densities up to about 30 times local values; it also asks whether the apparent size differences could be affected by observational biases such as surface-brightness dimming and signal-to-noise effects.
self_contained_problem:
Observations of early-type galaxies (ETGs)—galaxies dominated by an old stellar population, with elliptical or lenticular morphology and little ongoing star formation—at redshift z > 1 indicate that a substantial fraction are "superdense": they have effective (half-light) radii R_e ≲ 1 kpc, a factor of about 2–3 smaller than ETGs of comparable stellar mass at z ≈ 0, with stellar mass surface densities up to about 10 times and stellar volume densities up to about 30 times those of present-day ETGs. Local ETGs obey the Kormendy relation, an observed linear correlation between mean surface brightness ⟨μ⟩_e within R_e and log R_e.

(a) Identify the physical mechanism(s) by which ETGs at z > 1 attain such compact sizes and high central densities at formation.

(b) Determine a quantitative evolutionary scenario by which these superdense ETGs increase R_e (and decrease their stellar density) by the required factor of 2–3 between z ≳ 1 and z ≈ 0, in such a way that they end up on the local Kormendy relation, while preserving the old stellar populations (i.e., without significant new star formation).

(c) Assess whether observational systematics—in particular cosmological surface-brightness dimming (which scales as (1+z)^{-4} for bolometric flux), limited signal-to-noise in the outer low-surface-brightness wings of the light profile, and PSF effects—could account, in whole or in part, for the apparent compactness, rather than the size difference being intrinsic.
status_search_result: The compactness of high-z ETGs has been confirmed by multiple subsequent studies, ruling out observational biases as the dominant cause. The leading explanation for subsequent size growth is dry minor mergers, supported by both simulations and observations (e.g., Naab et al. 2009; López-Sanjuan et al. 2012; Bernardi et al. 2013), with size growing roughly as the square of mass for minor mergers. However, debate continues over whether minor mergers alone provide enough growth, with alternative/complementary scenarios (puffing up via AGN/stellar mass loss, progenitor bias, selection effects) still discussed. The problem is therefore considered partially resolved rather than definitively settled.

paper_title: The formation and evolution of early-type galaxies : solid results and open questions
context_brief: Viability of dry merging as a size-growth mechanism
original_question: How can major dissipationless, or dry, merging explain the gradual size increase of compact, superdense early-type galaxies at 1 < z < 2 while remaining consistent with the observed small-scale clustering of low-redshift early-type galaxies and the weak evolution of the high-mass end of their stellar mass function at 0 < z < 0.7? The question asks whether dry merging is viable as the main size-growth mechanism or whether other processes such as smooth envelope accretion or multiple frequent minor mergers are needed.
self_contained_problem:
Compact, "superdense" massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) observed at redshifts 1 < z < 2 are known to be substantially smaller (by factors of a few in effective radius) than local ETGs of comparable stellar mass, and they appear to grow gradually in size toward the present epoch. Consider the following structural/cosmological constraints on the size-growth mechanism:

(i) the small-scale (sub-Mpc) two-point correlation function of low-redshift (z ≲ 0.1) early-type galaxies, which constrains the rate of close pairs and hence the frequency of major dissipationless mergers;
(ii) the weak evolution of the high-mass end (M_* ≳ 10^11 M_⊙) of the ETG stellar mass function over 0 < z < 0.7, which limits how much mass can be added to already massive ETGs by major merging without overproducing the abundance of very massive systems.

Within this setup, determine whether major dissipationless ("dry") mergers between comparable-mass spheroids can simultaneously:
(a) reproduce the observed mean increase of the effective radius R_e of massive ETGs from z ~ 2 to z ~ 0 (roughly a factor of 3–5 at fixed stellar mass),
(b) be consistent with constraint (i), and
(c) be consistent with constraint (ii).

If major dry merging alone is insufficient, quantify the relative contributions required from alternative mechanisms — in particular smooth accretion of low-density stellar envelopes, and a sequence of multiple minor (mass ratio ≲ 1:5) dry mergers — needed to account for the observed size evolution while remaining consistent with (i) and (ii).
status_search_result: Subsequent literature has converged on the view that major dry mergers alone cannot reproduce the observed size growth of compact massive ETGs while respecting clustering and high-mass-end stellar-mass-function constraints; multiple minor dry mergers (mass ratios 1:5–1:10 or smaller) are now widely regarded as the dominant size-growth channel, supplemented by smooth envelope accretion in some scenarios. original_question: For the integer lattice Zⁿ with n > 3, calculate the numbers χ(Zⁿ) that govern the exact minimal-central-set calculations in this setting, and determine the structure of central sets in Zⁿ.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a group. For an element g ∈ G, define the involution s_g : G → G by s_g(x) = gx^{-1}g. A subset C ⊆ G is called symmetric with center g if s_g(C) = C, equivalently if gC^{-1}g = C. A finite subset C ⊆ G with |C| ≥ 2 is called central if for every finite subset F ⊆ G there exists h ∈ G such that hF h ⊆ ⋃_{c ∈ C} c·G·c (more precisely, a central set is one that meets every symmetric subset of G of sufficiently large size; equivalently, C is central if every finite coloring of G in which C is monochromatic admits a monochromatic symmetric subset of arbitrarily large size). Define
   χ(G) = min{ |C| : C ⊆ G is a central subset of G }.
For the abelian group G = Z^n with n > 3, determine the value of χ(Z^n) and describe the structure (up to translation and the natural action of GL_n(Z)) of all central subsets of Z^n.
status_search_result: No published computation of χ(Z^n) for n > 3 or classification of central sets in Z^n for n > 3 was found. Related work by Banakh, Protasov, Verbitsky and Vorobets addresses symmetric monochromatic subsets and coloring numbers of abelian groups, but the specific values χ(Z^n) for n > 3 and a structural description of central sets in higher-dimensional integer lattices appear to remain open.

original_question: Is there a connected compact group G and an integer r for which ms(G, r) < 1/r², where ms(G, r) is the largest ε such that every measurable r-coloring of G contains a measurable monochromatic symmetric subset of Haar measure at least ε? Let G be a connected compact topological group equipped with its normalized Haar measure μ. A subset A ⊆ G is called symmetric if there exists g ∈ G such that A = gA⁻¹g, i.e., A is invariant under the involution x ↦ gx⁻¹g for some g ∈ G (equivalently, symmetric about the point g in the sense of the group involution). Given r ∈ ℕ, a measurable r-coloring of G is a partition G = C₁ ⊔ … ⊔ Cᵣ into μ-measurable sets. Define

  ms(G, r) := sup { ε > 0 : for every measurable r-coloring of G there exists a measurable monochromatic symmetric subset A ⊆ Cᵢ (for some i) with μ(A) ≥ ε }.

Question 1: Does there exist a connected compact group G and an integer r ≥ 1 such that ms(G, r) < 1/r²?

self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. For a subset $A \subseteq X$, say that $A$ is symmetric (with respect to the action) if there exists a non-identity element $g \in G$ such that $gA = A$.

Now let $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a compact set of positive Lebesgue measure, and let $G$ be its isometry group (the group of Euclidean isometries of $\mathbb{R}^n$ that map $X$ onto itself), acting on $X$. Let $\mu$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$. For an integer $r \geq 2$, a measurable $r$-coloring of $X$ is a partition $X = C_1 \cup \cdots \cup C_r$ into $r$ Lebesgue-measurable subsets.

Define
$$ \mathrm{ms}(X, r) \;=\; \sup\{\varepsilon \geq 0 : \text{for every measurable } r\text{-coloring of } X \text{ there exists a monochromatic} $$
$$ \text{symmetric subset } A \subseteq C_i \text{ with } \mu(A) \geq \varepsilon\}, $$
where "monochromatic symmetric" means $A$ is contained in a single color class $C_i$ and $gA = A$ for some non-identity $g \in G$.

Problems:
(a) Classify (i.e., give a method to compute) $\mathrm{ms}(X, r)$ for arbitrary compact subsets $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ of positive Lebesgue measure, when $n > 2$.

(b) In particular, compute $\mathrm{ms}(X, r)$ for every regular polyhedron $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n > 2$, for all integers $r \geq 2$.

(c) Compute $\mathrm{ms}(T, 2)$, where $T$ is the regular tetrahedron in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (equivalently, compute $\mathrm{ms}(S_4 \times I, 2)$ where the symmetric group $S_4$ acts on the tetrahedron's symmetry structure and $I$ denotes the standard interval factor in this reformulation).

For a Lebesgue measurable subset A ⊂ [0,1], call A symmetric if there exists a point c ∈ ℝ such that A = 2c − A (i.e., A is invariant under the reflection x ↦ 2c − x). paper_title: SYMMETRY AND COLORINGS: SOME RESULTS AND OPEN PROBLEMS
original_question: How quickly do the sequences {ms([n], r)}_{n=1}^{∞} and {bms([n], r)}_{n=1}^{∞} converge to their common limit ms([0, 1], r)?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer n ≥ 1 let [n] = {1, 2, …, n}, equipped with the family of central symmetries s_c : x ↦ 2c − x (c ∈ ½ℤ). A subset B ⊆ [n] is called symmetric if s_c(B) = B for some c. A coloring of [n] is a map χ : [n] → {1, …, r}; a subset is monochromatic if χ is constant on it. Define

  MS([n], r) = min over all r-colorings χ of [n] of the maximum cardinality of a monochromatic symmetric subset of [n],
  ms([n], r) = MS([n], r) / n.

Analogously, a fractional r-coloring of [n] is a map χ : [n] → Δ_r, where Δ_r = {(p_1,…,p_r) ∈ ℝ_{≥0}^r : Σ p_i = 1}. The "monochromatic mass" in color i of a subset B is Σ_{x ∈ B} χ(x)_i. Define

  BMS([n], r) = inf over fractional r-colorings χ of the supremum, over symmetric subsets B ⊆ [n] and colors i, of Σ_{x ∈ B} χ(x)_i,
  bms([n], r) = BMS([n], r) / n.

For the unit interval [0, 1] equipped with central symmetries s_c(x) = 2c − x (c ∈ ℝ), and r-colorings χ : [0, 1] → {1, …, r} measurable in the appropriate sense, set

  ms([0, 1], r) = inf_χ sup{ λ(B) : B ⊆ [0,1] symmetric and monochromatic for χ },

where λ denotes Lebesgue measure. It is known that

  ms([0, 1], r) = lim_{n→∞} ms([n], r) = inf_{n ∈ ℕ} ms([n], r),
  ms([0, 1], r) = lim_{n→∞} bms([n], r) = inf_{n ∈ ℕ} bms([n], r),

for every r ∈ ℕ.

Problem. Determine the rate of convergence: for each fixed r ∈ ℕ, give sharp asymptotic bounds on ms([n], r) − ms([0, 1], r) and on bms([n], r) − ms([0, 1], r) as n → ∞.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in surveys on symmetry and colorings by Banakh, Verbitsky, Vorobets, and Protasov. Web searches did not reveal a published paper establishing sharp convergence rates for ms([n], r) and bms([n], r) toward ms([0, 1], r); related papers continue to investigate values and bounds for these invariants but do not appear to settle the rate of convergence. Status could not be conclusively verified.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
original_question: Generalize the notion of transversality from Volterra quadratic stochastic operators to arbitrary quadratic stochastic operators V(x) with heredity coefficients P_{ij,k}. In particular, define what it should mean for a non-Volterra or arbitrary QSO to be transversal, and then find necessary and sufficient conditions on the cubic heredity matrix P = (P_{ij,k}) that exactly characterize when the operator is transversal.
self_contained_problem:
A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) on the (m-1)-dimensional simplex
S^{m-1} = { x = (x_1,...,x_m) ∈ R^m : x_i ≥ 0, Σ x_i = 1 }
is a map V : S^{m-1} → S^{m-1} of the form
(V(x))_k = Σ_{i,j=1}^{m} P_{ij,k} x_i x_j,  k = 1,...,m,
where the heredity coefficients P_{ij,k} satisfy P_{ij,k} = P_{ji,k} ≥ 0 and Σ_{k=1}^{m} P_{ij,k} = 1 for every i,j.

A QSO V is called Volterra if P_{ij,k} = 0 whenever k ∉ {i,j}. For a Volterra QSO, writing (V(x))_k = x_k(1 + Σ_{i=1}^{m} a_{ki} x_i), one obtains a skew-symmetric matrix A = (a_{ki}) with a_{ki} = 2 P_{ki,k} - 1 (so that a_{ki} = -a_{ik} and |a_{ki}| ≤ 1). A skew-symmetric matrix A is called transversal if all its leading principal minors of even order are nonzero, and a Volterra QSO is called transversal when its associated skew-symmetric matrix A is transversal.

Problem. Extend the notion of transversality from Volterra QSO to the class of all (in particular non-Volterra) quadratic stochastic operators: propose a definition of "transversal QSO" applicable to an arbitrary cubic heredity tensor P = (P_{ij,k}) that reduces to the Volterra notion above in the Volterra case, and find necessary and sufficient conditions on P that exactly characterize when the corresponding QSO is transversal in the sense of this definition.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any work that defines transversality for arbitrary (non-Volterra) quadratic stochastic operators or that characterizes such operators in terms of the heredity tensor P_{ij,k}. Surveys and recent papers on QSOs (including superpositions of Volterra and permuted Volterra operators, and non-Volterra families) discuss dynamics and fixed/periodic points but do not appear to address this specific extension of transversality. The status is therefore reported as unknown.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Ergodicity for the three-parameter Volterra family
original_question: Consider the three-dimensional Volterra quadratic stochastic operator on S^2 defined by x' = x (1 + a y - b z), y' = y (1 - a x + c z), z' = z (1 + b x - c y), where a, b, c are in [-1,1]. The paper proves that if a, b, and c are all nonzero and have the same sign, then the ergodic theorem fails for this operator. Determine whether one can formulate a sufficient condition for the ergodic theorem to hold for this family, and in particular whether the parameter-sign condition appearing in Theorem 3 is sharp for separating ergodic and non-ergodic behavior.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^2 = \{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : x,y,z \ge 0,\ x+y+z = 1\}$ be the two-dimensional simplex. For parameters $a,b,c \in [-1,1]$, define the Volterra quadratic stochastic operator $V : S^2 \to S^2$ by
\[
x' = x(1 + ay - bz),\qquad y' = y(1 - ax + cz),\qquad z' = z(1 + bx - cy).
\]
For an initial point $p \in S^2$, denote the trajectory by $V^n(p)$, and say that the ergodic theorem holds for $V$ if for every $p \in S^2$ the Cesàro averages
\[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} V^k(p)
\]
converge as $n \to \infty$.

It is known that if $a$, $b$, $c$ are all nonzero and have the same sign, then the ergodic theorem fails for $V$. The problem is the following:

(a) Determine whether the condition that $a,b,c$ are all nonzero and of the same sign is also necessary for failure of the ergodic theorem; equivalently, determine whether for all remaining parameter choices $(a,b,c) \in [-1,1]^3$ (i.e., when at least one of $a,b,c$ is zero or the nonzero ones do not all share the same sign) the ergodic theorem holds for $V$.

(b) More generally, give a sufficient condition on $(a,b,c) \in [-1,1]^3$ under which the ergodic theorem holds for the operator $V$.
status_search_result: Subsequent works (e.g., "Ergodic Volterra Quadratic Transformations of the Simplex," arXiv:1205.3841, and later surveys/chapters such as "Ergodic Volterra Quadratic Mappings of the Simplex," 2024) provide a description of ergodic properties of Volterra QSOs on the 2-simplex and analyze the parameter regimes (cases where parameters have mixed signs versus all-same-sign), indicating that the same-sign nonzero condition is essentially the obstruction to ergodicity, with full analyses given in special cases. The original sharpness/sufficiency question thus appears to have been substantially addressed but is reported across several papers with case-by-case analyses rather than a single unified theorem in the original formulation.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
original_question: Develop a general dynamical-systems theory for ℓ-Volterra quadratic stochastic operators. This should include, at minimum, the construction of Lyapunov functions for ℓ-Volterra QSOs, a description of the limit sets of their trajectories, and other core structural results about their asymptotic dynamics.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^{m-1}=\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m: x_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m x_i=1\}$ denote the $(m-1)$-dimensional standard simplex. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) is a map $V:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ defined by
$$ (Vx)_k = \sum_{i,j=1}^{m} P_{ij,k}\, x_i x_j, \qquad k=1,\dots,m, $$
where the coefficients satisfy $P_{ij,k}=P_{ji,k}\ge 0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^m P_{ij,k}=1$ for all $i,j$.

Fix an integer $\ell\in\{0,1,\dots,m\}$. The QSO $V$ is called an $\ell$-Volterra QSO if there exists a subset $I=\{i_1,\dots,i_\ell\}\subset\{1,\dots,m\}$ of cardinality $\ell$ such that
$$ P_{ij,k}=0 \quad\text{whenever } k\notin\{i,j\}\cup I, $$
i.e. the only "non-Volterra" coordinates allowed in the support of $P_{ij,\cdot}$ lie in the distinguished set $I$. (For $\ell=0$ this recovers the classical Volterra QSOs.) Iteration of $V$ yields a discrete-time dynamical system $x^{(n+1)}=V(x^{(n)})$ on $S^{m-1}$, whose trajectory starting at $x^{(0)}$ has $\omega$-limit set $\omega(x^{(0)})$.

Develop a general theory of the dynamical systems generated by $\ell$-Volterra QSOs for arbitrary $m$ and $\ell$. In particular:

(a) Construct Lyapunov functions $\varphi:S^{m-1}\to\mathbb{R}$ (i.e. functions which are monotone along every trajectory of $V$) for general $\ell$-Volterra QSOs.

(b) Describe the structure of the set $\omega(x^{(0)})$ of limit points of trajectories for every initial point $x^{(0)}\in S^{m-1}$.

(c) Establish the further core structural results about the asymptotic behaviour of these operators (e.g.\ characterisation of fixed points, basins of attraction, ergodic properties).
status_search_result: Subsequent work (notably Rozikov–Zada, "ℓ-Volterra Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Lyapunov Functions, Trajectories", Appl. Math. Inf. Sci. 6 (2012)) constructs Lyapunov functions for ℓ-Volterra QSOs under coefficient restrictions and gives upper bounds on ω-limit sets, and describes some fixed-point sets. However, unlike pure Volterra QSOs, ω(x⁰) is not in general contained in the fixed-point set, and a complete general theory (full description of limit sets, basins, ergodic behaviour for arbitrary m and ℓ) has not been established. Hence the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Analogue of F-QSO theorem for ξ-QSOs
original_question: Let ξ = {E_1, ..., E_q} be a partition of the species set E, and define a ξ-QSO by requiring P_{ij,k} = 0 whenever both parent indices i and j lie in the same block E_p. Determine whether an analogue of Theorem 5 holds for every ξ-QSO; that is, whether such operators always have a unique fixed point and whether every trajectory converges to it, as happens for F-QSOs.
self_contained_problem:
Let $m\ge 2$ and let $E=\{1,2,\dots,m\}$ be a finite set (the species set). Denote the $(m-1)$-dimensional simplex by
$$S^{m-1}=\Bigl\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m:\ x_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m x_i=1\Bigr\}.$$
A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) on $S^{m-1}$ is a map $V:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ defined by
$$(Vx)_k=\sum_{i,j=1}^{m} P_{ij,k}\,x_i x_j,\qquad k=1,\dots,m,$$
where the heredity coefficients satisfy
$$P_{ij,k}=P_{ji,k}\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{m}P_{ij,k}=1\quad\text{for all }i,j.$$
For $x^{(0)}\in S^{m-1}$, the trajectory is the sequence $x^{(n+1)}=Vx^{(n)}$, $n\ge 0$.

Now fix a partition $\xi=\{E_1,\dots,E_q\}$ of $E$, i.e.\ $E=E_1\cup\cdots\cup E_q$ with $E_p\cap E_r=\emptyset$ for $p\ne r$. A QSO is called a $\xi$-QSO if its coefficients additionally satisfy
$$P_{ij,k}=0\quad\text{whenever there exists } p\in\{1,\dots,q\}\text{ such that } i,j\in E_p.$$

Question: Is it true that, for every partition $\xi$ of $E$ and every $\xi$-QSO $V$, the operator $V$ has a unique fixed point in $S^{m-1}$ and every trajectory $\{x^{(n)}\}_{n\ge 0}$ starting from any $x^{(0)}\in S^{m-1}$ converges to that fixed point?
status_search_result: Subsequent works have studied ξ-QSOs (and the related ξ(s)- and ξ(a)-QSOs) on the 2-dimensional simplex, classifying them into multiple nonconjugate classes and analyzing dynamics for several specific partitions/classes. These studies reveal varied dynamical behaviors (including non-unique fixed points and non-global convergence in some classes), so the proposed analogue of the F-QSO theorem does not hold uniformly. A complete general answer for arbitrary partitions ξ and arbitrary dimension does not appear to be established.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
original_question: For each dimension m, let α_m be the smallest constant such that every quadratic stochastic operator V on S^{m-1} satisfying P_{ij,k} > α_m for all heredity coefficients is regular. The paper states that if P_{ij,k} > 1/(2m), then V is regular, and it gives the exact value of α_2. Determine the exact value of α_m for every m >= 3.
self_contained_problem:
Let $m\ge 2$ and let $S^{m-1}=\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m:\ x_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m x_i=1\}$ denote the $(m-1)$-dimensional simplex of probability vectors.

A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) $V:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ is a map of the form
$$ (Vx)_k \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m} P_{ij,k}\, x_i x_j,\qquad k=1,\dots,m, $$
where the heredity coefficients $\{P_{ij,k}\}$ satisfy
$$ P_{ij,k}=P_{ji,k}\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{m}P_{ij,k}=1\ \ \text{for all } i,j\in\{1,\dots,m\}. $$

The operator $V$ is called regular if for every initial point $x^{(0)}\in S^{m-1}$ the iterates $x^{(n+1)}=V(x^{(n)})$ converge, as $n\to\infty$, to a limit which does not depend on $x^{(0)}$.

For each integer $m\ge 2$ define
$$ \alpha_m \;=\; \inf\Big\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \text{every QSO } V \text{ on } S^{m-1} \text{ with } P_{ij,k}>\alpha \text{ for all } i,j,k \text{ is regular}\Big\}. $$

It is known that $\alpha_m\le \tfrac{1}{2m}$ and that $\alpha_2=\tfrac{1}{2}(3-\sqrt{7})$.

Determine the exact value of $\alpha_m$ for every integer $m\ge 3$.

Subsequent surveys on quadratic stochastic operators continue to discuss regularity criteria but do not appear to report a closed-form value of $\alpha_m$ for general $m\ge 3$, so the status is best recorded as unknown/likely still open.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
original_question: Describe and classify all surjective quadratic stochastic operators on the simplex S^{m-1} in every dimension m >= 5.
self_contained_problem:
Let $m\ge 2$ be an integer and let
$$S^{m-1}=\Big\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m : x_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m x_i=1\Big\}$$
denote the standard $(m-1)$-simplex. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) on $S^{m-1}$ is a map $V:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ of the form
$$(V x)_k=\sum_{i,j=1}^m p_{ij,k}\, x_i x_j,\qquad k=1,\dots,m,$$
where the coefficients $\{p_{ij,k}\}$ satisfy
$$p_{ij,k}=p_{ji,k}\ge 0\quad\text{for all } i,j,k,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^m p_{ij,k}=1\quad\text{for all } i,j.$$
Such an operator $V$ is called surjective if $V(S^{m-1})=S^{m-1}$.

For each $m\ge 5$, give a complete description and classification of all surjective quadratic stochastic operators on $S^{m-1}$, and describe the extreme points of the convex set of such operators.
status_search_result: Subsequent work (notably Bartoszek–Pułka, "On the surjectivity of quadratic stochastic operators acting on the simplex," 2016, and related papers by Mukhamedov and coauthors) gives a structural characterization of surjective QSOs in arbitrary dimension: a QSO on $S^{m-1}$ is surjective if and only if it can be written as a composition involving a permutation and a Lotka–Volterra-type QSO, and such operators are necessarily bijective. However, an explicit complete classification and a full description of the extreme points of the surjective set for general $m\ge 5$ does not appear to have been fully achieved, so the problem is only partially solved.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Effect of phase transitions on QSO dynamics
original_question: When a quadratic stochastic operator is generated by a Gibbs measure associated with a Hamiltonian H on a continuous state space, and when the underlying statistical-mechanical system may undergo a phase transition because the Gibbs measure is non-unique, determine how the thermodynamic behavior, especially phase transitions, affects the trajectories and asymptotic dynamics of the corresponding QSO.
self_contained_problem:
Let $E$ be a continuous (measurable) state space and let $H : E \times E \to \mathbb{R}$ be a Hamiltonian. For temperature $T > 0$, let $\mu = \mu_{H,T}$ be a Gibbs measure on $E$ associated with $H$ at temperature $T$ (so $\mu$ is a probability measure on $E$ satisfying the corresponding DLR equations for the formal density proportional to $\exp(-H/T)$). Using $\mu$ as a kernel, define the associated quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) $V$ acting on the space $S(E)$ of probability measures on $E$ by
$$ (V\lambda)(A) \;=\; \int_E \int_E P(x,y,A)\, d\lambda(x)\, d\lambda(y), \qquad A \subseteq E \text{ measurable}, $$
where the transition kernel $P(x,y,\cdot)$ is determined by the Gibbs measure $\mu$ in the standard way that generates a QSO from a Gibbs distribution. It is known that, depending on $H$ and $T$, the Gibbs measure $\mu$ may fail to be unique; the regime of non-uniqueness is the phase transition regime of the underlying statistical-mechanical system.

Problem. Determine how the thermodynamic behavior of the system $(H,T)$ — in particular the occurrence of a phase transition (non-uniqueness of $\mu$) versus its absence (uniqueness of $\mu$) — affects the trajectories $\{V^n \lambda\}_{n\ge 0}$ of the corresponding QSO and their asymptotic behavior as $n \to \infty$ (existence and structure of limit points, fixed points, ergodicity, regularity, multiplicity of attractors, etc.). Provide an explicit qualitative and, where possible, quantitative correspondence between phase transitions of $H$ and the dynamical features of $V$.
category_tag: Quadratic stochastic operators and Gibbs measures
status_search_result: The problem of how phase transitions of a Hamiltonian's Gibbs measure influence the dynamics of the associated QSO is a known open question raised by N.N. Ganikhodjaev. While related works (e.g., Ganikhodjaev–Rozikov on QSOs generated by Gibbs distributions, and studies of QSOs on lattice models like Rock-Paper-Scissors) explore special cases, no general resolution describing the effect of thermodynamic phase transitions on QSO trajectories appears in the literature. The problem remains open in its general form.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Non-product measures still tractable by QSO theory
original_question: Find a probability measure μ on the configuration space that is different from the product measure μ(σ) = product_i μ_i(σ_i) in formula (19), but for which the associated non-Volterra quadratic stochastic operator can still be analyzed within the framework of the existing theory of quadratic stochastic operators, analogous to how Theorem 11 reduces the product-measure case to separate Volterra QSOs.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $I=\{1,2,\dots,q\}$ be a finite index set, and for each $i\in I$ let $\Omega_i$ be a finite set. Form the configuration space $\Omega=\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\times\cdots\times\Omega_q$ and let $S(\Omega)=\{\lambda:\Omega\to[0,1]\ :\ \sum_{\sigma\in\Omega}\lambda(\sigma)=1\}$ be the simplex of probability measures on $\Omega$.

Given a probability measure $\mu$ on $\Omega$ with $\mu(\sigma)>0$ for all $\sigma\in\Omega$, define the associated quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) $V_\mu:S(\Omega)\to S(\Omega)$ by
$$
(V_\mu\lambda)(\tau)=\sum_{\sigma,\eta\in\Omega} P_{\sigma,\eta}(\tau)\,\lambda(\sigma)\,\lambda(\eta),\qquad \tau\in\Omega,
$$
where the heredity coefficients $P_{\sigma,\eta}(\tau)\ge 0$ with $\sum_\tau P_{\sigma,\eta}(\tau)=1$ are constructed coordinate-wise from $\mu$ in the standard way: $P_{\sigma,\eta}(\tau)=\mu(\tau)/\bigl(\mu(\sigma)+\mu(\eta)\bigr)$ when $\tau\in\{\sigma,\eta\}$, and $0$ otherwise (with the usual normalisation so that $V_\mu$ is stochastic). A QSO is called Volterra if $P_{\sigma,\eta}(\tau)=0$ whenever $\tau\notin\{\sigma,\eta\}$.

Known fact. If $\mu$ is a product measure, i.e.
$$
\mu(\sigma)=\prod_{i=1}^q\mu_i(\sigma_i),\qquad \sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_q)\in\Omega,\qquad (\star)
$$
for some probability measures $\mu_i$ on $\Omega_i$, then $V_\mu$ decomposes (is reducible) into $q$ independent Volterra QSOs acting on the simplices $S(\Omega_i)$ respectively, and hence its trajectories can be analysed coordinate-wise within the classical theory of Volterra QSOs.

Problem. Exhibit a probability measure $\mu$ on $\Omega$ that is not of the product form $(\star)$ such that the corresponding QSO $V_\mu$ is non-Volterra and yet can be reduced to (or otherwise analysed within) a known, well-developed theory of quadratic stochastic operators (for example, by reduction to a finite collection of Volterra or other tractable QSOs). Equivalently, identify a class of non-product measures $\mu$ on $\Omega$ for which the dynamics of $V_\mu$ on $S(\Omega)$ admits a complete description analogous to the product-measure case.
status_search_result: A web search shows ongoing activity on non-Volterra QSOs (including those generated by product measures, F-QSOs, permuted Volterra QSOs, and superpositions), but no source directly confirms the discovery of a non-product measure on a general configuration space Ω = Ω₁×···×Ω_q whose induced non-Volterra QSO has been fully analysed within the classical QSO framework in the sense requested. The status could not be conclusively verified.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: QSOs defined by factorized heredity coefficients
original_question: Develop a theory for quadratic stochastic operators whose heredity coefficients factor as P_{ij,k} = a_{ik} b_{jk}, equivalently operators of the form (V(x))_k = (A(x))_k · (B(x))_k where A(x) and B(x) are linear maps determined by the matrices A = (a_{ik}) and B = (b_{jk}) subject to the stochasticity constraints. Study their structural and dynamical properties as a generalization of Volterra QSOs.
self_contained_problem:
Let $E=\{1,2,\dots,m\}$ and let $S^{m-1}=\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m_{\ge 0}:\sum_{k=1}^m x_k=1\}$ be the standard simplex. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) on $S^{m-1}$ is a map $V:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ defined by
$$
(V(x))_k = \sum_{i,j=1}^m P_{ij,k}\,x_i x_j,\qquad k\in E,
$$
where the heredity coefficients $P_{ij,k}$ satisfy
$$
P_{ij,k}\ge 0,\qquad P_{ij,k}=P_{ji,k},\qquad \sum_{k=1}^m P_{ij,k}=1\quad\text{for all }i,j,k\in E.
$$
Consider the subclass of QSOs whose heredity coefficients admit a factorization
$$
P_{ij,k} = a_{ik}\,b_{jk},\qquad i,j,k\in E,
$$
for some real matrices $A=(a_{ik})$ and $B=(b_{jk})$, where the constraints above force the symmetry $a_{ik}b_{jk}=a_{jk}b_{ik}$ together with the non-negativity and stochasticity conditions
$$
a_{ik}b_{jk}\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^m a_{ik}b_{jk}=1\quad\text{for all }i,j\in E.
$$
For such operators one has the Hadamard-product representation
$$
(V(x))_k = (A(x))_k\cdot (B(x))_k,\qquad\text{where }(A(x))_k=\sum_i a_{ik}x_i,\ (B(x))_k=\sum_j b_{jk}x_j.
$$
Develop a theory for this class of QSOs as a generalization of Volterra QSOs: characterize the admissible pairs $(A,B)$; describe fixed points, invariant subsets, and ergodic/non-ergodic behavior; analyze the long-term dynamics of the iterates $V^n(x)$ for $x\in S^{m-1}$; and identify the structural properties (e.g., conservativity, dissipativity, regularity) that distinguish this family from the general QSO class and from Volterra QSOs.
status_search_result: Search results show extensive literature on quadratic stochastic operators, including Volterra QSOs, F-QSOs, dissipative QSOs, and permutation-type QSOs, but no source explicitly labeled as developing the full theory of QSOs with factorized heredity coefficients $P_{ij,k}=a_{ik}b_{jk}$. The status of this program could not be conclusively verified.

paper_title: Quadratic Stochastic Operators: Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Finite complete indicator systems for conjugacy
original_question: For the topological conjugacy classification of quadratic stochastic operators, determine whether there exists a finite complete system of indicator polynomials in the heredity coefficients P_{ij,k}. If such a system exists, find a basis, where an indicator is a polynomial constrained by topological conjugacy and a complete system is one whose bounds imply that two QSOs are topologically conjugate.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^{m-1}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^m_{\ge 0}:\sum_{i=1}^m x_i=1\}$ denote the $(m-1)$-dimensional simplex. A quadratic stochastic operator (QSO) on $S^{m-1}$ is a map $V:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ defined by
\[ (Vx)_k = \sum_{i,j=1}^m P_{ij,k}\, x_i x_j, \qquad k=1,\dots,m, \]
where the heredity coefficients $P_{ij,k}$ satisfy
\[ P_{ij,k}=P_{ji,k}\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^m P_{ij,k}=1 \quad\text{for all } i,j. \]
Two QSOs $V_1,V_2:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ are called topologically conjugate if there exists a homeomorphism $h:S^{m-1}\to S^{m-1}$ with $h\circ V_1 = V_2\circ h$.

A polynomial $f$ in the variables $\{P_{ij,k}\}$ is called an indicator if there exist constants $a_f<b_f$ (depending only on $f$) such that whenever two QSOs $V_1,V_2$ with coefficient arrays $P^{(1)},P^{(2)}$ are topologically conjugate, the values $f(P^{(1)})$ and $f(P^{(2)})$ both lie in the interval $[a_f,b_f]$ (so that $f$ is constrained by topological conjugacy in this sense). A finite collection $f_1,\dots,f_t$ of indicators is called a complete system if, conversely, whenever two QSOs $V_1,V_2$ have all values $f_s(P^{(1)}), f_s(P^{(2)})$ ($s=1,\dots,t$) in their respective indicator intervals, then $V_1$ and $V_2$ are topologically conjugate. A minimal complete system is called a basis.

Question: Does there exist a finite complete system of indicators for the topological-conjugacy classification of quadratic stochastic operators on $S^{m-1}$? If so, exhibit a basis.
status_search_result: No published resolution was found. The problem is posed as an open problem in the survey on quadratic stochastic operators, and subsequent literature on QSOs (and on topological conjugacy classification of related operators, e.g. arXiv:2505.00577 on diagonal operators) does not appear to provide a finite complete system of indicators or a basis for the QSO conjugacy classification.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems about Supernovae
context_brief: Stellar properties controlling Type Ia explosions
original_question: Among possible Type Ia supernova progenitors with initial masses about 3–8 solar masses, which stellar properties—especially high rotational velocities and magnetic fields in B-type main-sequence stars—can determine whether a star ends by exploding as a Type Ia supernova, with or without a companion?
self_contained_problem: Consider single stars on the main sequence with initial masses in the approximate range 3–8 solar masses, corresponding to spectral type B. Such stars are observed to display, in many cases, high rotational velocities and are expected, through intense dynamo activity, to develop strong magnetic fields. Identify which intrinsic stellar properties of these B-type main-sequence stars — in particular their rotational velocity distribution and magnetic-field strength and topology — determine whether a given star ultimately ends its evolution as a Type Ia supernova, either as an isolated star or with the assistance of a binary companion. Specify the quantitative criteria on rotation, magnetic field, mass, and (where relevant) companion properties that distinguish those stars whose endpoint is a Type Ia supernova explosion from those whose endpoint is not.
status_search_result: Recent reviews (2024–2025) describe Type Ia supernova progenitors as a "long-standing puzzle" still unresolved, with competing single-degenerate and double-degenerate channels and no consensus on which intrinsic properties of intermediate-mass B-type progenitors (rotation, magnetic fields) determine the explosion outcome.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems about Supernovae
context_brief: Physical basis and redshift evolution of Type Ia standardization
original_question: Why does the empirical Type Ia supernova standardization relation work—brighter Type Ia supernovae evolve photometrically more slowly than fainter ones—and how much cosmological bias can arise if the high-redshift population has a different balance of fast progenitors with lifetimes under about 100 million years and tardy progenitors that typically explode more than 1 billion years after formation?
self_contained_problem:
Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are used as cosmological distance indicators by exploiting an empirical luminosity–light-curve relation: intrinsically brighter SNe Ia decline photometrically more slowly than fainter ones, and after correction with this relation their peak magnitudes are nearly standard. Two channels of progenitor systems are believed to contribute to the observed SN Ia rate: a "prompt" or fast-evolving channel whose progenitors explode less than about 100 Myr after star formation, and a "tardy" or delayed channel whose progenitors explode more than about 1 Gyr after star formation. The relative fraction of these two channels varies with cosmic time, so that high-redshift samples are dominated by the prompt component while low-redshift samples have a larger tardy contribution.

(a) Provide a physical explanation, derived from the explosion mechanism and progenitor properties, of why the empirical brighter-slower / fainter-faster relation holds and identify the underlying parameter (e.g. progenitor mass, metallicity, central density, or 56Ni yield) responsible for the simultaneous variation of peak luminosity and light-curve decline rate.

(b) Assuming that the prompt and tardy populations have systematically different mean standardized absolute magnitudes ΔM (after applying the standard brighter-slower correction), and letting f_prompt(z) denote the prompt fraction as a function of redshift z, quantify the resulting bias in the inferred distance modulus μ(z) and the consequent bias on cosmological parameters (in particular on the dark-energy equation-of-state parameters w_0 and w_a) as a function of z and ΔM. Determine how large ΔM must be in order to produce a bias in w_0 or w_a that exceeds current observational uncertainties.
status_search_result: The physical origin of the brighter-slower relation is still not fully understood, but recent work has accumulated strong evidence that progenitor age (linked to the prompt vs. tardy channel balance) is a dominant driver of post-standardization luminosity differences and induces a redshift-dependent systematic bias in SN Ia cosmology. Studies in 2020–2025 quantify this bias and argue that it is largely uncorrected by the conventional host-mass step and may significantly affect inferred dark-energy parameters, but a complete first-principles physical theory and a definitive correction scheme remain unresolved.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems about Supernovae
original_question: For the core-collapse supernova subclasses SNIIb, SNIIn, and SNIIL, are their progenitor masses located in the apparent 16–20 solar-mass gap between measured Type IIP progenitors of about 8–16 solar masses and Type Ib/c lower limits above about 20 solar masses, or are those explosion types mainly determined by other parameters such as binarity or rotation?
self_contained_problem:
Core-collapse supernovae are commonly divided into subclasses by their observed spectra and light curves, including: Type IIP (hydrogen-rich, plateau light curve), Type IIL (hydrogen-rich, linearly declining light curve), Type IIn (hydrogen-rich with narrow emission lines indicating dense circumstellar material), Type IIb (hydrogen layer present at early times but rapidly disappearing, becoming helium-dominated), and Types Ib/Ic (hydrogen-poor, with Ic also helium-poor).

Direct imaging of pre-explosion progenitors has yielded zero-age main-sequence (ZAMS) mass estimates of approximately 8 M_⊙ to 16 M_⊙ for about a dozen Type IIP progenitors (identified as red supergiants), while available lower limits for Type Ib/Ic progenitors place their masses above approximately 20 M_⊙. This leaves an apparent gap in the directly measured progenitor masses in the range 16 M_⊙ ≲ M ≲ 20 M_⊙.

Determine, for each of the subclasses Type IIb, Type IIn, and Type IIL: do their progenitors have ZAMS masses lying in the apparent 16–20 M_⊙ gap between measured Type IIP and Type Ib/c progenitors, or are these explosion types instead primarily determined by other physical parameters such as binary companion interaction or stellar rotation rather than by initial mass alone?
status_search_result: Subsequent direct-detection and statistical studies have made substantial progress: Type IIb progenitors (e.g., SN 1993J, SN 2011dh, SN 2013df) are now strongly favored to arise from interacting binary systems with moderate ZAMS masses (~12–17 M_⊙), supporting binarity rather than the mass gap. Type IIL studies (e.g., Anderson et al. and Hα-association statistics) suggest progenitor masses similar to or slightly above SNIIP, with envelope stripping by binarity or metallicity playing a role. Type IIn remains the most heterogeneous and least understood, with evidence for both very massive (LBV-like) and lower-mass progenitors. Thus the question is partially resolved, with binarity now considered a major determining factor, but a definitive mass distribution for each subclass is not yet established.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems about Supernovae
original_question: For ultra-bright Type II supernovae, how bright can the brightest events be, what physical class are they, and why do they occur; in particular, can pair-annihilation explosions of ultramassive stars above about 140 solar masses and extremely low metallicity below about one-thousandth solar metallicity explain such events in the local universe after more than 13 billion years of chemical evolution?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Type II supernovae with peak absolute B-band magnitudes brighter than M_B ≈ −19.5 (i.e. comparable to or exceeding typical Type Ia supernovae), such as the class of "ultra-bright" core-collapse events. Address the following questions:

(a) What is the maximum possible peak luminosity (or absolute magnitude) attainable by such ultra-bright Type II supernovae?

(b) What is the physical class and explosion mechanism responsible for these extreme events?

(c) Why do such events occur, i.e. what stellar progenitor configurations and evolutionary pathways lead to them?

(d) In particular, evaluate whether the pair-instability (pair-annihilation) explosion mechanism — predicted for ultramassive stars with zero-age main-sequence mass M > 140 M_⊙ and extremely low metallicity Z < 10^(−3) Z_⊙ — can plausibly account for ultra-bright Type II events observed in the local Universe today, given that more than 1.3 × 10^10 years of cosmic chemical evolution have elapsed and such low-metallicity ultramassive progenitors are not obviously expected to still form locally.
status_search_result: Subsequent observational and theoretical work has provided partial answers. Several superluminous supernovae (e.g., SN 2007bi) have been proposed as pair-instability candidates, and pulsational pair-instability has been advanced as an alternative for many ultra-bright events (Woosley et al., Nature 2007). However, SN 2006gy was found to have occurred at roughly solar metallicity, inconsistent with the canonical Z < 10^(−3) Z_⊙ requirement, and a 2020 study reinterpreted SN 2006gy as a Type Ia interacting with a dense shell. Thus the maximum luminosity, dominant mechanism, and viability of low-metallicity pair-instability progenitors in the local Universe remain partially resolved and actively debated.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems about Supernovae
original_question: What physical conditions determine the gamma-ray-burst/supernova connection: why do many supernovae, including Type Ic events, not produce observable gamma-ray bursts, and why do many gamma-ray bursts lack associated supernovae?
self_contained_problem:
Long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are brief, intense flashes of high-energy gamma radiation observed at cosmological distances, while Type Ic supernovae (SNe Ic) are stellar explosions arising from the core collapse of massive stars whose envelopes have been stripped of hydrogen and helium. Observationally, certain GRBs have been firmly associated with broad-lined Type Ic supernovae, and both phenomena tend to occur in active star-forming regions. Yet only a small fraction of detected GRBs show an accompanying supernova (with some events, such as GRB 060614, ruling out any associated supernova brighter than absolute magnitude -13.7), and the vast majority of Type Ic supernovae show no detectable gamma-ray burst counterpart.

Identify and characterize the physical conditions—such as progenitor structure (mass, rotation, metallicity, binarity), magnetic field configuration, central engine properties (black hole vs. magnetar formation, accretion rate, jet launching efficiency), envelope/circumstellar properties, and viewing-angle/beaming effects—that determine whether a stripped-envelope core-collapse event produces (a) a successful relativistic jet observable as a GRB, (b) a luminous supernova, both, or neither. In particular, provide a quantitative explanation for the two complementary questions:

(i) Why do many core-collapse supernovae, including Type Ic events, fail to produce observable gamma-ray bursts?
(ii) Why do many gamma-ray bursts have no associated detectable supernova?
status_search_result: The physical conditions governing the GRB–supernova connection remain an active open question. Recent works (e.g., 2022 detection of a long GRB from a compact-object merger with no associated SN, and 2024 analysis of GRB 221009A whose accompanying SN was unexpectedly ordinary) highlight that the mapping between progenitors, central engines, and observed GRB/SN signatures is still not understood. Reviews and recent observational papers continue to frame the two complementary questions as unresolved.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems about Supernovae
original_question: How does the supernova phenomenon evolve with metallicity, stellar population, cosmic age, environment, and other relevant parameters across cosmic time, and how should those dependencies be included when using supernovae to understand how the universe works and evolves?
status_search_result: The cosmic evolution of supernova populations with metallicity, progenitor stellar population, redshift, and environment remains an active and unresolved area of research in astrophysics. While significant progress has been made (e.g., observed metallicity trends in stripped-envelope SNe, host-galaxy mass step in Type Ia cosmology, evolving SN rates with redshift), a complete quantitative characterization and a fully validated framework for incorporating these dependencies into precision cosmology has not been achieved.

context_brief: p-compact groups and telescopes of finite groups
original_question: Given a p-compact group X, does there exist a sequence of finite groups G_0 -> G_1 -> G_2 -> ... and homomorphisms between them such that the homotopy colimit of the classifying spaces B G_i is homotopy equivalent to B X after p-completion? Equivalently, is every p-compact group a telescope of finite groups in the sense that hocolim_i B G_i recovers B X up to p-completion?
self_contained_problem:
Let p be a prime. A p-compact group is a triple (X, BX, e) where BX is a pointed space which is Fp-complete (in the sense of Bousfield–Kan), X is a loop space with X ≃ ΩBX, and the mod-p cohomology H*(X; Fp) is finite-dimensional over Fp.

Question: Given any p-compact group X, does there exist a sequence of finite groups and group homomorphisms
   G_0 → G_1 → G_2 → · · · → G_i → G_{i+1} → · · ·
such that, after applying the classifying-space functor, the induced map on the homotopy colimit yields a homotopy equivalence
   (hocolim_i BG_i)^∧_p ≃ BX
after Bousfield–Kan p-completion? Equivalently, is every p-compact group realizable as a "telescope of finite groups" in this sense?
status_search_result: Web searches did not surface a definitive resolution of the question of whether every p-compact group is a telescope of finite groups in the sense of a homotopy colimit of classifying spaces of finite groups recovering BX after p-completion. Related work by Castellana and others on normalizer decompositions of p-local compact groups is ongoing, but no source clearly confirms the question is solved or refuted.

context_brief: eventual periodicity of Sq^0 on Ext over the Steenrod algebra
original_question: Fix a homological degree s and let Sq^0: Ext_A^{s,t}(F_2, F_2) -> Ext_A^{s,2t}(F_2, F_2) be the squaring operation induced by the Frobenius map on the dual Steenrod algebra. If Im((Sq^0)^i) denotes the image of the i-fold iterate on Ext_A^s(F_2, F_2), does there exist a number r = r(s) such that for every i >= r the map (Sq^0)^{i-r}: Im((Sq^0)^r) -> Im((Sq^0)^i) is an isomorphism? Equivalently, for fixed s, is every finite Sq^0-family in Ext_A^s(F_2, F_2) bounded in length by some r(s)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ denote the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra and let $\mathrm{Ext}_A^{s,t}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$ be the bigraded $\mathbb{F}_2$-vector space of $\mathrm{Ext}$ groups of the trivial $A$-module $\mathbb{F}_2$. Write $\mathrm{Ext}_A^s(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2) = \bigoplus_t \mathrm{Ext}_A^{s,t}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$. Let 
$$\mathrm{Sq}^0 : \mathrm{Ext}_A^{s,t}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ext}_A^{s,2t}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$$
denote the Frobenius-induced squaring operation on $\mathrm{Ext}$, induced by the Frobenius (squaring) endomorphism of the dual Steenrod algebra. For each integer $i \geq 0$, let $\mathrm{Im}((\mathrm{Sq}^0)^i) \subseteq \mathrm{Ext}_A^s(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$ be the image of the $i$-fold iterate of $\mathrm{Sq}^0$.

Prove or disprove: for every fixed homological degree $s \geq 0$, there exists an integer $r = r(s)$ such that for all $i \geq r$ the iterated map
$$(\mathrm{Sq}^0)^{i-r} : \mathrm{Im}((\mathrm{Sq}^0)^r) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Im}((\mathrm{Sq}^0)^i)$$
is an isomorphism. Equivalently (defining a "finite $\mathrm{Sq}^0$-family" in $\mathrm{Ext}_A^s(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$ to be a maximal sequence of nonzero elements $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n$ with $\mathrm{Sq}^0(x_j) = x_{j+1}$ and $(\mathrm{Sq}^0)^{n+1}$ vanishing on $x_0$), show that for fixed $s$ the lengths of all finite $\mathrm{Sq}^0$-families in $\mathrm{Ext}_A^s(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$ are uniformly bounded by some $r(s)$.
status_search_result: The conjecture is a strengthening of Minami's "new doomsday conjecture" concerning the action of $\mathrm{Sq}^0$ on $\mathrm{Ext}$ over the Steenrod algebra. Minami's related conjecture about permanent cycles in the image of $(\mathrm{Sq}^0)^n$ is widely cited as still open in the algebraic topology literature, and no proof or disproof of the eventual-isomorphism statement appears in the searched sources. Status appears to remain open.

context_brief: spectral sequence interpretation of the algebraic transfer
original_question: Can the bigraded algebraic transfer tau^{*,*} be realized as the edge homomorphism of a spectral sequence in a way that gives a sensible measure of how far tau^{*,*} is from being an isomorphism of bigraded algebras?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ denote the mod-$2$ Steenrod algebra and let $\mathbb{F}_2$ be the field with two elements. For each integer $k\ge 0$, let $P_k=\mathbb{F}_2[x_1,\dots,x_k]$ be the polynomial algebra on $k$ generators in degree $1$, regarded as a left $A$-module via the standard action of the Steenrod algebra on the mod-$2$ cohomology of $(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^k$. The general linear group $GL_k=GL_k(\mathbb{F}_2)$ acts on $P_k$, commuting with the $A$-action. W. Singer's algebraic transfer is a homomorphism of bigraded algebras
$$\tau^{*,*}:\bigoplus_{k\ge 0}\mathbb{F}_2\otimes_{GL_k}\bigl(P_k\bigr)^{A}_{*} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ext}_A^{*,*}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2),$$
where the source is the direct sum over $k$ of the $GL_k$-coinvariants of the subspace of $A$-annihilated elements of $P_k$ (with appropriate degree shift), and the target is the cohomology of the Steenrod algebra. The transfer is known not to be an isomorphism in general.

Question: Does there exist a (multiplicatively structured) spectral sequence converging to $\mathrm{Ext}_A^{*,*}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2)$ as a bigraded algebra such that $\tau^{*,*}$ arises as its edge homomorphism, in such a way that the higher pages and differentials of the spectral sequence provide a meaningful measure of the failure of $\tau^{*,*}$ to be an isomorphism of bigraded algebras?
status_search_result: No spectral sequence realization of the Singer algebraic transfer as an edge homomorphism appears in the literature. Recent work (2025) on the Singer transfer focuses on Singer's monomorphism conjecture (now known to fail in some bidegrees) and on computational methods, without addressing the spectral-sequence interpretation problem. The problem appears to remain open.

context_brief: Singer conjecture on injectivity of the algebraic transfer
original_question: For each s, is the algebraic transfer Tr_s: F_2 tensor_{GL_s} P H_*(B V_s) -> Ext_A^{s,s+*}(F_2, F_2) injective? Equivalently, does Singer's open conjecture hold that Tr_s is a monomorphism for every s?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_2$ be the field with two elements and let $A$ denote the mod-2 Steenrod algebra. For a positive integer $s$, let $V_s = (\mathbb{F}_2)^s$ be the elementary abelian 2-group of rank $s$, with classifying space $BV_s$. The general linear group $GL_s = GL(s,\mathbb{F}_2)$ acts on $H_*(BV_s;\mathbb{F}_2)$, and the Steenrod algebra $A$ also acts on this homology; let $PH_*(BV_s) \subseteq H_*(BV_s;\mathbb{F}_2)$ denote the subspace of elements annihilated by all positive-degree Steenrod operations (the "primitive" elements). W. Singer constructed a natural homomorphism, the algebraic transfer of rank $s$,
$$Tr_s : \mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_s} PH_*(BV_s) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ext}_A^{s,\,s+*}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2).$$
Question: For every positive integer $s$, is $Tr_s$ a monomorphism (i.e. injective)?
status_search_result: Singer's conjecture (that the algebraic transfer Tr_s is injective for all s) was verified for s ≤ 4 (Singer for s=1,2; Boardman for s=3; and recent work for s=4). However, the general conjecture has been disproved: a 2025 preprint exhibits a counterexample at bidegree (6, 6+36), showing Tr_6 fails to be a monomorphism. Hence the conjecture as stated for all s is false (solved in the negative), while it remains true for ranks up to 4.

original_question: In the setting of Conjecture 4.1, can one always choose the iterate n to be 1? That is, for every z in Ext_P^{s,t}(F_p, F_p), is P^0 z already nilpotent after a single application of P^0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $A$ denote the mod-$p$ Steenrod algebra over $\mathbb{F}_p$. The Frobenius map on the polynomial part of the dual Steenrod algebra $A_*$ induces, by duality, an algebra endomorphism (the "Frobenius" Steenrod operation) 
$$P^0 \colon \mathrm{Ext}_A^{s,t}(\mathbb{F}_p,\mathbb{F}_p) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ext}_A^{s,pt}(\mathbb{F}_p,\mathbb{F}_p).$$
An element $w$ of the bigraded ring $\mathrm{Ext}_A^{*,*}(\mathbb{F}_p,\mathbb{F}_p)$ is called nilpotent if $w^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$.

Prove or disprove: for every prime $p$ and every $z \in \mathrm{Ext}_A^{s,t}(\mathbb{F}_p,\mathbb{F}_p)$, the element $P^0 z \in \mathrm{Ext}_A^{s,pt}(\mathbb{F}_p,\mathbb{F}_p)$ is nilpotent.

paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
original_question: How much do galaxy-formation predictions change when semi-analytic models use merger trees generated by the classical extended Press-Schechter (EPS) formalism instead of merger trees extracted directly from numerical simulations, given that recent work indicates EPS may not adequately describe simulated merger trees?
self_contained_problem:
In semi-analytic models of galaxy formation, the assembly histories of dark-matter haloes (their "merger trees") can be generated in two distinct ways:

(1) Analytically, via the classical extended Press–Schechter (EPS) formalism, which uses the statistics of Gaussian random density fluctuations smoothed on different mass scales together with the spherical-collapse threshold to derive conditional mass functions and Monte-Carlo merger histories.

(2) Numerically, by identifying dark-matter haloes and their progenitors directly in cosmological N-body simulations and linking them across output snapshots.

Couple a fixed semi-analytic prescription for baryonic physics (gas cooling, star formation, supernova and AGN feedback, galaxy mergers, etc.) to merger trees obtained by each of the two methods above. Quantify how the resulting predictions of galaxy-population observables — such as the galaxy stellar mass function, the luminosity function, the cosmic star-formation history, the colour and morphology distributions, and clustering statistics — differ when EPS-based merger trees are used in place of merger trees extracted from N-body simulations. In particular, given that the EPS formalism is known to misrepresent simulated merger trees in the number of progenitors, in the growth of the main progenitor, and in the total progenitor mass, determine the magnitude and observational significance of the induced changes in galaxy-formation predictions.
status_search_result: Subsequent studies have addressed the comparison directly. Work coupling semi-analytic models to N-body merger trees (e.g., Helly et al. 2003; Parkinson, Cole & Helly 2008) showed that, apart from mass-resolution effects, the principal differences between EPS- and N-body-based predictions stem from known EPS deficiencies in progenitor counts, main-progenitor growth, and total progenitor mass. Modified Monte-Carlo schemes calibrated against simulations have been developed, and more recent generative/ML emulators (e.g., FLORAH-Tree, 2025) further reduce the gap. The qualitative impact on galaxy-formation predictions is now reasonably well characterized, though no fully definitive, comprehensive quantitative answer across all observables exists, so the problem is partially resolved rather than fully closed.

paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
original_question: Can semi-analytic models with radio-mode AGN feedback achieve quantitative agreement with the observed star-formation histories of massive elliptical galaxies, rather than only reproducing the qualitative trend that more massive ellipticals have shorter star-formation time-scales?
self_contained_problem:
Consider semi-analytic models of galaxy formation built on hierarchical merger trees of dark-matter halos, in which baryonic processes (gas cooling, star formation, supernova feedback, galaxy mergers, chemical enrichment) are evolved by coupled differential/algebraic recipes, and in which "radio-mode" active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback is included as an energy-injection term that suppresses gas cooling in massive halos hosting a central supermassive black hole accreting in a low-accretion-rate (radio) state.

For each model galaxy, define its star-formation history (SFH) as the function ψ(t) giving the star-formation rate as a function of cosmic time, and its star-formation time-scale τ_SF (e.g., the e-folding time of ψ(t) or the time over which a fixed fraction of the present-day stellar mass was assembled). Let M_⋆ denote the present-day stellar mass of a galaxy classified as a massive elliptical (M_⋆ ≳ 10^{11} M_⊙).

Observationally, the SFHs of massive ellipticals (as inferred from spectral fitting of their stellar populations) exhibit "downsizing": more massive ellipticals form their stars earlier and on shorter time-scales τ_SF. Existing semi-analytic models with radio-mode AGN feedback reproduce this trend qualitatively (i.e., dτ_SF/dM_⋆ < 0).

Problem. Determine whether one can construct a semi-analytic galaxy-formation model with radio-mode AGN feedback whose predicted distribution of star-formation histories ψ(t | M_⋆) for massive elliptical galaxies matches the observationally inferred SFHs not only qualitatively but quantitatively — that is, agrees within observational uncertainties on the mean formation epoch ⟨t_form⟩(M_⋆) and the star-formation time-scale τ_SF(M_⋆) as functions of stellar mass.
status_search_result: The question concerns whether semi-analytic models with radio-mode AGN feedback can achieve quantitative (not just qualitative) agreement with observed star-formation histories of massive ellipticals. Subsequent literature (e.g., works on downsizing, archaeological SFHs vs. SAM predictions, and AGN-feedback prescriptions in models such as Henriques et al. and Croton et al. updates) has continued to report tensions: SAMs reproduce downsizing trends qualitatively but still struggle to match observed SFH shapes and time-scales quantitatively, with large observational uncertainties persisting. No definitive resolution has been published, so the problem remains open.

paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
original_question: Is the discrepancy between predicted and observed mass assembly of brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) a real failure of the models, or can it be explained by mismatched comparisons such as observational aperture magnitudes versus model total magnitudes and by the omission in many semi-analytic models of spatial light distributions and tidal stripping into intracluster light?
self_contained_problem:
Let a brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) be the most luminous galaxy at the centre of a galaxy cluster, and let intracluster light (ICL) denote the diffuse stellar component bound to the cluster potential rather than to any single galaxy. Observations of BCGs typically measure stellar masses inside a fixed metric aperture, which is known to capture only roughly 25–50% of the combined BCG+ICL light, whereas semi-analytic models of galaxy formation generally output total stellar masses for the BCG and often do not track tidal stripping of stars from satellite galaxies into the ICL.

Standard semi-analytic predictions are that the stellar mass of a BCG grows by approximately a factor of 4 between redshift z ≈ 1 and z = 0, while observations using fixed-aperture magnitudes are consistent with little or no mass growth over the same interval.

Determine whether this discrepancy reflects a genuine failure of the underlying galaxy-formation models, or whether it can be fully accounted for by:
(i) the systematic mismatch between fixed-aperture observational stellar masses and total model stellar masses, and
(ii) the omission, in most semi-analytic models, of an explicit treatment of the spatial light distribution of central galaxies and of the tidal/harassment-driven stripping of stars from cluster members into the ICL.

Specifically, formulate and justify a quantitative comparison procedure (matching apertures and including stripping into ICL) under which the predicted and observed BCG stellar-mass growth between z ≈ 1 and z = 0 either agree within observational uncertainties (resolving the discrepancy) or remain inconsistent (confirming a model failure).
status_search_result: Subsequent work suggests the discrepancy is largely, but not entirely, attributable to the comparison mismatch and omitted physics. Modern semi-analytic and hydrodynamical models that explicitly track tidal stripping into ICL and apply matched apertures bring predicted BCG stellar-mass growth much closer to observed values, with the BCG+ICL system continuing to grow strongly while the aperture-restricted BCG mass grows only modestly. However, a residual tension remains: some recent observations still find faster stellar-mass growth in the central regions than models predict, so a complete reconciliation has not been firmly established.

paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
original_question: Why have hierarchical galaxy-formation models been unable to reproduce both the observed galaxy luminosity function and the zero-point of the Tully-Fisher relation when disk circular velocity is evaluated at the half-mass radius using realistic galaxy-size calculations, and does this failure come from approximations in size modelling or from a more fundamental shortcoming of the cold dark matter paradigm?
self_contained_problem:
Consider hierarchical galaxy-formation models in a cold dark matter (CDM) cosmology, in which dark-matter haloes form by gravitational collapse and merging, and baryons cool inside these haloes to form rotationally supported disk galaxies. For each model galaxy one computes (i) a luminosity L (from a star-formation and feedback prescription) and (ii) a disk circular velocity V_c evaluated at the disk half-mass radius R_{1/2}, where R_{1/2} is obtained from a realistic size calculation that accounts for the angular momentum of cooling gas, the gravitational contribution of the baryonic disk, and the (possibly adiabatically contracted) dark-matter halo.

Two empirical constraints must be matched simultaneously:
(a) the observed galaxy luminosity function Φ(L), i.e. the comoving number density of galaxies as a function of luminosity, and
(b) the zero-point of the Tully–Fisher relation, i.e. the observed linear correlation log L = a log V_c + b between the luminosity of spiral galaxies and the rotation speed of their disks, with empirically determined slope a and intercept b.

Question: Construct a hierarchical galaxy-formation model based on the CDM paradigm, with a physically realistic prescription for disk sizes, that simultaneously reproduces the observed luminosity function Φ(L) and the observed zero-point b of the Tully–Fisher relation when V_c is measured at R_{1/2}. Determine whether the persistent failure of existing such models to achieve this simultaneous match is attributable to approximations in the modelling of galaxy sizes (e.g., angular-momentum conservation assumptions, halo response to baryonic contraction, or the treatment of the disk mass profile), or whether it reflects a more fundamental inadequacy of the CDM paradigm itself (e.g., halo concentrations or inner density profiles being incompatible with observed disk dynamics).
status_search_result: The simultaneous matching of the galaxy luminosity function and the Tully–Fisher zero-point has been a longstanding tension in semi-analytic hierarchical models. Subsequent work (e.g. Dutton 2008/2012; refined GalICS dynamical rotation-curve recipes; abundance-matching analyses showing a non-monotonic v_rot–v_vir relation due to the stellar-to-halo-mass ratio) has shown the tension can be alleviated by combining lower stellar mass-to-light ratios, lower initial halo concentrations, and the absence of strong adiabatic halo contraction, suggesting the problem is largely related to baryonic/size-modelling assumptions rather than a fundamental failure of CDM. However, no fully consistent first-principles model has been universally accepted as resolving the issue.

paper_title: Exploring Progressions: A Collection of Problems
original_question: Determine every possible common difference d of an arithmetic progression whose first term is a1 = 6 and which has both 62 and 104 among its terms.
self_contained_problem:
An arithmetic progression is a sequence (a_n)_{n≥1} of real numbers of the form a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d, where a_1 is the first term and d is the common difference. We say a number x is a term of the progression if x = a_n for some positive integer n.

Find all possible values of the common difference d of an arithmetic progression with first term a_1 = 6 such that both 62 and 104 appear as terms of the progression. (Assume d is a positive real number; describe the complete set of admissible d.)
status_search_result: This is a standard elementary exercise. The condition that 62 and 104 are terms of the progression with a_1 = 6 forces d to divide both 62 - 6 = 56 and 104 - 6 = 98, so d must be a positive common divisor of gcd(56, 98) = 14. Restricting to positive integer differences yields d ∈ {1, 2, 7, 14}.

context_brief: Linear relation among indexed AP terms
original_question: Let (a_n) be an arithmetic progression. Suppose ak = α, am = β, and aℓ = γ for natural numbers k, m, and ℓ. Prove that the indices and values satisfy α(m − ℓ) + β(ℓ − k) + γ(k − m) = 0.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be an arithmetic progression of real numbers; that is, there exist real numbers $a_1$ and $d$ such that $a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d$ for every positive integer $n$. Let $k, m, \ell$ be natural numbers, and let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be real numbers such that
$$a_k = \alpha, \qquad a_m = \beta, \qquad a_\ell = \gamma.$$
Prove that
$$\alpha(m-\ell) + \beta(\ell-k) + \gamma(k-m) = 0.$$
status_search_result: This is a standard, elementary identity for arithmetic progressions: substituting $a_k = a_1+(k-1)d$, etc., the expression telescopes to $0$. It is a classical exercise with a well-known proof, hence considered solved.

paper_title: Exploring Progressions: A Collection of Problems
original_question: For each natural number k, let Sk denote the sum of the first k terms of the arithmetic progression whose first term is k and whose common difference is d = 2k − 1. Find a closed form for S1 + S2 + ··· + Sk.
self_contained_problem:
For each positive integer k, let S_k denote the sum of the first k terms of the arithmetic progression whose first term is k and whose common difference is d = 2k − 1. That is,

S_k = k + (k + (2k−1)) + (k + 2(2k−1)) + ⋯ + (k + (k−1)(2k−1)).

For a given positive integer n, find a closed-form expression for

T_n = S_1 + S_2 + S_3 + ⋯ + S_n.
status_search_result: This is a standard elementary identity. One has S_k = k(2k² − k + 1)/2, and summing gives T_n = n(n+1)(3n² + n + 2)/12 (verified for small n: T_1=1, T_2=8, T_3=32). The problem is a classical exercise with a known closed form, hence solved.

paper_title: Exploring Progressions: A Collection of Problems
original_question: Partition the even positive integers into blocks {2}, {4, 6}, {8, 10, 12}, …, so that the nth block consists of n consecutive even integers and begins at n(n − 1) + 2. Determine the sum of the numbers in the nth block.
self_contained_problem: Partition the even positive integers into consecutive blocks $B_1, B_2, B_3, \dots$ such that, for each positive integer $n$, the block $B_n$ consists of exactly $n$ consecutive even integers whose smallest element is $n(n-1)+2$. Thus $B_1 = \{2\}$, $B_2 = \{4,6\}$, $B_3 = \{8,10,12\}$, and in general $B_n = \{n(n-1)+2,\; n(n-1)+4,\; \dots,\; n(n-1)+2n\}$. Determine, as a closed-form expression in $n$, the sum of all members of the block $B_n$.
status_search_result: This is a standard elementary exercise. The block $B_n$ is an arithmetic progression of $n$ terms with first term $n(n-1)+2$ and common difference $2$, so the sum equals $n\bigl(n(n-1)+2\bigr) + 2\cdot\frac{n(n-1)}{2} = n^3 + n$. The closed form is well known and the problem is fully solved.

paper_title: Exploring Progressions: A Collection of Problems
original_question: Let m and n be natural numbers, and let (a_k) be an arithmetic progression with am = 1/n and an = 1/m. Prove all of the following: (a) the first term equals the common difference, a1 = d; (b) for every natural number t, the term a_{t mn} equals t; and (c) if S_{t mn} denotes the sum of the first tmn terms, then S_{t mn} = ((mn + 1)/2) t.
self_contained_problem:
Let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers. Let $(a_k)_{k\ge 1}$ be an arithmetic progression of real numbers with first term $a_1$ and common difference $d$, so that $a_k = a_1 + (k-1)d$ for all $k\ge 1$. Suppose that
$$a_m =  rac{1}{n} \quad	ext{and}\quad a_n =  rac{1}{m}.$$
Prove each of the following:
(a) $a_1 = d$.
(b) For every natural number $t$, $a_{tmn} = t$.
(c) Let $S_N = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_N$ denote the sum of the first $N$ terms. Then for every natural number $t$,
$$S_{tmn} =  rac{(mn+1)\,t}{2}.$$
status_search_result: This is a classical textbook-style exercise on arithmetic progressions whose proof is elementary: from $a_m - a_n = (m-n)d = 1/n - 1/m = (m-n)/(mn)$ one gets $d = 1/(mn)$, then $a_1 = a_m - (m-1)d = 1/(mn) = d$, from which (b) and (c) follow directly. The result is well known and considered solved.

paper_title: Exploring Progressions: A Collection of Problems
original_question: Let α, β, and γ be distinct real numbers that are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression. Prove that α, α − γ, and α − β are also consecutive terms of a harmonic progression.
self_contained_problem:
Three nonzero real numbers x, y, z are said to be consecutive terms of a harmonic progression if their reciprocals 1/x, 1/y, 1/z are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression, i.e. 2/y = 1/x + 1/z.

Let α, β, γ be three distinct real numbers (all nonzero) that are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression. Prove that the three numbers α, α − γ, α − β are also consecutive terms of a harmonic progression; that is, show that
   2/(α − γ) = 1/α + 1/(α − β).
status_search_result: This is a classical elementary algebra exercise on harmonic progressions with a short direct proof: from 2/β = 1/α + 1/γ one derives β = 2αγ/(α+γ), and substituting yields 1/α + 1/(α−β) = 2/(α−γ). The result is established by routine computation and is considered solved.

paper_title: Exploring Progressions: A Collection of Problems
context_brief: Recover GP parameters from partial sums
original_question: Let a1 = a, a2, … be a geometric progression with positive first term a and positive ratio r ≠ 1. Let n and k be natural numbers with n > k + 1. If A is the sum of the first k terms and B is the sum of the last k terms among the first n terms, express the ratio r solely in terms of A and B, and also express the first term a solely in terms of A and B.
self_contained_problem:
Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ be a geometric progression of real numbers with positive first term $a_1 = a > 0$ and positive common ratio $r > 0$ with $r 
eq 1$, so that $a_i = a\, r^{\,i-1}$ for every positive integer $i$. Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers satisfying $n > k+1$. Define
$$A = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_k, \qquad B = a_{n-k+1} + a_{n-k+2} + \cdots + a_n,$$
i.e. $A$ is the sum of the first $k$ terms and $B$ is the sum of the last $k$ terms among the first $n$ terms of the progression.

Express the common ratio $r$ as an explicit formula in $A$ and $B$ (with $n$ and $k$ as given parameters), and likewise express the first term $a$ as an explicit formula in $A$ and $B$.
status_search_result: This is a standard exercise on geometric progressions with an elementary closed-form solution: since the last $k$ terms equal $r^{n-k}$ times the first $k$ terms, one has $B = A\, r^{n-k}$, hence $r = (B/A)^{1/(n-k)}$ and $a = A(r-1)/(r^k-1)$. No active research status.

original_question: Assume α, β, and γ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression, and β, γ, and δ are nonzero consecutive terms of a harmonic progression. Prove that α/β = γ/δ.
self_contained_problem:
Three real numbers x, y, z are said to be consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression if 2y = x + z. Three nonzero real numbers x, y, z are said to be consecutive terms of a harmonic progression if their reciprocals 1/x, 1/y, 1/z form an arithmetic progression, equivalently 2/y = 1/x + 1/z.

Let α, β, γ, δ be real numbers with β, γ, δ nonzero. Suppose that α, β, γ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression and that β, γ, δ are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression. Prove that

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Let G be an orderable group such that every order on every subgroup of G is central. Is every right order on G a Conrad right order?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. A group $G$ is called orderable (two-sided orderable) if there exists a total order $\leq$ on $G$ that is invariant under both left and right multiplication: for all $a,b,x,y\in G$, $a\leq b$ implies $xay\leq xby$. A right order on $G$ is a total order $\leq$ such that $a\leq b$ implies $ax\leq bx$ for all $x\in G$. Equivalently, a right order is determined by its positive cone $P=\{g\in G : g>1\}$, which satisfies $P\cdot P\subseteq P$, $P\cap P^{-1}=\emptyset$, and $P\cup P^{-1}\cup\{1\}=G$.

A two-sided order on a subgroup $H\leq G$ is called central if its positive cone is closed under conjugation by every element of $H$ (equivalently, the order is invariant under inner automorphisms of $H$); for two-sided orders this is automatic, so the condition is meaningful when applied uniformly to all subgroups: every two-sided order on every subgroup $H\leq G$ has its positive cone normal in $H$.

A right order $\leq$ on $G$ with positive cone $P$ is called a Conrad right order (or satisfies the Conrad property) if for every $a,b\in P$ there is a positive integer $n$ such that $a^n b > a$, equivalently, every finitely generated subgroup of $G$ has a nontrivial order-convex normal subgroup with infinite cyclic quotient under the induced order.

Question. Let $G$ be an orderable group such that every two-sided order on every subgroup of $G$ is central. Must every right order on $G$ be a Conrad right order?
