Call a group $G$ orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is bi-invariant, i.e. $a\le b$ implies $xay\le xby$ for all $x,y\in G$. Call a partial order $\preceq$ on $G$ a partial group order if it is invariant under left and right multiplication. Define an O*-group to be a group $G$ with the property that every partial group order on $G$ extends to a total bi-invariant order on $G$.

A class $\mathcal{K}$ of groups is said to be axiomatically closed (or to be the axiomatic closure of a subclass $\mathcal{K}_0\subseteq\mathcal{K}$) if $\mathcal{K}$ consists of exactly those groups that satisfy every first-order sentence in the language of groups that holds in every member of $\mathcal{K}_0$.

Question: Is the class of orderable groups equal to the axiomatic closure of the class of O*-groups?

No source found that announces a resolution.

original_question: Is every orderable group H embeddable in an orderable group G so that any G-invariant partial order on H has an extention to a total order on G?
self_contained_problem:
A group $H$ is called orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $H$ that is bi-invariant, i.e. $a\le b$ implies $xay\le xby$ for all $x,y,a,b\in H$. If $H$ is a subgroup of a group $G$, a partial order $\preceq$ on $H$ is called $G$-invariant if it is preserved under conjugation by every element of $G$, i.e. $a\preceq b$ implies $gag^{-1}\preceq gbg^{-1}$ for all $g\in G$ and all $a,b\in H$ (and $\preceq$ is also bi-invariant under multiplication within $H$).

Question: Is it true that every orderable group $H$ can be embedded into some orderable group $G$ with the following property: every $G$-invariant partial order on $H$ extends to a bi-invariant total order on $G$?

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Let W* be the class of orderable groups G such that every G-invariant weakly abelian partial order extends to a weakly abelian total order. Is W* \ O* non-empty?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. Let $G$ be a group, written multiplicatively. A partial order $\le$ on $G$ is called $G$-invariant (or two-sided invariant) if for all $a,b,x,y \in G$, $a \le b$ implies $xay \le xby$. The positive cone of $\le$ is $P = \{g \in G : g \ge e\}$; an invariant partial order on $G$ corresponds to a subset $P \subseteq G$ with $P \cdot P \subseteq P$, $P \cap P^{-1} = \{e\}$, and $gPg^{-1} \subseteq P$ for every $g \in G$. The order is total (a left-and-right invariant linear order) if additionally $P \cup P^{-1} = G$.

A $G$-invariant partial order $\le$ on $G$ is called weakly abelian if for all $a, b \in G$ with $a > e$ and $b > e$, one has $b^{-1} a b < a^n$ for some positive integer $n$ (equivalently, no strictly positive element is "infinitely larger" than its conjugates).

A group $G$ is called orderable if it admits a $G$-invariant total order. Define the following classes of orderable groups:
- $\mathcal{O}^* = \{G : G \text{ is orderable, and every } G\text{-invariant partial order on } G \text{ extends to a } G\text{-invariant total order on } G\}$.
- $\mathcal{W}^* = \{G : G \text{ is orderable, and every } G\text{-invariant weakly abelian partial order on } G \text{ extends to a } G\text{-invariant weakly abelian total order on } G\}$.

Question. Is $\mathcal{W}^* \setminus \mathcal{O}^*$ nonempty? Equivalently, does there exist an orderable group $G$ such that every $G$-invariant weakly abelian partial order on $G$ extends to a weakly abelian total order, but some $G$-invariant partial order on $G$ fails to extend to any $G$-invariant total order?
status_search_result: The question appears in a well-known list of unsolved problems in ordered and orderable groups, and no published resolution was located. The available sources only restate the question as open; no proof or counterexample establishing whether $\mathcal{W}^* \setminus \mathcal{O}^*$ is empty was found.

original_question: Let F be the free group of finite rank ≥ 2. Does there exist a finite subset S ⊂ F such that there is a unique total order on F under which all elements from S are positive?
self_contained_problem:

Does there exist a finite subset $S \subset F$ such that there is exactly one total (bi-invariant) order on $F$ under which every element of $S$ is positive?

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Let G be an abelian-by-nilpotent ordered group. (i) Is G order-embeddable in a divisible ordered group? (ii) If G is also nilpotent-by-abelian, is G order-embeddable in a divisible ordered group?
self_contained_problem:
A totally ordered group is a group $G$ equipped with a total order $\leq$ that is invariant under both left and right multiplication: for all $a,b,x,y \in G$, $a \leq b$ implies $xay \leq xby$. A totally ordered group $D$ is called divisible if for every $d \in D$ and every positive integer $n$ there exists $x \in D$ with $x^n = d$. An order-embedding of an ordered group $G$ into an ordered group $H$ is an injective group homomorphism $\varphi : G \to H$ such that for all $a,b \in G$, $a \leq b$ if and only if $\varphi(a) \leq \varphi(b)$. A group $G$ is abelian-by-nilpotent if it has a normal abelian subgroup $A \trianglelefteq G$ such that $G/A$ is nilpotent; it is nilpotent-by-abelian if it has a normal nilpotent subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$ such that $G/N$ is abelian.

(i) Let $G$ be an abelian-by-nilpotent totally ordered group. Is $G$ order-embeddable in a divisible totally ordered group?

(ii) If, in addition, $G$ is nilpotent-by-abelian, is $G$ order-embeddable in a divisible totally ordered group?

paper_title: On Some Open Problems on Maximal Curves
context_brief: Existence of a Frobenius-dimension-3 maximal curve with ε_2 = 3.
original_question: Does there exist an F_{q^2}-maximal curve X over the finite field F_{q^2} whose Frobenius linear series D = |(q+1)P_0| has projective dimension 3 and whose generic D-order sequence has third entry ε_2 = 3, equivalently whose D-order sequence is (0, 1, 3, q)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $q$ be a prime power and let $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ be the finite field with $q^2$ elements. A smooth, projective, geometrically irreducible curve $X$ defined over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ of genus $g$ is called $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-maximal if the number of its $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-rational points attains the Hasse–Weil upper bound, i.e.\ $\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}) = q^2 + 1 + 2gq$. For such a curve, fix an $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-rational point $P_0 \in X$ and consider the complete linear series $D = |(q+1)P_0|$, called the Frobenius (or natural) linear series of $X$. Let $r := \dim D$ be its projective dimension. Associated with $D$ there is a generic order sequence $0 = \varepsilon_0 < \varepsilon_1 < \cdots < \varepsilon_r$, the integers giving the possible orders of contact (intersection multiplicities) of hyperplanes with the image of the morphism defined by $D$ at a generic point of $X$.

Question: Does there exist an $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-maximal curve $X$ (for some prime power $q$) such that the Frobenius linear series $D = |(q+1)P_0|$ has projective dimension $r = 3$ and such that the generic $D$-order sequence is exactly
$$(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3) = (0,1,3,q),$$
i.e.\ with third entry $\varepsilon_2 = 3$?
status_search_result: The question is answered affirmatively: an explicit $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-maximal curve with Frobenius dimension 3 and $D$-order sequence $(0,1,3,27)$ is constructed for $q=27$, settling case (A).

paper_title: On Some Open Problems on Maximal Curves
context_brief: Existence of a Frobenius-dimension-3 maximal curve with ε_2 = 2 and the large exceptional value of j_2(P).
original_question: Does there exist an F_{q^2}-maximal curve X over F_{q^2} whose Frobenius linear series has projective dimension 3, whose generic D-order sequence satisfies ε_2 = 2, and for which there is an F_{q^2}-rational point P such that the second (D, P)-order is j_2(P) = q + 1 - floor((2/3)(q + 1))?
self_contained_problem:
Let $q$ be a prime power and let $X$ be a projective, geometrically irreducible, non-singular algebraic curve defined over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$. Recall that $X$ is called $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-maximal if the number of its $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-rational points attains the Hasse–Weil upper bound $q^2 + 1 + 2gq$, where $g$ is the genus of $X$.

For an $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-maximal curve $X$, the Frobenius linear series $\mathcal{D}$ is the complete linear series cut out on $X$ by the divisor $(q+1)P_0$ for any $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-rational point $P_0$ (this series is independent of the chosen point). Let $r$ denote the projective dimension of $\mathcal{D}$ (the Frobenius dimension of $X$). Associated with $\mathcal{D}$ are:
- the generic $\mathcal{D}$-order sequence $0 = \varepsilon_0 < \varepsilon_1 < \cdots < \varepsilon_r$, the strictly increasing sequence of integers attained as orders of contact of hyperplane sections at a generic point of $X$;
- for each point $P \in X$, the $(\mathcal{D},P)$-order sequence $0 = j_0(P) < j_1(P) < \cdots < j_r(P)$, the Hermitian invariants of $\mathcal{D}$ at $P$.

Question. Does there exist a prime power $q$ and an $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-maximal curve $X$ whose Frobenius dimension equals $3$, whose generic $\mathcal{D}$-order sequence satisfies $\varepsilon_2 = 2$, and which has an $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-rational point $P$ such that
$$j_2(P) = q + 1 - \left\lfloor \tfrac{2}{3}(q+1) \right\rfloor\,?$$
status_search_result: The question is answered affirmatively by an explicit construction: the function field $F = K(z,t)$ over $K = \mathbb{F}_{49}$ defined by $z^{16} = t(t+1)^6$ yields an $\mathbb{F}_{49}$-maximal curve with Frobenius dimension $3$, generic $\mathcal{D}$-order sequence $(0,1,2,7)$, and an $\mathbb{F}_{49}$-rational place $P$ with $j_2(P) = 3 = 8 - \lfloor \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot 8\rfloor$ (here $q=7$). Thus the problem is solved.

paper_title: Multi-Head Finite Automata: Characterizations, Concepts and Open Problems
original_question: What is the exact state complexity of simulating a nondeterministic two-way one-head finite automaton by a deterministic two-way one-head finite automaton? More precisely, given a 2NFA(1), how many states are sufficient and how many are necessary in the worst case for an equivalent 2DFA(1)?
self_contained_problem:
A two-way one-head finite automaton over a finite alphabet Σ is a finite-state machine equipped with a read-only input tape (with left and right end-markers) and a single head that may move left, right, or stay, until it accepts or rejects. Such a machine is called a 2DFA(1) if its transition relation is deterministic and a 2NFA(1) if it is nondeterministic. Two automata are equivalent if they accept the same language.

For a 2NFA(1) with n states, let f(n) denote the smallest integer such that every n-state 2NFA(1) admits an equivalent 2DFA(1) with at most f(n) states. Determine f(n) exactly; equivalently, determine matching upper and lower bounds on the number of states sufficient and necessary, in the worst case, to simulate an arbitrary n-state 2NFA(1) by an equivalent 2DFA(1). In particular, decide whether f(n) is bounded by a polynomial in n.
status_search_result: The problem of the state-complexity cost of simulating two-way nondeterministic finite automata by two-way deterministic ones is the classical Sakoda–Sipser question (1978). It is widely regarded as a central open problem in automata theory, with known formal connections to the L vs. NL question (Berman–Lingas, Kapoutsis). Only special cases (unary languages, sweeping/oblivious 2DFAs, outer-nondeterministic 2NFAs, etc.) have been resolved; the general question remains open.

paper_title: Multi-Head Finite Automata: Characterizations, Concepts and Open Problems
context_brief: Conversion bounds between one-head data-independent and data-dependent automata
original_question: Determine tight conversion bounds between one-head data-independent finite automata and one-head data-dependent finite automata. In particular, when a language is recognized by a one-head data-independent finite automaton, what description-size blow-up is required to convert it into an equivalent one-head data-dependent deterministic, nondeterministic, or alternating finite automaton, and what bounds hold in the reverse direction?
self_contained_problem:
A one-head finite automaton is a finite automaton (deterministic, nondeterministic, or alternating) that reads its input via a single head moving on a tape containing the input word. Such an automaton is called data-independent (or oblivious) if the sequence of head positions during a computation depends only on the length of the input word and not on the specific symbols of the input; otherwise it is called data-dependent. The description size of an automaton is measured by its total number of states (or by the total length of a standard encoding of its transition function).

For each pair (X, Y) with X ∈ {data-independent} and Y ∈ {data-dependent deterministic, data-dependent nondeterministic, data-dependent alternating} (and the analogous pairs in the reverse direction), determine tight upper and lower bounds on the description-size blow-up needed to convert a one-head finite automaton of type X recognizing a language L into an equivalent one-head finite automaton of type Y recognizing the same language. That is, find a function f(n) such that every type-X automaton with n states can be converted to an equivalent type-Y automaton with at most f(n) states, and exhibit a family of languages witnessing that this bound cannot be improved (up to constants), for each of the six conversion directions.
status_search_result: The problem was posed as an open problem in the survey on multi-head finite automata by Holzer, Kutrib, and Malcher. Related work (Holzer, MFCS 1997; later papers on data-independent vs. data-dependent multi-head automata, and on tight hierarchies of data-independent multi-head automata) studies the broader k-head setting and shows that many conversions yield non-recursive trade-offs, but no published source found in the search establishes tight conversion bounds for the one-head data-independent vs. data-dependent case. Status could not be confirmed from the available sources.

paper_title: Normals, subnormals and an open question
original_question: Let S be a densely defined operator on a Hilbert space with invariant domain. For each vector f in D(S), define the cyclic portion S_f by first setting D_f = {p(S)f : p belongs to C[Z]}, then H_f as the closure of D_f, and finally S_f as the restriction of S to D_f acting in the Hilbert space H_f. If every cyclic portion S_f is subnormal for every f in D(S), must the original operator S itself be subnormal?
self_contained_problem:
Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $S$ be a densely defined linear operator in $H$ with domain $\mathcal{D}(S)$ such that $S\mathcal{D}(S)\subseteq \mathcal{D}(S)$ (i.e., $\mathcal{D}(S)$ is invariant under $S$, so that $p(S)f$ is well defined for every polynomial $p\in\mathbb{C}[Z]$ and every $f\in\mathcal{D}(S)$).

Recall that a densely defined operator $T$ in a Hilbert space $K$ is called subnormal if there exist a Hilbert space $\widetilde{K}\supseteq K$ and a densely defined normal operator $N$ in $\widetilde{K}$ such that $\mathcal{D}(T)\subseteq \mathcal{D}(N)$ and $Tf=Nf$ for all $f\in\mathcal{D}(T)$.

For each $f\in\mathcal{D}(S)$, define the cyclic portion of $S$ at $f$ as follows:
- $\mathcal{D}_f := \{p(S)f : p\in\mathbb{C}[Z]\}$,
- $H_f := \overline{\mathcal{D}_f}$ (the closure taken in $H$),
- $S_f := S\!\restriction_{\mathcal{D}_f}$, considered as an operator in the Hilbert space $H_f$.

Question: If $S_f$ is subnormal for every $f\in\mathcal{D}(S)$, must $S$ itself be subnormal?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not turn up a published resolution of this question. The problem is posed as an open question in the operator-theory literature on unbounded subnormal operators, and no subsequent paper located by the search clearly settles whether subnormality of every cyclic portion of a densely defined operator with invariant domain forces subnormality of the operator itself.

paper_title: An Experimental Mathematics Perspective on the Old, and still Open, Question of When To Stop?
original_question: Let β_n denote the Chow-Robbins stopping boundary after n tosses, meaning that one should stop as soon as the number of heads minus the number of tails is at least β_n. The paper highlights the specific unresolved case n = 8: is β_8 equal to 2? Equivalently, after eight tosses with five heads and three tails, is it optimal in the infinite-horizon game to stop immediately and take the certain payoff 5/8 = 0.625, or to continue playing because the true expected payoff from that state eventually exceeds 5/8?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following infinite-horizon optimal stopping problem (the Chow–Robbins game). A fair coin is tossed repeatedly. After any number of tosses the player may stop; if the player stops after a total of n tosses with H heads and T = n − H tails, the payoff is H/n. The player may also continue forever (in which case the payoff is the limit, which is 1/2 almost surely). Let V(H,T) denote the supremum, over all stopping rules, of the expected payoff starting from a state with H heads and T tails already accumulated. It is known that the optimal policy has the form: stop in state (H,T) with n = H + T tosses if and only if H − T ≥ β_n, for a sequence of integer thresholds β_n.

Question: Is β_8 = 2? Equivalently, in the state with H = 5 heads and T = 3 tails (so the current empirical mean is 5/8 = 0.625), is it optimal to stop immediately, i.e., does V(5,3) = 5/8? Determine whether stopping is optimal in the position (H,T) = (5,3), or whether instead V(5,3) > 5/8.

Subsequent work (e.g., the Catalan-triangle approach, arXiv:2205.13499, 2022) reaffirmed exact solutions for almost all n.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: How should confirmation theory resolve the black raven paradox, namely the tension between the claim that observing black ravens confirms the hypothesis that all ravens are black, the logical equivalence of 'all ravens are black' with 'all non-black things are non-ravens', and the apparently absurd conclusion that observing a white sock therefore confirms that all ravens are black?
self_contained_problem:
Hempel's raven paradox arises from three apparently plausible principles in confirmation theory:

(i) (Nicod's criterion) For predicates R and B, the universal hypothesis "for all x, R(x) → B(x)" is confirmed by observing an instance a satisfying R(a) ∧ B(a).

(ii) Applying (i) with R replaced by ¬B and B replaced by ¬R: the hypothesis "for all x, ¬B(x) → ¬R(x)" is confirmed by observing an instance a satisfying ¬B(a) ∧ ¬R(a).

(iii) (Equivalence condition) If two hypotheses are logically equivalent, then any observation that confirms one confirms the other. Since "∀x (R(x) → B(x))" and "∀x (¬B(x) → ¬R(x))" are logically equivalent, observations of the form ¬B(a) ∧ ¬R(a) confirm "all R are B" as well.

Taking R(x) = "x is a raven" and B(x) = "x is black", (iii) yields the conclusion that observing a white sock (a non-black non-raven) confirms the hypothesis that all ravens are black, which appears absurd.

Problem: Provide a formal theory of confirmation — specifying a precise quantitative or qualitative confirmation relation between evidence and hypotheses — that (a) clearly identifies which of the principles (i)–(iii) must be modified or restricted, (b) accounts for the intuition that observing black ravens provides substantially more confirmation of "all ravens are black" than observing white socks does (or explains rigorously why such a difference of degree is or is not warranted), and (c) does so in a way that is consistent across reformulations of the hypothesis under logical equivalence and choice of predicates.
status_search_result: The raven paradox remains a debated foundational problem in confirmation theory and inductive logic. While Bayesian analyses (Good, Hosiasson-Lindenbaum, Fitelson & Hawthorne, Vranas, and others) offer partial resolutions showing that white socks do confirm the hypothesis but only to a tiny degree under certain priors, there is no universally accepted resolution; competing approaches differ on which of Nicod's criterion, the equivalence condition, or background assumptions to revise. The problem is typically classified as open / unresolved in the philosophy of science and inductive logic literature.

status_search_result: The question of a universally applicable, reparametrization-invariant proper prior on non-compact parameter spaces (extending the finite-uniform and Jeffreys principles) remains a long-standing open problem in objective Bayesian statistics and universal induction. No publication identified that resolves this problem.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: How should Solomonoff-style induction be extended or clarified so that it can be compared to Carnap’s confirmation theory and Laplace’s rule, accommodate continuous model classes, and incorporate prior knowledge in a principled way?
self_contained_problem:
Solomonoff's universal a priori probability is defined, for binary strings $x\in\{0,1\}^*$, by
$$M(x) \;=\; \sum_{p:\, U(p)=x*} 2^{-|p|},$$
where $U$ is a fixed universal monotone Turing machine and the sum is over all minimal programs $p$ that produce $x$ as a prefix of their output. Solomonoff induction predicts the next symbol via the conditional $M(x_{n+1}\mid x_1\dots x_n)$, and corresponds to a Bayesian mixture over the countable class of all lower semicomputable semimeasures with the universal prior $2^{-K(\nu)}$.

Develop a principled extension/clarification of Solomonoff-style universal induction that simultaneously achieves the following:

(a) Provides an explicit, formal correspondence (or precisely demarcated divergence) between universal induction and Carnap's continuum of inductive methods (the $\lambda$-confirmation functions $c_\lambda$ on a first-order monadic language) together with Laplace's rule of succession $P(x_{n+1}=1\mid x_1,\dots,x_n) = (k+1)/(n+2)$ for $k$ successes in $n$ trials; in particular, identify which choices of universal machine, prior, or hypothesis class recover $c_\lambda$ or Laplace's rule as special cases or limits.

(b) Generalizes the construction from the countable class of lower semicomputable semimeasures to genuinely continuous (uncountable) model classes $\mathcal{M}=\{\mu_\theta : \theta\in\Theta\}$ over a continuous parameter space $\Theta$ (e.g.\ a measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$), specifying a computable or constructive notion of universal prior on $\Theta$, and proving convergence and loss-bound theorems analogous to Solomonoff's $\sum_{n=1}^\infty E[(M(x_n=1\mid x_{<n})-\mu(x_n=1\mid x_{<n}))^2]\le \tfrac{1}{2}\ln 2 \cdot K(\mu)$ for the true measure $\mu\in\mathcal{M}$.

(c) Provides a principled mechanism for incorporating arbitrary prior background knowledge $B$ (expressed, say, as a finite or computable set of constraints, equations, or observed data) into the universal prior, yielding a modified universal predictor $M_B$ that (i) remains dominant over the relevant class given $B$, (ii) reduces to standard $M$ when $B$ is vacuous, and (iii) admits convergence guarantees relative to $B$.

State and prove the corresponding consistency/convergence and dominance theorems for the proposed framework.
status_search_result: The question is a programmatic open problem in the foundations of universal induction. There is no single agreed solution; partial work exists (e.g., Hutter and others on continuous classes via integration over parameter spaces, and Rathmanner–Hutter "A Philosophical Treatise of Universal Induction" relating Solomonoff to Carnap and Laplace), but a unified principled framework satisfying all three desiderata has not been established. Status remains effectively open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: Can one identify a nonempty class of 'natural' universal Turing machines or universal semimeasures, or even a single best such machine or semimeasure, that has favorable invariance properties strong enough to control the additive and multiplicative constants that otherwise pervade algorithmic information theory?
self_contained_problem:
Background. In algorithmic information theory, a universal Turing machine (UTM) U is a Turing machine such that for every Turing machine M there exists a constant c_M with K_U(x) ≤ K_M(x) + c_M for all finite binary strings x, where K_M(x) denotes the length of a shortest M-program that outputs x. A universal (lower-semicomputable) semimeasure (USM) is a function m on finite binary strings that is lower semicomputable, satisfies Σ_x m(x) ≤ 1, and dominates every lower-semicomputable semimeasure up to a multiplicative constant. The invariance theorem guarantees that quantities such as K_U and m are defined only up to additive (respectively multiplicative) constants that depend on the choice of U or m, and this freedom is responsible for many of the additive O(1) and multiplicative Θ(1) terms appearing throughout the theory.

Problem. Define a precise, nonempty class C of UTMs (or USMs) deserving to be called "natural" by means of a finite list of explicit invariance/robustness properties P_1, …, P_n (for instance, properties such as: optimality up to small constants relative to a wide class of reference machines; stability under standard simulations and prefix encodings; minimality of the constants in the invariance theorem when compared to specified machine families; canonicity with respect to a chosen universal model of computation), and prove:

(a) that the intersection ∩_i C_i of the classes determined by each property P_i is nonempty; and
(b) that every element of C provides quantitative control over the additive constants in K_U (or the multiplicative constants in m) appearing in standard results of algorithmic information theory, in the sense that for any two U, U' ∈ C the difference |K_U(x) − K_{U'}(x)| can be bounded by an explicit, small, computable constant uniformly in x.

Stronger form. Exhibit a single UTM U* (respectively USM m*) — a "best" universal machine — together with a precise optimality criterion which U* (resp. m*) provably satisfies, and which singles it out uniquely up to a controlled, explicitly bounded equivalence.

Either produce such a class C (and ideally such a U* or m*) with proofs of (a) and (b), or show that no such class with the required properties can exist.
status_search_result: The problem of identifying a class of "natural" universal Turing machines or universal semimeasures, or a single best such machine, that would tame the additive/multiplicative constants of algorithmic information theory is a long-standing foundational open problem. Surveys of Kolmogorov complexity and AIT continue to highlight the dependence of K and of universal semimeasures on the choice of reference machine as an unresolved foundational issue, with no widely accepted canonical "natural" UTM or USM having been established.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: Which generalized classes of semimeasures, Bayesian mixtures over those classes, and corresponding generalized randomness notions yield robust convergence results, and can structural conditions such as denseness characterize when such convergence holds and when it fails?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. Let $\mathcal{X}=\{0,1\}$ and consider sequences in $\mathcal{X}^\infty$. A semimeasure on $\mathcal{X}^*$ is a function $\nu:\mathcal{X}^*\to[0,1]$ with $\nu(\epsilon)\le 1$ and $\nu(x)\ge \nu(x0)+\nu(x1)$ for all finite strings $x$; it is a (probability) measure when these inequalities are equalities. Given a countable class $\mathcal{M}$ of semimeasures together with a strictly positive prior weight $w:\mathcal{M}\to(0,1]$ with $\sum_{\nu\in\mathcal{M}} w(\nu)\le 1$, the Bayesian mixture is
$$\xi_{\mathcal{M}}(x)=\sum_{\nu\in\mathcal{M}} w(\nu)\,\nu(x).$$
For a true measure $\mu\in\mathcal{M}$, one studies posterior convergence of the predictive ratios $\xi_{\mathcal{M}}(x_{n+1}\mid x_{1:n})\to \mu(x_{n+1}\mid x_{1:n})$ along sequences $x_{1:\infty}$, where the convergence may be required $\mu$-almost surely, on every $\mu$-Martin-Löf random sequence, or on every sequence random with respect to a generalized randomness notion derived from $\xi_{\mathcal{M}}$ itself.

Known facts. Restrict to the class of Bernoulli measures $\mu_\theta$, $\theta\in\Theta\subseteq[0,1]$. It is known that if $\Theta$ is dense in $[0,1]$ then the mixture $\xi_\Theta$ predicts correctly on every $\mu_\theta$-random sequence for $\theta\in\Theta$, while if $\Theta$ has a gap (an open subinterval disjoint from $\Theta$) then convergence can fail on some random sequence.

Problem. Identify general classes $\mathcal{M}$ of semimeasures (extending beyond the computably enumerable universal class) such that:

(a) the corresponding Bayesian mixture $\xi_{\mathcal{M}}$ admits a well-defined generalized randomness notion (e.g. defined by Martin-Löf-type tests with respect to $\xi_{\mathcal{M}}$);

(b) for every $\mu\in\mathcal{M}$, the posterior $\xi_{\mathcal{M}}(\cdot\mid x_{1:n})$ converges to $\mu(\cdot\mid x_{1:n})$ on every sequence that is random in this generalized sense.

In particular, determine whether a topological/structural condition of "denseness" of $\mathcal{M}$ in an appropriate ambient space of semimeasures characterizes exactly when such robust convergence holds, and identify a structural property (analogous to the gappy/dense dichotomy for Bernoulli classes) whose violation provably forces convergence to fail on some random sequence.
status_search_result: The literature (Hutter and collaborators, 2003–2007) establishes the dense-vs-gappy dichotomy for Bernoulli subclasses and constructs universal semimeasures that fail to converge on some Martin-Löf random sequences. A general characterization, in terms of denseness or another structural property, of which classes of semimeasures yield posterior convergence on all (generalized) random sequences does not appear to have been established; the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: When AIXI is specialized to a sequence-prediction task, does it predict sequences as well as Solomonoff’s universal prediction scheme even though AIXI does not literally reduce to Solomonoff prediction and the universal prior M is defined on inputs rather than directly on outputs?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Fix a finite alphabet of observations $\mathcal{O}$, a finite alphabet of actions $\mathcal{A}$, and a finite alphabet of rewards $\mathcal{R}\subset[0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q}$. Let $U$ be a fixed universal monotone Turing machine, and define Solomonoff's universal semimeasure on input strings by
$$M(x)\;=\;\sum_{p:\;U(p)=x*}2^{-\ell(p)},$$
where the sum runs over minimal programs $p$ that, when fed to $U$, output a string having $x\in(\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{R})^{*}$ as a prefix, and $\ell(p)$ is the length of $p$ in bits.

Solomonoff's universal predictor. For sequences $z_{1:\infty}\in\mathcal{O}^{\infty}$ generated by an unknown computable measure $\mu$, Solomonoff's universal sequence prediction scheme predicts $z_{n+1}$ from $z_{1:n}$ using the conditional
$$M_{\mathrm{seq}}(z_{n+1}\mid z_{1:n})\;=\;\frac{M_{\mathrm{seq}}(z_{1:n+1})}{M_{\mathrm{seq}}(z_{1:n})},$$
where $M_{\mathrm{seq}}$ is the universal semimeasure defined directly on output sequences.

AIXI. The AIXI agent at time $n$, having observed history $h_{<n}=a_1 o_1 r_1\cdots a_{n-1}o_{n-1}r_{n-1}$, chooses
$$a_n^{\mathrm{AIXI}}\;=\;\arg\max_{a_n}\sum_{o_n r_n}\!\cdots\!\max_{a_m}\sum_{o_m r_m}\!\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{k=n}^{m}r_k\Bigr)\,M(o_1 r_1\cdots o_m r_m\mid a_1\cdots a_m),$$
for a finite horizon $m$, where $M$ is conditioned on the action sequence (actions are inputs, not predicted by $M$).

Prediction specialization. Specialize AIXI to a pure sequence-prediction task: the agent must output a guess $\hat z_n\in\mathcal{O}$ for the next symbol $z_n$ of an unknown computable sequence and receives reward $r_n=1$ iff $\hat z_n=z_n$ (and $0$ otherwise). Identify $a_n$ with $\hat z_n$ and $o_n r_n$ with $(z_n,\mathbb{1}[\hat z_n=z_n])$.

Question. Even though, in this specialization, AIXI does not literally reduce to Solomonoff's universal sequence prediction scheme—because $M$ is the universal semimeasure on input/interaction strings rather than directly on output sequences—does the AIXI policy nonetheless achieve sequence-prediction performance comparable to Solomonoff's universal predictor? Concretely: prove or disprove that for every computable measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{O}^{\infty}$, the expected number of prediction errors made by AIXI on $\mu$-distributed sequences is finite (or bounded by a constant multiple of the corresponding bound for Solomonoff's scheme), and quantify any loss in performance relative to Solomonoff prediction.
status_search_result: The question of whether AIXI, when specialized to sequence prediction, performs as well as Solomonoff's universal predictor was raised as an open problem in the universal induction/AIXI literature. Subsequent work on AIXI (computability, optimality variants, AIXI^tl, limit-computable approximations) does not appear to have settled this specific equivalence/comparison question. No source found in the search explicitly resolves it, so it appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: For which restricted environmental classes—such as Markov, factorizable, forgetful, relevant, asymptotically learnable, farsighted, uniform, or pseudo-passive environments—can one define and prove general value bounds or optimality properties for AIXI?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the universal reinforcement-learning agent AIXI, defined as follows. An environment is a conditional probability measure $\mu(o_{1:n}r_{1:n}\mid a_{1:n})$ over sequences of observations $o_t$ and rewards $r_t\in[0,1]$ given a sequence of actions $a_t$ chosen from finite alphabets. For a policy $\pi$, the expected future $\mu$-value at time $k$ with horizon $m$ is 
$$V^\pi_\mu(\ae_{<k}) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_\mu\!\left[\sum_{t=k}^{k+m} r_t \,\Big|\, \ae_{<k},\, a_{k:k+m}\sim\pi\right].$$
The Bayes-optimal AIXI policy with respect to a class $\mathcal{M}$ of environments and prior $w:\mathcal{M}\to(0,1]$ with $\sum_\nu w_\nu \le 1$ is the policy maximizing $V^\pi_\xi$, where $\xi(\,\cdot\,)=\sum_{\nu\in\mathcal{M}} w_\nu\,\nu(\,\cdot\,)$. When $\mathcal{M}$ is the class of all lower semicomputable chronological semimeasures with universal Solomonoff-type prior, this defines AIXI.

Recall the following restricted environment classes:
(i) $n$-Markov: the conditional distribution of $(o_t,r_t)$ given history depends only on the last $n$ action–percept pairs.
(ii) Factorizable: $\mu$ factorizes into independent episodes of bounded length.
(iii) Forgetful: the influence of the initial history on future percepts vanishes uniformly.
(iv) Relevant: only finitely much past information is needed to predict the future to arbitrary accuracy.
(v) Asymptotically learnable: there exists a policy whose predictions converge to the true conditional in $\mu$-probability.
(vi) Farsighted: the limit $\lim_{m\to\infty} V^\pi_\mu$ exists for the relevant policies.
(vii) Uniform: the per-step rewards have a structure that is uniform across histories.
(viii) Pseudo-passive (and passive): the agent's actions do not influence (resp. only weakly influence) future percepts.

Problem. For each of the above restricted classes $\mathcal{C}$, determine whether one can prove a nontrivial general value bound or optimality property for the Bayes-optimal AIXI policy $\pi^\xi$ relative to the best informed policy $\pi^\mu$, of the form
$$V^{\pi^\xi}_\mu - V^{\pi^\mu}_\mu \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{(in some appropriate sense)}$$
uniformly or $\mu$-almost surely for every $\mu\in\mathcal{C}$, and identify the largest such class for which a meaningful bound or optimality theorem can be established.
status_search_result: Partial progress exists. Hutter's 2005 monograph and follow-up work establish self-optimizingness of Bayes-optimal agents on classes such as ergodic MDPs, factorizable, forgetful, relevant, (pseudo-)passive and asymptotically learnable environments, and Leike's 2016 thesis "Nonparametric General Reinforcement Learning" extends asymptotic optimality results in mean and Cesàro senses for restricted classes. However, fully general value bounds or strong optimality properties for AIXI itself across all of these classes (especially uniform and farsighted) remain incomplete; recent work (e.g., 2025 "Value Under Ignorance in Universal Artificial Intelligence") continues to refine the picture, indicating the question is partially solved rather than fully resolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: Which mathematically precise intelligence-related properties—such as creativity, problem solving, pattern recognition, classification, learning, induction, deduction, building analogies, optimization, surviving in an environment, language processing, and planning—does AIXI satisfy as a rational agent?
self_contained_problem:
Let AIXI denote the universal reinforcement-learning agent defined as follows. Fix a finite action set A, a finite percept set E = O × R where O is a set of observations and R ⊂ ℚ ∩ [0,1] is a finite set of rewards. For an interaction history of length t, write a_{1:t} = a_1 a_2 … a_t and e_{1:t} = e_1 e_2 … e_t with e_k = (o_k, r_k). Let M be the class of all lower semi-computable chronological semimeasures over (A × E)^∞, and let ξ(e_{1:t} ‖ a_{1:t}) := Σ_{ν∈M} 2^{-K(ν)} ν(e_{1:t} ‖ a_{1:t}) be the universal Solomonoff–Hutter mixture, where K(·) denotes prefix Kolmogorov complexity. For a fixed lifetime m ≥ 1 and discount γ_k ≥ 0 with Σγ_k < ∞, define AIXI by

  a_t^{AIXI} := arg max_{a_t} Σ_{e_t} … max_{a_m} Σ_{e_m} (Σ_{k=t}^{m} γ_k r_k) ξ(e_{1:m} ‖ a_{1:m}),

acting at every time step t given the past history a_{<t} e_{<t}.

Provide mathematically precise formal definitions, within this framework, of each of the following intelligence-related properties of an agent — (i) creativity, (ii) problem solving, (iii) pattern recognition, (iv) classification, (v) learning, (vi) induction, (vii) deduction, (viii) building analogies, (ix) optimization, (x) surviving in an environment, (xi) language processing, (xii) planning — and, for each property, prove or disprove that AIXI satisfies it as a rational agent.
status_search_result: No formal mathematical results are known that systematically establish (or refute) such intelligence-related properties of AIXI. Subsequent work on AIXI has focused on optimality notions (Pareto/self-optimizing), legg–Hutter universal intelligence, asymptotic non-learnability results (Leike & Hutter), and variants such as AIXI_tl and BayesExp, but the listed properties (creativity, analogy-building, language processing, etc.) have not received agreed-upon formal definitions or proofs in the AIXI framework.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: How does the learning speed and quality of AIξ compare with standard reinforcement-learning algorithms such as TD(λ) and Q-learning, especially in environments where AIXI-style elimination of inconsistent environment programs may behave differently from existing efficient algorithms?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the universal Bayesian reinforcement-learning agent AIξ defined as follows. Fix a universal prefix Turing machine and let M be the class of all lower semicomputable chronological semimeasures over interaction histories. Let ξ(·) = Σ_{ν∈M} 2^{-K(ν)} ν(·) be the universal mixture, where K(ν) is the prefix Kolmogorov complexity of ν. At each time step k, given history h_{<k} = a_1 o_1 r_1 … a_{k-1} o_{k-1} r_{k-1} (where a_i are actions, o_i observations, r_i ∈ [0,1] rewards), the AIξ agent chooses

  a_k = argmax_{a_k} Σ_{o_k r_k} … max_{a_m} Σ_{o_m r_m} (r_k + … + r_m) · ξ(o_1 r_1 … o_m r_m | a_1 … a_m),

for some horizon m. Now consider classical reinforcement-learning algorithms operating on finite Markov decision processes with state space S, action space A, transition kernel P(s'|s,a) and bounded reward r(s,a):
 (i) Q-learning, with update Q_{t+1}(s_t,a_t) = (1-α_t) Q_t(s_t,a_t) + α_t (r_t + γ max_{a'} Q_t(s_{t+1}, a'));
 (ii) TD(λ), with eligibility-trace update for value-function estimation under a fixed policy.

Provide a quantitative comparison, in terms of either expected total reward up to time T or sample/regret bounds, between AIξ and each of TD(λ) and Q-learning, in finite ergodic Markov environments. Specifically:

(a) Establish nontrivial upper and lower bounds on the regret or learning-time of AIξ as a function of T, |S|, |A|, the mixing time, and the description complexity K(μ) of the true environment μ ∈ M.

(b) Compare these bounds with the corresponding finite-time performance bounds known for Q-learning and TD(λ) in the same environment, and determine whether AIξ asymptotically dominates, is dominated by, or is incomparable to these algorithms in (1) learning speed and (2) asymptotic quality of the learned policy.

(c) Identify environment classes where the AIξ-style elimination of inconsistent environment programs (Bayesian posterior contraction over M) provably yields strictly faster convergence than Q-learning or TD(λ), and environment classes where it does not.

Existing AIξ analyses give asymptotic optimality results rather than comparable rates, and standard Q-learning/TD(λ) sample-complexity bounds have not been juxtaposed with AIξ guarantees. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: How robust is AIXI to observations that contain irrelevant information, especially when that irrelevant input is complex or non-computable rather than computably generated noise, and under what conditions can AIXI separate such irrelevant input from the information relevant for future observations and rewards?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $\mathcal{O}$ and $\mathcal{R}\subseteq[0,1]$ be finite sets of observations and rewards, and let $\mathcal{A}$ be a finite set of actions. Write $\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{R}$ for percepts. An environment is a probability measure $\mu$ on infinite interaction histories $a_1 x_1 a_2 x_2 \dots \in (\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{X})^\infty$, specifying for every history the conditional distribution $\mu(x_t\mid a_1 x_1\cdots a_{t-1} x_{t-1} a_t)$ over the next percept. The agent AIXI is defined, with horizon discount and a universal lower-semicomputable semimeasure $\xi$ (Solomonoff's universal mixture over all lower-semicomputable chronological semimeasures), as the policy
$$ a_t^{\mathrm{AIXI}} = \arg\max_{a_t}\sum_{x_t}\max_{a_{t+1}}\sum_{x_{t+1}}\cdots \Big(\sum_{k=t}^{\infty}\gamma_k r_k\Big)\,\xi(x_t x_{t+1}\cdots\mid a_1 x_1\cdots a_t a_{t+1}\cdots),$$
for some bounded discount sequence $\gamma_k \geq 0$ with $\sum_k \gamma_k < \infty$.

Decompose each observation as $o_t = (u_t, v_t)\in\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{V}$, where $u_t$ is the "useful" component and $v_t$ is an "irrelevant" component, in the precise sense that the conditional distribution
$$\mu(u_{t+1}, r_{t+1}\mid a_1 x_1\cdots a_t x_t a_{t+1}) = \mu(u_{t+1}, r_{t+1}\mid a_1 u_1 r_1\cdots a_t u_t r_t a_{t+1})$$
depends only on the past useful components and rewards (so $v_{1:t}$ carries no information about future $u$'s and $r$'s given past $u$'s and $r$'s). Assume the marginal process $(v_t)_{t\ge 1}$ is generated independently (or independently conditioned on the agent's actions) from a source $\nu$.

Question. Establish, or refute by counterexample, the following form of robustness of AIXI:

(a) If $\nu$ is a computable (lower-semicomputable) source — i.e., $(v_t)$ is computably generated noise — show that the asymptotic value attained by AIXI on $\mu$ equals the asymptotic value of AIXI on the marginalized environment $\mu_{\mathcal U,\mathcal R}$ obtained by removing the $v$-component (i.e., AIXI's policy and expected discounted reward are unaffected, in the limit, by the presence of $v_{1:\infty}$).

(b) More generally, allow $\nu$ to be a non-computable / Kolmogorov-complex source for $(v_t)$. Identify necessary and sufficient conditions on $\nu$, on the encoding of $(u_t, v_t)$ into $o_t$, and on the discount sequence $(\gamma_k)$ under which AIXI's behavior and value remain (asymptotically) invariant under replacement of $\mu$ by $\mu_{\mathcal U,\mathcal R}$. In particular, determine whether complexity of $v$ alone can cause AIXI to suffer arbitrarily large value loss compared with the optimal policy on $\mu$, and characterize the cases in which AIXI provably "separates" the irrelevant input $v$ from the relevant signal $(u, r)$.
status_search_result: No published result establishes general robustness of AIXI to complex or non-computable but irrelevant components of observations. Discussions of AIXI's optimality (e.g., embedded-agency surveys) note that even basic optimality results for AIXI require strong realizability/computability assumptions on the environment, and the question of separating irrelevant non-computable inputs from relevant signals does not appear to have been resolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: Can the 'prediction with expert advice' paradigm be extended from passive prediction and active learning to the full reinforcement-learning setting in a way that produces a viable alternative or dual to AIXI, or does the failure of such an extension instead show that AIXI occupies a distinguished position?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. In the prediction-with-expert-advice (PEA) framework, a learner observes, at each round t = 1, 2, ..., the predictions of a (finite or countable) class E of experts, issues its own prediction, and then receives an outcome and incurs a bounded loss. Classical results provide regret bounds of the form L_T(learner) − inf_{e ∈ E} L_T(e) = o(T) (e.g., O(√(T log |E|))), so that the learner competes with the best expert in hindsight without any probabilistic assumption on the outcome sequence. PEA has been generalized to the active-learning setting, where the learner additionally chooses queries that influence which information is revealed but not the outcomes themselves.

Reinforcement-learning setting. Consider a general (history-based, possibly non-Markovian) reinforcement-learning interaction between an agent and an unknown environment: at each time t the agent selects an action a_t ∈ A, the environment returns an observation o_t ∈ O and a bounded reward r_t ∈ [0, 1], where the environment is an arbitrary computable (or merely measurable) function from interaction histories to distributions over (o_t, r_t). Let Π be a given countable class of "expert" policies π : (A × O × R)^* → A. The agent's cumulative reward up to horizon T is V_T(agent) = Σ_{t=1}^T r_t.

Question. Does there exist an agent (a single policy, possibly randomized and history-dependent) that, for every environment in a sufficiently rich class (e.g., the class of all lower-semicomputable environments, or all stochastic environments) and for every countable expert class Π, achieves a sublinear regret guarantee of the form

   sup_{π ∈ Π} E[V_T(π)] − E[V_T(agent)] = o(T) as T → ∞,

where the expectations are taken in the true environment with the agent (resp. expert π) controlling the actions? Equivalently, can the PEA paradigm be lifted from passive prediction and active learning to the full reinforcement-learning case so as to yield a universal "experts-style" agent dual to AIXI? Or, alternatively, prove an impossibility result showing that no such agent exists for any sufficiently expressive expert class, thereby exhibiting a distinguished status for the Bayes-optimal AIXI construction.
status_search_result: The question of extending prediction-with-expert-advice to the full reinforcement-learning setting (with a regret guarantee against an arbitrary policy class in arbitrary environments) is widely cited as an open problem in the universal-AI literature. The PEA paradigm has been extended to active learning, but no general PEA-style agent for the full RL case dual to AIXI has been established, and no definitive impossibility theorem singling out AIXI has been proved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: How does the intelligence order relation compare, both theoretically and on restricted problem classes, to conventional IQ tests and other intelligence or performance measures, and does narrowing the order relation to specific classes of environments reveal principled connections between apparently different domain-specific performance metrics?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let an agent be a (possibly stochastic) policy π that, at each time step t = 1, 2, …, receives an observation o_t and reward r_t ∈ [0,1] from an environment μ and outputs an action a_t. An environment μ is a computable conditional probability measure over observation–reward sequences given action sequences. Let E denote a class of such environments, and for each μ ∈ E let

   V^π_μ := E_μ[ Σ_{t=1}^∞ γ_t · r_t ],

where (γ_t) is a fixed nonnegative summable discount sequence. For a chosen prior w : E → (0,1] with Σ_μ w(μ) ≤ 1, define the universal value

   Υ(π; E, w) := Σ_{μ ∈ E} w(μ) · V^π_μ.

The Intelligence Order Relation (IOR) on agents (relative to (E, w)) is the preorder

   π ⪰_{E,w} π'   ⇔   Υ(π; E, w) ≥ Υ(π'; E, w),

with strict version ≻_{E,w}. When E is the class of all lower-semicomputable chronological environments and w(μ) = 2^{-K(μ)} (Kolmogorov complexity prior), call ⪰_{E,w} the universal IOR.

Problem. Provide a rigorous comparative analysis of the IOR and other measures of agent performance:

(1) (General comparison.) Determine the formal relationship between the universal IOR ⪰_{E,w} and standard human-intelligence tests modeled as score functions S : Agents → ℝ (e.g., IQ-style batteries formalized as finite collections of task-environments with weighted scoring). Specifically, does there exist a choice of (E, w) such that ⪰_{E,w} agrees, up to a monotone transformation, with a given score function S on a prescribed class of agents? Characterize necessary and sufficient conditions on S for such an (E, w) to exist.

(2) (Restriction to subclasses.) For natural restricted environment classes E' ⊂ E — for instance, finite-state Markov decision processes, fully observable deterministic environments, sequence-prediction environments, ergodic environments, or bandit problems — identify the resulting restricted IOR ⪰_{E', w'} and prove whether it coincides with, refines, or is incomparable to the canonical performance metrics used for that class (e.g., expected cumulative regret for bandits, average reward for ergodic MDPs, log-loss for sequence prediction). In each case, exhibit either an equivalence theorem (the restricted IOR induces the same total preorder on agents as the standard metric) or a separation (a pair of agents ordered oppositely by the two preorders).

(3) (Principled unification.) Decide whether varying E' across a family of subclasses yields a principled hierarchy of performance measures, in the sense that the restricted IORs form a consistent refinement structure linking apparently different domain-specific metrics into a single framework, or whether obstructions (e.g., prior dependence, non-monotonicity under environment-class inclusion) prevent such a unification.

Goal: produce theorems that either (a) establish concrete equivalences/refinements between the (restricted) IOR and existing intelligence/performance measures, or (b) demonstrate provable incompatibilities.
category_tag: Universal artificial intelligence / agent performance measures
status_search_result: The comparison between the Intelligence Order Relation (universal intelligence measure of Legg–Hutter) and conventional IQ tests or other domain-specific performance measures remains an active research direction; subsequent work (e.g., Hernández-Orallo and collaborators on anytime universal intelligence tests, and Hutter's later surveys) discusses partial connections but does not provide a definitive equivalence theorem. No publication appears to fully resolve the formal comparison or principled unification questions.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: Once a computable version of the intelligence order relation is available, what experimental behavior does it exhibit across different problem spaces, does it correlate with human IQ test scores, and in restricted domains such as classification or sequence prediction does it rank algorithms in a way that agrees with standard performance measures and observed real-world performance?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $\mathcal{E}$ denote a class of computable reward-summable environments $\mu:(\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{R})^{*}\to[0,1]$ with rewards in $[0,1]$ and bounded total reward, and let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the class of (possibly stochastic) agents $\pi:(\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{R})^{*}\to\mathcal{A}$. For an agent $\pi$ interacting with an environment $\mu$, let $V^{\pi}_{\mu}\in[0,1]$ denote the expected total discounted reward. Fix a universal prefix Turing machine $U$ and let $K(\mu)$ denote the prefix Kolmogorov complexity of $\mu$. The Legg–Hutter intelligence order relation is the partial preorder on $\mathcal{A}$ defined by
$$\pi_1 \succeq \pi_2 \iff \forall \mu\in\mathcal{E}:\ V^{\pi_1}_{\mu}\ \ge\ V^{\pi_2}_{\mu},$$
and the universal intelligence of $\pi$ is
$$\Upsilon(\pi) = \sum_{\mu\in\mathcal{E}} 2^{-K(\mu)} V^{\pi}_{\mu}.$$
Both $\succeq$ and $\Upsilon$ are uncomputable in general.

Problem. Construct an explicit computable approximation $\widehat{\Upsilon}$ (equivalently a computable surrogate $\widehat{\succeq}$ of the intelligence order relation), e.g. by restricting $\mathcal{E}$ to a time/space-bounded sub-class of computable environments and replacing $K$ with a resource-bounded complexity measure, and then establish the following:

(a) Prove convergence/consistency: as the resource bound tends to infinity, $\widehat{\Upsilon}\to\Upsilon$ pointwise on a meaningful subclass of agents, and characterize the rate of convergence.

(b) Empirically (or via probabilistic analysis on a specified random model of test instances) determine the distribution of $\widehat{\Upsilon}(\pi)$ across natural agent families and problem spaces, and decide whether $\widehat{\Upsilon}$, when applied to models of human subjects on inductive-inference test batteries (such as C-Test–style sequence-completion problems), produces a quantity that is significantly correlated with measured IQ scores.

(c) For the restricted domains of (i) supervised classification with a fixed loss $\ell$ and (ii) deterministic sequence prediction with log-loss, prove or disprove that the ordering induced by $\widehat{\succeq}$ on standard algorithm classes (e.g., $k$-NN, decision trees, SVMs, neural networks; Laplace/Krichevsky–Trofimov/CTW/LZ-based predictors) coincides, up to ties, with the ordering induced by classical risk or per-symbol redundancy on natural benchmark distributions.

State and resolve each of (a), (b), (c).
status_search_result: The problem of defining a computable approximation of the Legg–Hutter intelligence order relation and experimentally validating it (correlation with human IQ-style tests, agreement with standard performance measures on classification/sequence prediction) remains an open research program. While related work exists on AIXI approximations (e.g., MC-AIXI-CTW), Hernández-Orallo's anytime universal intelligence tests, and the C-Test, no published result establishes the full experimental characterization requested. No definitive resolution was found.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Cosmological origin of the thermodynamic arrow
original_question: What is the cosmological origin of the universal thermodynamic arrow of time? In particular, should the present arrow be explained by a special low-entropy condition at the big bang, by a Boltzmann-style giant fluctuation in an eternal universe, or by some other mechanism; and if the low-entropy condition is tied to the big bang, how can one understand the consequences for oscillating-universe models, where the thermodynamic arrow would otherwise have to reverse direction?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a universe modeled by a time-symmetric fundamental dynamics (for instance, a Hamiltonian or unitary evolution on a phase space or Hilbert space) together with a coarse-graining that defines a Boltzmann-type entropy S(t). Empirically, S(t) is observed to increase monotonically in one temporal direction, defining a universal thermodynamic arrow of time.

Provide a cosmological account of the origin of this arrow by addressing the following:

(a) Determine whether the observed monotonic increase of S(t) can be explained by postulating a special low-entropy boundary condition at the big bang (a "past hypothesis"), and formulate precisely what such a condition must require of the initial macrostate so that typical microstates compatible with it evolve toward higher-entropy macrostates.

(b) Evaluate the alternative hypothesis, due to Boltzmann, that the universe is eternal and in global thermal equilibrium, and that the present low-entropy state is a giant statistical fluctuation. Show, using the relative measures of fluctuations of given size in an equilibrium ensemble, whether or not this hypothesis is consistent with the observation that the present state of the universe is not the smallest fluctuation compatible with current memories and records (the "Boltzmann brain" / typicality problem).

(c) Assuming the low-entropy condition is attached to the big bang, analyze the consequences for a recollapsing or oscillating cosmological model. In particular, decide whether the thermodynamic arrow must reverse during the contracting phase, and reconcile this with the dynamical requirement that causally connected regions of the universe cannot simultaneously support oppositely directed thermodynamic arrows.

(d) If neither (a) nor (b) is satisfactory, propose an alternative mechanism (for example, based on quantum cosmology, decoherence, or a dynamical selection principle) that derives the universal thermodynamic arrow from the underlying time-symmetric laws together with cosmological structure, and verify its compatibility with the constraints in (c).
category_tag: arrow of time and cosmological initial conditions
status_search_result: The cosmological origin of the thermodynamic arrow of time remains an open foundational problem. Recent reviews and research (e.g., works by Carroll, Wallace, Goldstein–Tumulka, Albert, and others through the 2020s) continue to debate the past hypothesis, Boltzmann-fluctuation scenarios (now pressured by the Boltzmann-brain problem), and quantum-cosmological alternatives, with no consensus resolution.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
original_question: Why do electromagnetic absorbers, and more generally physical absorptive processes, pick out only one temporal direction? In the case of retarded versus advanced Maxwell fields, if absorbers and thermalization can account for retarded shadows and the absence of incoming high-frequency radiation, what explains the fact that all absorbers absorb in the same time direction rather than admitting the time-reversed alternative with advanced correlations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider classical electrodynamics governed by the time-symmetric Maxwell equations, which admit, for any prescribed source current, both retarded Green-function solutions (in which the field at a spacetime point depends on the source on its past light cone) and advanced Green-function solutions (in which the field depends on the source on its future light cone). Empirically, all observed macroscopic radiation phenomena are described by purely retarded fields: emitters cast "retarded shadows" on absorbers in their causal future, and there is a generic absence of incoming, coherently focused high-frequency radiation that would correspond to advanced correlations.

A standard partial explanation invokes absorbers (matter, including the radiation-dominated early universe) which thermalize incoming coherent radiation and thereby suppress advanced-type correlations. However, this explanation presupposes that absorbers act in a single, common temporal direction.

Provide a derivation, from time-symmetric microscopic dynamics together with admissible cosmological/boundary conditions, of the following fact: every physical absorber in the observable universe absorbs in one and the same direction of time, rather than the time-reversed alternative in which absorption (equivalently, anti-thermalization producing advanced coherent outgoing radiation) occurs in the opposite temporal direction. In particular, identify the structural ingredient — be it an initial low-entropy condition, a cosmological boundary condition, a statistical-mechanical principle, or otherwise — that selects a single global absorptive arrow of time and explain why this selection is "probable" (typical) rather than requiring a fine-tuned hypothesis comparable to a special low-entropy initial micro-state.
category_tag: Arrow of time and absorber theory
status_search_result: The question of why all absorbers act in the same temporal direction is a long-standing foundational problem connected to Wheeler-Feynman absorber theory and the cosmological arrow of time. Recent literature (2020s philosophy-of-physics and arXiv preprints, including discussions of time-symmetric quantum mechanics and generalized absorber theory) continues to debate the issue, with no consensus derivation from time-symmetric dynamics alone; explanations typically invoke either a special cosmological boundary condition or a thermodynamic/low-entropy past hypothesis, both of which remain contested.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Initial homogeneity and the Weyl tensor condition
original_question: Is the relevant low-entropy condition of the early universe best understood as primordial homogeneity, as Penrose’s vanishing-Weyl-tensor condition on past singularities, or as some closely related condition; and if the Weyl condition cannot be explained by absorptive matter in the way electromagnetic retardation can, must it instead be taken as the law-like ingredient that establishes the causal asymmetry of the universe by excluding future-relevant initial correlations?
self_contained_problem:
In general relativity, the thermodynamic arrow of time is widely associated with a very low-entropy condition imposed on the early universe. Two natural candidates for this condition are:

(a) Primordial homogeneity: the spatial geometry and matter distribution near the initial cosmological singularity are highly homogeneous and isotropic.

(b) The Weyl curvature condition: on every past singularity of spacetime, the Weyl conformal curvature tensor C_{abcd} of the Lorentzian metric vanishes (or is suitably bounded), while the Ricci part of the curvature, governed by the Einstein equations and the matter content, is unconstrained.

By contrast, the well-known explanation of the retardation asymmetry of classical electromagnetism — that physically realized solutions of Maxwell's equations are retarded rather than advanced — can be derived from the assumption that matter is sufficiently absorptive in the future, so that no incoming free radiation field is present.

Address the following:

1. Determine whether the appropriate low-entropy initial condition that selects the observed thermodynamic arrow of time in a general-relativistic universe is best formulated as primordial homogeneity, as the vanishing-Weyl-tensor condition on past singularities, or as some closely related geometric condition; in particular, give a precise mathematical formulation of the chosen condition and prove that it implies a monotonic increase of a suitable coarse-grained entropy along the cosmological time direction.

2. Show whether the Weyl condition can or cannot be derived, in analogy with electromagnetic retardation, from an assumption of "absorption" by the gravitational matter content in the future (e.g., from a future boundary condition on gravitational degrees of freedom together with the Einstein equations).

3. If no such derivation is possible, prove that the condition must instead be imposed as an independent law-like postulate, and that this postulate is what excludes future-relevant initial correlations and thereby establishes the causal asymmetry of the universe.
status_search_result: The Weyl curvature hypothesis remains an open conjecture in mathematical cosmology. Penrose has continued to advocate it (e.g., in his Conformal Cyclic Cosmology proposal, 2010 onward), but no derivation from a future-absorption-style boundary condition is known, and no rigorous theorem links it to monotone entropy growth in full generality. Partial results exist for specific models (e.g., Tod's work on isotropic singularities and conformal extension across the Big Bang), but the overall question of which initial condition correctly captures the low-entropy past, and whether it must be law-like, is still actively debated.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Black holes, singularities, and information loss
original_question: In the quantum-gravitational treatment of black holes, should one impose a time-symmetric Weyl-tensor condition on all spacelike singularities, and would doing so eliminate genuine black-hole interiors, horizons, or information loss? Because the black-hole interior is causally inaccessible and quantum gravity no longer sharply distinguishes past from future singularities, the unresolved issue is whether a symmetric singularity condition is the correct way to understand black-hole entropy and avoid the information-loss paradox.
self_contained_problem:
In a quantum-gravitational treatment of gravitational collapse, consider Penrose's Weyl curvature hypothesis, which in its original form requires the Weyl conformal tensor C_{abcd} of the spacetime metric to vanish (or be suitably bounded) at past spacelike singularities, thereby selecting a low-entropy initial state and providing a geometric origin for the thermodynamic arrow of time. In a regime where quantum gravity is taken to remove any sharp distinction between past-type and future-type spacelike singularities, one is led to consider a time-symmetric variant of this hypothesis: impose the same Weyl-tensor vanishing condition on every spacelike singularity of the spacetime, regardless of its temporal orientation.

Determine whether the following can be established:

(a) Imposing such a time-symmetric Weyl-tensor condition on all spacelike singularities is consistent with the standard formulation of black-hole thermodynamics (in particular with the area law for black-hole entropy and with the generalized second law), and is compatible with all current observational constraints on gravitational collapse and cosmology.

(b) Under this condition, no causally disconnected black-hole interior region and no event horizon can form in any classical or semiclassical solution describing gravitational collapse; equivalently, the symmetric Weyl condition forces the global causal structure to lack a true black-hole region in the sense of Hawking and Ellis.

(c) Consequently, the information-loss paradox associated with evaporating black holes does not arise, because the would-be interior and horizon are excluded by (b).

Either prove (a)–(c) within a precise framework for semiclassical or quantum gravity, or exhibit an obstruction (for example a spacetime satisfying the symmetric Weyl condition that nevertheless contains a genuine event horizon and causally hidden interior).
category_tag: Weyl curvature hypothesis and black-hole singularities
status_search_result: The Weyl curvature hypothesis remains a conjectural proposal of Penrose, with no accepted proof or refutation. Recent work (e.g. 2025 preprints on conservative resolutions of the singularity problem, and Weyl-invariant dilaton-gravity models replacing singularities by baby universes) explores related time-symmetric scenarios, but no consensus exists on whether a symmetric Weyl condition prevents horizon/interior formation or resolves information loss. The question is therefore considered open.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Initial conditions for partial Schrödinger waves
original_question: Can the global intrinsic dynamics of the Wheeler-DeWitt framework determine the initial conditions of the partial Schrödinger waves that appear in the semiclassical WKB regime? Since the WKB approximation yields approximately autonomous matter-wave evolution along quasi-classical geometries but does not by itself justify an ensemble of trajectories, the unresolved problem is how the full, timeless quantum state fixes the initial data for the branch-dependent partial waves observed as evolving quasi-classical worlds.
self_contained_problem:
Consider canonical quantum gravity coupled to matter fields, formulated through the Wheeler–DeWitt constraint
\[ \hat{\mathcal{H}}\,\Psi[h_{ij},\phi] = 0, \]
where $\Psi$ is a timeless wave functional defined on superspace (the space of three-metrics $h_{ij}$ and matter configurations $\phi$). In the semiclassical (WKB) regime, one writes
\[ \Psi[h_{ij},\phi] \;\approx\; \sum_\alpha A_\alpha[h_{ij}]\,e^{i S_\alpha[h_{ij}]/\hbar}\,\chi_\alpha[h_{ij},\phi], \]
where each $S_\alpha$ satisfies the Hamilton–Jacobi equation of vacuum gravity, defining a congruence of quasi-classical geometries, and each "partial Schrödinger wave" $\chi_\alpha$ is shown to obey, to leading order in $\hbar$, an approximately autonomous Schrödinger-type evolution equation along the WKB time parameter associated with $S_\alpha$.

Because the WKB ansatz preserves the global superposition of all branches $\alpha$, it does not by itself select an ensemble of trajectories nor prescribe initial data for the individual matter wave functions $\chi_\alpha$.

Problem. Determine whether the global intrinsic dynamics encoded in the full Wheeler–DeWitt state $\Psi$ (together with whatever boundary or regularity conditions are imposed on it, e.g.\ in the neighborhood of the classical singularity) uniquely fixes the initial conditions of each partial Schrödinger wave $\chi_\alpha$ to be used in the WKB region of superspace far from the big bang. Concretely: provide a derivation, from the timeless equation $\hat{\mathcal{H}}\Psi=0$ alone, of the initial data $\chi_\alpha\big|_{\Sigma_0}$ on a spacelike slice $\Sigma_0$ in each WKB branch, or prove that no such derivation is possible without additional structure.
status_search_result: Searches on the Wheeler–DeWitt equation and its WKB / Born–Oppenheimer semiclassical expansion (including work extending the expansion to arbitrary orders and addressing unitarity) show that while the leading-order emergence of Schrödinger-type evolution along WKB branches is well established, there is no widely accepted derivation of the initial data for the branch-dependent partial waves directly from the timeless Wheeler–DeWitt state. The question of how (or whether) the global quantum gravity state fixes these branch initial conditions remains a foundational open problem connected with proposals such as Hartle–Hawking and tunneling boundary conditions.

original_question: Does there exist a 2-knot group with unsolvable word problem? Here K_2 is the class of groups of 2-knots, so the question asks whether some group of a 2-knot has no algorithm deciding, for an arbitrary word in its generators, whether that word represents the identity element.
self_contained_problem:
An n-knot is a smooth (or locally flat topological) embedding of the n-sphere S^n into the (n+2)-sphere S^{n+2}, considered up to ambient isotopy. The group of an n-knot K is the fundamental group π_1(S^{n+2} \ K) of the complement. A finitely generated group G is said to have solvable word problem if there exists an algorithm which, given any finite word w in a fixed finite set of generators (and their inverses), decides whether w represents the identity element of G; otherwise the word problem is unsolvable.

Question: Does there exist a 2-knot K ⊂ S^4 whose knot group π_1(S^4 \ K) has unsolvable word problem?
category_tag: High-dimensional knot groups and decision problems
status_search_result: The question of whether some 2-knot group has unsolvable word problem appears to remain open. While it is known that there exist 3-knot groups with unsolvable word problem (e.g., universal 3-knot groups containing every finitely presented group), no such construction is known for 2-knots, and the problem is stated as a conjecture (expected answer: yes) in the literature on higher-dimensional knot groups.

context_brief: TV convergence in stationary ergodic G/G/m FCFS
original_question: Consider the multi-server first-come-first-served queue G/G/m with interarrival times {(t_n)} and service times {(sigma_n)} such that the two-dimensional sequence {(sigma_n, t_n)} is stationary ergodic, the stability condition E sigma_1 < m E t_1 holds, and the Kiefer-Wolfowitz workload vector starts from the zero initial value. Is it true that, under these assumptions alone and without any further mixing or regenerative condition, the distribution of the workload vector converges in total variation to a stationary distribution as n tends to infinity?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a first-come-first-served queue with $m\ge 1$ identical parallel servers. Customers are indexed by $n\in\mathbb{Z}$; customer $n$ arrives at time $T_n=\sum_{k<n} t_k$, where $t_n>0$ is the interarrival time between customers $n$ and $n+1$, and requires service time $\sigma_n>0$. Assume the bivariate sequence $\{(\sigma_n,t_n)\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}$ is stationary and ergodic on some probability space, with $\mathbb{E}\sigma_1<\infty$, $\mathbb{E}t_1<\infty$, and the stability condition
$$\mathbb{E}\sigma_1 < m\,\mathbb{E}t_1.$$
Let $W_n=(W_n^{(1)},\dots,W_n^{(m)})\in\mathbb{R}_+^m$ denote the Kiefer–Wolfowitz workload vector at the arrival epoch of customer $n$, with components arranged in non-decreasing order. It satisfies the recursion
$$W_{n+1}=R\bigl((W_n+\sigma_n e_1 - t_n \mathbf{1})^+\bigr),$$
where $e_1=(1,0,\dots,0)$, $\mathbf{1}=(1,1,\dots,1)$, $(\cdot)^+$ is componentwise positive part, and $R$ reorders coordinates in non-decreasing order. Assume the initial condition $W_0=0$.

Under the stability condition there exists a stationary distribution $\pi$ on $\mathbb{R}_+^m$ to which the workload vector converges weakly along the Loynes construction. Question: is it always true, under only the assumptions above (stationarity and ergodicity of $\{(\sigma_n,t_n)\}$, the stability condition, and $W_0=0$), and without imposing any additional mixing, regenerative, or independence assumption, that
$$\sup_{A\subset \mathbb{R}_+^m}\bigl|\mathbb{P}(W_n\in A)-\pi(A)\bigr|\;\longrightarrow\;0\qquad\text{as }n\to\infty,$$
that is, the law of $W_n$ converges to $\pi$ in total variation?
status_search_result: Searches for follow-up work resolving this conjecture (TV-convergence of the Kiefer–Wolfowitz workload vector in stationary ergodic G/G/m FCFS queues without further mixing assumptions) did not surface a definitive resolution. Related results address convergence under additional mixing or regenerative structure, but a confirmation or refutation of the conjecture in full generality could not be verified from the available sources.

context_brief: Tail asymptotics for two-server queue at rho=1
original_question: In the two-server queue case m = 2 with stationary waiting time D, when the load satisfies rho = 1 and the service-time distribution is subexponential (for example regularly varying), what is the asymptotic behavior of P(D > x) as x becomes large?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a FCFS queueing system with $m=2$ identical servers fed by a single renewal arrival stream with i.i.d. interarrival times $\{T_n\}_{n\geq 1}$ having mean $1/\lambda \in (0,\infty)$, and i.i.d. service times $\{S_n\}_{n\geq 1}$ (independent of $\{T_n\}$) with common distribution $B$ having finite mean $\mathbb{E}S_1 = 1/\mu$. Define the traffic intensity $\rho = \lambda/(m\mu) = \lambda/(2\mu)$, and assume the system admits a stationary waiting-time distribution; let $D$ denote the stationary waiting time of a typical customer (the time the customer spends in the queue before service begins).

Assume the service-time distribution $B$ is subexponential, meaning $\overline{B}(x):=1-B(x)>0$ for all $x$ and $\overline{B^{*2}}(x)/\overline{B}(x)\to 2$ as $x\to\infty$, where $B^{*2}$ is the two-fold convolution of $B$. As a representative concrete subclass, one may take $B$ regularly varying at infinity, i.e. $\overline{B}(x) = x^{-\alpha} L(x)$ for some $\alpha>1$ and slowly varying $L$.

Consider the critical-load case $\rho=1$. Determine the asymptotic behavior of $\mathbb{P}(D > x)$ as $x \to \infty$, and identify the typical sample path leading to a large value of the stationary waiting time $D$. In particular, provide explicit asymptotics in the case where $B$ is regularly varying.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has addressed the critical (half-loaded) GI/GI/2 case with regularly varying service times. Notably, Blanchet–Chen–Lam (2015, Queueing Systems) "Tail Asymptotics for Delay in a Half-loaded GI/GI/2 Queue with Heavy-tailed Job Sizes" provides asymptotic bounds and identifies two qualitative regimes (finite vs. infinite variance) for the tail of $\mathbb{P}(D>x)$, identifying typical-path behavior (one extremely big job vs. two moderately big jobs). The bounds are tight up to slowly varying factors in the finite-variance regime, while sharp asymptotics with explicit constants for general subexponential $B$ at $\rho=1$ remain incomplete; the broader subexponential (non–regularly varying) case at $\rho=1$ is largely unresolved.
