paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Visibility Graphs of Points, Segments and Polygons
context_brief: Hamiltonian circuits in embedded segment visibility graphs
original_question: Does every segment visibility graph contain a Hamiltonian cycle that becomes a non-self-intersecting Hamiltonian circuit in the embedded segment visibility graph?
self_contained_problem:
Let S = {s_1, …, s_n} be a finite set of pairwise disjoint closed line segments in the plane in general position (no three endpoints collinear). The segment visibility graph G(S) is the graph whose vertex set consists of the 2n endpoints of the segments of S, and whose edges are: (i) the n segments of S themselves, and (ii) all pairs of endpoints {p, q} (belonging to possibly different segments) such that the open segment pq does not cross any segment of S, i.e. p and q are mutually visible. The embedded segment visibility graph G'(S) is the straight-line drawing of G(S) in which every vertex is placed at its corresponding endpoint and every edge is drawn as the straight-line segment between its endpoints.

A Hamiltonian cycle of G(S) is called non-self-intersecting (in the embedding) if, when its edges are drawn as straight-line segments in G'(S), no two of those edges cross.

Prove or disprove: For every such finite set S of pairwise disjoint segments in general position, the segment visibility graph G(S) admits a Hamiltonian cycle that is non-self-intersecting in the embedded graph G'(S).
status_search_result: The conjecture was resolved affirmatively by Hoffmann and Tóth, who proved that every segment visibility graph contains a non-crossing Hamiltonian cycle in its straight-line embedding, and gave an O(n log n) algorithm to construct it (building on results of Bose, Houle, and Toussaint on disjoint-compatible geometric matchings/spanning structures).

context_brief: Alternating paths in embedded segment visibility graphs
original_question: In the embedded segment visibility graph G′ of a set S of n disjoint segments, is there always an alternating path containing at least O(log n) segments of S?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S = \{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\}$ be a set of $n$ pairwise disjoint closed line segments in the plane (in general position, with no three endpoints collinear). The embedded segment visibility graph $G'$ of $S$ is defined as follows: its vertex set consists of the $2n$ endpoints of the segments in $S$; its edge set contains (i) every segment $s_i \in S$ (called a segment edge), and (ii) every visibility edge $pq$, where $p$ and $q$ are endpoints of two distinct segments such that the open line segment between $p$ and $q$ does not intersect any segment of $S$. An alternating path in $G'$ is a simple path that alternates between segment edges and visibility edges.

Prove or disprove: there is a constant $c > 0$ such that for every set $S$ of $n$ pairwise disjoint segments in general position, the embedded segment visibility graph $G'$ contains an alternating path that uses at least $c \log n$ segment edges of $S$.

paper_title: Recent developments and open problems in linear series
original_question: Let S be a finite set of points in P^N. Suppose there exists m such that a(S,m)/m = (a(S,1)+N-1)/N, where a(S,m) is the least degree of a divisor vanishing to order at least m on S. Must S then either lie in a hyperplane or be a star configuration? More generally, if the Waldschmidt constant satisfies e(S) = (a(S,1)+N-1)/N, must the same conclusion hold?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S = \{P_1, \dots, P_s\}$ be a finite set of distinct points in projective space $\mathbb{P}^N$ over an algebraically closed field, where $N \geq 2$. For a positive integer $m$, define
$$\alpha(S,m) = \min\{\deg F : F \in k[x_0,\dots,x_N] \text{ is a nonzero homogeneous form vanishing to order} \geq m \text{ at every } P_i\}.$$
In particular $\alpha(S,1) = \alpha(S)$ is the least degree of a hypersurface through $S$. The Waldschmidt constant of $S$ is defined as
$$\widehat{\alpha}(S) = \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{\alpha(S,m)}{m} = \inf_{m \geq 1} \frac{\alpha(S,m)}{m}.$$
A star configuration of points in $\mathbb{P}^N$ is the set of all $\binom{d}{N}$ pairwise intersections of $N$ of $d$ given hyperplanes in $\mathbb{P}^N$ that meet properly (i.e., no $N+1$ of the hyperplanes share a common point and any $N$ meet in exactly one point), for some $d \geq N$.

It is known that
$$\frac{\alpha(S,m)}{m} \geq \widehat{\alpha}(S) \geq \frac{\alpha(S) + N - 1}{N}.$$

Question: 

(a) Suppose there exists a positive integer $m$ such that
$$\frac{\alpha(S,m)}{m} = \frac{\alpha(S) + N - 1}{N}.$$
Must $S$ either be contained in a hyperplane of $\mathbb{P}^N$, or be a star configuration?

(b) Suppose instead that
$$\widehat{\alpha}(S) = \frac{\alpha(S) + N - 1}{N}.$$
Must the same conclusion hold; that is, is $S$ necessarily contained in a hyperplane or a star configuration?
status_search_result: No published resolution of this characterization-of-equality problem was located. Recent work (e.g., on Chudnovsky-type bounds, symbolic defects of star configurations, and the containment problem) continues to study related lower bounds and equality cases without settling the conjectured dichotomy. The problem appears to remain open.

context_brief: Cohomology of monomial subschemes on surfaces
original_question: With the same notation, let Y be a general subscheme of a smooth projective surface S corresponding to a monomial ideal I, and let D be a divisor on S. Find conditions on S, I, and D that determine or constrain the cohomology of I_Y ⊗ O_S(D), ideally giving criteria that force h^0(I_Y ⊗ O_S(D)) = max{0, h^0(O_S(D)) - n}.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a smooth complex projective surface and let $I \subset \mathcal{O}_S$ be a sheaf of ideals defined locally as a monomial ideal: at each point $p$ of its support, after a choice of local coordinates $(x,y)$ on $S$, the stalk $I_p$ is generated by monomials $x^a y^b$. Let $Y \subset S$ denote a general subscheme corresponding to such a monomial ideal $I$ (i.e. $Y$ is the zero-dimensional or one-dimensional scheme cut out by $I$ at a general configuration of points of $S$), and write $n = h^0(\mathcal{O}_S/\mathcal{I}_Y) = \operatorname{length}(\mathcal{O}_Y)$ when $Y$ is zero-dimensional (more generally $n$ denotes the appropriate "number of conditions" imposed by $Y$). For a divisor $D$ on $S$ with associated line bundle $\mathcal{O}_S(D)$, consider the twisted ideal sheaf cohomology
$$ h^0(S, \mathcal{I}_Y \otimes \mathcal{O}_S(D)). $$

The naive (expected) value of this quantity, assuming $Y$ imposes independent conditions on $|D|$, is
$$ \max\{0,\; h^0(S, \mathcal{O}_S(D)) - n\}. $$

Problem. Determine geometric or numerical conditions on the triple $(S, I, D)$ that control $h^0(S, \mathcal{I}_Y \otimes \mathcal{O}_S(D))$. In particular, find sufficient conditions on $S$, on the monomial ideal $I$ (e.g. on its Newton diagram / generators), and on $D$ (e.g. positivity, intersection-theoretic, or numerical conditions) which guarantee
$$ h^0(S, \mathcal{I}_Y \otimes \mathcal{O}_S(D)) \;=\; \max\{0,\; h^0(S, \mathcal{O}_S(D)) - n\}, $$
and more generally describe or conjecturally describe the higher cohomology $h^i(S, \mathcal{I}_Y \otimes \mathcal{O}_S(D))$.

status_search_result: The problem is posed as a general open question about the cohomology of ideal sheaves of general monomial subschemes on surfaces, generalizing classical interpolation/Nagata-type problems. While many partial results exist for specific cases (e.g., fat points, ordinary multiple points on $\mathbb{P}^2$ via the SHGH conjecture, and Harbourne-type conjectures), no general criterion forcing the expected value $h^0 = \max\{0, h^0(\mathcal{O}_S(D)) - n\}$ for arbitrary monomial ideals on arbitrary smooth projective surfaces appears to be known. The problem remains open.

original_question: Let X be a projective manifold with large algebraic fundamental group and let L be an ample line bundle on X. Given a positive number N, does there exist a finite étale cover p: X'→X such that either (1) the Seshadri number of p^*L at every point of X' is greater than N, or (2) the Seshadri number of p_e^*(p_1^*L \otimes p_2^*L) along the diagonal in X'	imes X' is greater than N? If not in general, what condition on the fundamental group of X guarantees such a positive answer?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective variety, and let $L$ be an ample line bundle on $X$. Recall that the Seshadri constant of $L$ at a point $x \in X$ is
$$\varepsilon(L;x) = \inf_{C \ni x} \frac{L \cdot C}{\mathrm{mult}_x C},$$
where the infimum is over irreducible curves $C \subset X$ passing through $x$. For a closed subvariety $D \subset X$, the Seshadri constant of $L$ along $D$ is defined analogously using multiplicity along $D$. Say that $X$ has large algebraic fundamental group if for every positive-dimensional closed irreducible subvariety $Z \subset X$ with normalization $\tilde Z \to Z$, the image of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{alg}}(\tilde Z) \to \pi_1^{\mathrm{alg}}(X)$ is infinite.

Assume $X$ has large algebraic fundamental group, and fix a real number $N > 0$. Let $p_1, p_2 : X \times X \to X$ be the two projections, and for a finite étale cover $p_e : Y \to X \times X$ let $\Delta_Y \subset Y$ denote the preimage of the diagonal $\Delta \subset X \times X$.

(1) Does there exist a finite étale cover $p : X' \to X$ such that $\varepsilon(p^*L; x') > N$ for every $x' \in X'$?

(2) Does there exist a finite étale cover $p_e : Y \to X \times X$ such that the Seshadri constant of $p_e^*(p_1^*L \otimes p_2^*L)$ along $\Delta_Y$ is greater than $N$?

(3) If neither (1) nor (2) holds in this generality, identify a condition on $\pi_1(X)$ (e.g.\ residual finiteness) that guarantees an affirmative answer.
status_search_result: Part (1) of the problem (originally a conjecture of J.-M. Hwang) was answered affirmatively by G. and L. F. Di Cerbo (arXiv:1411.1033, 2014): if $X$ has large algebraic fundamental group and $L$ is ample, then for any $N>0$ there is a finite étale cover $p:X'\to X$ with $\varepsilon(p^*L;x)\geq N$ at every point. They also proved an analogous statement for big and nef $L$ assuming $\pi_1(X)$ is large and residually finite. The diagonal version (2) and the precise optimal hypothesis on $\pi_1(X)$ in (3) do not appear to have been completely settled.

paper_title: Recent developments and open problems in linear series
original_question: Let (R,m) be a regular local ring of dimension n and let I⊂R be an ideal of big height e. Determine whether the strengthened symbolic-power containments listed in Problem 2.8.2 hold, namely whether I^(m) is contained in m^{rn-r}I^r for m≥rn, in m^{rn-r-(n-1)}I^r for m≥ rn-(n-1), in m^{re-r}I^r for m≥re, and in m^{re-r-(e-1)}I^r for m≥ re-(e-1).
status_search_result: These strengthened containments refine the Harbourne–Huneke type conjectures on symbolic powers in regular local rings. The basic containments $I^{(hr)} \subseteq I^r$ and $I^{(hr-h+1)} \subseteq I^r$ (Harbourne's conjecture) are known to fail in general (counterexamples exist), but stable versions and the further-strengthened forms with extra factors $\mathfrak{m}^{rn-r}$ or $\mathfrak{m}^{re-r}$ remain active research topics. Recent surveys (Grifo 2018/2019; Grifo–Huneke and follow-ups including the "stable Harbourne–Huneke" results) treat these as open problems in general, with progress in special cases (monomial ideals, F-pure rings, certain configurations of points, space monomial curves), but no full resolution.

paper_title: Recent developments and open problems in linear series
original_question: Let f:Y→B be a morphism from a smooth projective threefold to a smooth curve whose general fiber is a smooth surface. Fix an integer g>0. Is there a constant b(Y,g) such that every vertical curve C contained in a fiber, with geometric genus g, satisfies C^2 ≥ -b(Y,g), where self-intersection is computed inside the fiber containing C?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f: Y \to B$ be a surjective morphism from a smooth complex projective threefold $Y$ to a smooth projective curve $B$ such that the general fiber of $f$ is a smooth projective surface. Fix an integer $g > 0$. For a vertical curve $C \subset Y$ (i.e., an irreducible curve contained in some fiber $F = f^{-1}(b)$, $b \in B$) of geometric genus $g$, let $C^2$ denote the self-intersection of $C$ computed inside the (possibly singular or non-reduced) surface fiber $F$ containing it.

Question: Does there exist a constant $b(Y, g)$, depending only on $Y$ and $g$, such that
$$C^2 \geq -b(Y, g)$$
for every vertical curve $C \subset Y$ of geometric genus $g$?
status_search_result: The bounded negativity conjecture, even for a single complex projective surface, remains open in general (known only in special cases such as surfaces with anticanonical Kodaira dimension ≥ 0 and some other settings). The fibered/family version asking for a uniform bound $b(Y,g)$ across all surface fibers of a threefold fibration is a strengthening that does not appear to have been resolved; recent literature on bounded negativity, Harbourne constants, and weighted variants treats it as an outstanding problem.

paper_title: Recent developments and open problems in linear series
original_question: Let X be the blow-up of P^2 at r general points, let D be an effective divisor on X, and let E be a (-1)-curve. For the restriction map from the complete linear system |D| to |D|_E|, must all base points in the image come from a fixed base curve of |D|, and, if |D| has no fixed component, must the restriction map have maximal rank?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be the blow-up of the projective plane $\mathbb{P}^2$ at $r$ general points, let $D$ be an effective divisor on $X$, and let $E \subset X$ be a $(-1)$-curve (a smooth rational curve with self-intersection $-1$). Consider the complete linear system $|D|$ on $X$ and the restriction map
$$\rho \colon |D| \longrightarrow |D|_E|,$$
where $|D|_E|$ denotes the linear system on $E$ cut out by $|D|$. Prove or disprove the following two statements:

(1) Every base point of the image linear system $\rho(|D|) \subseteq |D|_E|$ on $E$ arises from a fixed base curve of $|D|$ on $X$ (i.e., it is the image on $E$ of a base curve component of $|D|$).

(2) If $|D|$ has no fixed component, then $\rho$ has maximal rank, meaning that $\rho$ is either injective or surjective as a linear map of vector spaces.
category_tag: linear systems on blow-ups of P^2
status_search_result: The conjecture is part of the circle of problems around the SHGH conjecture on linear systems on blow-ups of $\mathbb{P}^2$ at general points. No proof of this restriction-map statement (in full generality, for arbitrary effective $D$ and $(-1)$-curves $E$) appears in the literature; it is stated as a conjecture in surveys on linear series and remains open as far as accessible sources indicate.

paper_title: Recent developments and open problems in linear series
original_question: Let X be a smooth projective surface in characteristic zero. Does there exist a constant b(X) such that every reduced irreducible curve C on X satisfies C^2 ≥ -b(X)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. A curve $C \subset X$ is called reduced and irreducible if its defining ideal sheaf is prime and has no embedded components. The self-intersection number $C^2 \in \mathbb{Z}$ is defined via the intersection pairing on the Néron–Severi group of $X$.

Prove or disprove: there exists a real constant $b(X) \ge 0$, depending only on $X$, such that
$$C^2 \;\ge\; -\,b(X)$$
for every reduced and irreducible curve $C \subset X$.
status_search_result: The Bounded Negativity Conjecture for smooth complex projective surfaces is a long-standing open problem, traceable back roughly a century. Recent work (2014–2025) addresses only special cases, weighted/weak variants, or particular surface classes (e.g., blow-ups, Fermat surfaces, line arrangements). A weak version has been established, but the full conjecture in characteristic zero remains open. It is known to fail in positive characteristic.

paper_title: Recent developments and open problems in linear series
context_brief: Very weak bounded negativity for smooth curves
original_question: Let X be a smooth projective surface in characteristic zero and let g>0. Does there exist a constant b_s(X,g) such that every smooth irreducible curve of geometric genus g on X satisfies C^2 ≥ -b_s(X,g)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and let $g > 0$ be an integer. Does there exist a positive constant $b_s(X,g)$, depending only on $X$ and $g$, such that for every smooth irreducible curve $C \subset X$ of geometric genus exactly $g$, the self-intersection number satisfies
$$C^2 \geq -\,b_s(X,g)\,?$$
status_search_result: This "very weak bounded negativity" statement is implied by the Weak Bounded Negativity Conjecture, which asserts a lower bound on self-intersection for reduced curves whose components have geometric genus bounded by g. A complete proof of the weak version (in characteristic zero) was given by X. Hao (arXiv:1708.09463), and further variations have been studied by Ciliberto–Fontanari and others. In particular, the bound for smooth irreducible curves of geometric genus g follows from these results, so the statement is established. (The full Bounded Negativity Conjecture, allowing arbitrary genus, remains open.)

paper_title: Observational properties of diffuse radio sources in Galaxy Clusters: Current knowledge and open questions
original_question: Do galaxy clusters that host ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos, meaning radio halos with GHz-frequency synchrotron spectral index around α ∼ 2 under the convention S ∝ ν^-α, have basic differences from galaxy clusters that host “classical” radio halos with typical spectral-index values around 1.2–1.4?
self_contained_problem:
Consider galaxy clusters that host diffuse, Mpc-scale, cluster-wide synchrotron radio emission known as "radio halos." Adopt the convention that the integrated synchrotron flux density obeys S(ν) ∝ ν^{−α}, where α is the spectral index measured at GHz frequencies. Call a radio halo "classical" if its GHz spectral index lies in the typical range α ≈ 1.2–1.4, and call it "ultra-steep-spectrum" if α ≈ 2. 

Determine whether galaxy clusters hosting ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos differ in basic physical properties (such as merger energetics/dynamical state, mass, thermal X-ray characteristics, or intracluster-medium turbulence) from galaxy clusters hosting classical radio halos, and characterize any such differences. In particular, decide whether less energetic cluster mergers leave a distinctive observational signature in the radio band that distinguishes the host clusters of ultra-steep-spectrum halos from those of classical halos.
status_search_result: Subsequent observational and theoretical work supports that ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos tend to occur in less massive clusters undergoing less energetic mergers, are typically under-luminous for their mass, and are consistent with predictions of turbulent re-acceleration models (and disfavor purely hadronic origin). However, the sample of confirmed USSRHs remains small and a complete statistical characterization of the differences between USSRH-hosting and classical-halo-hosting clusters is still being assembled (e.g., LOFAR and MeerKAT surveys). The question is therefore partially resolved rather than fully settled.

paper_title: Observational properties of diffuse radio sources in Galaxy Clusters: Current knowledge and open questions
context_brief: Integrated spectra of halos and relics
original_question: For radio halos and relics in galaxy clusters, what are their well-defined integrated radio spectra from roughly hundred-MHz frequencies to GHz frequencies, and what do the spectral shapes and spectral-index values reveal about the underlying relativistic electron population and the re-acceleration processes that generate the diffuse emission?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the diffuse synchrotron radio emission observed in galaxy clusters, namely radio halos (Mpc-scale, centrally located, low-surface-brightness sources) and radio relics (elongated, peripheral sources associated with merger shocks). For such a source, the integrated radio flux density S(ν) as a function of frequency ν determines the integrated radio spectrum, often characterized by a (possibly frequency-dependent) spectral index α(ν) defined by S(ν) ∝ ν^α. The shape of this spectrum encodes information about the energy distribution N(E) of the underlying relativistic electron population and about in-situ (re-)acceleration mechanisms (e.g., turbulent reacceleration in the intracluster medium for halos, and diffusive shock acceleration at merger shocks for relics), competing against synchrotron and inverse-Compton energy losses.

Problem: For a representative sample of radio halos and radio relics in galaxy clusters, determine the integrated radio spectra S(ν) over the frequency range from approximately 100 MHz to several GHz with sufficient accuracy to characterize their detailed spectral shapes (pure power law, broken power law, high-frequency steepening/cutoff, low-frequency flattening, or curvature). Then, from the measured spectral shapes and spectral-index values:

(a) infer the energy distribution N(E) of the relativistic electrons producing the observed emission, including the location and form of any spectral break or cutoff; and

(b) discriminate among proposed origin mechanisms for the diffuse emission—in particular, secondary (hadronic) models versus primary turbulent re-acceleration models for halos, and diffusive shock (re-)acceleration scenarios for relics—by comparing the predicted spectral signatures of each mechanism with the observed integrated spectra.
category_tag: Galaxy cluster radio halos and relics
status_search_result: Since 2011 the number of halos and relics with integrated spectra spanning ~100 MHz to GHz has grown substantially through LOFAR, uGMRT, MeerKAT and JVLA observations, with curved/steepening spectra now confirmed in several halos (Coma, A3562, MACSJ0717, AS1063, El Gordo) and high-frequency steepening in many relics, broadly supporting turbulent re-acceleration for halos and DSA/re-acceleration at shocks for relics. However, the sample with well-defined integrated spectra remains limited, hadronic versus re-acceleration discrimination is not fully settled, and alternative mechanisms (e.g., magnetic reconnection from the fluctuation dynamo) are still being explored, so the broader question is partially solved.

paper_title: Observational properties of diffuse radio sources in Galaxy Clusters: Current knowledge and open questions
original_question: Which galaxy clusters contain both a firmly detected shock front and a radio relic with a clear spatial and physical connection, and does a larger sample of such systems support the view that relics are produced by merger-driven shocks with Mach numbers less than or approximately equal to 3?
self_contained_problem:
In the intracluster medium of merging galaxy clusters, two observational signatures are of interest: (i) shock fronts, defined as surfaces across which the X-ray surface brightness and gas temperature exhibit discontinuities consistent with the Rankine–Hugoniot jump conditions for a Mach number M > 1, as detected with high-resolution X-ray imaging; and (ii) radio relics, defined as elongated, often peripheral, polarized regions of diffuse synchrotron emission with steep radio spectra and Mpc-scale extent. A "clear spatial and physical connection" between a shock front and a radio relic means that the X-ray-detected shock surface coincides spatially with the outer edge of the relic and that the Mach number inferred independently from the X-ray jump is consistent with the Mach number inferred from the relic's integrated radio spectral index under the diffusive shock acceleration relation M^2 = (2α − 3)/(2α + 1), where α is the integrated spectral index of the relic.

Identify the set S of galaxy clusters for which both a shock front (in the above sense) is firmly detected and a radio relic with such a clear spatial and physical connection to that shock front has been observed. Determine, for the clusters in S, the empirical distribution of Mach numbers, and decide whether this distribution supports the hypothesis that radio relics are produced by merger-driven shocks with Mach numbers M ≲ 3.
category_tag: Galaxy cluster radio relics and merger shocks
status_search_result: Subsequent observational and simulation work has expanded the catalog of clusters where X-ray–detected shock fronts coincide with radio relics (e.g., A520, A754, CIZA J2242.8+5301, the Sausage and Toothbrush relics, A2744, A3667, etc.), and the inferred X-ray Mach numbers are typically in the range 1.5–3, broadly consistent with the M ≲ 3 hypothesis. However, a persistent discrepancy exists in which radio-derived Mach numbers tend to exceed X-ray-derived ones, and recent simulation studies (e.g., TNG-Cluster, 2024) describe shock surfaces as composites with broad Mach distributions peaking at 2–4.5. The qualitative picture of low-Mach merger shocks producing relics is supported, but the underlying acceleration mechanism and Mach-number tension remain unresolved.

paper_title: Observational properties of diffuse radio sources in Galaxy Clusters: Current knowledge and open questions
context_brief: Population status of ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos
original_question: Are ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos a genuine population of diffuse cluster radio sources rather than only two confirmed objects, and would finding more such halos provide observational support for the turbulent re-acceleration model of radio-halo formation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider diffuse, Mpc-scale synchrotron radio emission ("radio halos") from the intracluster medium of merging galaxy clusters. A radio halo is said to be ultra-steep-spectrum (USSRH) if its integrated spectral index α (defined by flux density S_ν ∝ ν^(−α)) satisfies α ≳ 1.5 between roughly 0.1 and 1.4 GHz. The turbulent re-acceleration model of halo formation, in which mildly relativistic electrons in the ICM are stochastically re-accelerated by merger-driven MHD turbulence, predicts that:
(i) the synchrotron spectra of halos steepen above a break frequency that depends on the energetics of the merger; and
(ii) less energetic mergers (typically in lower-mass clusters) produce halos with lower break frequencies, so that a substantial fraction of halos detectable at low radio frequencies (≲ 300 MHz) should appear ultra-steep, while being undetectable or missed in observations at ~1.4 GHz.

Question: Do ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos constitute a genuine, statistically populated class of diffuse cluster radio sources (as opposed to a handful of isolated objects), and does the observed abundance and luminosity distribution of such halos provide quantitative observational support for the turbulent re-acceleration model of radio-halo formation?
category_tag: galaxy cluster radio halos / turbulent re-acceleration
status_search_result: Subsequent LOFAR observations have substantially expanded the sample of ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos beyond the two early objects. Recent low-frequency studies report that a large fraction (e.g. ~64% in one LOFAR sample of 11 halos) of cluster radio halos show α < −1.5, consistent with the turbulent re-acceleration prediction that ~50% or more of halos at ~120 MHz should be ultra-steep. This supports USSRHs as a genuine population and provides observational backing for the turbulent re-acceleration scenario, although a fully statistical census awaits completion of LOFAR all-sky surveys, so the question is partially resolved rather than definitively closed.

paper_title: Observations and Open Questions in Beam-Beam Interactions
original_question: Are the observed long-range-loss dependencies on opposing beam intensity and transverse emittance nearly universal for a well-tuned collider operating away from harmful resonances, and if so, do they also hold in the LHC, which has several long-range beam-beam interactions per turn?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a circular hadron collider in which two counter-rotating bunched beams cross at one or more interaction points and additionally experience several parasitic long-range (electromagnetic) beam-beam encounters per revolution at non-zero transverse separation. For a stored bunch, let the relative particle loss rate L attributable to long-range beam-beam interactions be measured as a function of (i) the opposing beam's bunch intensity N (number of particles per bunch) and (ii) the transverse emittance ε of the opposing beam, while the machine is tuned away from low-order betatron resonances harmful to single-particle stability.

Empirical observations from one such collider show that, in this regime, L exhibits specific functional dependencies on N and ε (e.g., monotone increasing in N and decreasing in ε with characteristic scaling exponents).

Question: Prove or disprove that these observed dependencies of long-range beam-beam loss rate on (N, ε) are essentially universal — i.e., independent of machine-specific parameters — for any well-tuned collider operated away from harmful resonances and possessing several long-range beam-beam encounters per turn. In particular, determine whether the same dependencies govern long-range beam-beam losses in a collider with the geometry and lattice of the Large Hadron Collider (multiple long-range encounters per turn around each of the main interaction points).

The question concerns an empirical universality conjecture for long-range beam-beam loss scaling, raised as an open question to be tested at the LHC. Subsequent LHC operational studies have characterized long-range beam-beam effects (e.g., dynamic aperture, diffusion, losses), but a clean confirmation or refutation of strict universality of the (N, ε) dependence across machines does not appear to have been firmly established in the literature reviewed.

original_question: Why did KEKB achieve a maximum vertical beam-beam parameter of only 0.09 in the higher-energy ring when beam-beam simulations predicted 0.15, and what mechanisms were limiting further luminosity increase under crab-cavity operation?

paper_title: Observations and Open Questions in Beam-Beam Interactions
original_question: What quantitative theoretical model can explain why, in SPS and similar hadron-collider observations, proton losses became more sensitive to high-order resonances when the opposing anti-proton bunch emittance was reduced to nearly match the proton emittance, even though the beam-beam parameter was about 40% lower?
self_contained_problem:
Consider two counter-rotating bunched hadron beams (a proton bunch and an antiproton bunch) interacting at one or more crossing points in a circular collider. The strength of the long-range and head-on beam-beam force experienced by a test proton is characterized by the linear beam-beam parameter
  ξ = N r_p β* / (4π γ σ²),
where N is the opposing antiproton bunch population, r_p the classical proton radius, γ the relativistic factor, β* the optical β-function at the interaction point, and σ the rms transverse size of the opposing (antiproton) bunch. Assume the proton bunch has fixed transverse rms emittance ε_p and the antiproton bunch has rms emittance ε_a, with σ² ∝ ε_a at the interaction point.

Empirical observation in collider operation has shown the following: when ε_a ≫ ε_p (large antiproton emittance), proton losses driven by nonlinear betatron resonances of order ≥ 10 are weak; when ε_a is reduced so that ε_a ≈ ε_p, proton losses on these high-order resonances become substantially stronger, even though the increase of σ caused by the smaller ε_a makes the nominal beam-beam parameter ξ approximately 40% lower than in the large-ε_a configuration.

Develop a quantitative theoretical model — based on the nonlinear single-particle dynamics of a proton in the field of a Gaussian (or arbitrary radially symmetric) opposing bunch, including the dependence of resonance driving terms, dynamic aperture, and diffusion rates on the ratio ε_p/ε_a — that predicts and explains this enhancement of high-order resonance-driven proton losses as ε_a is decreased toward ε_p, despite the simultaneous reduction of ξ by roughly 40%. The model should reproduce, at least at the scaling level, the experimentally observed sensitivity of proton lifetime to high-order resonance tunes as a function of the emittance ratio.
status_search_result: Searches return general literature on beam-beam effects in proton-antiproton colliders (SPS, Tevatron) and on high-order resonance-driven losses with unequal emittances, but no source explicitly providing a quantitative theoretical model that reproduces the observed enhanced sensitivity to high-order resonances when the opposing-bunch emittance is reduced toward the proton emittance while ξ drops ~40%. The current status of a closed-form/quantitative model for this specific phenomenon could not be verified.

paper_title: Observations and Open Questions in Beam-Beam Interactions
original_question: Why did the RHIC pi coherent beam-beam mode appear without causing an instability even though it lies outside the incoherent spectrum and was theoretically expected to be undamped, and what damping mechanism, if any, would control this mode in the LHC?
self_contained_problem:
Consider two counter-rotating bunched particle beams in a circular collider that interact at one or more interaction points through the nonlinear beam–beam force. In the rigid-bunch (two-particle) coherent dipole model, the small-amplitude transverse coherent oscillations of the two bunches decompose into two normal modes: the sigma (0) mode, in which both bunches oscillate in phase at the unperturbed betatron tune Q_0, and the pi mode, in which they oscillate out of phase at a tune Q_0 + Y·xi, where xi is the beam–beam parameter and Y is the Yokoya factor (Y ≈ 1.21–1.33 for round Gaussian bunches with one head-on collision). Because the pi-mode tune lies outside the incoherent single-particle tune spread [Q_0, Q_0+xi] generated by the beam–beam force, standard Landau damping by the incoherent spectrum is absent, and theoretical analysis predicts that, in the presence of machine impedance, the pi mode should be undamped and therefore drive a coherent instability.

Empirically, in the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) the pi coherent beam–beam mode is observed as a clear spectral line outside the incoherent spectrum, yet no associated coherent instability develops.

Tasks:
(a) Identify and rigorously characterize the physical/mathematical mechanism that damps, or otherwise stabilizes against machine impedance, the pi coherent beam–beam mode in RHIC despite its tune lying outside the incoherent beam–beam tune spread, reconciling the observation with the prediction of an undamped pi mode in the rigid-bunch coherent model.
(b) Determine whether the same mechanism, or a different one, would be effective in stabilizing the pi mode in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) under its nominal collision optics and beam parameters, and quantify the required damping rate as a function of the beam–beam parameter xi, the Yokoya factor Y, the impedance budget, the chromaticity, the tune separation between the two beams, and the available external feedback.
category_tag: Beam-beam coherent modes and Landau damping
status_search_result: The stability of the pi coherent beam–beam mode and the mechanism damping it in hadron colliders is a long-standing open problem in accelerator physics. Subsequent literature (e.g., studies by Buffat, Pieloni, Tambasco and collaborators on coherent beam–beam modes and Landau damping in the LHC) continues to investigate damping mechanisms (lattice nonlinearities, octupoles, noise-induced decoherence, tune split between rings, head-on and long-range beam–beam tune spread) without a single, universally agreed quantitative explanation for the absence of pi-mode instability at RHIC or a definitive prescription for LHC.

paper_title: Observations and Open Questions in Beam-Beam Interactions
original_question: For possible future LHC crab-cavity operation, how sensitive are the beams to cavity phase noise and to synchro-betatron resonances driven by dispersion in the crab cavities, and are there additional beam-dynamics limitations that detailed studies should uncover before implementation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a high-energy circular hadron collider (such as the LHC) equipped with transverse deflecting "crab" RF cavities used to compensate the geometric luminosity loss arising from a finite crossing angle at the interaction points. A bunch is described by its 6-D phase-space coordinates, and the crab cavities impart a transverse momentum kick whose magnitude depends on the longitudinal position of each particle (and on the cavity phase relative to the synchronous particle). Two specific effects are of interest:

1. Cavity phase noise. Suppose the crab-cavity RF phase fluctuates stochastically with a power spectral density S(f). Derive quantitative expressions and tolerance limits relating S(f) (and amplitude noise) to the resulting transverse emittance growth rate of the stored beam, taking into account the betatron tune spread and the synchrotron sidebands. Determine the maximum allowable noise level (over the relevant frequency band) such that the emittance growth and luminosity lifetime remain compatible with collider operation.

2. Synchro-betatron resonances driven by dispersion in the crab cavities. With nonzero dispersion D and dispersion derivative D' at the location of the crab cavity, classify and quantify the synchro-betatron resonance conditions m·Q_x + n·Q_y + p·Q_s = integer that are excited (including those introduced by the crab kick itself and higher-order multipole content of the cavity field), compute their driving terms and stop-band widths, and assess their impact on dynamic aperture and beam lifetime for off-momentum particles.

Finally, identify and analyze any additional beam-dynamics limitations (e.g., impedance-coupling with crab-cavity noise, long-range and head-on beam-beam interplay, nonlinear multipole content) that constrain the operability of crab cavities in such a collider, and establish the corresponding tolerance budget.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since the question was posed. Theory, simulations, and beam-based measurements relating crab-cavity RF noise to transverse emittance growth have been published (e.g., Phys. Rev. Accel. Beams 27, 051001 (2024) on noise-driven emittance growth and 27, 071001 (2024) on impedance effects), and synchro-betatron resonances driven by crab cavities and large Piwinski angle have been analyzed (Phys. Rev. Accel. Beams 24, 041002 (2021); HL-LHC studies). Tolerances and cures have been derived and partially validated experimentally, but ongoing HL-LHC commissioning continues to refine the full set of beam-dynamics limitations, so the broader question is partially solved.

paper_title: Observations and Open Questions in Beam-Beam Interactions
original_question: Do longitudinally flat bunch profiles in large-Piwinski-angle luminosity schemes for the LHC genuinely produce lower transverse diffusion than Gaussian bunches when evaluated in more detailed beam-beam studies, and if they do, can such flat-profile schemes remain attractive even without very large Piwinski angles and very high bunch intensities?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a high-energy hadron collider in which two counter-rotating bunched beams cross at an interaction point with a finite crossing angle. For a bunch with rms transverse size σ_x, rms bunch length σ_z, and half crossing angle θ_c, define the Piwinski parameter Φ = (σ_z/σ_x) tan(θ_c). Model the longitudinal charge density of each bunch in two ways: (i) a Gaussian profile ρ_G(s) ∝ exp(−s²/(2σ_z²)), and (ii) a longitudinally flat (uniform) profile ρ_F(s) of the same total charge and rms length. In either case, the test particle in the opposing beam undergoes the nonlinear beam-beam kick at every turn, accumulated over many crossings, leading to a transverse diffusion coefficient D_⊥ characterizing the long-term spread of transverse action variables.

Questions:
(a) In a regime of large Piwinski angle Φ ≫ 1, with high bunch intensity, does the flat longitudinal profile ρ_F yield a strictly smaller transverse diffusion coefficient D_⊥ than the Gaussian profile ρ_G when evaluated under a detailed self-consistent beam-beam tracking model that includes all relevant nonlinear resonances, dynamic-beta and hourglass effects, and noise sources?

(b) If the answer to (a) is affirmative, does the inequality D_⊥(ρ_F) < D_⊥(ρ_G) continue to hold in regimes where Φ is moderate (not large) and bunch intensity is moderate (not extreme), so that flat longitudinal profiles remain advantageous outside the large-Piwinski, high-intensity limit?
status_search_result: No definitive resolution was located. Subsequent accelerator-physics literature on large-Piwinski-angle and flat-bunch luminosity schemes for the LHC/HL-LHC discusses potential benefits of flat longitudinal profiles, but a conclusive comparative quantification of transverse beam-beam diffusion that confirms or refutes the advantage in moderate regimes was not identified.

paper_title: Bimagic Squares of Bimagic Squares and an Open Problem
context_brief: Bimagic-sum invariance in nested square constructions
original_question: For the three tabulated families of bimagic squares — order 256×256 with listed subgroups 64×64, 16×16, and 4×4; order 625×625 with listed subgroups 125×125, 25×25, and 5×5; and order 2401×2401 with listed subgroups 343×343, 49×49, and 7×7 — prove mathematically the observed property stated by the source: for k = 4, 5, and 7, in the first sub-group the bimagic sum S2 is the same, summarized by the pattern k^4 → k^3 → k^2 → k^1.
self_contained_problem:
A bimagic square of order n is an n×n array filled with positive integers such that every row, every column, and both main diagonals have the same sum S₁ (the magic sum), and such that the array obtained by replacing each entry by its square is again a magic square; the common sum of squares in rows, columns, and diagonals is denoted S₂ and called the bimagic sum.

Consider the following nested constructions. For each prime power base k ∈ {4, 5, 7}, form a bimagic square of order k⁴ × k⁴ whose entries are the integers 1, 2, …, k⁸. Suppose this square admits a hierarchy of "sub-group" partitions: the k⁴ × k⁴ square is partitioned into k² × k² blocks of size k³ × k³ (the first sub-group), each k³ × k³ block is partitioned into k² × k² blocks of size k × k (here viewed at scale k², k¹), giving a nested sequence of orders

   k⁴ → k³ → k² → k¹.

Concretely the three families considered are:
 • k = 4: orders 256 → 64 → 16 → 4,
 • k = 5: orders 625 → 125 → 25 → 5,
 • k = 7: orders 2401 → 343 → 49 → 7.

Empirically, in each of these three families one observes that the bimagic sum S₂ taken over each k³ × k³ sub-block of the first sub-group is the same constant (independent of which sub-block of order k³ is chosen).

Prove rigorously that for k ∈ {4, 5, 7} (and in the general scheme k⁴ → k³ → k² → k¹), every k³ × k³ sub-block of the first sub-group of the bimagic square of order k⁴ has the same bimagic sum S₂. Equivalently, identify the structural property of the construction that forces this invariance and give a mathematical proof.
status_search_result: A web search for the specific invariance property k⁴ → k³ → k² → k¹ of bimagic sums in nested bimagic squares of orders 256, 625, and 2401 did not return any published proof or refutation. General literature on bimagic squares (Wikipedia, MathWorld, recent papers on existence of normal bimagic squares of even order) does not address this particular sub-block invariance claim, so the status appears unresolved in the accessible literature.

original_question: Suppose f and g are non-constant meromorphic functions that share four distinct values, and one of those four shared values is shared by counting multiplicities, meaning that for that one value the two functions take the value at exactly the same points with the same multiplicities, while for the other three values only the sets of shared points are assumed to coincide. Must the conclusion of Nevanlinna's Four-Value Theorem still follow, namely that after relabelling the values the cross-ratio (a1, a2, a3, a4) equals -1, a1 and a2 are Picard values of both functions, and g is a Mobius transformation of f that fixes a3 and a4 and permutes a1 and a2?
self_contained_problem:
Let f and g be non-constant meromorphic functions on the complex plane. For a value a ∈ ℂ ∪ {∞}, say that f and g share a IM (ignoring multiplicities) if f^{-1}(a) = g^{-1}(a) as sets, and share a CM (counting multiplicities) if in addition every point z₀ in this common preimage is a zero of f − a (interpreted appropriately at ∞) of the same multiplicity as it is for g − a.

Nevanlinna's Four-Value Theorem states: if f and g are non-constant meromorphic functions sharing four distinct values a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄ ∈ ℂ ∪ {∞} all CM, then (after relabelling) the cross-ratio (a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄) = −1, the values a₁ and a₂ are Picard exceptional values of both f and g, and g is a Möbius transformation of f that fixes a₃ and a₄ and interchanges a₁ and a₂.

Question (the (1+3) Four-Value Problem): Suppose f and g are non-constant meromorphic functions that share four distinct values a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, where one of these values is shared CM and the remaining three are shared IM. Must the same conclusion as in Nevanlinna's Four-Value Theorem hold — namely, that after relabelling, (a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄) = −1, a₁ and a₂ are Picard values of both f and g, and g is a Möbius transformation of f fixing a₃, a₄ and permuting a₁, a₂?
status_search_result: The general (1+3) four-value problem (also known as Gundersen's question, equivalent to whether 3 IM + 1 CM forces 4 CM) remains open. Partial results exist; in particular, a 2024 work establishes the conclusion under the additional hypothesis that at least one of f, g has finite order. The unrestricted case is still unresolved.

original_question: For each positive integer n, determine C(n), the number of Costas arrays of order n. In particular, do Costas arrays exist for every order n > 0, and if not, which positive integers n satisfy C(n) = 0?
self_contained_problem:
A Costas array of order n is an n×n array with exactly one dot in each row and one dot in each column (i.e., a permutation matrix of size n×n) such that all the displacement vectors between distinct pairs of dots are distinct. Equivalently, a permutation f: {1,…,n} → {1,…,n} is a Costas permutation if for every integers i, j, k with 1 ≤ i, j, j+k ≤ n and k ≠ 0, the equality f(i+k) − f(i) = f(j+k) − f(j) implies i = j. Let C(n) denote the number of Costas arrays of order n.

(a) For every positive integer n, determine the value of C(n).

(b) Decide whether C(n) > 0 holds for every positive integer n; if not, determine explicitly the set X = { n ∈ ℤ_{>0} : C(n) = 0 } of orders for which no Costas array exists.
status_search_result: The problem is widely regarded as open. No closed-form expression for C(n) is known, and the existence question is famously unresolved: as of recent enumeration efforts (covering orders up to roughly 29 exhaustively, with partial searches extending much further), it is still unknown whether Costas arrays exist for order n = 32 and n = 33, the smallest orders where existence has not been decided. Asymptotic gaps between known upper and lower bounds for C(n) also remain open.

original_question: Define the degrees of freedom of a Costas array of order n as the smallest k <= n for which there exist indices i1 < i2 < ... < ik in [n] such that, for any prescribed values f1, ..., fk in [n], there is at most one Costas permutation f:[n]->[n] with f(ij)=fj for all j. Determine this quantity for Costas arrays of order n, and if possible improve the definition so it captures the phenomenon more effectively.
self_contained_problem: A Costas permutation of order $n$ is a bijection $f:[n]\to[n]$ (where $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$) such that all vectors $(j-i,\,f(j)-f(i))$ with $1\le i<j\le n$ are distinct; equivalently, for every nonzero integer $h$ the function $i\mapsto f(i+h)-f(i)$ is injective on its domain. Define the degrees of freedom of Costas permutations of order $n$ to be the smallest integer $k\le n$ for which there exist indices $i_1<i_2<\cdots<i_k$ in $[n]$ with the following property: for every prescribed tuple of values $(f_1,\dots,f_k)\in[n]^k$, the set $\{f:[n]\to[n]\,:\,f(i_j)=f_j\text{ for }j=1,\dots,k\}$ contains at most one Costas permutation. Determine this quantity as a function of $n$, and, if possible, propose an improved definition that better captures the phenomenon of how few coordinates suffice to determine a Costas permutation.
status_search_result: The problem of determining the degrees of freedom of Costas arrays of order n is listed as an open problem. Partial results exist: studies have shown the number of degrees of freedom is surprisingly small and have proved partial results for Golomb and Welch Costas permutations, but no closed-form determination for general n is known.

original_question: Determine whether sporadic Costas arrays form only a finite set, or whether they instead arise from one or more still-unknown generally applicable construction techniques.
self_contained_problem:
A Costas array of order n is an n×n permutation matrix (equivalently, a permutation f of {1,2,…,n}) with the property that all the vectors connecting pairs of its 1-entries are pairwise distinct; equivalently, for every nonzero integer h with |h| < n and every pair of integers i ≠ j in the appropriate range, f(i+h) − f(i) = f(j+h) − f(j) implies i = j. Two main families of Costas arrays are known to exist for infinitely many orders: the Welch construction and the Golomb (Lempel) construction, both based on primitive roots in finite fields. A Costas array is called "generated" if it can be obtained directly from one of these algebraic constructions (using their standard parameters), and "emergent" if it arises from a generated array via a documented operation such as addition or removal of a corner 1, taking sub-arrays, or related transformations. A Costas array that is neither generated nor emergent is called sporadic. Sporadic Costas arrays are presently known only for finitely many orders n with 6 ≤ n ≤ 27, and exhaustive enumeration becomes computationally infeasible for moderately larger n.

Settle the status of sporadic Costas arrays: prove either that the set of sporadic Costas arrays (over all orders n) is finite, or exhibit one or more general construction techniques (independent of the Welch and Golomb families and their known emergent transformations) that produce infinitely many sporadic Costas arrays.
status_search_result: The problem of whether sporadic Costas arrays are finite in number, or whether some yet-undiscovered general construction produces them, remains open. original_question: Do there exist finite-order sporadic Costas arrays of order n > 1 whose dots also form a configuration of non-attacking queens on an n x n chessboard? If such arrays exist, how many are there, and can they be constructed systematically?
self_contained_problem:
A Costas array of order $n$ is an $n\times n$ array containing exactly $n$ dots, with one dot in each row and one dot in each column (equivalently, the dots are the graph of a permutation of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$), such that the $\binom{n}{2}$ displacement vectors connecting distinct pairs of dots are all distinct. Costas arrays can be constructed by certain algebraic methods based on primitive roots in finite fields (the Welch and Lempel–Golomb constructions and their variants); arrays produced by those constructions, or obtained from them by elementary symmetries (rotations, reflections, and the transformations that arise from those constructions), are called generated. Costas arrays that arise as sub-arrays from such algebraic constructions are called emergent. A Costas array is called sporadic if it is neither generated nor emergent.

A configuration of non-attacking queens on the $n\times n$ chessboard is a placement of $n$ queens, one in each row and column, such that no two queens lie on a common diagonal (neither of the two diagonal directions).

Question: Does there exist an integer $n>1$ and a sporadic Costas array of order $n$ whose dots simultaneously form a configuration of $n$ non-attacking queens on the $n\times n$ chessboard? If such arrays exist, determine how many there are (for each such $n$, or in total) and give a systematic construction.
status_search_result: The problem of finding Costas arrays whose dots also form a non-attacking-queens configuration appears to remain open. It is known that such an array, if it exists, must be sporadic, and the prevailing conjecture in the literature is that no such arrays exist; however, no proof has been published, and the search results found do not report a resolution of the question.

original_question: Describe the cycle structure of Costas permutations under iteration. In particular, for a specific Costas permutation or a specific family, determine the full cycle decomposition, whether cycles of a given length can occur, the longest cycle length, and the smallest positive integer k for which the k-fold iterate equals the identity permutation.
self_contained_problem:
A Costas array of order n is an n×n array with exactly one dot in each row and each column such that all (n choose 2) displacement vectors between pairs of distinct dots are distinct. Equivalently, a Costas permutation of order n is a bijection f : [n] → [n] (where [n] = {1, 2, …, n}) whose graph is a Costas array; that is, for every choice of integers i, j, k with 1 ≤ i < i+k ≤ n and 1 ≤ j < j+k ≤ n with (i, j) ≠ (i+k, j+k) lying in [n], the equation f(i+k) − f(i) = f(j+k) − f(j) implies (i, j) = (i+k, j+k); equivalently, the differences f(i+k) − f(i) are distinct for each fixed k ∈ {1, …, n−1} as i varies.

Let I : [n] → [n] denote the identity permutation, and define iterates of f by f^(0) = I and f^(k+1)(i) = f(f^(k)(i)) for all i ∈ [n] and k ∈ ℕ. The cycle of i ∈ [n] under f is the (finite) set {f^(k)(i) : k ∈ ℕ}.

Investigate the cycle structure of Costas permutations under iteration. In particular, address the following:

(a) For specified Costas permutations or specified families of Costas permutations (for instance, the Welch and Lempel–Golomb families arising from primitive roots of finite fields), determine the full cycle decomposition.

(b) Determine, for such a permutation or family, which cycle lengths can occur and which are forbidden.

(c) Determine the longest cycle length appearing in such a permutation or family.

(d) Determine the order of f, that is, the smallest positive integer k such that f^(k) = I.
status_search_result: The problem of describing the cycle structure of Costas permutations under iteration is listed as one of the open problems in the literature on Costas arrays. Some partial results exist for specific algebraic families (e.g., Welch and Golomb/Lempel constructions), but no general description of cycle decomposition, longest cycle length, or order of Costas permutations is known.

original_question: For each unpredictably emergent Costas-array construction method obtained by adding one or more dots to an existing Costas array, determine whether there is a finite threshold N beyond which that method never produces a Costas array of order n > N.
self_contained_problem:
A Costas array of order n is an n×n permutation matrix (equivalently, a permutation f:{1,...,n}→{1,...,n}) such that all the n(n−1)/2 displacement vectors between distinct pairs of its dots are pairwise distinct; equivalently, for every nonzero integer h with |h|<n, the function i ↦ f(i+h)−f(i) is injective on its domain.

A "dot-addition" construction method is a deterministic procedure that takes a Costas array A of order m as input, augments it by adjoining one or more new dots (e.g., placed at corner positions or otherwise) to form an (m+k)×(m+k) permutation matrix B, and outputs B whenever B happens to satisfy the Costas property. Such a method is called unpredictably emergent if there is no known sufficient condition, depending only on m (or on m together with auxiliary parameters), guaranteeing in advance that the augmented array B will be Costas; whether B is Costas must be verified a posteriori. Several specific unpredictably emergent methods of this kind are known (for instance, single corner-dot additions to Welch–Rickard or Golomb–Rickard arrays, as well as analogous two-dot or interior-dot variants).

Problem. For each such unpredictably emergent dot-addition construction method M, decide whether there exists a finite threshold N = N(M) ∈ ℕ such that M produces no Costas array of any order n > N. Equivalently, determine for each method M whether the set of orders n for which M yields at least one Costas array is finite, and if so, exhibit such a bound.
status_search_result: The problem of bounding the orders of Costas arrays produced by unpredictably emergent dot-addition methods remains open. Exhaustive computer searches have verified that several such methods (e.g., the Rickard-type constructions) yield no new Costas arrays up to order 300, but no proof of a finite cutoff N for any of these methods is known. The problem is listed among open problems in the Costas-array literature and surveys.

original_question: Develop a stochastic search algorithm for Costas arrays that continues to work at larger orders of practical interest, especially orders 30, 31, 32, and 33.
self_contained_problem:
A Costas array of order $n$ is an $n\times n$ array with exactly one mark in each row and each column (equivalently, a permutation $f:\{1,\dots,n\}\to\{1,\dots,n\}$) such that all $\binom{n}{2}$ displacement vectors between distinct marks are distinct. Equivalently, for every triple of integers $(i,j,k)$ with $1\le i<i+k\le n$ and $1\le j<j+k\le n$ and $k\ne 0$, one has
$$f(i+k)-f(i)\ne f(j+k)-f(j) \quad\text{whenever } i\ne j.$$
The existence problem for Costas arrays at certain orders remains unresolved; in particular, no Costas array is known for orders $32$ and $33$, and only a handful are known for orders $30$ and $31$, while complete enumerations have only been carried out up through order $29$.

Design a stochastic (randomized) search algorithm for Costas arrays which is effective at orders $n=30,31,32,33$. Specifically, exhibit such an algorithm together with evidence that it can locate Costas arrays of these orders (or, in the case of $n=32,33$, decisively succeed in producing one if any exist), within practical computational resources.
status_search_result: No stochastic search method to date has been shown to reliably find Costas arrays at orders 32 and 33; existence at these orders is unknown, and only a few examples are known at orders 30 and 31. Bayesian analyses suggest the rarity of Costas permutations makes naive stochastic search ineffective at these orders. Large-scale parallel constraint-based local search has been studied but has not produced new arrays at these problematic orders.

original_question: Suppose a Costas array has the property that after adding one blank row at the top, every cyclic shift of the rows still yields a non-square array with the Costas property. Must the original Costas array be an exponential Welch W1 array?
self_contained_problem:
A Costas array of order n is an n×n array with exactly one dot in each row and each column such that all the (n choose 2) vectors (difference vectors) connecting pairs of dots are distinct. More generally, an m×n array (with m ≠ n) is said to have the Costas property if it has at most one dot in each row and at most one dot in each column, and all difference vectors between pairs of dots are distinct.

For an odd prime p and a primitive root g modulo p, the exponential Welch construction W1 produces a Costas array A of order p−1 by placing a dot at row i and column j if and only if j ≡ g^{i-1} (mod p), for 1 ≤ i, j ≤ p−1.

Now let A be any Costas array of order n. Form the (n+1)×n array A' obtained by inserting a blank row above the first row of A. Consider all n+1 cyclic shifts of the rows of A' (i.e., for k = 0, 1, …, n, move the top k rows to the bottom in order). Suppose that every such cyclic shift yields an (n+1)×n array (necessarily non-square) that has the Costas property.

Question: Must A be (equivalent to) an exponential Welch W1 array?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in a list of open problems on Costas arrays. Web search did not surface a published resolution characterizing exactly the Costas arrays for which adding a blank top row yields the Costas property under all cyclic row shifts. Recent works on Welch arrays with 1-gap rows discuss related structures but do not appear to settle this inverse characterization, so the status is treated as unknown.

original_question: For G2 Costas arrays constructed over finite fields of characteristic 2, determine the four parity populations ee, eo, oe, and oo, namely the numbers of dots whose coordinates are respectively even-even, even-odd, odd-even, and odd-odd.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let q = 2^k with k ≥ 2, and let F_q be the finite field with q elements. A Costas array of order n is an n × n array containing exactly n dots (one in each row and one in each column) such that the (n choose 2) displacement vectors between distinct pairs of dots are all distinct.

The Golomb (G2) construction over F_q produces a Costas array of order q − 2 as follows. Fix two primitive elements α, β of F_q. For 1 ≤ i, j ≤ q − 2, place a dot at position (i, j) if and only if
   α^i + β^j = 1.
The resulting (q − 2) × (q − 2) array is a Costas array, called a G2 Costas array.

For any Costas array, define its four parity populations
   ee = #{ dots (i, j) : i even and j even },
   eo = #{ dots (i, j) : i even and j odd  },
   oe = #{ dots (i, j) : i odd  and j even },
   oo = #{ dots (i, j) : i odd  and j odd  }.

Problem. For q = 2^k (k ≥ 2), determine, as a function of q and of the choices of primitive elements α, β, the four parity populations ee, eo, oe, oo of the G2 Costas array of order q − 2 constructed above. In particular, give closed-form expressions (or tight characterizations) for these four counts in the characteristic-2 case.

original_question: Let p be a prime, let C be a nonzero element of the finite field F(p), and let alpha be a primitive root modulo p. Determine the number of integers i in [p-1] that satisfy the congruence i ≡ C alpha^i (mod p).
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $\mathbb{F}_p$ denote the finite field with $p$ elements, let $C \in \mathbb{F}_p^{*}$ be a nonzero element, and let $\alpha$ be a primitive root modulo $p$ (i.e., a generator of the cyclic group $\mathbb{F}_p^{*}$). Consider the congruence
$$ i \equiv C\,\alpha^{i} \pmod{p}. $$
Determine, as a closed-form expression (or sharp asymptotic / exact formula) in terms of $p$, $C$, and $\alpha$, the number of integers $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, p-1\}$ that satisfy this congruence.

original_question: For the families of Welch W1 and Golomb G2 Costas arrays, determine the maximal pairwise cross-correlation quantities defined by the paper as Ψ_W1(p) and Ψ_G2(q), classify primes and prime powers into the cases stated in Problem 21, prove the listed formulas and exceptional cases, derive formulas for the local minima, and show where the maxima are attained in the non-safe cases described there.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $g$ be a primitive root modulo $p$. The exponential Welch Costas permutation $f_g$ on $\{0,1,\dots,p-2\}$ is defined by $f_g(i) = g^i \bmod p - 1$. Two Welch permutations $f_{g_1}$ and $f_{g_2}$ are said to be produced by different primitive roots, written $f_{g_1} \stackrel{pr}{\neq} f_{g_2}$, if $g_1 \not\equiv g_2 \pmod p$.

Let $q$ be a prime power and let $\alpha,\beta$ be primitive elements of the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$. The Golomb Costas permutation $f'_{\alpha,\beta}$ on $\{1,\dots,q-2\}$ is defined by the relation $\alpha^{i} + \beta^{f'_{\alpha,\beta}(i)} = 1$.

For two permutations $f_1, f_2$ of a common index set of size $N$ and integers $(u,v)$ with $|u|<N$, define the cross-correlation
$$\Psi_{f_1,f_2}(u,v) = \#\{ i : f_1(i+u) = f_2(i) + v \}.$$

Define
$$\Psi_{W_1}(p) = \max_{(u,v)} \max_{f_1 \stackrel{pr}{\neq} f_2} \Psi_{f_1,f_2}(u,v),$$
$$\Psi_{G_2}(q) = \max_{(u,v)} \max_{f'_1 \neq f'_2} \Psi_{f'_1,f'_2}(u,v),$$
the maxima being taken over pairs of distinct Welch (resp. Golomb) Costas permutations as above.

A prime $p$ is called safe if $(p-1)/2$ is also prime.

Problem.

(a) Prove that with respect to $\Psi_{W_1}(p)$ and $\Psi_{G_2}(p)$, the primes $p$ split into three groups according to whether $p$ is a safe prime, $p$ is a non-safe prime of a specified second class, or $p$ is a non-safe prime of the third class, and determine the corresponding closed-form values (or sharp bounds) of $\Psi_{W_1}(p)$ and $\Psi_{G_2}(p)$ in each class, including all exceptional small cases.

(b) Prove the analogous trichotomy classification of prime powers $q$ with respect to $\Psi_{G_2}(q)$, with the corresponding formulas and exceptional cases.

(c) For non-safe primes $p$, prove that
$$\Psi_{W_1}(p) = \max_{f_1 \stackrel{pr}{\neq} f_2} \Psi_{f_1,f_2}(0,0),$$
i.e. the maximum is attained at the shift $(u,v)=(0,0)$. For prime powers $q \notin \{16,19\}$ that are non-safe and such that $q-1$ is not prime, prove that
$$\Psi_{G_2}(q) = \max_{f'_1 \neq f'_2} \Psi_{f'_1,f'_2}(0,0).$$

(d) Derive explicit formulas for the local minima of $\Psi_{W_1}$ and $\Psi_{G_2}$ in terms of arithmetic invariants of $p$ and $q$ (e.g. the smallest prime divisor of $p-1$ or $q-1$).
status_search_result: Subsequent work (notably the 2020 IEEE Transactions on Information Theory note "A Note on the Cross-Correlation of Costas Permutations") settles part of the conjecture: for primes $p\ge 5$, the maximal cross-correlation of distinct Welch Costas permutations equals $(p-1)/t$ where $t$ is the smallest prime divisor of $(p-1)/2$ when $p$ is not safe, and is at most $1+\sqrt{p}$ when $p$ is safe. The corresponding Golomb result is proved only for a smaller subfamily of size $\varphi(q-1)$, and the authors note the bound can fail for the full Golomb family of size $\varphi(q-1)^2$. Hence the trichotomy classification and formulas are partially proved, with the full Golomb case and several exceptional/local-minimum statements still open.

original_question: Let C(m,n,N) denote the number of m x n Golomb rectangles containing N dots, where a Golomb rectangle is a rectangular dot pattern whose autocorrelation takes exactly the three values {N, 1, 0}. Determine C(m,n,N). In particular, for fixed m and n find the largest N with C(m,n,N) > 0, and for fixed N find the smallest m and n with C(m,n,N) > 0.
self_contained_problem:
A two-dimensional binary pattern is an m×n array A = (a_{i,j}) with entries in {0,1}, where the 1's are called "dots" and the 0's are called "blanks". The (discrete) autocorrelation of A is the function defined, for integer shifts (s,t) with |s|<m and |t|<n, by

  R(s,t) = Σ_{i,j} a_{i,j} · a_{i+s,j+t},

where a_{k,l} = 0 whenever (k,l) lies outside the m×n grid. Let N be the number of dots in A (so R(0,0)=N). Call A an m×n Golomb rectangle (with N dots) if N > 2 and the set of values { R(s,t) : (s,t) ranges over all admissible shifts } equals exactly {N, 1, 0}; equivalently, every nonzero shift of A overlaps the original pattern in either exactly one dot or no dots.

Let C(m,n,N) denote the number of m×n Golomb rectangles containing exactly N dots (counted as labeled subsets of the m×n grid, without identifying patterns related by symmetry).

(a) Determine a formula or effective procedure for computing C(m,n,N) for all positive integers m, n, N.
(b) For each fixed pair (m,n), determine the largest integer N = N_max(m,n) for which C(m,n,N) > 0.
(c) For each fixed integer N > 2, determine the smallest values of m and n (in an appropriate sense, e.g. minimizing m+n or the area mn) for which C(m,n,N) > 0.
status_search_result: No closed-form enumeration of C(m,n,N) appears in the literature. Available work on Golomb rectangles (Robinson, 1985 and later) provides bounds, special constructions, and computer searches for optimal cases, but the general counting problem and the determination of extremal m, n, N remain unresolved. The problem appears to still be open.

original_question: Find exact formulas for the two fundamental extremal functions for Golomb rulers: the minimum possible length n of a Golomb ruler with a given number m of points, and the maximum possible number of points m in a Golomb ruler of a given length n.
self_contained_problem:
A Golomb ruler is a finite set of nonnegative integers $\{a_0 < a_1 < \dots < a_{m-1}\}$ such that all pairwise differences $a_j - a_i$ (for $0 \le i < j \le m-1$) are distinct. The number of points of the ruler is $m$, and its length is $a_{m-1} - a_0$ (equivalently, one may assume $a_0 = 0$ and the length is $a_{m-1}$). Define the two extremal functions:

- $G(m)$ = the minimum possible length of a Golomb ruler with exactly $m$ points;
- $M(n)$ = the maximum possible number of points of a Golomb ruler of length $n$.

Provide an exact closed-form formula for $G(m)$ as a function of the integer $m \ge 1$, and an exact closed-form formula for $M(n)$ as a function of the integer $n \ge 0$.
status_search_result: No closed-form exact formula is known for either the minimum length of an optimal Golomb ruler with m points or the maximum number of points of a Golomb ruler of length n. Optimal lengths have been verified computationally only up to 28 marks (as of distributed search results through 2023), and research has focused on asymptotic bounds and constructions (e.g., Singer, Bose–Chowla) producing near-optimal rulers. The problem of giving exact formulas remains open.

original_question: What is the actual low-temperature magnetic-domain structure of pure LiHoF4, an insulating dipolar Ising ferromagnet whose Ho3+ moments order below about 1.53 K along the crystalline c axis, and can experiments verify the predicted rich structure in which the ground-state domains consist of parallel antiferromagnetically aligned sheets whose sizes and possible branching depend on demagnetization effects and sample geometry?
self_contained_problem:
Consider LiHoF4, an insulating dipolar Ising ferromagnet in which the Ho3+ magnetic moments order below approximately Tc ≈ 1.53 K, with their easy axis along the crystalline c direction. Treat the system as a three-dimensional lattice of classical Ising dipoles interacting solely via the magnetic dipole–dipole interaction (the long-range, angularly anisotropic interaction U(r) ∝ [1 − 3(ẑ·r̂)^2]/|r|^3 between parallel moments aligned along c).

For a finite macroscopic sample of given shape (and hence demagnetization factor N), the competition between bulk dipolar energy and surface/demagnetization energy is predicted to produce a ground-state domain configuration consisting of parallel sheet-like domains of alternating magnetization (an "antiferromagnetic" stacking of ferromagnetic sheets), whose characteristic width grows as N decreases, with a uniformly magnetized state attained in the limit of an infinitely long, thin sample. For sufficiently thick samples, the predicted optimal pattern develops a hierarchical branching structure near the sample surfaces.

Problem: Determine experimentally the actual low-temperature magnetic-domain structure of pure LiHoF4 as a function of sample geometry and demagnetization factor, and verify (or refute) the predicted features: (i) the existence of parallel antiferromagnetically stacked sheet domains in the ordered phase, (ii) the predicted dependence of domain width on demagnetization factor, and (iii) the appearance of a branched domain pattern in thick samples.
status_search_result: Subsequent experiments have made significant progress: scanning Hall-probe microscopy below 40 mK (Biltmo & Henelius / Kjäll et al. type studies, and later imaging works) directly observed a multi-domain state in LiHoF4 with parallel/cylinder-like domains a few microns wide, and a 2022 Nature paper reported emergent mesoscale antiferromagnetism near the quantum critical point. These confirm the qualitative picture of antiferromagnetically stacked sheet/cylinder domains and shape dependence, but full quantitative verification of the predicted branched pattern in thick samples and detailed N-dependence of the domain width remains incomplete, so the problem is best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: Collective Phenomena in the LiHoxY1−xF4 Quantum Ising Magnet: Recent Progress and Open Questions
context_brief: Hyperfine effects in the global phase diagram
original_question: What quantitatively accurate role do Ho hyperfine interactions play in the global concentration-temperature-transverse-field phase diagram of LiHoxY1−xF4, especially in regimes where the ferromagnetic or spin-glass critical temperature drops below roughly 0.5 K and the hyperfine interaction inhibits quantum fluctuations and strongly renormalizes the critical transverse field?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the diluted dipolar quantum Ising magnet defined as follows. On a tetragonal (LiYF4-type) lattice, place Ho^{3+} ions independently at random with concentration x ∈ (0,1] at each rare-earth site, the remaining sites being occupied by non-magnetic Y^{3+}. To each Ho^{3+} site i associate (i) an effective low-energy doublet described by a Pauli operator σ_i^z (longitudinal Ising component) with transverse component σ_i^x, and (ii) a nuclear spin I_i = 7/2 coupled to the electronic moment by an on-site hyperfine interaction A_0 I_i · S_i (with S_i the full electronic angular momentum projected onto the relevant crystal-field manifold). The Ho-Ho electronic moments interact through the long-range magnetic dipolar interaction (with both longitudinal Ising couplings and off-diagonal terms generated by a transverse field). A uniform transverse magnetic field B_x is applied along a crystallographic a-axis.

The microscopic Hamiltonian thus has the schematic form
H = (1/2) Σ_{i ≠ j} ε_i ε_j [ J_{ij}^{zz} σ_i^z σ_j^z + (off-diagonal dipolar terms induced by B_x) ] − Γ(B_x) Σ_i ε_i σ_i^x + A_0 Σ_i ε_i I_i · S_i,
where ε_i ∈ {0,1} are i.i.d. Bernoulli(x) site occupations, J_{ij}^{zz} are the dipolar couplings on the LiYF4 lattice, and Γ(B_x) is the transverse-field-induced tunneling splitting computed from the full Ho^{3+} crystal-field spectrum.

Problem. Determine, by quantitatively accurate (e.g. unbiased quantum Monte Carlo) calculations, the global phase diagram of this model in the three-dimensional parameter space (x, T, B_x), with the full hyperfine term retained. In particular:
(a) Compute the boundary between the paramagnetic phase and the ordered (ferromagnetic for x close to 1, spin-glass for intermediate x) phase as a surface T_c(x, B_x).
(b) Quantify how the hyperfine interaction renormalizes the critical transverse field B_x^c(x, T) in the regime where T_c(x, B_x = 0) ≲ 0.5 K, where suppression of quantum fluctuations by the nuclear spins is non-negligible.
(c) Determine how the hyperfine coupling alters the location and nature of the quantum critical points and quantum critical lines, including any modifications to the universality class of the transitions.
status_search_result: Subsequent works (e.g. Schechter–Stamp; Tabei et al.; quantum Monte Carlo studies of the diluted dipolar Ising model with renormalized transverse field; and more recent quantum-annealing microscopics work, ~2021) have made progress incorporating hyperfine effects, often by approximating them via a renormalization of the transverse field. However, a fully quantitative determination of the global x–T–B_x phase diagram of LiHoxY1−xF4 with the complete hyperfine structure retained—particularly the spin-glass regime and the strongly hyperfine-renormalized low-temperature quantum critical region—has not been definitively achieved, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Collective Phenomena in the LiHoxY1−xF4 Quantum Ising Magnet: Recent Progress and Open Questions
original_question: Do transverse-field-induced random fields in diluted ferromagnetic LiHoxY1−xF4, for example at Ho concentration x = 0.44, produce Griffiths singularity effects in the paramagnetic regime just above the ferromagnetic transition temperature Tc, and what systematic experimental investigation is needed to test the claimed susceptibility-scaling behavior?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the diluted dipolar Ising magnet LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4, in which magnetic Ho^{3+} ions (Ising-like, with easy axis along the crystallographic c-direction) are randomly substituted by non-magnetic Y^{3+} ions at concentration 1-x. When a magnetic field B_x is applied transverse to the Ising axis, the combination of B_x-induced off-diagonal admixing of crystal-field states and the dilution-induced loss of local crystalline symmetry generates, through the long-range dipolar couplings, effective random longitudinal fields acting on the Ising degrees of freedom. Fix the Ho concentration x = 0.44, which lies in the diluted ferromagnetic regime with a finite ferromagnetic transition temperature T_c(B_x) > 0 for sufficiently small B_x.

(a) Determine whether the transverse-field-induced random longitudinal fields produce Griffiths-type singularities in the paramagnetic phase at temperatures just above T_c(B_x); that is, decide whether the linear and nonlinear magnetic susceptibilities exhibit non-analytic Griffiths behavior (e.g. essential singularities or power-law tails associated with rare large ferromagnetic clusters in the random-field environment) for T just above T_c(B_x).

(b) Identify the precise scaling form of the magnetic susceptibility χ(T, B_x) as a function of temperature and transverse field that would be predicted by such a random-field Griffiths scenario, and specify how this scaling could be distinguished experimentally from non-Griffiths smearing of the transition.
status_search_result: The question was raised as an open problem calling for further experimental and theoretical investigation. Subsequent work (e.g. numerical linked-cluster studies of Griffiths–McCoy singularities in the dilute transverse-field Ising model, Phys. Rev. E 99, 032129 (2019), and observations in related random quantum Ising magnets such as PrTiNbO6) has explored Griffiths phenomena in similar models, but no definitive systematic experimental confirmation of the proposed Griffiths singularity scaling of the susceptibility in LiHo_{0.44}Y_{0.56}F_4 just above T_c has been established. The status thus appears still open.
