paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
context_brief: Standardization of models, definitions, and analyses
original_question: How should the field standardize initial-state model implementations, initial-anisotropy definitions ε_n, Glauber Monte Carlo variations, and experimental flow analyses so that heavy-ion results can be compared consistently across models and measurements?
self_contained_problem:
In relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the transverse geometry of the participating nucleons in a single event is commonly characterized by the complex initial-anisotropy coefficients

  ε_n e^{i n Φ_n} = − ⟨ r^n e^{i n φ} ⟩ / ⟨ r^n ⟩,   n ≥ 2,

where (r, φ) are polar coordinates around the event's center of mass in the transverse plane and the average ⟨·⟩ is taken with respect to a participant or energy-density distribution generated by a Glauber Monte Carlo (or analogous) initial-state model. Different models, however, employ different choices for: (i) the weight used in the average (number of participants, number of binary collisions, deposited energy, smeared Gaussian profiles of varying width, etc.); (ii) the recentering and rotation conventions used to define Φ_n; (iii) the cumulant variants of ε_n; (iv) parameters of the Glauber Monte Carlo such as the nucleon–nucleon inelastic cross section, nucleon size and shape, minimal inter-nucleon exclusion distance, and treatment of nucleon substructure; and (v) the experimental flow analysis methods used to extract harmonic flow coefficients v_n (event-plane, scalar-product, two- and multi-particle cumulants, Lee–Yang zeros, etc.), which respond differently to event-by-event fluctuations and non-flow correlations.

Problem. Formulate a unified, publicly available framework for initial-state modeling and flow analysis with the following properties:

(a) A canonical mathematical definition of the eccentricities ε_n (including their phases Φ_n, weights, and cumulant generalizations) that fixes all averaging and centering conventions.

(b) A standardized specification of Glauber Monte Carlo implementations: precise prescriptions for nucleon sampling, nucleon–nucleon collision criteria, energy/entropy deposition rules, and a documented set of physical parameters and their uncertainties, so that two independent implementations of the specification yield statistically identical event ensembles.

(c) A standardized set of estimators for experimental flow observables v_n{method} together with explicit mathematical relations expressing each estimator as moments/cumulants of the underlying single-event flow distribution P(v_n), so that values quoted under different methods can be inter-converted.

(d) A consistency criterion (for example, in terms of measurable ratios such as v_n{2}/v_n{4} versus ε_n{2}/ε_n{4}) that allows model and experimental quantities to be compared on the same footing across collision systems and energies.

State whether such a framework can be constructed so that (a)–(d) are simultaneously well-defined and mutually compatible, and exhibit it explicitly if so.
status_search_result: The question is a community-level standardization challenge in heavy-ion phenomenology. While substantial progress has been made (e.g., the TRENTo parametric initial-condition model, public Glauber MC codes such as PHOBOS Glauber, and Bayesian model-to-data frameworks like JETSCAPE), no single universally adopted standard for ε_n definitions, Glauber MC variants, and experimental flow methods has been agreed upon. The issue therefore appears to remain open in practice.

paper_title: Some open problems in control theory.
context_brief: periodic stabilization in dimensions two or three
original_question: In dimensions 2 and 3, suppose a control system satisfies small-time reachability together with a Lie algebra condition. Do these hypotheses imply the existence of a periodic stabilizing feedback or periodic stabilization mechanism? The source states that positive answers are already known in the other dimensions from the author's work.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a smooth control-affine system on $\mathbb{R}^n$ of the form
$$\dot x = f(x,u), \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}^n,\ u \in \mathbb{R}^m,$$
with $f$ smooth and $f(0,0)=0$. Recall:

(a) The system is small-time locally controllable at $(0,0)$ if for every $T>0$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\eta>0$ such that for every $x_0,x_1\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with $|x_0|+|x_1|\le\eta$, there is a measurable control $u:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^m$ with $\|u\|_\infty\le\varepsilon$ steering the state from $x_0$ at time $0$ to $x_1$ at time $T$.

(b) The system satisfies the Lie algebra rank condition at $0$ if the Lie algebra generated by the vector fields $x\mapsto f(x,u)$, $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$, evaluated at $0$, equals $\mathbb{R}^n$.

(c) The origin is locally asymptotically stabilizable by means of periodic time-varying feedback if there exist $T>0$ and a continuous map $u:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^m$ with $u(0,t)=0$ and $u(x,t+T)=u(x,t)$ for all $(x,t)$, such that $0$ is a locally asymptotically stable equilibrium of the closed-loop system $\dot x = f(x,u(x,t))$.

For $n\in\{4,5,6,\dots\}$ it is known that (a) and (b) together imply (c). Question: does the same implication hold when $n=2$ or $n=3$? That is, in dimensions two and three, does small-time local controllability together with the Lie algebra rank condition at $0$ imply local asymptotic stabilizability of $0$ by means of a continuous periodic time-varying feedback law?
category_tag: Periodic stabilization of nonlinear control systems
status_search_result: The implication from small-time local controllability (with the Lie algebra rank condition) to local asymptotic stabilizability by continuous periodic time-varying feedback is established for state-space dimensions $n\ge 4$ (Coron). The cases $n=2,3$ remain singled out as open problems in Coron's overview of his main works in control theory; no resolution in dimensions two or three has been located in subsequent literature.

paper_title: Some open problems in control theory.
context_brief: blowup avoidance for nonlinear heat equation
original_question: For a one-dimensional heat equation with a cubic nonlinearity, can the blowup phenomenon be avoided by a suitable control strategy?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the one-dimensional semilinear heat equation with cubic nonlinearity on the bounded interval (0,1):

  y_t(t,x) - y_{xx}(t,x) = y(t,x)^3 + 1_{\omega}(x) u(t,x), \quad (t,x) \in (0,T)\times(0,1),
  y(t,0) = y(t,1) = 0, \quad t \in (0,T),
  y(0,x) = y_0(x), \quad x \in (0,1),

where \omega \subset (0,1) is a fixed nonempty open subinterval (the control region), 1_{\omega} is its indicator function, and u \in L^2((0,T)\times(0,1)) is an internal control supported in \omega. It is known that, in the absence of control (u \equiv 0), there exist smooth initial data y_0 for which the solution y blows up in finite time, i.e., \lim_{t \to T^*} \|y(t,\cdot)\|_{L^\infty(0,1)} = +\infty for some T^* < +\infty.

Question: For every initial datum y_0 (say in H^1_0(0,1) or smoother) and every T>0, does there exist a control u \in L^2((0,T)\times \omega) such that the corresponding solution y of the controlled equation exists globally on [0,T] (i.e., the blowup phenomenon is avoided)?

Equivalently: can the blowup of solutions of the cubic semilinear heat equation in one space dimension always be prevented by a suitable internal control localized on \omega?
status_search_result: Search results indicate active research on controllability and blowup of semilinear heat equations, including feedback controllability of blowup points and prevention-of-blowup results in related settings, but no source clearly resolves the specific question of whether internal controls can prevent blowup for the one-dimensional cubic semilinear heat equation. The status appears to remain open or at least not definitively settled in the literature surveyed.

paper_title: Some open problems in control theory.
original_question: Is the Navier-Stokes equation controllable?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a bounded smooth domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ ($d=2$ or $3$):
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0, \qquad \text{in } (0,T)\times\Omega,$$
with prescribed initial datum $u(0,\cdot)=u_0$ in a suitable function space (e.g.\ $L^2_{\mathrm{div}}(\Omega)$ or $H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\Omega)$), and with the no-slip boundary condition $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, where $\Gamma\subset\partial\Omega$ is a fixed nonempty open subset of the boundary on which one is allowed to prescribe a boundary control $u|_{(0,T)\times\Gamma}=g$ (with $g$ chosen in an appropriate trace space and consistent with incompressibility).

Question: Is the Navier–Stokes system controllable in the following sense? For every $T>0$, every initial state $u_0$, and every target state $u_1$ (in the chosen function space), does there exist a boundary control $g$ on $(0,T)\times\Gamma$ such that the corresponding solution satisfies $u(T,\cdot)=u_1$? Equivalently, decide global exact (or null) controllability of the Navier–Stokes equations under the no-slip boundary condition outside the control region.
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made: local exact controllability is known, and small-time global exact controllability has been established by Coron, Marbach, and Sueur for Navier slip-with-friction boundary conditions (and extensions to curved boundaries). However, the global exact (or null) controllability of the Navier–Stokes equations under the classical no-slip boundary condition on the uncontrolled part of the boundary remains an open problem (a question originally posed by J.-L. Lions).

original_question: If Y is a smooth convex billiard table and the billiard flow on Y is an integrable Hamiltonian system with two degrees of freedom, must Y be an ellipse?
self_contained_problem:
Let $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth, strictly convex domain with smooth boundary $\partial Y$. The billiard flow inside $Y$ is the dynamical system describing a point particle that moves in straight lines inside $Y$ and reflects elastically off $\partial Y$ (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection). This flow can be realized as a Hamiltonian system with two degrees of freedom; equivalently, the associated billiard map on the cylinder of inward-pointing unit tangent vectors based at $\partial Y$ preserves a smooth area form.

The billiard flow on $Y$ is called (Liouville-)integrable if there exists a smooth first integral, functionally independent of the energy on an open set of full measure, that is invariant under the billiard map (so that the phase space is foliated, away from a singular set, by invariant curves on which the dynamics is conjugate to a rotation).

Prove or disprove: if the billiard flow on $Y$ is integrable in the above sense, then $\partial Y$ is an ellipse.
status_search_result: This is the classical Birkhoff conjecture on integrable convex billiards. The full conjecture remains open. Important partial results include: Bialy's theorem (if all of phase space is foliated by invariant curves, the table is a disk); Avila–De Simoi–Kaloshin (nearly circular integrable domains are ellipses, 2016); Kaloshin–Sorrentino's local Birkhoff conjecture for perturbations of ellipses (Annals of Math, 2018); and Bialy–Mironov's result for centrally symmetric domains and Kaloshin et al.'s extension to nearly centrally symmetric domains (GAFA, 2024). The general (non-perturbative) case is unresolved.

original_question: Construct a strictly convex C^1-smooth billiard table with positive entropy, and also construct a convex C^2-smooth billiard table with positive entropy.
self_contained_problem:
Consider planar billiards: given a bounded region $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ whose boundary is a closed convex curve, the billiard map acts on the unit tangent bundle restricted to the boundary by the rule of specular reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection). Known examples of convex billiard tables with positive metric (or topological) entropy include the Bunimovich stadium and its generalizations, whose boundaries are only $C^1$ and fail to be strictly convex (containing straight segments).

Solve the following two construction problems.

(a) Construct a strictly convex billiard table $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ whose boundary is a $C^1$-smooth closed curve and whose billiard map has positive metric entropy with respect to the natural invariant (Liouville) measure.

(b) Construct a convex billiard table $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ whose boundary is a $C^2$-smooth closed curve and whose billiard map has positive metric entropy.
status_search_result: Recent work (Bessa–Dias Carneiro–Pacífico-style and the 2022 result of Bessa et al., "Billiards in generic convex bodies have positive topological entropy") establishes that a $C^2$-open and dense set of smooth convex bodies have billiard maps with a hyperbolic basic set, hence positive topological entropy. This gives genericity-type answers but not an explicit construction; the problem in its strict-convexity $C^1$ form (a) and explicit $C^2$ form (b) remains widely cited as open. Status is best described as partially solved.

original_question: A semi-dispersive billiard table is one whose boundary has dispersive inward-convex components together with neutral components such as line segments. Is every semi-dispersive billiard table hyperbolic?
self_contained_problem:
A planar billiard table is a compact, connected region $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with piecewise smooth boundary $\partial Y$, on which the billiard flow is defined by free motion in the interior together with elastic reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) at smooth points of the boundary. A boundary component is called dispersive if it is smooth and strictly convex when viewed from the inside of $Y$ (so that it scatters parallel beams of trajectories), and neutral if it is a straight line segment. Call $Y$ a semi-dispersive billiard table if every smooth component of $\partial Y$ is either dispersive or neutral, and at least one component is dispersive.

The billiard flow is called hyperbolic if it has nonzero Lyapunov exponents almost everywhere with respect to the natural invariant (Liouville) measure on the unit tangent bundle restricted to $Y$.

Question: Is every semi-dispersive billiard table (in the above sense) hyperbolic?
status_search_result: A targeted search returned the original problem listing and general literature on semi-dispersing billiards (hard ball systems, Boltzmann–Sinai hypothesis, transversal fundamental theorem). No source was found that explicitly resolves the question of whether every planar semi-dispersive billiard table (dispersive arcs plus neutral line-segment components) is hyperbolic. The status therefore appears unverified from available sources.

original_question: If the limit h = lim_{n -> infinity} log f_Y(n) / n exists for a hyperbolic billiard table Y, must this finite positive number coincide with the topological entropy of the billiard map?
self_contained_problem:
Let $Y$ be a hyperbolic billiard table (a planar billiard table whose associated billiard map on the boundary phase space is hyperbolic, e.g. a Sinai dispersing billiard or a Bunimovich-type billiard). Assume that the set of periodic points of any given period of the billiard map is finite, and let $f_Y(n)$ denote the number of periodic points whose minimal period is at most $n$. Suppose that the limit
$$h \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\log f_Y(n)}{n}$$
exists and satisfies $0 < h < \infty$. Must $h$ equal the topological entropy of the billiard map?

original_question: Does there exist an irrational polygon whose billiard flow is not ergodic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a simple polygon. The billiard flow on $P$ is the dynamical system describing a point particle moving in straight lines inside $P$ at unit speed and reflecting off the boundary $\partial P$ according to the law of equal angles (and undefined at vertices). This flow preserves Liouville (Lebesgue) measure on the unit tangent bundle $P\times S^1$. The polygon $P$ is called rational if every interior angle is a rational multiple of $\pi$, and irrational otherwise. The billiard flow is ergodic if every flow-invariant measurable subset of the phase space has either zero or full Liouville measure.

Construct an explicit example of an irrational polygon $P$ (i.e., a simple polygon at least one of whose interior angles is an irrational multiple of $\pi$) whose billiard flow is not ergodic with respect to Liouville measure; equivalently, decide whether such a polygon exists.
status_search_result: The problem of exhibiting an irrational polygon whose billiard flow fails to be ergodic appears to remain open. Surveys on polygonal billiards (e.g., Masur–Tabachnikov; Schwartz's ICM survey; the blog post "On the ergodicity of billiards in non-rational polygons") describe the ergodicity question for irrational polygons as unresolved, with no known theorem confirming or precluding ergodicity in general and no explicit nonergodic example.

original_question: Does every polygon admit at least one periodic billiard orbit?
self_contained_problem:
A billiard trajectory in a polygon $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ is the trajectory of a point particle moving in straight lines inside $P$ and reflecting off the boundary according to the law of equal angles (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection); trajectories that hit a vertex are considered undefined at that point. Such a trajectory is called periodic if, after finitely many reflections, the particle returns to its initial position with its initial direction.

Question: Does every polygon $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ (i.e. every simply connected planar region bounded by finitely many line segments) admit at least one periodic billiard trajectory?
status_search_result: The general question remains open. Known partial results: Fagnano (1775) gave a periodic orbit in every acute triangle; Masur (1986) established existence of periodic orbits in every rational polygon (all angles rational multiples of π); Holt (1993) handled right triangles; and Schwartz proved existence for every obtuse triangle whose angles are all at most 100°. The case of general (irrational) polygons, and even general obtuse triangles, is still unresolved.

original_question: For a rational polygon P, the quadratic constants c_*(P) and c^*(P) are defined by inequalities c_*(P) l^2 <= f_P(l) <= c^*(P) l^2 for all sufficiently large l. Find efficient estimates for these quadratic constants.
self_contained_problem:
Let P be a rational polygon, that is, a polygon in the Euclidean plane all of whose interior angles are rational multiples of π. A billiard trajectory in P is the path of a point mass moving in straight lines inside P and reflecting from the boundary according to the law of equal angles (with trajectories hitting a vertex left undefined). A periodic billiard trajectory is one that closes up after finitely many reflections; periodic trajectories occur in parallel families ("strips") of equal length, and one defines

  f_P(ℓ) = number of strips of periodic billiard trajectories in P of length at most ℓ.

It is known that there exist constants 0 < c_*(P) ≤ c^*(P) < ∞ such that

  c_*(P) ℓ^2  ≤  f_P(ℓ)  ≤  c^*(P) ℓ^2

for all sufficiently large ℓ. The numbers c_*(P) and c^*(P) are called the quadratic constants of P.

Problem: Provide efficient (computable, sharp, or otherwise quantitatively useful) estimates for the quadratic constants c_*(P) and c^*(P) of a rational polygon P. In particular, give methods that, for as wide a class of rational polygons as possible, produce explicit upper and lower bounds on c_*(P) and c^*(P), and ideally identify the limit c(P) = lim_{ℓ→∞} f_P(ℓ)/ℓ^2 when it exists.
status_search_result: The quadratic bounds on the counting function f_P(ℓ) for periodic billiard orbits in rational polygons are due to Masur (existence of quadratic upper and lower bounds). Exact asymptotics (Siegel–Veech-type constants) are known only for special families (e.g., Veech polygons such as the regular n-gons and lattice surfaces), where c_*(P) = c^*(P) = c(P) can be computed via Eskin–Masur–Zorich theory. For a general rational polygon, no efficient or sharp estimates of c_*(P), c^*(P) are known, and the problem of computing or bounding them effectively is widely regarded as open.

original_question: Let F_*(n) denote a partial billiard complexity obtained by coding only orbit families satisfying additional restrictions; for example, periodic complexity counts periodic-orbit codes. Find nontrivial explicit bounds on such partial billiard complexities for a general polygon.
self_contained_problem:
Let $P$ be a polygon in the plane and consider the billiard flow on $P$: a point particle moves in straight lines inside $P$ and reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) on the sides, with trajectories meeting a vertex left undefined. Code each billiard orbit by the sequence of sides it hits, so that a finite trajectory of combinatorial length $n$ corresponds to a word of length $n$ in the alphabet of sides of $P$. The (full) billiard complexity $F(n)$ is the number of distinct admissible words of length $n$ realized by some billiard orbit in $P$.

A partial billiard complexity $F_*(n)$ is obtained by counting only those length-$n$ codes that come from orbits satisfying a prescribed restriction. Important examples include:
- the periodic complexity $f_P(n)$, the number of distinct codes of length $n$ realized by periodic billiard orbits in $P$;
- complexities counting only codes of orbits that are uniformly distributed, only codes of saddle connections, or only codes avoiding a prescribed subset of sides; and other natural restrictions.

Problem. For a general (not necessarily rational) polygon $P$, find nontrivial, explicit upper and/or lower bounds, as functions of $n$, for partial billiard complexities $F_*(n)$. In particular, give explicit nontrivial bounds for the periodic complexity $f_P(n)$ valid for every polygon $P$.
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., 2023–2025 papers on the complexity of polygonal billiards) establishes cubic complexity bounds for rational and typical polygons and superlinear lower bounds on periodic complexity for certain irrational polygons, but no explicit nontrivial bounds for partial billiard complexities of a general polygon are known. The problem of finding such bounds is still listed as open in surveys on polygonal billiards.

original_question: Does there exist an integer d >= 3 such that for every polygon the full billiard complexity has a cubic lower bound and also an upper bound by a polynomial of degree d?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a polygon (a connected planar region bounded by finitely many straight segments). The billiard flow on $P$ is the geodesic flow of a point particle moving with unit speed inside $P$ and reflecting elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) at each side; trajectories meeting a vertex are undefined. Label the sides of $P$ by symbols from a finite alphabet $\mathcal{A}$. To each (one-sided or two-sided) billiard trajectory associate the infinite word over $\mathcal{A}$ recording the labels of the sides hit in order. The full billiard complexity $f_P(n)$ is defined as the number of distinct words of length $n$ that occur as factors of any such trajectory in $P$.

Question: Does there exist an integer $d\ge 3$ such that, for every polygon $P$, there are constants $c_1=c_1(P)>0$, $c_2=c_2(P)>0$ and an integer $n_0=n_0(P)$ with
$$c_1\, n^3 \;\le\; f_P(n)\;\le\; c_2\, n^d \qquad\text{for all } n\ge n_0\,?$$
status_search_result: Recent work establishes cubic complexity growth for typical/rational polygons and obtains polynomial lower bounds for special families (e.g., almost every right triangle), but a uniform polynomial upper bound of fixed degree d valid for every polygon, together with a cubic lower bound for every polygon, has not been proved. The conjecture appears to remain open, with only partial progress.

original_question: For a compact smooth Riemannian manifold, is security equivalent to flatness? In other words, is every secure compact smooth Riemannian manifold flat, and every flat one secure?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold. For points $x,y \in M$, let $\Gamma(x,y)$ denote the set of geodesic segments in $M$ from $x$ to $y$. A finite set $B \subset M \setminus \{x,y\}$ is called a blocking set for the pair $(x,y)$ if every geodesic segment in $\Gamma(x,y)$ passes through at least one point of $B$. The pair $(x,y)$ is called secure if there exists a finite blocking set for it. The manifold $(M,g)$ is called secure if every pair of points $(x,y) \in M \times M$ is secure.

The manifold $(M,g)$ is called flat if its sectional curvature vanishes identically.

It is known that every compact flat Riemannian manifold is secure. Prove or disprove: a compact smooth Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is secure if and only if it is flat.
status_search_result: The conjecture that a compact smooth Riemannian manifold is secure iff it is flat remains open in general. Partial results are known: compact flat manifolds are secure; compact nonpositively curved manifolds with the finite blocking property are flat (Burns–Gutkin, Lafont–Schmidt); and 2-dimensional secure tori are flat (Bangert–Gutkin, 2008). The full conjecture in arbitrary dimension and curvature is not resolved.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Continuous measurement-based feedback versus direct coherent feedback
original_question: For a quantum system controlled either by continuous measurement-based feedback or by coherent feedback implemented through direct system-auxiliary coupling, what is the exact relationship between the two control paradigms when both are given the same dissipative resources? Is coherent feedback through direct coupling superior to continuous measurement-based feedback under those conditions, and if it is superior, does the advantage remain when the added dissipative resources are removed?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum system S (the "primary" system) coupled to an auxiliary quantum system A, with the goal of stabilizing, preparing, or otherwise controlling the state of S. Two distinct feedback paradigms are available:

(i) Continuous measurement-based feedback: A is continuously measured (a Markovian, irreversible coupling that produces a classical measurement record), and the measurement record is used in real time to modulate Hamiltonian or other parameters acting on S. Mathematically the joint evolution is described by a stochastic master equation conditioned on the measurement record, with an actuation Hamiltonian H_c(t) that is a (causal) functional of the record.

(ii) Coherent feedback via direct system–auxiliary coupling: S and A are coupled only through a unitary (Hamiltonian) interaction H_SA, with no measurement performed. The reduced dynamics of S are obtained by tracing over A, and any irreversible (dissipative) channels acting on A or S are specified explicitly as part of the model.

Assume that in both paradigms the same dissipative resources are available: i.e., the same Lindblad dissipators acting on S and A (with the same rates) are present, so that the only structural difference between the two setups is whether the S–A coupling is mediated by measurement-plus-classical-control or by a direct Hamiltonian interaction.

Questions:
(a) Determine the precise mathematical relationship between paradigms (i) and (ii) under this matched-resource assumption. Specifically, characterize the set of completely positive trace-preserving evolutions of S that can be realized by (i) and the set realizable by (ii), and determine whether one set is contained in the other.

(b) Decide whether paradigm (ii) is strictly superior to paradigm (i) for some control task (for example, achieving strictly higher steady-state fidelity to a target state, or strictly faster convergence) when both have access to the same dissipative resources.

(c) If (ii) is strictly superior in part (b), determine whether this superiority persists when the shared dissipative resources are removed, i.e., when in (ii) only the unitary S–A coupling (and the intrinsic dissipation of S) is retained while in (i) only the measurement of A and the corresponding classical actuation on S is retained.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made on comparing coherent and measurement-based feedback. For linear quantum systems, work by Yamamoto (2014) shows coherent feedback can exactly match measurement-based feedback performance with ideal controllers and can also achieve tasks measurement-based feedback cannot. Experimental and theoretical comparisons (e.g., Liu et al., Phys. Rev. X 6, 011022 (2016)) study driven-dissipative vs. measurement-based entanglement stabilization, and other works (e.g., Phys. Rev. A 97, 062341) replace measurement feedback by coherent feedback for state preparation. However, a fully general resource-matched characterization for arbitrary nonlinear quantum systems—including the question of whether coherent feedback's advantage persists once shared dissipative resources are removed—does not appear to be settled in full generality, so the problem as posed is partially solved.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Measurement restrictions and geodesic entropy extraction
original_question: For feedback protocols implemented through irreversible coupling, can one quantitatively characterize how much performance is lost when the controller is restricted to measurement followed by conditional feedback, and can that loss be related to geodesic evolutions in the joint system-auxiliary Hilbert space that extract entropy as quickly as possible?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum system $S$ coupled to an auxiliary quantum system $A$, both modeled on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_S$ and $\mathcal{H}_A$, with joint Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_S \otimes \mathcal{H}_A$. Two cooling/feedback paradigms are compared:

(i) Coherent Feedback Control (CFC): a unitary interaction $U(t) = \exp(-i H t)$ generated by a Hamiltonian $H$ on $\mathcal{H}_S \otimes \mathcal{H}_A$, with a fixed bound $\|H\| \le E$ on its operator norm, that transfers entropy from $S$ to $A$. Under such a norm bound, the quickest possible extraction of all entropy from $S$ into $A$ is achieved when the joint pure state of $S\otimes A$ evolves along a geodesic of the Fubini–Study metric on the projective Hilbert space $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{H}_S \otimes \mathcal{H}_A)$.

(ii) Measurement-and-Feedback Control (MFC): the controller is restricted to (a) performing a (possibly generalized) measurement on $A$ after a system–auxiliary interaction, and (b) applying a unitary on $S$ conditioned on the classical outcome.

For an arbitrary initial state $\rho_S$ of the system (with the auxiliary prepared in a fixed pure reference state) and a fixed Hamiltonian energy budget $\|H\|\le E$ for any system–auxiliary coupling used, define the cooling time $T_{\mathrm{CFC}}(\rho_S, E, \varepsilon)$ (resp. $T_{\mathrm{MFC}}(\rho_S, E, \varepsilon)$) as the infimum over admissible CFC (resp. MFC) protocols of the time required to bring $S$ to a state with von Neumann entropy at most $\varepsilon$.

Problem. Provide a quantitative characterization of the gap
$$\Delta(\rho_S, E, \varepsilon) \;=\; T_{\mathrm{MFC}}(\rho_S, E, \varepsilon) \;-\; T_{\mathrm{CFC}}(\rho_S, E, \varepsilon),$$
i.e. the performance loss incurred by restricting the controller from coherent feedback through irreversible coupling to measurement-plus-conditional-feedback. In particular, derive sharp lower (and, if possible, matching upper) bounds on $\Delta$ expressed in terms of geometric data of the joint Hilbert space — for example, the Fubini–Study length of the optimal CFC geodesic that extracts entropy from $S$ and a quantitative measure of how far MFC trajectories must deviate from such geodesics — and characterize the protocols (if any) for which the bound is saturated.
status_search_result: Searches for a quantitative comparison between measurement-based feedback and coherent (irreversible-coupling) feedback in terms of geodesic entropy extraction in the joint system–auxiliary Hilbert space did not turn up a definitive resolution. Related literature on measurement-based quantum thermal machines and quantum feedback control discusses performance trade-offs but does not appear to provide a sharp geometric characterization of the loss as posed. Status is therefore reported as unknown.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
original_question: Because coherent feedback implemented by unitary system-auxiliary interactions is naturally periodic rather than continuously dissipative, what forms of Hamiltonian are needed to realize continuous or quasi-continuous quantum feedback control, and in which regimes can one derive simple analytic formulas for the resulting steady-state control performance?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum control setting in which a target quantum system, with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_S$, is coupled to an auxiliary quantum system ("controller"), with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A$, by a joint unitary interaction $U(t) = \exp(-i H_{SA} t/\hbar)$ on $\mathcal{H}_S \otimes \mathcal{H}_A$ generated by a (possibly time-dependent) Hamiltonian $H_{SA}$. Such "coherent feedback" via unitary system–auxiliary interactions is intrinsically periodic: in the absence of dissipation or reset of the auxiliary, the joint evolution recurs and does not by itself generate a non-trivial steady state on the system alone.

Formulate and answer the following:

(a) Characterize the classes of joint Hamiltonians $H_{SA}$ (possibly augmented by repeated re-initialization, weak-coupling limits, continuous exchange of an auxiliary bath mode, or similar mechanisms) that yield genuinely continuous or quasi-continuous coherent feedback dynamics on the reduced state $\rho_S(t) = \mathrm{Tr}_A[\,U(t)(\rho_S(0)\otimes\rho_A)U(t)^\dagger\,]$, in the sense that $\rho_S(t)$ obeys an autonomous master equation (Lindblad-type or otherwise) admitting a non-trivial steady state $\rho_S^{\mathrm{ss}}$.

(b) Identify regimes — for example, weak coupling, fast re-initialization of the auxiliary, Markovian limits, or linear (Gaussian) systems — in which closed-form analytic expressions for the steady-state performance (such as fidelity to a target state, purity, entanglement, or a quadratic cost) of the resulting coherent-feedback loop can be derived, and exhibit such expressions.
status_search_result: The general question of which Hamiltonians realize quasi-continuous coherent feedback and when closed-form steady-state performance exists remains open. Partial progress exists: for linear (Gaussian) quantum systems, coherent $H^\infty$/LQG frameworks yield analytic controller designs via Lyapunov/Riccati equations, and recent work has produced closed-form steady-state covariance results under continuous monitoring with unitary feedback. However, no general theory characterizing the required Hamiltonians or yielding analytic steady-state performance beyond linear or weak-coupling regimes has been established.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Limits of linear networks for quantum error correction
original_question: For linear quantum systems coupled irreversibly through quantum fields, also called quantum linear networks, can one prove that such linear networks cannot implement quantum error correction, meaning correction of errors on arbitrary unknown quantum states?
self_contained_problem:
Consider linear quantum systems that are coupled irreversibly to one another through bosonic quantum fields (quantum linear networks). Concretely, such a system consists of a finite collection of quantum harmonic oscillators with quadratic Hamiltonians and linear couplings to input/output bosonic field channels, governed by quantum stochastic differential equations whose Heisenberg dynamics preserve the linear span of the canonical position and momentum (quadrature) operators. Quantum error correction means a procedure that, given an arbitrary unknown quantum state subjected to an error from a specified error class, recovers the original state without requiring prior knowledge of that state.

Problem: Prove (or disprove) that no quantum linear network of the above form can implement quantum error correction; that is, show that within the class of linear quantum systems coupled through quantum fields there exists no encoding-decoding scheme capable of correcting errors on arbitrary unknown quantum states.
status_search_result: A targeted search did not surface a definitive impossibility theorem establishing that linear quantum networks cannot perform quantum error correction on arbitrary unknown states. Related work investigates passive error correction of linear optics networks via unitary/error averaging and feedback-based schemes, but these address restricted error/state classes rather than refuting or confirming the general impossibility claim. The status therefore appears unresolved in the publicly available literature found.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Time-dependent control in linear feedback networks
original_question: In linear feedback networks, how much performance improvement is obtained by adding time-dependent external control to systems and couplings that have usually been treated as time-independent, and how does the size of that improvement vary across different classes of quantum-control problems?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a linear quantum feedback network: a collection of quantum systems whose internal dynamics are generated by quadratic Hamiltonians in canonical bosonic mode operators, interconnected through linear coupling channels (e.g., a cascaded or feedback configuration of input-output systems described by quantum stochastic differential equations of Hudson–Parthasarathy type). In the standard setting the system Hamiltonians H_k and the inter-system coupling operators L_{kj} are time-independent, and one optimizes a control performance functional J (for example, steady-state cooling, squeezing generation, state stabilization fidelity, entanglement production rate, or LQG-type cost) over the choice of these time-independent parameters.

Now allow each H_k(t) and each coupling L_{kj}(t) to depend on time, subject to the same physical admissibility constraints (e.g., quadratic in mode operators, bounded coupling strengths). Define the performance gap

  Δ(P) = sup_{time-dependent admissible networks} J(P) − sup_{time-independent admissible networks} J(P),

for a given class P of linear-feedback-network control problems.

(a) Quantify Δ(P): provide rigorous upper and lower bounds on the achievable improvement obtained by introducing time-dependent external control of the Hamiltonians and couplings, as a function of the network size, available control bandwidth, and the cost functional J.

(b) Determine how Δ(P) varies across natural classes P of such control problems (e.g., state preparation, dissipation engineering, parameter estimation, noise rejection, robust stabilization), identifying classes where time dependence yields strictly greater performance and, if any, classes where time-independent networks are optimal.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
original_question: In the regime of good quantum control, what are the optimal control protocols when the auxiliary controller itself experiences significant damping, so that the controller is not an ideal noiseless auxiliary?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum system $S$ with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_S$ that is to be controlled via coherent (i.e., non-measurement-based) feedback. The controller is an auxiliary quantum system $A$ with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A$, coupled to $S$ via some interaction Hamiltonian $H_{SA}$ together with possible time-dependent control Hamiltonians $H_c(t)$ acting on $S\otimes A$. Assume the joint system evolves according to a Markovian master equation
$$\dot{\rho} = -i[H_S + H_A + H_{SA} + H_c(t),\rho] + \mathcal{D}_S[\rho] + \gamma\,\mathcal{D}_A[\rho],$$
where $\mathcal{D}_S$ is a (possibly weak) dissipator on $S$ and $\mathcal{D}_A$ is a Lindblad dissipator acting only on the auxiliary $A$ with damping rate $\gamma>0$ that is not negligible (so that the controller itself is significantly noisy and cannot be treated as an ideal noiseless ancilla). Work in the "regime of good control," meaning the coherent control of $S$ alone (in the absence of the controller's damping) would achieve high-fidelity performance for a given task such as state preparation, gate implementation, or stabilization of a target state $\rho_{\mathrm{tgt}}$.

Problem: Determine the optimal coherent feedback control protocols — i.e., the optimal choices of $H_{SA}$, $H_c(t)$, and the structure of the auxiliary $A$ — that maximize task fidelity (e.g., $\mathrm{Tr}[\rho_S(T)\rho_{\mathrm{tgt}}]$ at a final time $T$, or steady-state fidelity) when the auxiliary controller itself is subject to significant damping at rate $\gamma$. Characterize how the optimal protocol and the achievable fidelity depend on $\gamma$ and on the structure of $\mathcal{D}_A$.
status_search_result: Recent literature (e.g., learning-based LQG design for quantum coherent feedback, 2025; reviews of optimal quantum control) indicates that no closed-form optimal coherent feedback protocols are known when the auxiliary controller itself is significantly damped; numerical optimization yields only local optima due to nonconvex realizability constraints. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
original_question: How does noise in the time-dependent control Hamiltonian H(t) affect the fidelity of a quantum-control protocol, and can noise in the Hamiltonian that applies control be handled by the same methods used to handle noise in the auxiliary controller?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a finite-dimensional quantum system S coupled to an auxiliary quantum system A, with combined Hilbert space H = H_S ⊗ H_A. The joint evolution is governed by a time-dependent control Hamiltonian H(t) acting on H, whose role is to steer the evolution of S so as to implement a target unitary (or, more generally, a target completely positive trace-preserving map) U_target on S with high fidelity. Given an initial state ρ(0) on H, the realized evolution is the unitary propagator U(T) = T exp(-i ∫_0^T H(t) dt), and the achieved fidelity is measured by some standard fidelity functional F(U(T), U_target).

Suppose now that two independent sources of noise are present:
(i) noise on the auxiliary system A (e.g. stochastic perturbations of A's free Hamiltonian, or coupling of A to an external bath, modeled by a Lindblad dissipator L_A acting on A); and
(ii) noise on the control Hamiltonian itself, modeled by replacing H(t) with H(t) + δH(t), where δH(t) is a stochastic operator-valued process (for instance Gaussian white noise on the control amplitudes, multiplicative noise on each control field, or pulse-shape distortion).

Provide a quantitative analysis of the following:

1. Derive an expression (or rigorous bounds) for the expected loss of fidelity E[1 - F(U(T), U_target)] as a functional of the statistical properties (mean, covariance, spectral density) of δH(t), for a given control protocol H(t).

2. Determine whether noise of type (ii) on the control Hamiltonian can be suppressed or compensated by the same techniques (e.g. dynamical decoupling, optimal-control robustification, filter-function methods, decoherence-free subspaces, quantum error correction on the auxiliary) that are used to handle noise of type (i) on the auxiliary system, and characterize the regimes (noise spectrum, control bandwidth, protocol duration T) in which such a unified treatment is possible or provably impossible.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as one of twenty open problems in quantum control and remains open in the general form stated. While there is extensive literature on robust optimal control, filter functions, and dynamical decoupling addressing control-field noise, no comprehensive resolution unifying control-Hamiltonian noise with auxiliary-system noise has been established. No source confirms a definitive solution.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
original_question: For open-loop quantum control, where the task is to vary a Hamiltonian H = sum_n c_n H_n in time to obtain a desired evolution, which control objectives and which available sets of control Hamiltonians H_n make the control problem easy, with the time-dependent-control complexity scaling polynomially in the logarithm of the system size? Does the class of easy objectives depend nontrivially on the chosen set of available Hamiltonians?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an open-loop quantum control setting in which a quantum system of Hilbert-space dimension N evolves under a time-dependent Hamiltonian of the form
   H(t) = Σ_n c_n(t) H_n,
where {H_n} is a fixed finite set of Hermitian "control Hamiltonians" available to the experimenter, and the real-valued coefficients c_n: [0,T] → ℝ are classical control functions that may be varied essentially arbitrarily in time. A control objective is a specification of a desired property of the resulting unitary evolution U(T) = T-exp(−i ∫₀ᵀ H(t) dt) (for example, implementing a target unitary up to a prescribed accuracy, or steering an initial state to a target state).

Define the "time-dependent-control complexity" of an objective, given a control set {H_n}, to be the minimum description complexity (e.g., piecewise-constant pulse count plus bit-precision, or any equivalent reasonable measure) of a control schedule {c_n(t)} that achieves the objective. Call the control problem "easy" for a given pair (objective, {H_n}) if this complexity scales polynomially in log N as N → ∞.

Characterize, as completely as possible, the pairs (control objective, set of available control Hamiltonians {H_n}) for which the open-loop control problem is easy in the above sense. In particular, determine whether the class of "easy" objectives depends nontrivially on the choice of the available set {H_n}: i.e., do there exist objectives that are easy for some admissible control sets but provably not easy for others?

A general characterization of "easy" open-loop control objectives in terms of polylog(N) control complexity remains an active research topic (related to quantum compiling, Solovay–Kitaev-type results, and quantum speed limits), but no comprehensive answer has been established in the literature, and no source claims a resolution of this specific question.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Feedforward control in mesoscopic quantum systems
original_question: Are there situations in mesoscopic quantum systems where feedforward control is useful, where feedforward means that the controller receives information about the noise realization without interacting with the system rather than obtaining information only through the system as in feedback control? If such situations exist, what explicit examples demonstrate the feedforward-control paradigm, and how does feedforward control compare with feedback control in those examples?
self_contained_problem:
Consider open quantum systems in the mesoscopic regime, modeled as quantum systems coupled to an environment that produces noise affecting the system's dynamics. In the standard feedback paradigm, a controller obtains information about the system only by performing measurements on the system itself (or on its output field) and uses that information to adjust the system's Hamiltonian or dissipators. By contrast, define feedforward control as any control scheme in which the controller receives information about the realization of the environmental noise without interacting with the system, and then uses this information (for example, by applying a Hamiltonian or unitary correction conditioned on the noise realization) to steer the system toward a desired target.

Address the following:

(a) Exhibit explicit physical scenarios in mesoscopic quantum systems (e.g., superconducting circuits, quantum dots, optomechanical or nanomechanical devices, mesoscopic quantum transport setups) in which such feedforward control is meaningful and yields a control advantage. For each scenario, specify:
   - the system Hamiltonian and noise model (e.g., a stochastic classical field, a measured ancillary bath mode, or a probed environmental degree of freedom),
   - the precise mechanism by which the controller acquires information about the noise without disturbing the system,
   - the control law mapping noise records to actuation on the system,
   - a quantitative figure of merit (such as fidelity to a target state, gate error, stabilization rate, or transport current) demonstrating the benefit.

(b) For each example, compare quantitatively the achievable performance of feedforward control with that of optimal measurement-based feedback control acting on the same system under the same noise model, and identify regimes (in coupling strength, bandwidth, measurement efficiency, or noise spectrum) where one paradigm strictly outperforms the other.

(c) Determine whether there exist mesoscopic quantum control problems for which feedforward control is provably useful — i.e., achieves a strictly better figure of merit than any feedback strategy — or, conversely, prove that no such advantage is possible in a specified class of models.
status_search_result: While various works since 2013 have explored feedforward operations in photonic and superconducting platforms (e.g., one-way quantum computing with active feed-forward, quantum teleportation, electro-optic feedforward loops, and coherent feedback in mesoscopic transport), no comprehensive resolution of the open question — systematically identifying mesoscopic quantum settings where feedforward outperforms feedback and providing a general comparative framework — appears in the literature. The status of the original problem as a research program therefore remains unresolved as a whole.

paper_title: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation on graphs: recent results and open problems
original_question: Let a graph be obtained as a limit of a network of thin tubes or guides joined at junctions, and let a nonlinear Schrödinger equation be posed on the shrinking tube system before the limit is taken. Does the vanishing-transverse-size limit produce a nonlinear Schrödinger equation on the limiting graph, and if so, which vertex boundary conditions appear at the junction? More specifically, how do the limiting vertex conditions depend on the way the tubes and junction are shrunk and on the boundary conditions imposed on the tube walls, such as Neumann or Dirichlet conditions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a metric graph $\mathcal{G}$ realized as the singular limit of a family $\{\Omega_\varepsilon\}_{\varepsilon>0}$ of three-dimensional (or two-dimensional) "fat" domains consisting of thin tubes of transverse size $\varepsilon$ glued at junction regions, the tubes shrinking to the edges of $\mathcal{G}$ and the junctions to its vertices as $\varepsilon\to 0$. On each $\Omega_\varepsilon$ pose the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation
$$ i\,\partial_t \psi_\varepsilon = -\Delta \psi_\varepsilon + \kappa\,|\psi_\varepsilon|^{2\sigma}\psi_\varepsilon \quad\text{in } \Omega_\varepsilon, $$
with prescribed boundary conditions on $\partial\Omega_\varepsilon$ (for instance, Neumann or Dirichlet on the lateral walls of the tubes), where $\kappa\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\sigma>0$ are fixed.

(a) Show (or determine the conditions under which it is true) that as $\varepsilon\to 0$ suitably rescaled solutions $\psi_\varepsilon$ converge to a function $\psi$ defined on the metric graph $\mathcal{G}$, and that $\psi$ satisfies a nonlinear Schrödinger equation
$$ i\,\partial_t \psi = -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}} \psi + \kappa'\,|\psi|^{2\sigma}\psi \quad \text{on each edge of } \mathcal{G}, $$
where $\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$ is the edgewise Laplacian and the wave function satisfies certain self-adjoint vertex (matching) conditions at every vertex $v$ of $\mathcal{G}$.

(b) Identify which family of self-adjoint vertex conditions (e.g., Kirchhoff/standard, $\delta$-type, $\delta'$-type, decoupled Dirichlet, or more general $U(d_v)$-parametrized couplings, where $d_v$ is the degree of $v$) is selected in the limit, and characterize the dependence of these vertex conditions on:
   (i) the geometry and rate of shrinking of the junction relative to the tubes (e.g., relative scaling of junction volume vs.\ tube cross-section);
   (ii) the boundary condition imposed on the lateral walls of the tubes (Neumann vs.\ Dirichlet, or mixed);
   (iii) the nonlinearity exponent $\sigma$ and sign of $\kappa$.
category_tag: NLS on metric graphs / thin-tube limits
status_search_result: In the linear setting, the thin-tube approximation problem is well-developed: any self-adjoint vertex coupling on a quantum graph can be approximated by Schrödinger operators on shrinking branched manifolds (e.g., Exner–Post-type results). For the genuinely nonlinear NLS case, however, only partial and model-specific results exist (Ginzburg–Landau reductions, transparent vertex conditions for solitons in Y-junctions and tubular networks studied numerically/heuristically). A full rigorous derivation of NLS on a metric graph as the vanishing-transverse-size limit of NLS on fat graphs, together with classification of the resulting vertex conditions in terms of junction geometry and lateral boundary conditions, does not appear to be available; the problem is generally regarded as open.

paper_title: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation on graphs: recent results and open problems
original_question: Is the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on trees well posed? More precisely, for a tree graph equipped with the relevant vertex coupling conditions, can one prove existence, uniqueness, and appropriate continuous dependence for solutions in the natural energy spaces, analogous to the well-posedness theory available for the star-graph case?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a metric tree graph: a finite or locally finite connected graph with no cycles, in which each edge $e$ is identified with an interval $[0,\ell_e]$ (with $\ell_e\in(0,\infty]$ for unbounded edges), so that $\mathcal{T}$ is a one-dimensional metric space. A function $u:\mathcal{T}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ is identified with a collection $\{u_e\}_{e}$ of functions on the edges. Equip $\mathcal{T}$ with Kirchhoff (free) vertex coupling: at every vertex $v$, the function values along incident edges agree, and the sum of the outgoing derivatives vanishes,
$$\sum_{e\succ v} \partial_e u_e(v,t) = 0.$$
Let $H^1(\mathcal{T})$ denote the energy space of continuous functions on $\mathcal{T}$ whose restriction to each edge belongs to $H^1$, with the natural Hilbertian norm. Consider the Cauchy problem for the nonlinear Schrödinger equation
$$ i\,\partial_t u(x,t) = -\Delta_{\mathcal{T}}\, u(x,t) + \kappa\, |u(x,t)|^{p-1} u(x,t),\qquad x\in\mathcal{T},\ t\in\mathbb{R}, $$
where $\Delta_{\mathcal{T}}$ is the edgewise Laplacian with the Kirchhoff vertex conditions above, $\kappa\in\{-1,+1\}$ is the focusing/defocusing sign, and $p>1$ is energy-subcritical, with initial datum $u(\cdot,0)=u_0\in H^1(\mathcal{T})$.

Prove (or disprove) that this Cauchy problem is well posed in the energy space $H^1(\mathcal{T})$: namely, that for every $u_0\in H^1(\mathcal{T})$ there exists a unique solution $u\in C([0,T);H^1(\mathcal{T}))$ on a maximal time interval depending only on $\|u_0\|_{H^1(\mathcal{T})}$, that the solution depends continuously on the initial datum, and that the mass $\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^2(\mathcal{T})}^2$ and the energy
$$E(u) = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_e \int_0^{\ell_e} |\partial_x u_e|^2\,dx + \tfrac{\kappa}{p+1}\sum_e \int_0^{\ell_e} |u_e|^{p+1}\,dx$$
are conserved along the flow, in analogy with the corresponding well-posedness theory available on a star graph.
status_search_result: Local and global well-posedness of the energy-subcritical NLS in the energy space $H^1$ on general (noncompact) metric graphs—including trees—with Kirchhoff vertex conditions has by now been established as a standard fact, following the Cazenave-style argument combined with the Sobolev embedding $H^1(\mathcal{G})\hookrightarrow L^\infty(\mathcal{G})$ for metric graphs. It is routinely invoked, e.g., in the literature on ground states and standing waves for NLS on metric graphs (Adami–Serra–Tilli and many subsequent works), and in studies of NLS on specific tree-like graphs (tadpole, star, trees).

paper_title: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation on graphs: recent results and open problems
original_question: Can the orbital-stability and instability analysis for standing waves of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation be extended from star graphs to more complex graphs, such as trees or graphs with loops? In such settings, where explicit formulas for stationary states are generally unavailable, can one still identify standing-wave branches and verify the spectral and variational conditions needed to prove stability or instability?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a metric graph, that is, a finite or countable collection of edges (each identified with a closed interval $[0,\ell_e]$, $\ell_e\in(0,\infty]$) glued at vertices. On $\mathcal{G}$ consider the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation
$$ i\,\partial_t \Psi(t,x) = -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}\,\Psi(t,x) - |\Psi(t,x)|^{2\sigma}\Psi(t,x),\qquad x\in\mathcal{G},\ \sigma>0, $$
where $\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$ is the Laplacian on $\mathcal{G}$ acting edgewise as $d^2/dx^2$ with Kirchhoff (or another self-adjoint) coupling at each vertex: continuity of $\Psi$ across the vertex and vanishing of the sum of outgoing derivatives. Standing waves are solutions of the form $\Psi(t,x)=e^{i\omega t}\Phi_\omega(x)$ with $\omega>0$, where the profile $\Phi_\omega$ solves the stationary equation
$$ -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}\Phi_\omega + \omega \Phi_\omega - |\Phi_\omega|^{2\sigma}\Phi_\omega = 0 $$
together with the vertex coupling. Orbital stability is understood in the standard sense: the orbit $\{e^{i\theta}\Phi_\omega:\theta\in\mathbb{R}\}$ is stable in $H^1(\mathcal{G})$ under the NLS flow.

For star graphs (finitely many half-lines meeting at a single vertex), all stationary states can be written in closed form via solitons and Jacobi elliptic functions, and orbital stability/instability of the resulting branches has been analyzed by spectral and variational techniques (Vakhitov–Kolokolov / Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss criteria together with a count of negative eigenvalues of the linearization).

Question. Extend this analysis to more complex metric graphs $\mathcal{G}$, in particular:
(a) finite or infinite trees with multiple internal vertices, and
(b) graphs containing loops (such as the tadpole, dumbbell, or "looping-edge" graphs consisting of a circle with attached half-lines).

Specifically, on such graphs (where explicit closed-form expressions for the stationary profiles are generally unavailable), identify continuous branches $\omega\mapsto \Phi_\omega$ of nontrivial $H^1(\mathcal{G})$ solutions of the stationary equation, and verify the spectral conditions (Morse index of the constrained linearized operator) and the variational/Vakhitov–Kolokolov slope condition $\partial_\omega\|\Phi_\omega\|_{L^2}^2$ needed to determine the orbital stability or instability of each such branch.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since the question was posed: orbital (in)stability of standing-wave branches has been established on a number of non-star metric graphs, including tadpole graphs (with both power and logarithmic nonlinearities), dumbbell graphs, and "looping-edge" graphs with Kirchhoff or δ'-type vertex conditions, often via implicit-function/perturbation arguments combined with Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss theory and Krein extension methods. However, a general theory covering arbitrary trees and graphs with loops, including the systematic verification of spectral and variational criteria when no explicit profile is available, is not yet complete; results are still graph-by-graph. Hence the broad question is partially solved.

paper_title: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation on graphs: recent results and open problems
original_question: Do multisoliton states exist for the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on star graphs, and what happens when several solitons collide simultaneously at a vertex? In particular, can one construct or analyze solutions representing more than one incoming or outgoing soliton interacting through the junction?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation on a star graph G consisting of N≥2 half-lines (edges) e_1,...,e_N joined at a common vertex v. On each edge e_j, parametrize points by x∈[0,∞) with x=0 corresponding to v, and let ψ_j(t,x) denote the wavefunction component on edge e_j. The dynamics on each edge is governed by

  i ∂_t ψ_j = -∂_x^2 ψ_j - |ψ_j|^{2σ} ψ_j,  x>0, j=1,...,N,

with σ>0 (e.g. the cubic case σ=1), supplemented at the vertex by a self-adjoint coupling such as the Kirchhoff condition
  ψ_1(t,0) = ψ_2(t,0) = ... = ψ_N(t,0),  Σ_{j=1}^N ∂_x ψ_j(t,0+) = 0,
or a δ-type condition Σ_j ∂_x ψ_j(t,0+) = α ψ(t,0) with α∈ℝ.

A "soliton" on edge e_j is a localized traveling-wave profile of the form
  φ_{c,v_0}(t,x) = e^{i(v_0 x/2 - (v_0^2/4 - c)t)} R_c(x - v_0 t - x_0),
where R_c is the solitary-wave profile of the homogeneous line NLS (e.g. R_c(y) = (c(σ+1))^{1/(2σ)} sech^{1/σ}(σ√c · y) for the focusing power nonlinearity).

Question. Do there exist, for the NLS evolution above on the star graph, "multisoliton" solutions, i.e. solutions ψ(t)=(ψ_1(t),...,ψ_N(t)) which, as t→±∞, asymptotically decompose into a finite collection of solitons of the above form moving along the edges, with at least two solitons either incoming toward or outgoing from the vertex? Furthermore, analyze the simultaneous collision of several solitons at the vertex: construct or rigorously describe the scattering map relating the incoming asymptotic soliton data to the outgoing asymptotic soliton data when two or more solitons reach the junction v at the same time.
status_search_result: Search results show some progress on related questions: integrable matrix NLS on star graphs admits multisoliton solutions via Hirota's method under special integrability assumptions, and fast-soliton scattering through a Y-junction has been analyzed in the cubic case. However, no general rigorous construction or classification of multisoliton solutions on star graphs with standard (e.g. Kirchhoff or δ) vertex conditions, including simultaneous multi-soliton collisions at the vertex, has been clearly established in the search evidence. The status of the general problem appears unresolved, with only partial results in special regimes.

paper_title: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation on graphs: recent results and open problems
original_question: Can one extend the time interval over which the post-collision dynamics of a fast soliton on a graph is accurately approximated by outgoing solitary waves? More specifically, beyond the logarithmic-in-velocity timescale obtained in the paper, are there longer timescales of validity, perhaps depending on the initial data or on the vertex interaction, for which the outgoing-wave approximation remains accurate?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation on a star graph $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of $N$ half-lines joined at a single vertex $v$:
$$ i\partial_t \psi_j(t,x) = -\partial_x^2 \psi_j(t,x) - |\psi_j(t,x)|^2 \psi_j(t,x), \qquad x>0,\ j=1,\dots,N, $$
where $\psi=(\psi_1,\dots,\psi_N)$ satisfies a self-adjoint vertex condition at $v$ (for instance, a Kirchhoff or $\delta$-type condition characterized by a coupling parameter $\alpha$). Let
$$ \phi_v(x) = \sqrt{2}\, v\, \mathrm{sech}(v x)\, e^{i v^2 t/2}\, e^{i v x} $$
denote the standard fast solitary wave of velocity $v\gg 1$ on a single half-line, and consider initial data of the form $\psi(0,\cdot)$ supported on one edge and equal to a fast soliton of velocity $v$ traveling toward the vertex.

It is known that, after the collision with the vertex, the solution is approximated, in $H^1$ on each edge, by a superposition of outgoing solitary waves with reflection/transmission coefficients given by the linear scattering problem at $v$, and that this approximation is valid up to a timescale of order $\log v / v$ (logarithmic in the velocity).

Question: Can the time interval of validity of the outgoing-solitary-wave approximation for the post-collision dynamics be extended beyond this logarithmic-in-velocity timescale? In particular, do there exist longer timescales of validity—possibly depending on the initial data (such as its profile, phase, or energy) or on the choice of vertex interaction—on which the post-collision solution remains accurately approximated, in a suitable norm, by a sum of outgoing solitary waves with the prescribed scattering amplitudes?
category_tag: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation on metric graphs
status_search_result: The available literature on fast soliton scattering on star graphs establishes a logarithmic-in-velocity timescale for the outgoing-soliton approximation, but no published result has been found extending this timescale or proving a sharp upper bound. Subsequent work on NLS on graphs has focused on stationary states, scattering and ground states rather than improving the post-collision time of validity, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation on graphs: recent results and open problems
original_question: Can one develop a rigorous mathematical theory for the capture and generation of solitons in nonlinear Schrödinger dynamics on graphs? More specifically, in dynamical regimes that lie between the standing-wave regime and the fast-soliton-scattering regime, can one explain when junction interactions or graph geometry trap a soliton, create a new one, or transfer mass into a localized coherent structure?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{G}=(V,E)$ be a metric graph: a connected multigraph in which each edge $e\in E$ is identified with an interval $I_e\subset\mathbb{R}$ (finite or half-infinite), and the edges are glued at the vertices. On $\mathcal{G}$ consider the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation
$$ i\,\partial_t \psi(t,x) = -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}\,\psi(t,x) - |\psi(t,x)|^{2\sigma}\psi(t,x), \qquad x\in\mathcal{G},\ t\in\mathbb{R}, $$
where $\psi:\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{C}$, $\sigma>0$, and $-\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$ is the Laplacian on $\mathcal{G}$ defined with Kirchhoff (or, more generally, prescribed self-adjoint) boundary conditions at each vertex $v\in V$. A soliton is a solitary-wave solution of the NLS equation on the line $\mathbb{R}$, of the form $\phi_{c,\omega}(x-ct)e^{i\theta(t,x)}$, where $\phi_{c,\omega}$ is the standard NLS soliton profile of speed $c$ and frequency $\omega$.

Two limiting dynamical regimes are well understood:
(i) the standing-wave regime, in which the soliton velocity is small and the solution stays close to a stationary state localized near a vertex;
(ii) the fast-soliton-scattering regime, in which a soliton with large velocity $c\to\infty$ hits a vertex and splits into transmitted/reflected solitons whose amplitudes are governed, to leading order, by the scattering matrix of the linear Laplacian on $\mathcal{G}$.

Problem. Develop a rigorous mathematical theory of soliton dynamics on metric graphs in the intermediate regime between (i) and (ii). Specifically, formulate and prove theorems that, for initial data of the form $\psi_0(x)=\phi_{c,\omega}(x-x_0)$ on an incoming half-line of $\mathcal{G}$ with moderate $c$, characterize quantitatively (in terms of $c$, $\omega$, the vertex conditions, and the topology/geometry of $\mathcal{G}$):
(a) capture: when the soliton is trapped near a vertex or a compact subgraph, converging on long time scales to a localized coherent structure (e.g., a nonlinear bound state);
(b) generation: when a new soliton (not present in the incoming data) emerges on an outgoing edge after the interaction;
(c) mass transfer: the amount of $L^2$-mass that is asymptotically carried by each emerging coherent structure versus radiated away as dispersion.

Provide quantitative criteria (sufficient conditions and, where possible, sharp thresholds) under which (a), (b), or (c) occur.
status_search_result: No rigorous mathematical theory of soliton capture and generation on metric graphs in the intermediate-velocity regime appears in the literature. Existing rigorous results address either standing waves/ground states or the fast-soliton scattering limit; numerical and physical studies of soliton generation on networks exist but do not provide a rigorous proof. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Some open problems
original_question: For the same generic single-input time-optimal control problem qdot = f(q) + u g(q) with |u| ≤ 1 on a 3-dimensional manifold, let sw(q) denote the smallest local uniform bound on the number of switching points of sufficiently short time-optimal trajectories near q, with sw(q) = ∞ if arbitrarily close optimal trajectories can have infinitely many switching points. Is sw(q) finite for every point q in M?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a generic single-input control-affine system on a smooth 3-dimensional manifold $M$ of the form
$$\dot q = f(q) + u\, g(q), \qquad |u(t)| \le 1,$$
where $f, g$ are smooth vector fields on $M$ and admissible controls are measurable functions with values in $[-1,1]$. A trajectory is called time-optimal if it minimizes the time needed to steer between its endpoints among all admissible trajectories with the same endpoints. A switching point of an admissible bang-bang trajectory is a time at which the control $u(t)$ changes sign.

For each point $q \in M$, define $\mathrm{sw}(q)$ to be the smallest nonnegative integer $N$ with the following property: there exist a neighborhood $U$ of $q$ and a time $T>0$ such that every time-optimal trajectory $\gamma:[0,t_\gamma]\to M$ contained in $U$ with $t_\gamma \le T$ has at most $N$ switching points. Set $\mathrm{sw}(q) = \infty$ if no such finite $N$ exists, i.e., if there exist time-optimal trajectories arbitrarily close to $q$, of arbitrarily short duration, having arbitrarily many switching points.

Question: For a generic pair $(f,g)$, is $\mathrm{sw}(q) < \infty$ for every $q \in M$?
status_search_result: The question of whether a uniform local bound on the number of switching points exists for time-optimal trajectories of generic single-input control-affine systems on 3-dimensional manifolds appears to remain open. Related work by Agrachev–Sigalotti and Agrachev–Biolo establishes finite switching bounds in regular regions and under specific Lie-bracket conditions, but a finite bound at every point — including a "bad" lower-dimensional subset — has not been established. No source found that resolves the question in full generality.

paper_title: Some open problems
original_question: Let M be a real analytic manifold and let f and g be real analytic vector fields in the time-optimal control system qdot = f(q) + u g(q), |u| ≤ 1. If two points are connected by some time-optimal trajectory, is there always a time-optimal trajectory joining the same endpoints whose set of switching points is at most countable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a real analytic manifold, and let $f$ and $g$ be real analytic vector fields on $M$. Consider the single-input time-optimal control system
$$\dot q(t) = f(q(t)) + u(t)\, g(q(t)), \qquad |u(t)| \le 1,$$
with measurable controls $u:[0,T]\to[-1,1]$. A trajectory $q:[0,T]\to M$ is called time-optimal if it minimizes the transfer time $T$ among all admissible trajectories joining $q(0)$ to $q(T)$. For an admissible control $u$, a switching point of the corresponding trajectory is a time $t\in(0,T)$ such that $u$ is not constant (equivalently, not equal to $+1$ identically or $-1$ identically) on any open neighborhood of $t$.

Question: Suppose two points $q_0, q_1 \in M$ are joined by some time-optimal trajectory. Does there always exist a time-optimal trajectory from $q_0$ to $q_1$ whose set of switching points is at most countable?
status_search_result: The general problem appears to remain open. Partial results are known: for three-dimensional real-analytic single-input systems, time-optimal trajectories are bang-bang with finitely many switchings under nondegeneracy assumptions; and a 2018 result shows that for generic control-affine systems, optimal controls are smooth outside a countable set of times (so genericity gives countable switchings). However, no source confirms the full general statement for arbitrary real-analytic single-input systems.

paper_title: Some open problems
original_question: Let Δ ⊂ TM be a bracket-generating distribution defining a sub-Riemannian structure on a manifold M, and let γ0, γ1 : [0,1] → M be smooth admissible paths with the same starting point q0 and linearly independent initial velocities at q0. Must there always exist an admissible path from γ0(1) to γ1(1) whose length is strictly less than the length of the broken path obtained by concatenating γ0 and γ1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold equipped with a sub-Riemannian structure given by a bracket-generating distribution $\Delta \subset TM$ together with a smoothly varying inner product on $\Delta$. An absolutely continuous path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$ is called admissible if $\dot\gamma(t) \in \Delta_{\gamma(t)}$ for almost every $t$, and its length is $\ell(\gamma) = \int_0^1 \|\dot\gamma(t)\|\,dt$. 

Suppose $\gamma_0,\gamma_1:[0,1]\to M$ are two smooth admissible paths sharing the common starting point $\gamma_0(0)=\gamma_1(0)=q_0$, and such that the initial velocities $\dot\gamma_0(0)$ and $\dot\gamma_1(0)$ are linearly independent vectors in $\Delta_{q_0}$. Consider the broken concatenation that follows $\gamma_0$ in reverse from $\gamma_0(1)$ to $q_0$ and then follows $\gamma_1$ from $q_0$ to $\gamma_1(1)$; its length equals $\ell(\gamma_0)+\ell(\gamma_1)$.

Prove or disprove: there always exists an admissible path from $\gamma_0(1)$ to $\gamma_1(1)$ whose length is strictly less than $\ell(\gamma_0)+\ell(\gamma_1)$.
status_search_result: The "cutting corners" question is affirmatively resolved by the theorem of Hakavuori and Le Donne (Inventiones Math. 206 (2016), 693–704), which proves that in any sub-Riemannian manifold a length-minimizing curve cannot contain a corner (a point where left and right tangent vectors are linearly independent admissible vectors). Consequently, the broken concatenation described, having a corner at $q_0$, is not length-minimizing between its endpoints, so a strictly shorter admissible connection between $\gamma_0(1)$ and $\gamma_1(1)$ always exists.

paper_title: Some open problems
original_question: For the same endpoint-map setting in sub-Riemannian geometry, can length-minimizing singular curves issuing from a fixed point q0 fill a subset of M of positive measure, or is their image always measure-theoretically small?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth connected manifold equipped with a sub-Riemannian structure: a smooth bracket-generating distribution $\Delta \subset TM$ together with a smooth fiberwise inner product on $\Delta$. An absolutely continuous curve $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$ is called horizontal if $\dot\gamma(t)\in\Delta_{\gamma(t)}$ for almost every $t$, and its length is $\ell(\gamma)=\int_0^1 \lVert\dot\gamma(t)\rVert\,dt$. Fix a point $q_0\in M$ and consider the endpoint map $\mathrm{End}_{q_0}:\Omega_{q_0}\to M$, $\gamma\mapsto\gamma(1)$, defined on the Hilbert manifold $\Omega_{q_0}$ of horizontal curves issuing from $q_0$ with square-integrable controls. A horizontal curve $\gamma\in\Omega_{q_0}$ is called singular (or abnormal) if $\mathrm{End}_{q_0}$ fails to be a submersion at $\gamma$. A horizontal curve is length-minimizing if its length equals the sub-Riemannian distance between its endpoints.

Let
$$S(q_0) \;=\; \bigl\{\gamma(1) : \gamma\in\Omega_{q_0}\text{ is singular and length-minimizing}\bigr\}\subset M.$$

Question: Does there exist a sub-Riemannian manifold $(M,\Delta,g)$ and a point $q_0\in M$ such that $S(q_0)$ has positive Lebesgue (volume) measure in $M$, or is $S(q_0)$ always a measure-zero subset of $M$?
status_search_result: This question is a form of the (minimizing) Sard conjecture in sub-Riemannian geometry. It remains open in full generality. The strongest known result, established for analytic rank-2 distributions on 3-dimensional analytic manifolds, shows that the set reached from $q_0$ by singular horizontal paths has Hausdorff dimension at most 1, in particular Lebesgue measure zero. Recent work on subdifferentials and the minimizing Sard conjecture provides further partial results, but the general case is still open.

paper_title: Some open problems
original_question: For the Engel distribution, that is, a rank-2 distribution in ℝ4 with n3(q) = 3 and n4(q) = 4, what is the C1 classification of the germs of sub-Riemannian spheres at points lying on the optimal singular curve through the point? Equivalently, how should one classify these 3-dimensional hypersurface singularities in ℝ4 up to local C1 diffeomorphism?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Delta$ be a rank-2 distribution on $\mathbb{R}^4$ (a smooth subbundle of rank 2 of $T\mathbb{R}^4$) endowed with a smooth sub-Riemannian metric $g$ on $\Delta$. For a point $q\in\mathbb{R}^4$, let $\Delta^1(q)=\Delta(q)$ and inductively define $\Delta^{k+1}(q)=\Delta^k(q)+[\Delta,\Delta^k](q)$, and set $n_k(q)=\dim\Delta^k(q)$. Assume that at every point $q\in\mathbb{R}^4$ one has $n_2(q)=3$ and $n_3(q)=4$ (the Engel condition; equivalently, $\Delta$ is an Engel distribution).

For such a structure, through every point $q_0$ there passes a unique (up to reparametrization) singular (abnormal) horizontal curve, and sufficiently small arcs of this curve are length-minimizing. For $r>0$ small, let $S_r(q_0)\subset\mathbb{R}^4$ denote the sub-Riemannian sphere of radius $r$ centered at $q_0$, i.e. the set of points whose sub-Riemannian distance from $q_0$ equals $r$. Let $q\in S_r(q_0)$ be a point lying on the singular curve through $q_0$.

Problem. Classify, up to local $C^1$-diffeomorphism of $(\mathbb{R}^4, q)$, the germs at $q$ of the 3-dimensional hypersurface singularities $S_r(q_0)$ that arise in this Engel setting.
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g. Ardentov–Sachkov on the flat Engel sub-Riemannian sphere, and studies on front asymptotics near abnormal geodesics) describes the asymptotics and shows non-subanalyticity of the Engel sphere at the abnormal poles, but no full local $C^1$ classification of these hypersurface singularities appears to be available. The problem appears to remain open.
