paper_title: Some open problems
original_question: Let Δ ⊂ TM be a smooth vector distribution on a manifold M. Suppose Δ is singular transitive, meaning that any two points of M can be joined by a concatenation of singular curves of Δ. Does this singular transitivity force the full symmetry group of Δ—the diffeomorphisms Φ with Φ_*Δ = Δ—to be a finite-dimensional Lie group?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $\Delta \subset TM$ be a smooth vector distribution on $M$ (a smooth subbundle, or more generally a smooth submodule of the tangent sheaf). A smooth curve $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$ is called horizontal for $\Delta$ if $\dot\gamma(t)\in\Delta_{\gamma(t)}$ for almost every $t$. Among horizontal curves one distinguishes the so-called singular (or abnormal) curves: these are the critical points of the endpoint map on the space of horizontal curves with fixed initial point (equivalently, horizontal curves admitting a nontrivial abnormal Pontryagin extremal lift in $T^*M$).

Say that $\Delta$ is singular transitive on $M$ if any two points of $M$ can be joined by a finite concatenation of singular curves of $\Delta$. Define the symmetry group of $\Delta$ to be
$$\mathrm{Sym}(\Delta) := \{\Phi \in \mathrm{Diff}(M) : \Phi_*\Delta = \Delta\}.$$

Question: Does singular transitivity of $\Delta$ imply that $\mathrm{Sym}(\Delta)$ is a finite-dimensional Lie group?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return any source explicitly resolving the question of whether singular transitivity of a smooth distribution forces its symmetry pseudogroup to be a finite-dimensional Lie group. No paper claiming a proof or counterexample was located, so the status remains unverified.

paper_title: Some open problems
original_question: For each n > 3, determine the smallest integer μ(n) such that any convex plane curve run μ(n) times admits arbitrarily small perturbations as a nondegenerate closed curve in ℝn, and decide whether every regular closed curve in ℝn has Frenet-frame length strictly greater than μ(n) times the length of the standard closed geodesic SO(2) ⊂ O(n).
self_contained_problem:
Work in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n>3$. A smooth closed curve $\gamma:S^1\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is called nondegenerate if at every point the derivatives $\gamma'(t),\gamma''(t),\ldots,\gamma^{(n)}(t)$ are linearly independent; equivalently, $\gamma$ admits a well-defined Frenet $n$-frame, viewed as a closed curve $F_\gamma:S^1\to O(n)$. A convex plane curve is a smooth simple closed curve in $\mathbb{R}^2\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ bounding a convex region; "running it $k$ times" means the $k$-fold cover $S^1\to S^1\to\mathbb{R}^n$. Let $SO(2)\subset O(n)$ denote the standard closed geodesic (a great circle of length $2\pi\sqrt{2}$ in $O(n)$ with its bi-invariant Riemannian metric).

Define $\mu(n)$ to be the smallest positive integer $k$ such that, for every convex plane curve $C\subset\mathbb{R}^2\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, the $k$-fold covering of $C$ admits arbitrarily $C^\infty$-small perturbations that are nondegenerate closed curves in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

(a) Determine $\mu(n)$ explicitly for every $n>3$.

(b) Decide whether, for every regular (i.e. nondegenerate) closed curve $\gamma$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the length of the Frenet frame $F_\gamma$ in $O(n)$ is strictly greater than $\mu(n)$ times the length of the standard closed geodesic $SO(2)\subset O(n)$.
status_search_result: A targeted web search for the quantity $\mu(n)$ governing perturbation of multiply-covered convex plane curves into nondegenerate curves in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the conjectured Frenet-frame length inequality involving $SO(2)\subset O(n)$, did not return any source resolving the question for general $n>3$. No paper announcing a determination of $\mu(n)$ or a proof/disproof of the length inequality was located, so the status remains unverified.

paper_title: Some open problems
original_question: For a fixed compact 3-dimensional contact manifold with a chosen contact distribution, can one define a natural averaging or heat-type evolution on the space of sub-Riemannian metrics that converges, possibly after suitable rescaling, to a nonzero generalized metric preserved by the Reeb field, even when no smooth Reeb-invariant metric exists? This includes understanding whether the discrete averaging scheme or the continuous equation ∂h/∂t = c{uh,{uh,h}} can produce meaningful limiting Hamiltonians with controlled singularities.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) smooth 3-dimensional manifold equipped with a contact structure, i.e. a smooth rank-2 distribution $\xi \subset TM$ given as the kernel of a 1-form $\alpha$ with $\alpha \wedge d\alpha$ nowhere vanishing. Normalize $\alpha$ (within its conformal class defining $\xi$) so that the associated Reeb vector field $R$ is the unique vector field satisfying $\alpha(R)=1$ and $d\alpha(R,\cdot)=0$.

A sub-Riemannian metric on $(M,\xi)$ is a smooth positive-definite quadratic form $g$ on the bundle $\xi$. Equivalently, it is encoded by its (fiberwise) dual Hamiltonian $h\colon T^*M 	o \mathbb{R}$, the smooth nonnegative function on $T^*M$ that is a positive-semidefinite quadratic form on each cotangent fiber, with kernel exactly the annihilator of $\xi$, and whose restriction to $\xi^*$ is dual to $g$. Let $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$ denote the canonical Poisson bracket on $T^*M$, and let $u\colon T^*M	o \mathbb{R}$ be the linear-on-fibers function $u(\lambda) = \langle \lambda, R(\pi(\lambda))angle$ corresponding to the Reeb field $R$ (with $\pi\colon T^*M	o M$).

A sub-Riemannian metric (or its Hamiltonian $h$) is called Reeb-invariant if the flow of $R$ preserves it; equivalently $\{u,h\}=0$. It is known that smooth Reeb-invariant sub-Riemannian metrics typically do not exist on a given $(M,\xi,\alpha)$.

Question. For an arbitrary closed contact 3-manifold $(M,\xi)$ with chosen contact form $\alpha$, does there exist a natural averaging/diffusion process on the space of sub-Riemannian Hamiltonians on $\xi$ that produces a nontrivial Reeb-invariant limit, possibly only as a generalized (non-smooth) object? More specifically:

(a) Discrete scheme. Do there exist sequences of positive smooth functions $\varepsilon_n, c_n$ on $M$ and an iterative averaging procedure along the Reeb flow such that, starting from any smooth sub-Riemannian Hamiltonian $h_0$, the iterates converge (in a suitable distributional or measure-theoretic sense, after rescaling) to a nonzero limiting Hamiltonian $h_\infty$ with $\{u,h_\infty\}=0$ and with controlled (e.g. measure-valued or current-valued) singularities?

(b) Continuous scheme. Consider the ``heat along the Reeb field'' evolution
$$\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = c\,\{u h,\,\{u h,\,h\}\},$$
with $c$ a positive (possibly time-dependent) function, in the space of sub-Riemannian Hamiltonians on $\xi$. Does this equation admit, for generic smooth initial data, long-time solutions that converge as $t\to\infty$ (after appropriate rescaling) to a nontrivial generalized Hamiltonian $h_\infty$ that is Reeb-invariant in the sense $\{u,h_\infty\}=0$, with singularities of a controlled type?

Formulate, in either or both of the above settings, the existence and basic regularity of such limiting Reeb-invariant generalized sub-Riemannian metrics on every closed contact 3-manifold.
status_search_result: The problem was posed as an exploratory/imprecise open question about a Ricci-flow-like dynamics on sub-Riemannian metrics on contact 3-manifolds. Subsequent literature on sub-Riemannian curvature, Ricci-type bounds, and tightness for contact 3-manifolds (e.g. work on generalized Ricci curvature bounds, canonical curvature in contact sub-Riemannian geometry, and quantitative tightness via sub-Riemannian methods) develops related geometric tools but does not appear to construct or analyze the proposed Reeb-heat flow ∂h/∂t = c{uh,{uh,h}} or establish convergence to a Reeb-invariant generalized metric. No source found that resolves the question, so it appears to remain open.

original_question: Let S be a numerical semigroup and let H(S) = N \ S be its set of gaps. Determine the genus g(S) = |H(S)| from a minimal system of generators of S when the embedding dimension e(S) is at least 3.
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement $H(S) = \mathbb{N} \setminus S$. Elements of $H(S)$ are called the gaps of $S$, and the genus of $S$ is $g(S) = |H(S)|$. Every numerical semigroup $S \neq \mathbb{N}$ admits a unique minimal system of generators $\{n_1 < n_2 < \cdots < n_e\}$, where $e = e(S)$ is the embedding dimension of $S$ (so $S = \{a_1 n_1 + \cdots + a_e n_e : a_i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and $\gcd(n_1,\dots,n_e) = 1$).

Problem: Provide a closed-form expression (or algorithm of analogous explicit nature to the formulas known in the case $e(S) = 2$, where $g(S) = (n_1-1)(n_2-1)/2$) that, for every numerical semigroup $S$ with embedding dimension $e(S) \geq 3$, determines the genus $g(S)$ as a function of a minimal system of generators $\{n_1, \dots, n_e\}$ of $S$.
status_search_result: The problem of giving a general closed formula for the genus of a numerical semigroup in terms of its minimal generators when the embedding dimension is at least 3 is widely regarded as open. It has been shown that no polynomial formula can compute the Frobenius number or genus for embedding dimension 3 in general, although partial results exist for special classes (e.g., symmetric and pseudo-symmetric semigroups, and algorithmic procedures for the embedding dimension 3 case). For embedding dimension ≥ 4, the problem remains open in even stronger forms.

original_question: Decide whether every numerical semigroup S satisfies Wilf's conjectured inequality e(S)g(S) <= (e(S) - 1)(F(S) + 1), where e(S) is the embedding dimension, g(S) is the genus, and F(S) is the Frobenius number.
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset S of the non-negative integers that contains 0, is closed under addition, and has finite complement in the non-negative integers. For such an S, define:
- the Frobenius number F(S) as the largest integer not in S;
- the genus g(S) as the cardinality of the set of non-negative integers not in S;
- the embedding dimension e(S) as the cardinality of the minimal set of generators of S (equivalently, |(S \ {0}) \ ((S \ {0}) + (S \ {0}))|).

Decide whether the inequality
    e(S) · g(S) ≤ (e(S) − 1) · (F(S) + 1)
holds for every numerical semigroup S.
status_search_result: Wilf's conjecture, posed in 1978, remains open in general as of 2024–2025. It has been verified computationally for all numerical semigroups up to genus 100 (verification published October 2024) and proved for several large families (e.g., semigroups with sufficiently large maximum primitive, gluings, second-level semigroups), but no general proof or counterexample is known.

original_question: For a modular numerical semigroup S(a, b, 1), find formulas for the Frobenius number F(S(a, b, 1)), multiplicity m(S(a, b, 1)), type t(S(a, b, 1)), and embedding dimension e(S(a, b, 1)) in terms of the parameters a and b.
self_contained_problem:
A proportionally modular Diophantine inequality is an expression of the form $a x \bmod b \le c x$, where $a, b, c$ are positive integers. The set
$$S(a,b,c) \;=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{N} : a x \bmod b \le c x \,\}$$
is a numerical semigroup (a cofinite submonoid of $(\mathbb{N},+)$ containing $0$).

For a numerical semigroup $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, define:
- the Frobenius number $F(S) = \max(\mathbb{Z}\setminus S)$;
- the multiplicity $m(S) = \min(S\setminus\{0\})$;
- the embedding dimension $e(S)$, the cardinality of the (unique) minimal system of generators of $S$;
- the type $t(S) = \#\{\, z \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus S : z + s \in S \text{ for all } s \in S\setminus\{0\}\,\}$ (the number of pseudo-Frobenius numbers).

Specialize to the case $c = 1$, i.e.\ to the modular numerical semigroup
$$S(a,b,1) \;=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{N} : a x \bmod b \le x \,\}, \qquad a,b \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}.$$

Provide explicit closed-form expressions, in terms of the parameters $a$ and $b$ alone, for each of the four invariants
$$F\bigl(S(a,b,1)\bigr), \qquad m\bigl(S(a,b,1)\bigr), \qquad t\bigl(S(a,b,1)\bigr), \qquad e\bigl(S(a,b,1)\bigr).$$
status_search_result: A search indicates that while an algorithm of Euclidean-type complexity exists to compute the Frobenius number of S(a,b,1), and a formula for the genus g(S(a,b,1)) is known, no explicit closed-form formulas for F, m, t, and e of S(a,b,1) in terms of a and b appear in the literature; the problem is listed as open in the standard problem list on numerical semigroups.

original_question: Given a proportionally modular numerical semigroup by its minimal generators, find formulas for its Frobenius number, genus, and type directly from that minimal generating system.
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$. The Frobenius number $F(S)$ is the largest integer not in $S$, the genus $g(S)$ is the cardinality of $\mathbb{N}\setminus S$, and the type $t(S)$ is the cardinality of the set of pseudo-Frobenius numbers $\{x\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus S : x+s\in S\text{ for all }s\in S\setminus\{0\}\}$. Every numerical semigroup admits a unique minimal system of generators $\{n_1<n_2<\cdots<n_e\}$.

A numerical semigroup $S$ is called proportionally modular if there exist positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ with $c\le a$ such that
$$S=\{x\in\mathbb{N} : ax \bmod b \le cx\}.$$

Problem: Given a proportionally modular numerical semigroup $S$ specified by its minimal system of generators $\{n_1,\dots,n_e\}$, provide explicit closed-form formulas, expressed solely in terms of $n_1,\dots,n_e$, for each of the three invariants $F(S)$, $g(S)$, and $t(S)$.
status_search_result: Searches confirm that, although proportionally modular numerical semigroups have been characterized in terms of their minimal generators, no closed-form formulas for the Frobenius number, genus, or type in terms of the minimal generating system are known. The broader Frobenius problem is open for embedding dimension ≥ 3, and the proportionally modular case remains an open subproblem.

original_question: Characterize the numerical semigroups that can be written as quotients S / p = {x in N | px in S} of numerical semigroups of embedding dimension 3 by a positive integer, and determine whether every numerical semigroup arises in this way.
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$. The embedding dimension of $S$ is the cardinality of its unique minimal system of generators. Given a numerical semigroup $S$ and a positive integer $p$, the quotient of $S$ by $p$ is defined as
$$\frac{S}{p} = \{x \in \mathbb{N} : px \in S\},$$
which is itself a numerical semigroup.

(a) Give an algorithmic characterization of those numerical semigroups $T$ that can be expressed in the form $T = S/p$ for some numerical semigroup $S$ of embedding dimension $3$ and some positive integer $p$.

(b) Decide whether every numerical semigroup arises in this way, that is, whether for each numerical semigroup $T$ there exist a numerical semigroup $S$ of embedding dimension $3$ and a positive integer $p$ such that $T = S/p$. If not, exhibit a numerical semigroup that cannot be so expressed.
status_search_result: Part (b) has been resolved negatively: explicit families of numerical semigroups that are not quotients of any embedding-dimension-3 numerical semigroup have been constructed (e.g., families with generators of the form 2a+2^i, i=0,1,2,3, giving the first known examples of semigroups that are not 3-quotients). However, the characterization problem in part (a) — providing an algorithmic procedure to decide whether a given numerical semigroup is such a quotient — appears to remain open.

original_question: For a numerical semigroup S, determine the smallest possible number of irreducible numerical semigroups whose intersection equals S, and decide whether there is a universal constant N such that every numerical semigroup is an intersection of at most N irreducible numerical semigroups.
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset S ⊆ ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …} that contains 0, is closed under addition, and has finite complement in ℕ (the elements of ℕ \ S are called the gaps of S). A numerical semigroup S is irreducible if it cannot be expressed as the intersection of two numerical semigroups that strictly contain it. It is known that every numerical semigroup S can be written as a finite intersection S = S₁ ∩ S₂ ∩ ⋯ ∩ Sₙ with each Sᵢ irreducible; such a decomposition is called minimal if no Sᵢ may be omitted while still equaling S.

(a) For a given numerical semigroup S, determine the smallest possible integer n for which there exist irreducible numerical semigroups S₁, …, Sₙ with S = S₁ ∩ ⋯ ∩ Sₙ.

(b) Decide whether there exists a universal positive integer N (independent of S) such that every numerical semigroup can be expressed as the intersection of at most N irreducible numerical semigroups.
status_search_result: Part (b) appears to have been resolved in the negative: subsequent work has shown that the minimum number of irreducibles needed in a decomposition can be arbitrarily large, ruling out a universal bound N. Part (a), determining the exact minimum for a given numerical semigroup, remains an active research topic, with related conjectures (e.g., that the set of decomposition lengths is always an interval) only partially proved (e.g., for multiplicity at most 6).

original_question: Decide whether every system of proportionally modular Diophantine inequalities is equivalent to a system in which all proportions are equal to 1; equivalently, determine whether every numerical semigroup that admits a Toms decomposition can be expressed as an intersection of modular numerical semigroups.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of nonnegative integers. A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$.

Given positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ with $c \leq a$, the set
$$S(a,b,c) = \{ x \in \mathbb{N} : ax \bmod b \leq cx \}$$
is a numerical semigroup, called a proportionally modular numerical semigroup; the inequality $ax \bmod b \leq cx$ is called a proportionally modular Diophantine inequality, and the ratio $a/c$ is its proportion. When $c = 1$ the semigroup is simply called a modular numerical semigroup, and the inequality is called modular.

A system of proportionally modular Diophantine inequalities is a finite collection of such inequalities; its solution set is the intersection of the corresponding proportionally modular numerical semigroups. A numerical semigroup is said to admit a Toms decomposition if it is the solution set of some finite system of proportionally modular Diophantine inequalities, equivalently, if it can be written as a finite intersection of proportionally modular numerical semigroups.

Question: Is every system of proportionally modular Diophantine inequalities equivalent (i.e., has the same nonnegative integer solution set) to a system of inequalities all of which have proportion equal to $1$? Equivalently, can every numerical semigroup that admits a Toms decomposition be expressed as a finite intersection of modular numerical semigroups?
status_search_result: The question appears in a published numerical-semigroups problem list (2013) and is repeatedly referenced as an open question in subsequent literature on proportionally modular semigroups and Toms decompositions. Recent surveys and papers (through 2025) on irreducible decompositions of numerical semigroups still treat this reduction as an unresolved problem; no source found claiming a proof or counterexample.

original_question: For a given numerical semigroup S, let T range over all numerical semigroups with S = T/2. Find a formula, depending only on S, for the minimum Frobenius number among those doubles T.
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}_{0}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement $\mathbb{N}_{0}\setminus S$. The Frobenius number $F(S)$ is the largest integer not belonging to $S$ (defined when $S \ne \mathbb{N}_{0}$). For a numerical semigroup $T$ and a positive integer $d$, the quotient is $T/d := \{n \in \mathbb{N}_{0} : dn \in T\}$, which is again a numerical semigroup. A numerical semigroup $T$ is called a double of a numerical semigroup $S$ when $S = T/2$, i.e. $T = \{n \in \mathbb{N}_{0} : 2n \in T\text{ implies } n \in S\}$ — equivalently, $\{2s : s \in S\} \subseteq T$ and an integer $n$ lies in $S$ iff $2n \in T$.

Problem. Given a numerical semigroup $S$, let $\mathcal{D}(S) = \{T : T \text{ is a numerical semigroup with } T/2 = S\}$. Find a closed-form expression, depending only on invariants of $S$, for
$$\min_{T \in \mathcal{D}(S)} F(T).$$
status_search_result: A related problem on minimum genus among d-folds of a numerical semigroup was solved by Moscariello (arXiv:1512.00638), giving the formula g + ⌈(d-1)f/2⌉. However, that work concerns the genus, not the Frobenius number, and does not appear to provide the analogous closed formula for the minimum Frobenius number among doubles. No source found explicitly resolving the Frobenius-number version, so the status is unclear.

original_question: Let V_T be the Frobenius variety of numerical semigroups admitting a Toms decomposition. Determine whether V_T is the least Frobenius variety containing all numerical semigroups of embedding dimension 2.
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$. Its embedding dimension is the cardinality of its (unique) minimal system of generators. A Frobenius variety is a nonempty family $\mathcal{V}$ of numerical semigroups satisfying:
(i) if $S, T \in \mathcal{V}$ then $S \cap T \in \mathcal{V}$;
(ii) if $S \in \mathcal{V}$ and $S \neq \mathbb{N}$, then $S \cup \{F(S)\} \in \mathcal{V}$, where $F(S) = \max(\mathbb{N} \setminus S)$ is the Frobenius number of $S$.

A numerical semigroup $S$ is said to admit a Toms decomposition if there exist numerical semigroups $S_1, \dots, S_n$, each of embedding dimension $2$, such that
$$S = S_1 \cap S_2 \cap \cdots \cap S_n.$$
Let $\mathcal{V}_T$ denote the family of all numerical semigroups admitting a Toms decomposition; it is known that $\mathcal{V}_T$ is a Frobenius variety, and that every numerical semigroup of embedding dimension $2$ belongs to $\mathcal{V}_T$.

Determine whether $\mathcal{V}_T$ is the least (smallest under inclusion) Frobenius variety containing all numerical semigroups of embedding dimension $2$. Equivalently, decide whether every Frobenius variety that contains all numerical semigroups of embedding dimension $2$ must contain $\mathcal{V}_T$.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface a published resolution of this question. Subsequent literature on Frobenius (and Frobenius-restricted) varieties of numerical semigroups continues to develop the theory, but no source explicitly confirming or refuting that $\mathcal{V}_T$ is the least Frobenius variety containing all embedding-dimension-two numerical semigroups was located.

original_question: Characterize those Frobenius varieties whose associated trees satisfy the Bras-Amoros-type growth property that each level has more vertices than the preceding level.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}_0$. The elements of $\mathbb{N}_0 \setminus S$ are called the gaps of $S$, and the genus $g(S)$ is the number of gaps. Let $n_g$ denote the number of numerical semigroups of genus $g$. The Bras-Amorós conjecture asserts the strict monotonicity $n_{g+1} > n_g$ for all $g \geq 0$.

A Frobenius variety is a nonempty family $\mathcal{V}$ of numerical semigroups satisfying:
(i) if $S, T \in \mathcal{V}$, then $S \cap T \in \mathcal{V}$;
(ii) if $S \in \mathcal{V}$ and $S \neq \mathbb{N}_0$, then $S \cup \{F(S)\} \in \mathcal{V}$, where $F(S)$ denotes the Frobenius number of $S$ (the largest gap).

$$N_{h+1}(\mathcal{V}) > N_h(\mathcal{V}) \qquad \text{for every } h \geq 0.$$

original_question: Determine the Frobenius variety generated by the symmetric numerical semigroups.
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement $\mathbb{N}\setminus S$ in $\mathbb{N}$. The Frobenius number $F(S)$ of a numerical semigroup $S \neq \mathbb{N}$ is the largest integer not belonging to $S$. The genus $g(S)$ is the cardinality of $\mathbb{N}\setminus S$. A numerical semigroup $S$ is called symmetric if $g(S) = (F(S)+1)/2$ (equivalently, for every integer $z$, exactly one of $z$ and $F(S)-z$ lies in $S$).

A nonempty family $\mathcal{V}$ of numerical semigroups is called a Frobenius variety if it satisfies:
(i) if $S, T \in \mathcal{V}$, then $S \cap T \in \mathcal{V}$;
(ii) if $S \in \mathcal{V}$ and $S \neq \mathbb{N}$, then $S \cup \{F(S)\} \in \mathcal{V}$.

The intersection of an arbitrary family of Frobenius varieties is again a Frobenius variety, so for any family $\mathcal{F}$ of numerical semigroups there is a unique smallest Frobenius variety containing $\mathcal{F}$, called the Frobenius variety generated by $\mathcal{F}$.

Problem: Give an explicit description (a complete characterization of its members) of the Frobenius variety generated by the family of all symmetric numerical semigroups.
status_search_result: The question appears in a published problem list on numerical semigroups and is referenced in subsequent literature on Frobenius varieties (e.g., works on Frobenius restricted varieties and covarieties), without an explicit characterization being provided. No source found that claims a full description of the Frobenius variety generated by the symmetric numerical semigroups, so it appears to remain open.

original_question: Characterize the numerical semigroups that can be expressed as quotients of complete intersection numerical semigroups by a positive integer.
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$ (equivalently, $\gcd(S) = 1$). Every numerical semigroup admits a unique minimal system of generators $\{n_1,\dots,n_e\}$, and one writes $S = \langle n_1,\dots,n_eangle$. The integer $e$ is the embedding dimension of $S$.

To each numerical semigroup $S = \langle n_1,\dots,n_eangle$ one associates the semigroup ring $k[S] = k[t^{n_1},\dots,t^{n_e}] \subseteq k[t]$ over a field $k$, presented as $k[x_1,\dots,x_e]/I_S$, where $I_S$ is the kernel of the map sending $x_i \mapsto t^{n_i}$. The semigroup $S$ is called a complete intersection numerical semigroup if the toric ideal $I_S$ can be generated by exactly $e-1$ elements (equivalently, if $k[S]$ is a complete intersection ring).

For a numerical semigroup $T$ and a positive integer $d$, the quotient of $T$ by $d$ is defined to be
$$	frac{T}{d} = \{n \in \mathbb{N} : dn \in T\},$$
which is again a numerical semigroup.

Problem. Characterize the numerical semigroups $S$ that can be expressed as $S = T/d$, where $T$ is a complete intersection numerical semigroup and $d$ is a positive integer.

Subsequent work has addressed related questions—e.g., characterizing numerical semigroups that are quotients of symmetric or of flat semigroups, and constructing examples that are not k-quotients—but a full characterization of those that arise as quotients of complete intersection numerical semigroups by a positive integer does not appear to be available. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Among families of numerical semigroups closed under gluing, determine the least family that contains all numerical semigroups of maximal embedding dimension.
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$. Every numerical semigroup $S \neq \mathbb{N}$ has a unique minimal system of generators $\{n_1 < n_2 < \dots < n_e\}$; the integer $e = e(S)$ is called the embedding dimension of $S$, and the smallest nonzero element $m(S) = n_1$ is the multiplicity of $S$. It is known that $e(S) \le m(S)$, and $S$ is said to have maximal embedding dimension (MED) when $e(S) = m(S)$.

Given two numerical semigroups $S_1 = \langle a_1, \dots, a_r \rangle$ and $S_2 = \langle b_1, \dots, b_s \rangle$, and positive integers $\lambda \in S_2 \setminus \{b_1, \dots, b_s\}$ and $\mu \in S_1 \setminus \{a_1, \dots, a_r\}$ with $\gcd(\lambda, \mu) = 1$, $\lambda > 1$, $\mu > 1$, the gluing of $S_1$ and $S_2$ (with respect to $\lambda, \mu$) is the numerical semigroup
$$ S = \langle \mu a_1, \dots, \mu a_r,\; \lambda b_1, \dots, \lambda b_s \rangle. $$
A family $\mathcal{F}$ of numerical semigroups is said to be closed under gluing if every gluing of two members of $\mathcal{F}$ again belongs to $\mathcal{F}$.

Problem: Determine the smallest family $\mathcal{F}$ of numerical semigroups that is closed under gluing and contains every numerical semigroup of maximal embedding dimension.

No paper located in the search resolves it; related work studies properties (such as the Wilf inequality, complete intersection property, minimal free resolutions) preserved under gluing, but does not characterize the gluing closure of MED semigroups. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let n1, n2, n3 be pairwise relatively prime positive integers, and let u be a positive integer with u n2 == 1 mod n1. Find a formula, in terms of n1, n2, n3, for the multiplicity of the proportionally modular numerical semigroup S(u n2 n3, n1 n2, n3), equivalently for the invariant c3 needed to recover the Frobenius problem in embedding dimension 3.
self_contained_problem:
A proportionally modular numerical semigroup is a set of the form
S(a,b,c) = { x ∈ ℕ : a x mod b ≤ c x },
where a, b, c are positive integers and ℕ = {0,1,2,…}; this set is a numerical semigroup (a cofinite submonoid of ℕ).

The multiplicity of a numerical semigroup S, denoted m(S), is the smallest positive integer that belongs to S.

Let n₁, n₂, n₃ be pairwise relatively prime positive integers, and let u be a positive integer such that u n₂ ≡ 1 (mod n₁). Consider the proportionally modular numerical semigroup
S = S(u n₂ n₃, n₁ n₂, n₃) = { x ∈ ℕ : (u n₂ n₃) x mod (n₁ n₂) ≤ n₃ x }.

Problem: Find a closed-form formula, expressed only in terms of n₁, n₂, n₃ (and depending on u only through these data), for the multiplicity m(S) of S.

original_question: Characterize the numerical semigroups S for which the omega-primality omega(S) is different from the type t(S).
self_contained_problem:
A numerical semigroup is a subset S of the nonnegative integers N that is closed under addition, contains 0, and has finite complement in N. Let S be a numerical semigroup with minimal system of generators {n_1, ..., n_e}.

The type of S, denoted t(S), is the cardinality of the set PF(S) = {x ∈ Z \ S : x + s ∈ S for every s ∈ S \ {0}} of pseudo-Frobenius numbers of S.

For a nonzero element s ∈ S, the ω-primality of s in S, denoted ω_S(s), is the least positive integer N (or ∞ if no such N exists) such that whenever s divides a sum a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_n in S (i.e., (a_1 + ... + a_n) - s ∈ S) with each a_i ∈ S \ {0}, there exists a subset I ⊆ {1, ..., n} with |I| ≤ N such that s divides ∑_{i ∈ I} a_i in S. The ω-primality of S is defined by
   ω(S) = max{ ω_S(n_i) : i = 1, ..., e }.

It is known that ω(S) ≥ t(S) for every numerical semigroup S, and that equality ω(S) = t(S) holds for "most" numerical semigroups (in a computational sense), so that semigroups with ω(S) ≠ t(S) are comparatively rare.

Problem: Give an explicit characterization of the numerical semigroups S for which ω(S) ≠ t(S).
status_search_result: Web search returns work on computing ω-primality of numerical semigroups (algorithms, asymptotic ω-primality, mathematical programming approaches), but no source providing a complete characterization of numerical semigroups S satisfying ω(S) ≠ t(S). The status appears to remain open or at least unresolved in the literature surveyed, but no definitive resolution was located.

original_question: Determine whether the catenary degree function c(s) of a numerical semigroup is eventually periodic, meaning that there exist n in S and a threshold beyond which c(s + n) = c(s) for all s.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a numerical semigroup, that is, a cofinite submonoid of $(\mathbb{N},+)$. For $s \in S$, let
$$\mathsf{Z}(s) = \Big\{ (x_{n_1},\dots,x_{n_k}) \in \mathbb{N}^k : s = \sum_{i=1}^k x_{n_i} n_i,\; n_i \in S \setminus\{0\} \Big\}$$
denote the set of factorizations of $s$ in terms of the minimal generators of $S$. For two factorizations $x,y \in \mathsf{Z}(s)$, the distance is $d(x,y) = \max(|x-\gcd(x,y)|,|y-\gcd(x,y)|)$, where $|\cdot|$ is the sum of components and $\gcd$ is taken componentwise. For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, an $N$-chain from $x$ to $y$ is a sequence $x = z_0, z_1, \dots, z_r = y$ in $\mathsf{Z}(s)$ with $d(z_{i-1},z_i) \le N$ for each $i$. The catenary degree $c(s)$ is the least $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ such that for any $x,y \in \mathsf{Z}(s)$ there exists an $N$-chain from $x$ to $y$.

Question: Is the function $s \mapsto c(s)$ on $S$ eventually periodic? That is, does there exist $n \in S$ and an integer $s_0$ such that $c(s+n) = c(s)$ for all $s \in S$ with $s \ge s_0$?
status_search_result: The question (originally posed by F. Halter-Koch) was answered affirmatively by Chapman, Corrales, Miller, Miller, and Patel, who proved that both the catenary and tame degree functions on a numerical monoid are eventually periodic. The result appears in "The catenary and tame degrees on a numerical monoid are eventually periodic," Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society 97 (2014), 289–300.

    dψ/dt = (A + u(t) B) ψ,    ψ(0) = ψ_0 ∈ H,

 • A : D(A) ⊂ H → H is a skew-adjoint operator admitting an orthonormal Hilbert basis (φ_k)_{k∈ℕ} of eigenvectors, A φ_k = i λ_k φ_k with λ_k ∈ ℝ;

paper_title: On some open questions in bilinear quantum control
context_brief: Time-optimal transfer under an L1 control budget
original_question: Fix a bilinear quantum system dψ/dt = (A + u(t)B)ψ with first and second eigenstates φ_1 and φ_2 of the drift operator A. Suppose one imposes an a priori upper bound on the L^1 norm of the control u. Under that control-budget constraint, what is the smallest possible transfer time needed to steer the system from the first eigenstate φ_1 to the second eigenstate φ_2?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a bilinear quantum control system on a complex Hilbert space H of the form

  i dψ/dt = (A + u(t) B) ψ,

where A is a self-adjoint operator (the drift Hamiltonian) with pure point spectrum, B is a self-adjoint operator (the control Hamiltonian), u: [0,T] → ℝ is a scalar, measurable control, and ψ(t) ∈ H satisfies ‖ψ(t)‖ = 1. Let φ_1 and φ_2 denote eigenvectors of A associated with its first and second eigenvalues, respectively, and assume the pair (A,B) is such that φ_1 can be steered (exactly or approximately, up to a global phase) to φ_2 by some admissible control.

Given a fixed constant K > 0, define the admissible class of controls

  𝒰_K = { u : [0,T] → ℝ measurable, T > 0, ∫_0^T |u(t)| dt ≤ K }.

  T*(K) := inf { T > 0 : ∃ u ∈ 𝒰_K with support in [0,T] such that the solution ψ of the system with ψ(0) = φ_1 satisfies ψ(T) = e^{iθ} φ_2 for some θ ∈ ℝ }

(equivalently, in the approximate-controllability setting, the infimum of T such that ψ(T) can be made arbitrarily close to the orbit of φ_2). Compute or characterize T*(K) as a function of K, and in particular for "weakly coupled" systems (where an a priori L^1 bound on u is known to be incompatible with controllability in arbitrarily small time).

Consider a bilinear control system on an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space H of the form

    dψ/dt = (A + u(t) B) ψ,    ψ(t) ∈ H,    u : [0,T] → R,

where A is a (densely defined) skew-adjoint operator with purely discrete spectrum and an orthonormal basis (φ_n)_{n≥1} of eigenvectors A φ_n = i λ_n φ_n, and B is a (possibly unbounded) skew-symmetric operator. Assume the standing hypothesis (Assumption 1):

  (i) A is skew-adjoint with discrete spectrum {i λ_n};
  (ii) there exists an orthonormal basis (φ_n) of eigenvectors of A contained in the domain of B;
  (iii) for every u ∈ R, A + u B generates a strongly continuous unitary group on H.

For k > 0 define the operator |A|^{k/2} via functional calculus on the spectrum of A. The system (A,B) is called k-weakly-coupled if the domain of |A|^{k/2} is invariant under the propagators of A + uB and there exists C_k > 0 such that

    | Re ⟨ |A|^k ψ, B ψ ⟩ | ≤ C_k ⟨ |A|^{k/2} ψ, |A|^{k/2} ψ ⟩

for all ψ in the domain of |A|^{k/2}.

For N ≥ 1 let Π_N be the orthogonal projection onto span(φ_1,…,φ_N), and let ψ^N(t) denote the solution of the Galerkin truncation

    dψ^N/dt = Π_N (A + u(t) B) Π_N ψ^N,    ψ^N(0) = Π_N ψ(0).

Say that (A,B) admits good Galerkin approximations uniformly in the L^1 norm of the control if, for every ε > 0, every R > 0, and every initial datum φ_n, there exists N_0 such that for all N ≥ N_0 and all locally integrable controls u with ‖u‖_{L^1} ≤ R one has

    sup_{t ≥ 0} ‖ ψ(t) − ψ^N(t) ‖_H < ε,

with the bound depending only on ‖u‖_{L^1} and not on t.

Question. Does there exist a pair (A,B) with B unbounded that satisfies Assumption 1, is not k-weakly-coupled for any k > 0, yet still admits good Galerkin approximations uniformly in the L^1 norm of the control in the sense above?

Status appears to remain open/unresolved based on available evidence.

original_question: For incompressible fluid dynamics, especially at very large Reynolds number where viscosity is very small, is violent turbulence fundamentally caused by rough dependence on initial data rather than ordinary sensitive dependence on initial data? In this setting, rough dependence means that arbitrarily small perturbations of the initial condition can become substantial essentially instantly; for the Euler equations, at any nonzero time the solution map from initial data to the solution is continuous but nowhere locally uniformly continuous and nowhere differentiable. Does this mechanism, or the very large derivative of the Navier-Stokes solution map in the high-Reynolds-number regime, explain why sufficiently large-Reynolds-number turbulence develops violently in short time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider incompressible fluid dynamics on a smooth bounded (or periodic) spatial domain. The Navier–Stokes equations read
  ∂_t u + (u·∇)u = −∇p + ν Δu,  ∇·u = 0,
with prescribed initial data u(0)=u_0 in a suitable Sobolev space, where ν>0 is the kinematic viscosity and the Reynolds number is Re ~ 1/ν. The Euler equations correspond to ν=0:
  ∂_t u + (u·∇)u = −∇p,  ∇·u = 0.

Define the solution map S_t : u_0 ↦ u(t,·). For the Euler equations it is known that, for any t ≠ 0, S_t is continuous on the relevant Sobolev space but is nowhere locally uniformly continuous and nowhere Fréchet differentiable; equivalently, arbitrarily small perturbations of the initial condition can produce order-one changes in the solution after arbitrarily short time ("rough dependence on initial data"). For the Navier–Stokes equations with ν>0 the solution map is differentiable, but the operator norm of its Fréchet derivative admits an upper bound that grows like exp(C√(t·Re) + C_1 t).

Question. Is it true that, in the high-Reynolds-number regime, violent fully developed turbulence is fundamentally caused by this "rough dependence on initial data" mechanism (rather than the standard "sensitive dependence on initial data" of finite-dimensional chaos)? More precisely, does the norm of the Fréchet derivative of the Navier–Stokes solution map S_t (at fixed t>0) tend to infinity as Re → ∞, and does this divergence quantitatively account for the short-time onset of violent turbulent behavior at sufficiently large Reynolds number, while moderate-Reynolds-number turbulence is instead governed by ordinary chaotic sensitive dependence?
status_search_result: The conjecture remains open. Subsequent work has provided supporting analytical bounds (an exp(C√(t Re)+C_1 t) bound on the norm of the Navier–Stokes solution-map derivative) and numerical evidence of short-term unpredictability at high Reynolds number under periodic boundary conditions, but no proof that the derivative norm diverges as Re→∞ or a rigorous derivation that violent turbulence is caused by rough dependence has been established.

original_question: In predator-prey dynamics, does increasing the prey's nutrient supply or carrying capacity genuinely make extinction of both prey and predator more likely, or is that prediction only an artifact of a particular mathematical model? After rewriting a Rosenzweig-type predator-prey system in dimensionless form with the capacity-predation number H = h/b, where h is the half-saturation prey density for predation and b is the prey carrying capacity, does the apparent paradox disappear because increasing carrying capacity b and decreasing half-saturation h both lower the same governing dimensionless quantity and therefore represent the same effect?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Rosenzweig–MacArthur predator–prey system

  dN/dt = r N (1 - N/b) - a N P / (h + N),
  dP/dt = e a N P / (h + N) - m P,

where N(t) ≥ 0 is the prey density, P(t) ≥ 0 is the predator density, and r, b, a, h, e, m are positive constants: r is the prey intrinsic growth rate, b is the prey carrying capacity, a is the maximal predation rate, h is the half-saturation prey density for the Holling type-II functional response, e is the conversion efficiency, and m is the predator mortality.

The classical "paradox of enrichment" asserts that increasing the prey carrying capacity b destabilizes the coexistence equilibrium (via a Hopf bifurcation), so that limit-cycle oscillations of growing amplitude can drive both populations toward extinction.

(a) Rewrite the system in nondimensional form using rescaled time τ = r t and rescaled densities n = N/b, p = a P/(r b), and show that the resulting dynamics depend on b and h only through the single dimensionless capacity-predation number

  H = h / b,

together with the dimensionless parameters γ = e a / r and μ = m / r.

(b) Determine whether, within this nondimensional formulation, increasing the carrying capacity b and decreasing the half-saturation h are mathematically equivalent operations (both decreasing H), and in that sense represent the same biological effect.

(c) On the basis of (a)–(b), decide whether the prediction that increasing the prey's nutrient supply (carrying capacity) makes extinction of both species more likely is a genuine feature of the Rosenzweig–MacArthur framework or merely an artifact of a particular choice of parameters; in particular, address whether nondimensionalization through H = h/b "resolves" the paradox of enrichment.
status_search_result: The paradox of enrichment is a well-known prediction of Rosenzweig-type models since Rosenzweig (1971); the dimensional-analysis observation that b and h enter only through the ratio H = h/b is straightforward and has been noted in textbook treatments. However, whether this dimensional reformulation truly "resolves" the ecological paradox remains debated: empirical and theoretical work (e.g., Jensen & Ginzburg, Roy & Chattopadhyay, Fussmann et al.) shows the paradox can be mitigated by ratio-dependence, inducible defenses, or spatial structure rather than by rescaling alone. Status is therefore best described as partially solved / debated.

original_question: How can hundreds of phytoplankton species coexist while competing for only one or a few limiting nutrients, even though the principle of competitive exclusion predicts that at equilibrium only one or a few species should remain? Can a nonequilibrium model that combines turbulent water advection, species-specific drift relative to the water, regeneration of the limiting nutrient, and species-dependent nutrient uptake and growth explain sustained coexistence of many plankton species?
status_search_result: The paradox of the plankton, posed by Hutchinson (1961), has been addressed by many partial mechanistic resolutions: chaotic/turbulent mixing along fractal sets, mesoscale vortex transport barriers, oscillations and chaos in resource competition models, size-selective grazing, environmental fluctuations, and spatial heterogeneity have all been shown to permit coexistence of more species than limiting resources in specific models. No single universally accepted mechanism explains observed plankton diversity, and the question of whether nonequilibrium advection–reaction–diffusion models of the stated form can rigorously support coexistence of arbitrarily many species under realistic assumptions remains an active research topic. Hence the problem is best characterized as partially solved.

original_question: For a given closed subgroup H of GL(n, R), is there a general criterion that decides whether an n-manifold admits an integrable H-structure, rather than only case-by-case criteria for special geometric structures such as almost complex, symplectic, or foliation-type structures?
self_contained_problem:
Let $H \subseteq GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ be a closed subgroup. An $H$-structure on a smooth $n$-manifold $M^n$ is a reduction of the structure group of the frame bundle $F(M) \to M$ from $GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ to $H$, i.e., a principal $H$-subbundle $P \subseteq F(M)$. Such an $H$-structure is called integrable if every point of $M$ has an open neighborhood $U$ together with local coordinates $(x^1, \dots, x^n)$ on $U$ such that the coordinate frame $(\partial/\partial x^1, \dots, \partial/\partial x^n)$ is a local section of $P$ over $U$ (equivalently, $P$ is locally equivalent, as an $H$-structure, to the standard flat $H$-structure on $\mathbb{R}^n$).

Provide a general criterion, applicable to arbitrary closed subgroups $H \subseteq GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ and arbitrary smooth $n$-manifolds $M^n$, that determines whether $M$ admits an integrable $H$-structure. The criterion should be uniform in $H$, rather than tailored to particular geometric cases such as almost complex structures (with $H = GL(n/2,\mathbb{C})$), symplectic structures (with $H = Sp(n,\mathbb{R})$), or foliation structures.
status_search_result: The general integrability problem for $G$-structures (attributed to Calabi) has been resolved in many particular cases (almost complex, symplectic, foliations, etc.), each by different methods (e.g., Newlander–Nirenberg, Spencer cohomology, Guillemin's formal integrability theory). However, no uniform criterion applicable to arbitrary closed subgroups $H \subseteq GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ is known, and contemporary expositions suggest that such a uniform formulation may not be appropriate. The problem appears to remain open in its full generality.

context_brief: Optimal embeddings of real projective spaces
original_question: For each n, what is the minimal Euclidean dimension into which real projective n-space RP^n can be smoothly embedded? In particular, for RP^6, is the minimal embedding dimension 10 rather than the currently known upper bound 11 and the ruled-out value 8?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{RP}^n$ denote real projective $n$-space, the smooth manifold of lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. For each positive integer $n$, define the optimal embedding dimension $e(n)$ to be the smallest integer $N$ such that $\mathbb{RP}^n$ admits a smooth embedding into Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^N$.

(a) Determine $e(n)$ for every $n \geq 1$.

(b) In particular, determine $e(6)$. It is known that $\mathbb{RP}^6$ smoothly embeds in $\mathbb{R}^{11}$ and that $\mathbb{RP}^6$ does not smoothly embed in $\mathbb{R}^{8}$. Decide whether $\mathbb{RP}^6$ admits a smooth embedding into $\mathbb{R}^{10}$ (and, more generally, determine the exact value of $e(6) \in \{9, 10, 11\}$).
status_search_result: Donald M. Davis's continuously updated table of immersions and embeddings of real projective spaces lists, for $\mathbb{RP}^6$, a nonembedding result in $\mathbb{R}^8$ (Mahowald, 1962) and an embedding in $\mathbb{R}^{11}$ (Epstein–Schwarzenberger, 1962); whether $\mathbb{RP}^6$ embeds in $\mathbb{R}^9$ or $\mathbb{R}^{10}$ remains undetermined. The general problem of computing the optimal embedding dimension of $\mathbb{RP}^n$ for all $n$ is a classical open problem.

context_brief: Dolbeault-type invariants for almost complex manifolds
original_question: For an almost-complex manifold M, are the dimensions h^{p,q} defined as the kernel dimensions of the d-bar Laplacian independent of the choice of Hermitian metric, and if not, is there a replacement notion of h^{p,q} depending only on the almost-complex structure that extends Dolbeault cohomology from the integrable case?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a compact almost complex manifold of real dimension $2n$, with almost complex structure $J$. For each Hermitian metric $g$ compatible with $J$, decompose complex-valued differential forms into types $(p,q)$ using $J$, and define the operator $\bar\partial : \Omega^{p,q}(M) \to \Omega^{p,q+1}(M)$ as the $(0,1)$-component of the exterior derivative $d$ acting on $(p,q)$-forms. Let $\bar\partial^*$ be the formal adjoint of $\bar\partial$ with respect to $g$, and define the Dolbeault Laplacian
$$\Delta_{\bar\partial} = \bar\partial\,\bar\partial^* + \bar\partial^*\bar\partial$$
acting on $\Omega^{p,q}(M)$. Set
$$h^{p,q}(M, J, g) := \dim_{\mathbb{C}} \ker\bigl(\Delta_{\bar\partial}\bigr|_{\Omega^{p,q}(M)}\bigr).$$

(a) Is $h^{p,q}(M, J, g)$ independent of the choice of compatible Hermitian metric $g$ (depending only on $(M, J)$)?

(b) If the answer to (a) is negative, provide a definition of numerical invariants $h^{p,q}(M, J)$ that depends only on the almost complex structure $J$ and that, in the case where $J$ is integrable, recovers the usual Dolbeault cohomology dimensions $\dim_{\mathbb{C}} H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(M)$.
category_tag: Almost complex manifolds and Dolbeault cohomology
status_search_result: Part (a) has been answered negatively: Holt and Zhang (2020/2022, "Dolbeault cohomology for almost complex manifolds") showed on the Kodaira-Thurston manifold that $h^{0,1}$ depends on the choice of almost Hermitian metric. Part (b) — finding a fully satisfactory metric-independent replacement extending Dolbeault cohomology — remains an active area of research, with several proposed generalizations (Cirici-Wilson, Holt-Zhang, Tomassini and collaborators) and ongoing work on Bott-Chern/Aeppli analogues and on dimension 4 (e.g., 2023 work on the Kodaira-Spencer problem on almost Hermitian 4-manifolds).

original_question: For each n >= 3, determine all complex structures on the smooth manifold underlying complex projective space CP^n, including the possible existence and classification of non-Kahler complex structures beyond the standard algebraic one.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 3$ and let $M$ denote the smooth manifold underlying the complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$, equipped with its standard differentiable structure. A complex structure on $M$ is an integrable almost complex structure $J$ on $M$, equivalently the structure of a complex manifold whose underlying smooth manifold is $M$. Two such complex structures are equivalent if there is a biholomorphism between them inducing a diffeomorphism isotopic to the identity on $M$.

Determine all complex structures on $M$ up to equivalence. In particular, decide whether every complex structure on $M$ is biholomorphic to the standard algebraic structure of $\mathbb{CP}^n$, and if not, classify all non-Kähler complex structures on $M$.
status_search_result: The classification of complex structures on $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is a classical Hirzebruch problem. Under the Kähler assumption, uniqueness of the standard complex structure on $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is known (e.g., Hirzebruch–Kodaira and Yau for $n=2$, with extensions to higher $n$). However, without the Kähler hypothesis, the existence and classification of non-Kähler complex structures on the smooth manifold $\mathbb{CP}^n$ for $n \geq 3$ remains an open problem, as reflected in current surveys of non-Kähler complex geometry.

context_brief: Topological invariance of Hodge and Chern data
original_question: Which rational linear combinations of Hodge numbers and Chern characteristic numbers of a smooth complex projective variety are topological invariants, under oriented or unoriented homeomorphism or diffeomorphism, and which are not?
self_contained_problem:
Let $V$ be a smooth complex projective variety of complex dimension $n$. For $0\le p,q\le n$ let $h^{p,q}(V)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}} H^q(V,\Omega^p_V)$ denote its Hodge numbers, and let the Chern characteristic numbers of $V$ be the integers obtained by evaluating monomials of total weight $n$ in the Chern classes $c_1(TV),\dots,c_n(TV)\in H^*(V,\mathbb{Z})$ on the fundamental class $[V]$.

Consider rational linear combinations
$$L = \sum_{p,q} a_{p,q}\, h^{p,q} + \sum_{|I|=n} b_I\, c_I,$$
where $a_{p,q},b_I\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $c_I$ ranges over Chern monomials of degree $n$.

Determine, in each of the four equivalence relations on smooth complex projective varieties given by
(a) orientation-preserving diffeomorphism, (b) unoriented diffeomorphism, (c) orientation-preserving homeomorphism, (d) unoriented homeomorphism,
exactly which such linear combinations $L$ are invariant. In particular, decide whether the individual Hodge numbers $h^{p,q}$ and the individual Chern numbers $c_I$ are themselves invariants under each of these relations, and if not, characterize the full $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space of those that are.
category_tag: Hodge and Chern numbers of projective varieties
status_search_result: The problem has been solved. Kotschick proved that a rational linear combination of Chern numbers of smooth complex projective varieties is an oriented diffeomorphism invariant iff it is a linear combination of the Euler number and the Pontryagin numbers, and is a homeomorphism invariant iff it is a multiple of the Euler number. Kotschick and Schreieder then determined the Hodge ring of Kähler manifolds and combined it with the unitary bordism ring to characterize all rational linear combinations of Hodge numbers and Chern numbers that are (oriented/unoriented) homeomorphism or diffeomorphism invariants, completing the solution.

original_question: If a compact surface in Euclidean 3-space E^3 is of finite type, meaning that its position vector is a finite sum of Laplacian eigenmaps, must that surface be a sphere?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M \subset \mathbb{E}^3$ be a compact (closed, without boundary) smooth surface isometrically immersed in Euclidean 3-space, with position vector $\mathbf{x} : M \to \mathbb{E}^3$ and Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta$ acting componentwise on $\mathbf{x}$. The surface $M$ is said to be of finite type if its position vector admits a decomposition
$$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_0 + \mathbf{x}_{1} + \mathbf{x}_{2} + \cdots + \mathbf{x}_{k},$$
where $\mathbf{x}_0 \in \mathbb{E}^3$ is a constant vector and $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k$ are non-constant $\mathbb{E}^3$-valued maps on $M$ satisfying $\Delta \mathbf{x}_i = \lambda_i \mathbf{x}_i$ for pairwise distinct real numbers $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_k$.

Prove or disprove: every compact finite-type surface in $\mathbb{E}^3$ is a round sphere.
status_search_result: The conjecture, due to B.-Y. Chen (1980s), asserts that round spheres are the only compact finite-type surfaces in E^3. Recent literature (e.g. works on surfaces of finite Chen-type from 2015 onward) continues to refer to it as an open problem; partial results exist for special classes (ruled, quadric, tubes, surfaces with finite-type Gauss map), but no full resolution has been reported.

original_question: Classify all finite-type hypersurfaces of a hypersphere in E^{n+2}.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ denote the $(n+2)$-dimensional Euclidean space with its standard inner product, and let $S^{n+1}(r) \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ be a round hypersphere of radius $r$ centered at the origin. Recall the notion of finite-type submanifold introduced by B.-Y. Chen: an isometric immersion $x: M \to \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ of a connected Riemannian manifold $M$ is said to be of finite type if the position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k,$$
where $x_0$ is a constant vector in $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ and $x_1, \dots, x_k$ are non-constant $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued maps satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for pairwise distinct real eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k$ of the Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta$ of the induced metric on $M$. The smallest such integer $k$ is called the type of the immersion; in particular $M$ is of $k$-type.

Problem. Classify, up to congruence in $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$, all finite-type hypersurfaces $M^n$ of the hypersphere $S^{n+1}(r) \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$, i.e., all $n$-dimensional connected hypersurfaces $M \subset S^{n+1}(r)$ that are of finite type when viewed as submanifolds of the ambient Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$.
status_search_result: The general classification of finite-type hypersurfaces of a hypersphere in Euclidean space remains open. Only partial results are available: Takahashi characterized 1-type submanifolds as minimal submanifolds of the sphere, and 2-type hypersurfaces have been studied (e.g., Hasanis–Vlachos and others showing they have constant mean and scalar curvatures), with full classifications only under additional curvature or dimension hypotheses. No complete classification covering all types and dimensions has been established.

original_question: Are the only finite-type surfaces in the standard 3-sphere S^3 the minimal surfaces, the standard 2-spheres, and the products of two plane circles?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^3 \subset \mathbb{E}^4$ denote the unit 3-sphere standardly embedded in Euclidean 4-space. For a closed surface $M$ smoothly immersed in $S^3 \subset \mathbb{E}^4$, regard the position vector $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^4$ component-wise as smooth functions on $M$, and let $\Delta$ be the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced Riemannian metric on $M$. The immersion is said to be of finite type if the position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_{t_1} + x_{t_2} + \cdots + x_{t_k},$$
where $x_0$ is a constant vector in $\mathbb{E}^4$ and each non-constant $\mathbb{E}^4$-valued function $x_{t_i}$ satisfies $\Delta x_{t_i} = \lambda_{t_i} x_{t_i}$ for some real eigenvalue $\lambda_{t_i}$, with $k$ finite.

Three families of surfaces in $S^3$ are known to be of finite type:
(i) minimal surfaces in $S^3$;
(ii) standard 2-spheres in $S^3$ (i.e., intersections of $S^3$ with affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{E}^4$);
(iii) products of two plane circles, i.e., flat tori of the form $\{(r_1\cos\theta,\, r_1\sin\theta,\, r_2\cos\varphi,\, r_2\sin\varphi) : \theta,\varphi\in\mathbb{R}\}$ with $r_1^2+r_2^2=1$.

Question: Is every finite-type surface in $S^3$ (standardly embedded in $\mathbb{E}^4$) one of the surfaces in families (i), (ii), or (iii)?
status_search_result: The classification of finite-type surfaces in S^3 (in the sense of B.-Y. Chen's spectral decomposition) remains an active and open area of research. Surveys and recent papers on finite-type and finite Chen-type surfaces (e.g., works by Stamatakis–Al-Zoubi and subsequent literature) continue to treat the problem as unresolved, with results obtained only under additional restrictions (e.g., ruled, tubular, rotational, or factorable surfaces). No source confirming a full proof or counterexample to the conjecture was found.

original_question: For a Dupin hypersurface M contained in a hypersphere, when is M of finite type, and when does finite type force M to be isoparametric?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ denote the unit hypersphere, and let $M^{n-1}\subset S^{n}$ be a smooth, connected, oriented hypersurface. Recall the following notions.

(i) A curvature surface of $M$ is a connected submanifold $N\subset M$ such that for each $p\in N$, the tangent space $T_pN$ is equal to a smooth principal curvature distribution (an eigenspace of the shape operator). $M$ is called a Dupin hypersurface if along every curvature surface $N$ the corresponding principal curvature is constant. $M$ is called proper Dupin if, in addition, the number $g$ of distinct principal curvatures is constant on $M$, and each principal curvature has constant multiplicity.

(ii) $M$ is said to be isoparametric (in $S^{n}$) if all its principal curvatures are globally constant on $M$.

(iii) Let $x:M\to\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be the inclusion and $\Delta$ the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric. The submanifold $M$ is said to be of finite type if its position vector $x$ admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_{t_1} + x_{t_2} + \cdots + x_{t_k},$$
where $x_0$ is a constant vector in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, $k$ is a positive integer, and each $x_{t_i}:M\to\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a non-constant smooth map satisfying $\Delta x_{t_i}=\lambda_{t_i}x_{t_i}$ for distinct real eigenvalues $\lambda_{t_1}<\lambda_{t_2}<\cdots<\lambda_{t_k}$. The smallest such $k$ is the type of $M$. (Isoparametric hypersurfaces of $S^n$ are known to be of finite type.)

Resolve the following two questions:

(a) Give a characterization (necessary and sufficient geometric conditions) for a (proper) Dupin hypersurface $M\subset S^{n}$ to be of finite type.

(b) Determine whether every (compact, proper) Dupin hypersurface of $S^{n}$ that is of finite type must be isoparametric, and if not, classify all finite-type Dupin hypersurfaces in $S^{n}$ which fail to be isoparametric.
category_tag: Dupin hypersurfaces and finite type submanifolds
status_search_result: The two questions appear to remain open in general. They are explicitly recorded as unresolved problems in surveys on Dupin and isoparametric hypersurfaces, and recent work (e.g., classification of compact proper Dupin hypersurfaces with constant Lie curvatures, and constructions of compact Dupin hypersurfaces with non-constant Lie curvatures) has not produced a general characterization of the finite-type condition for Dupin hypersurfaces of a sphere or shown that finite type forces isoparametricity. No source found announces a complete solution.

original_question: If an n-dimensional submanifold of E^{n+2} is of 2-type, has constant mean curvature, and is not of null 2-type, must it lie in a hypersphere?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x : M 	o \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ be an isometric immersion of a connected $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold $M$ into Euclidean $(n+2)$-space. Let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of $M$ acting componentwise on $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued functions. The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type if it admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i, \qquad \Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i \;\; (i=1,\dots,k),$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ is a constant vector, the $x_i : M 	o \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ are non-constant maps, and $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k$ are pairwise distinct real numbers. The smallest such $k$ is the type of the immersion; if $k=2$, the immersion (and the submanifold) is called of 2-type. The immersion is said to be of null $k$-type if one of the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ in such a minimal decomposition equals $0$.

Let $H$ denote the mean curvature function of $M$ in $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$, i.e. the length of the mean curvature vector field. Assume:

(i) $x : M 	o \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ is of 2-type;
(ii) $H$ is constant on $M$;
(iii) $x$ is not of null 2-type.

Problem. Must $x(M)$ be contained in some hypersphere of $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$?
status_search_result: No published resolution of the problem was located. The question appears in B.-Y. Chen's lists of open problems on submanifolds of finite type and is restated in subsequent surveys (e.g. Chen's "Riemannian submanifolds: a survey" and his 2014 monograph "Total Mean Curvature and Submanifolds of Finite Type", 2nd ed.). While related cases (hypersurfaces of $\mathbb{E}^{n+1}$, null 2-type results, and partial classifications under additional curvature hypotheses) have been treated, the codimension-two non-null 2-type, constant-mean-curvature case as stated does not appear to have been settled.

original_question: Suppose x: M -> E^m is a k-type immersion with spectral decomposition x = c + x_1 + ... + x_k, and let E_i be the subspace of E^m spanned by {x_i(p) : p in M}. Classify the 2-type immersions for which the subspaces E_1 and E_2 are linearly independent.
self_contained_problem:
Let $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a connected Riemannian manifold $M$ into Euclidean $m$-space. The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite $k$-type if its position vector admits a spectral decomposition
$$x = c + x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k,$$
where $c \in \mathbb{E}^m$ is a constant vector and $x_1, \ldots, x_k : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ are non-constant smooth maps satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for pairwise distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_k$ of the Laplace operator $\Delta$ of $M$ (with the sign convention $\Delta f = -\operatorname{div}(\nabla f)$ on functions, extended componentwise to vector-valued maps).

For each $i \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$, let $E_i \subset \mathbb{E}^m$ denote the linear subspace spanned by the set $\{x_i(p) : p \in M\}$. The immersion $x$ (equivalently, the submanifold $M$) is called linearly independent if the subspaces $E_1, \ldots, E_k$ are linearly independent, i.e.\ their sum is direct.

Problem. Classify all linearly independent $2$-type isometric immersions $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$; that is, determine all submanifolds $M$ of Euclidean space whose spectral decomposition has the form $x = c + x_1 + x_2$ with $\Delta x_1 = \lambda_1 x_1$, $\Delta x_2 = \lambda_2 x_2$, $\lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2$, and such that the subspaces $E_1$ and $E_2$ are linearly independent.
status_search_result: The problem of classifying linearly independent 2-type immersions is listed among open problems on finite-type submanifolds, with partial results known (e.g., for hypersurfaces, spherical submanifolds, and immersions with geodesics of 2-type) but no complete classification appears to have been established. Surveys on submanifolds of finite type continue to list this as an outstanding classification problem.

original_question: An isometric immersion x: M -> E^m is called biharmonic when Δ^2 x = 0, equivalently ΔH = 0 for the mean curvature vector H. Other than minimal submanifolds of E^m, which submanifolds of E^m are biharmonic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x: M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a Riemannian manifold $M$ into Euclidean $m$-space, and let $H$ denote the mean curvature vector field of the immersion. Let $\Delta$ be the (rough/Laplace–Beltrami) Laplacian of $M$ acting componentwise on $\mathbb{E}^m$-valued functions, so that $\Delta x = -nH$ where $n = \dim M$. The immersion is called biharmonic if
$$\Delta^2 x = 0, \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad \Delta H = 0.$$
A submanifold is called minimal if $H \equiv 0$; every minimal submanifold of $\mathbb{E}^m$ is automatically biharmonic.

Determine all biharmonic submanifolds of $\mathbb{E}^m$ which are not minimal. In particular, decide whether there exist any biharmonic submanifolds of $\mathbb{E}^m$ other than the minimal ones.
status_search_result: This is Chen's biharmonic conjecture (1991), asserting that every biharmonic submanifold of Euclidean space is minimal. It is known to hold for surfaces in $\mathbb{E}^3$ (Chen, Jiang), for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^4$ (Hasanis–Vlachos, 1995), and for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^5$ (Fu–Hong–Zhan, 2021), as well as under various curvature/structural assumptions. The general conjecture remains open for hypersurfaces $M^n \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+1}$ with $n \geq 5$ and in higher codimension (even surfaces in $\mathbb{E}^4$ are not fully resolved). Surveys as recent as 2025 list the conjecture as still open in general.

original_question: Must every biharmonic hypersurface of a Euclidean space be minimal?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be an isometrically immersed hypersurface, and let $x : M^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ denote its position vector. Let $\Delta$ be the (non-positive) Laplace–Beltrami operator on $M^n$ induced by the metric pulled back from $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. The hypersurface is called biharmonic if 
$$\Delta^2 x = 0,$$
equivalently (by Beltrami's formula $\Delta x = n\,\mathbf{H}$, where $\mathbf{H}$ is the mean curvature vector) if $\Delta \mathbf{H} = 0$. The hypersurface is called minimal if $\mathbf{H} \equiv 0$.

Prove or disprove: every biharmonic hypersurface $M^n$ of Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is minimal.
status_search_result: Chen's biharmonic conjecture (1991) is confirmed for surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (Chen, Jiang), for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^4$ (Hasanis–Vlachos, 1995), and for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^5$ (Fu–Hong–Zhan, 2021). The general case for $n \ge 5$ remains open.

original_question: A null 2-type submanifold is one whose mean curvature vector satisfies ΔH = cH for some nonzero constant c. Does every null 2-type surface in Euclidean 4-space E^4 have constant mean curvature?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth orientable surface immersed in Euclidean 4-space $\mathbb{E}^4$, with mean curvature vector field $H$ (a normal vector field on $M$) and Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta$ acting componentwise on vector-valued functions via the induced metric. The surface $M$ is said to be of null 2-type if there exists a nonzero real constant $c$ such that
$$\Delta H = c\, H,$$
and $M$ is not of 1-type (equivalently, $H$ is not an eigenvector of $\Delta$ corresponding to a single eigenvalue arising from the position vector decomposition; more concretely, the position vector of $M$ in $\mathbb{E}^4$ admits a decomposition $x = x_0 + x_1$ with $x_0$ a constant vector and $\Delta x_1 = \lambda x_1$ failing — instead one has a two-component decomposition with one harmonic component).

Question: Must every null 2-type surface in $\mathbb{E}^4$ have constant mean curvature, i.e., must $\|H\|$ be a constant function on $M$?
status_search_result: Web searches turned up related results — null 2-type surfaces in $\mathbb{E}^3$ are known to be circular cylinders (Chen, 1988), null 2-type Chen surfaces have been studied (Li, 1994), and δ(3)-ideal null 2-type hypersurfaces in Euclidean spaces are known to have constant mean curvature — but no source was found establishing or refuting the general claim that every null 2-type surface in $\mathbb{E}^4$ has constant mean curvature. The status appears to remain unresolved in the general case.

original_question: Let N be an irreducible compact homogeneous manifold, immersed into a Euclidean space by its first standard immersion φ, and let M be a submanifold of N. When is M of finite type in the ambient Euclidean space via φ? In particular, when is M of 1-type or 2-type via φ?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $N$ be an irreducible compact homogeneous Riemannian manifold. Recall that on such a manifold the eigenspaces of the Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta$ acting on smooth functions are finite dimensional. If $\lambda>0$ is an eigenvalue of $\Delta$ with eigenspace $V_\lambda$ of dimension $m_\lambda$, choose an $L^2$-orthonormal basis $f_1,\dots,f_{m_\lambda}$ of $V_\lambda$ and set $x=c(f_1,\dots,f_{m_\lambda}):N\to\mathbb{E}^{m_\lambda}$. For a suitable positive constant $c$, the map $x$ is an isometric immersion into Euclidean space, called the standard immersion associated to $\lambda$; when $\lambda$ is the smallest positive eigenvalue, the resulting $\varphi:N\hookrightarrow\mathbb{E}^{m_1}$ is called the first standard immersion of $N$.
 
An isometric immersion $\psi:M\to\mathbb{E}^N$ of a compact Riemannian manifold $M$ is said to be of finite type if the position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$\psi=\psi_0+\psi_{t_1}+\psi_{t_2}+\cdots+\psi_{t_k},\qquad \Delta_M\psi_{t_j}=\lambda_{t_j}\psi_{t_j},$$
where $\psi_0$ is a constant vector in $\mathbb{E}^N$ and $\lambda_{t_1}<\cdots<\lambda_{t_k}$ are distinct positive eigenvalues of the Laplacian of $M$. The immersion is said to be of $k$-type; in particular it is of $1$-type if $k=1$ and of $2$-type if $k=2$.
 
Problem. Let $N$ be an irreducible compact homogeneous Riemannian manifold equipped with its first standard immersion $\varphi:N\to\mathbb{E}^{m_1}$, and let $M\subset N$ be a submanifold. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on $M$ (and on $N$) under which the composed isometric immersion $\varphi\!\restriction_M:M\to\mathbb{E}^{m_1}$ is of finite type. In particular, characterize those submanifolds $M\subset N$ for which $\varphi\!\restriction_M$ is of $1$-type, and those for which it is of $2$-type.
status_search_result: The problem is a well-known open problem in Bang-Yen Chen's program on finite-type submanifolds. Only partial results are known, mostly for specific ambient homogeneous spaces (spheres, projective spaces, and their hypersurfaces) and for special classes such as minimal or parallel mean curvature submanifolds. No general characterization for arbitrary irreducible compact homogeneous ambient $N$ has appeared in the literature accessible via the search.

original_question: Does every closed manifold of dimension at least 2 admit either a Riemannian metric or a Finsler metric whose geodesic flow is ergodic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) smooth manifold of dimension at least $2$. A Riemannian metric on $M$ is a smooth choice of inner product on each tangent space; a Finsler metric on $M$ is a smooth assignment of a Minkowski norm on each tangent space (a fiberwise smooth, positively homogeneous, strongly convex norm). Either type of metric induces a geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle $SM$, which preserves a canonical smooth measure (the Liouville measure for Riemannian metrics, or its analogue for Finsler metrics). The flow is called ergodic if every flow-invariant measurable subset of $SM$ has either zero or full measure with respect to this canonical measure.

Question: Does every closed smooth manifold of dimension at least $2$ admit either a Riemannian metric or a Finsler metric whose geodesic flow is ergodic?
status_search_result: The question appears in published lists of open problems on geodesics (Burns–Matveev) and is widely regarded as open. While ergodicity of the geodesic flow is established in many special cases (e.g., negatively curved manifolds, Weil–Petersson metric on moduli space, certain non-positively curved or rank-one manifolds), no general construction is known producing an ergodic Riemannian or Finsler metric on every closed manifold of dimension ≥ 2.

original_question: The existence of one hyperbolic prime closed geodesic on a Finsler S^2 implies the existence of infinitely many distinct prime closed geodesics.
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a Finsler metric on the 2-sphere $S^2$, i.e. a continuous function $F: TS^2 \to [0,\infty)$ that is smooth and positive on $TS^2 \setminus \{0\}$, positively homogeneous of degree one in the fiber variable, and whose vertical Hessian $\tfrac{1}{2}\partial^2(F^2)/\partial y^i \partial y^j$ is positive definite on $TS^2 \setminus \{0\}$. A closed geodesic is called prime if it is not an iterate of a shorter closed geodesic. The linearized Poincaré return map of a prime closed geodesic on a Finsler $S^2$ is a symplectic $2\times 2$ matrix; the geodesic is called hyperbolic if this map has two real eigenvalues different from $\pm 1$.

Prove or disprove: every Finsler 2-sphere $(S^2, F)$ that admits at least one hyperbolic prime closed geodesic admits infinitely many geometrically distinct prime closed geodesics.
status_search_result: A 2023 result establishes that every Finsler metric on $S^2$ with at least one prime closed geodesic that is not irrationally elliptic admits infinitely many geometrically distinct prime closed geodesics. Since hyperbolic closed geodesics are not irrationally elliptic, this confirms the conjecture (a "two-or-infinity" type theorem for Finsler $S^2$, related to and extending the Hofer–Wysocki–Zehnder conjecture).

original_question: Does every complete Riemannian manifold with finite volume have at least one closed geodesic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold (without boundary) such that the Riemannian volume of $M$ with respect to $g$ is finite. A closed geodesic is a non-constant smooth map $\gamma:S^1\to M$ that is a geodesic of $(M,g)$, i.e., a periodic geodesic of positive length.

Question: Must $(M,g)$ admit at least one closed geodesic?
status_search_result: The question (attributed to Bangert) is known to have an affirmative answer in dimension 2, where complete finite-volume Riemannian surfaces are known to carry even infinitely many geometrically distinct closed geodesics. In dimensions 3 and higher the problem is still open: the standard Birkhoff minimax arguments used in dimension 2 do not extend, and no general existence result is known.

original_question: Is there at least one closed magnetic geodesic in every positive energy level?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) connected Riemannian manifold and let $\sigma$ be a closed 2-form on $M$, called the magnetic form. The magnetic form induces a bundle map $Y:TM\to TM$ via $g(Y(v),w)=\sigma(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in T_xM$. A smooth curve $\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to M$ is called a magnetic geodesic for $(g,\sigma)$ if it satisfies the equation
$$\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma = Y(\dot\gamma),$$
where $\nabla$ is the Levi-Civita connection of $g$. Magnetic geodesics have constant kinetic energy $E(\gamma)=\tfrac{1}{2}|\dot\gamma|_g^2$, so they preserve every energy level $\{E=k\}$ for $k>0$. A magnetic geodesic is called closed if it is non-constant and periodic.

Question: Does there exist, for every closed Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$, every closed 2-form $\sigma$ on $M$, and every $k>0$, at least one closed magnetic geodesic with energy $k$?
status_search_result: The question of whether every positive energy level admits a closed magnetic geodesic is generally regarded as still open. Recent works (e.g., Asselle–Benedetti and follow-up papers from 2023–2025) confirm existence on low energy levels under curvature hypotheses, on almost every subcritical energy level, and on energies above the Mañé critical value, but the full problem on every positive energy level for arbitrary closed manifolds and magnetic forms remains unresolved.
