original_question: Can some or all groups of the following sorts be written as homomorphic images of nonprincipal ultraproducts of countable families of groups? This is Question 18 in(G. M. Bergman, Pacific J. Math., 274(2015) 451–495). (a) Infinite finitely generated groups of finite exponent. (b) For an infinite set X, the group of those permutations of X that move only finitely many elements. It is known that no group of permutations containing an element with exactly one infinite orbit can be written as an image of such an ultraproduct(ibid.).
self_contained_problem:
Let $\{G_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a countable family of groups and let $\mathcal{U}$ be a nonprincipal ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$. The ultraproduct $\prod_{\mathcal{U}} G_n$ is defined as the quotient of the direct product $\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}} G_n$ by the normal subgroup of sequences $(g_n)$ with $\{n : g_n = e\} \in \mathcal{U}$. Call a group $H$ a "countable ultraproduct image" if there exist such a family $\{G_n\}$ and such an ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ together with a surjective homomorphism $\prod_{\mathcal{U}} G_n \twoheadrightarrow H$.

Determine whether each of the following groups is a countable ultraproduct image:

(a) An infinite, finitely generated group $B$ of finite exponent (i.e., there exists $m\ge 1$ with $g^m = e$ for all $g\in B$, and $B$ is generated by finitely many elements but is infinite).

(b) For an infinite set $X$, the finitary symmetric group $\mathrm{FSym}(X)$ consisting of all permutations of $X$ that move only finitely many elements of $X$.

(It is known that no group of permutations of a set that contains an element having exactly one infinite orbit can be a countable ultraproduct image; this rules out the full symmetric group on an infinite set, but does not settle either (a) or (b).)
status_search_result: A 2025 preprint and Journal of Algebra paper "On homomorphic images of ultraproducts" answers several questions of Bergman from his 2015 Pacific J. Math. article, but its scope is limited to questions concerning abelian-image, direct products of finite groups, cotorsion groups, and ultrafilter comparability. It does not address Bergman's Question 18 regarding infinite finitely generated groups of finite exponent or the finitary symmetric group on an infinite set. No published resolution of either part (a) or (b) was located, so the question appears to remain open.

original_question: It is known that the group Zω has a subgroup whose dual is free abelian of rank 2ℵ0(see 17.24 in Archive). Does Zω have a subgroup whose dual is free ℵ0 abelian of still larger rank(the largest possible being 22)? This is Question 11 in(G. M. Bergman, Portugaliae Math., 69(2012) 69–84).
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{Z}^{\omega}$ denote the additive group of all functions $\omega \to \mathbb{Z}$ (equivalently, the direct product of countably many copies of $\mathbb{Z}$). For an abelian group $A$, write $A^{*} = \mathrm{Hom}(A, \mathbb{Z})$ for its dual. It is known that there exists a subgroup $G \le \mathbb{Z}^{\omega}$ whose dual $G^{*}$ is free abelian of rank $2^{\aleph_{0}}$. Since $|\mathbb{Z}^{\omega}| = 2^{\aleph_{0}}$, any subgroup $G \le \mathbb{Z}^{\omega}$ satisfies $|G^{*}| \le 2^{2^{\aleph_{0}}}$, so the rank of $G^{*}$ is at most $2^{2^{\aleph_{0}}}$.

Question: Does there exist a subgroup $G \le \mathbb{Z}^{\omega}$ whose dual $\mathrm{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z})$ is free abelian of rank strictly greater than $2^{\aleph_{0}}$? In particular, can the rank be made equal to $2^{2^{\aleph_{0}}}$?

original_question: Suppose B is a subgroup of the symmetric group S_Ω on an infinite set Ω. Will the amalgamated free product S_Ω*_B S_Ω of two copies of S_Ω with amalgamation of B be embeddable in S_Ω? This is a weakened form of the group case of Question 4.4 in(G. M. Bergman, Indag. Let $\Omega$ be an infinite set and let $S_\Omega$ denote the symmetric group on $\Omega$ (the group of all bijections $\Omega \to \Omega$). Let $B$ be a subgroup of $S_\Omega$, and form the amalgamated free product $S_\Omega *_B S_\Omega$ of two copies of $S_\Omega$ amalgamated along the common subgroup $B$. 

Question: Does there always exist a group embedding $S_\Omega *_B S_\Omega \hookrightarrow S_\Omega$?

(Note: It is known that there need not exist such an embedding whose restriction to $B$ is the identity, i.e., one respecting the amalgamated subgroup $B$. The question asks only whether some embedding into $S_\Omega$ exists, without requiring it to respect $B$.)

original_question: Prove that a simple(that is, without proper non-trivial connected normal subgroups) algebraic group M over an algebraically closed field cannot act definably, faithfully, and irreducibly on a simple group of finite Morley rank other than M/Z(M).

Recall that a group $N$ is said to be of finite Morley rank if there is a Morley rank function on the definable subsets of $N$ (in some structure in which $N$ is interpretable) taking finite values, and $N$ is called simple if it has no proper non-trivial normal subgroups. original_question: A graph is called a cograph if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to a path with 4 vertices. A graph is said to be chordal if it has no induced cycles with n vertices for every n ⩾ 4. For a finite group G, the enhanced power graph E(G) is the graph with vertex set G and edges {x, y} for all x ̸= y ∈ G such that ⟨x, y⟩ is cyclic. (a) For a given integer n ⩾ 4, determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups G such that E(G) has no induced cycles with n vertices. (b) Determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups G such that E(G) is chordal. In(Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18073) we proved that if the enhanced power graph of a given finite group is a cograph, then it is also chordal. Also the finite nonabelian simple groups whose enhanced power graph is a cograph are described, and additional information is obtained on finite nonabelian simple groups whose enhanced power graph has no induced cycles with 4 vertices.
self_contained_problem:
A graph is called a cograph if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to the path on 4 vertices. A graph is called chordal if, for every integer n ≥ 4, it contains no induced cycle on n vertices. For a finite group G, the enhanced power graph E(G) is the simple graph whose vertex set is G and whose edges are the pairs {x, y} with x ≠ y such that the subgroup ⟨x, y⟩ is cyclic.

Solve the following two problems:

(a) For each integer n ≥ 4, determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups G such that E(G) contains no induced cycle on n vertices.

(b) Determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups G such that E(G) is chordal.

original_question: (T. Breuer, R. M. Guralnick). Let G be a finite simple group and let p1, p2 be any(not necessarily distinct) prime divisors of |G|. Then can we always find Sylow pi-subgroups Hi such that G = ⟨H1, H2 ⟩?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite non-abelian simple group, and let $p_1$ and $p_2$ be any (not necessarily distinct) prime divisors of $|G|$. Does there always exist a Sylow $p_1$-subgroup $H_1$ of $G$ and a Sylow $p_2$-subgroup $H_2$ of $G$ such that 
$$G = \langle H_1, H_2 \rangle?$$
Equivalently, prove or disprove that every finite non-abelian simple group can be generated by two of its Sylow subgroups corresponding to any prescribed pair of prime divisors of its order (allowing the two primes to coincide, in which case $H_1$ and $H_2$ are two Sylow $p$-subgroups for the same prime $p$).
category_tag: generation of finite simple groups by Sylow subgroups
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made. Work of Breuer–Guralnick and subsequent results (e.g. Burness–Guest–Harper, "On the generation of simple groups by Sylow subgroups", arXiv:2204.04311) establish that any finite non-abelian simple group can be generated by a Sylow 2-subgroup and a Sylow r-subgroup for any prime r dividing |G|, and more generally by a π-subgroup and a π′-subgroup. The full statement allowing arbitrary, possibly equal, prime pairs (in particular the case p_1 = p_2) does not appear to be fully resolved in the literature surveyed.

original_question: Let G ⩽ Sym(Ω) be a finite primitive permutation group with a regular suborbit(that is, G has a trivial 2-point stabiliser). Then is it true that for all α, β ∈ Ω, there exists γ ∈ Ω such that the 2-point stabilisers Gα,γ and Gβ,γ are both trivial?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set and let $G \leq \mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$ be a primitive permutation group. For $\alpha, \beta \in \Omega$, write $G_{\alpha,\beta} = G_\alpha \cap G_\beta$ for the pointwise stabiliser of the pair $\{\alpha,\beta\}$. The orbits of a point stabiliser $G_\alpha$ on $\Omega$ are called the suborbits of $G$, and a suborbit $\Delta$ is called regular if $G_\alpha$ acts regularly on $\Delta$; equivalently, $G$ has a regular suborbit if and only if there exist $\alpha, \delta \in \Omega$ with $G_{\alpha,\delta} = 1$.

Assume $G$ has a regular suborbit. Decide whether the following statement is true: for every pair $\alpha, \beta \in \Omega$, there exists $\gamma \in \Omega$ such that
$$G_{\alpha,\gamma} = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad G_{\beta,\gamma} = 1.$$
status_search_result: This is the Burness–Giudici (BG) conjecture concerning the Saxl graph of a finite primitive permutation group of base size 2 (vertices $\Omega$, edges given by pairs with trivial joint stabiliser); the question asks whether every two vertices have a common neighbour. The conjecture is open in general but has been verified in many families, including primitive groups with socle PSL(2,q), PSU(3,q), Sz(q), or Ree(q), and various product-type and diagonal-type cases. No counterexample is known.

original_question: Conjecture: If N is a finite soluble group, then any regular subgroup in the holomorph Hol(N) of N is also soluble.
self_contained_problem:
Let $N$ be a finite group. The holomorph of $N$ is the semidirect product $\mathrm{Hol}(N) = N \rtimes \mathrm{Aut}(N)$, which acts faithfully and transitively on the underlying set of $N$ via $(n,\alpha)\cdot x = n\,\alpha(x)$. A subgroup $G \le \mathrm{Hol}(N)$ is called regular if it acts regularly on $N$ (that is, transitively and with trivial point stabilizers); equivalently, $|G|=|N|$ and $G$ acts transitively.

Prove or disprove: if $N$ is a finite soluble group, then every regular subgroup of $\mathrm{Hol}(N)$ is soluble.
category_tag: Holomorphs and regular subgroups of finite groups
status_search_result: The conjecture appears to remain open. Subsequent work has provided partial results: computational verification for small orders, and structural restrictions on hypothetical counterexamples (e.g., every non-abelian composition factor of a counterexample must be PSL(2,7) of order 168, and every maximal normal subgroup of N must have index 2). Recent papers explicitly treat the question as open and study related/generalized versions (e.g., insoluble transitive subgroups with soluble point stabilizers).

original_question: Does an analogue of Dunwoody’s theorem hold for totally disconnected locally compact groups, that is, must a tdlc group of rational discrete cohomological dimension at most 1 be topologically isomorphic to the fundamental group of a graph of profinite groups?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a totally disconnected locally compact (tdlc) Hausdorff topological group. Recall that for such a group one defines the rational discrete cohomological dimension $\mathrm{cd}_{\mathbb{Q}}(G)$ as the cohomological dimension of $G$ in the abelian category of rational discrete $G$-modules (i.e. $\mathbb{Q}$-vector spaces $V$ with a $G$-action such that the stabilizer of every $v\in V$ is open in $G$). A graph of profinite groups is a graph of groups (in the sense of Bass–Serre theory) whose vertex and edge groups are profinite groups, with edge maps being continuous injective homomorphisms; its fundamental group carries a natural tdlc topology in which the vertex (and edge) groups embed as compact open subgroups.

Dunwoody's theorem states that a discrete group has cohomological dimension at most $1$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ if and only if it is the fundamental group of a graph of finite groups whose vertex group orders are invertible in $\mathbb{Q}$ (equivalently, finite).

Question: If $G$ is a tdlc group with $\mathrm{cd}_{\mathbb{Q}}(G) \le 1$, must $G$ be topologically isomorphic to the fundamental group of a graph of profinite groups?
status_search_result: The analogue of Dunwoody's theorem has been established under additional hypotheses: a compactly generated, unimodular, CO-bounded tdlc group $G$ satisfies $\mathrm{cd}_{\mathbb{Q}}(G)\le 1$ if and only if $G$ is the fundamental group of a finite graph of profinite groups (Castellano–Corob Cook–Marchionna, arXiv:2201.10847). The authors explicitly state they could not prove the result in full generality and pose related questions, so the general case remains open.

original_question: Let G be a finite group, w a multilinear commutator group-word, and p a prime. Suppose that p divides the order |xy| whenever x is a w-value of p′-order in G and y is a w-value in G of order divisible by p. Is it true that then the verbal subgroup w(G) must be p-nilpotent? Without the assumption that w be multilinear, the answer is negative. An affirmative answer has been obtained in several special cases(J. Algebra, 609(2022), 926–936). Y. Contreras Rojas,
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $p$ be a prime. A multilinear commutator word (also called an outer commutator word) is a word obtained by nesting commutators using always pairwise distinct variables; formally, $w_1(x)=x$ is multilinear, and if $u(x_1,\dots,x_m)$ and $v(y_1,\dots,y_n)$ are multilinear commutator words on disjoint sets of variables, then $[u,v]$ is a multilinear commutator word. For a word $w(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, a $w$-value in $G$ is any element of the form $w(g_1,\dots,g_n)^{\pm 1}$ with $g_i\in G$, and the verbal subgroup $w(G)$ is the subgroup generated by all $w$-values. An element of $G$ has $p'$-order if its order is coprime to $p$.

Suppose that $w$ is a multilinear commutator word and that the following condition holds in $G$: for every $w$-value $x\in G$ of $p'$-order and every $w$-value $y\in G$ whose order is divisible by $p$, the prime $p$ divides the order of the product $xy$.

Question: Must the verbal subgroup $w(G)$ be $p$-nilpotent (i.e., must $w(G)$ have a normal Hall $p'$-subgroup)?

Algebra 609). No general resolution for arbitrary multilinear commutator words appears in the literature.

original_question: By definition, a constructible totally disconnected, locally compact(tdlc) group is the result of a sequence of profinite extensions and ascending HNN-extensions starting from the trivial group. As in the discrete case, soluble constructible tdlc groups have type F P∞ (G. C. Cook, I. Castellano, J. Algebra, 543(2020), 54–97). Are soluble tdlc groups of type F P∞ constructible?
self_contained_problem:
A topological group is called totally disconnected and locally compact (tdlc) if it is Hausdorff, locally compact, and its connected component of the identity is trivial. Within the class of tdlc groups, define the class of constructible tdlc groups recursively as the smallest class such that:
(i) the trivial group is constructible;
(ii) if N is a compact (equivalently, profinite) tdlc group, H is constructible, and 1 → N → G → H → 1 is a short exact sequence of tdlc groups (a profinite extension), then G is constructible;
(iii) if H is constructible and G is an ascending HNN-extension of H along a continuous, injective, open endomorphism of H (in the topological/tdlc sense), then G is constructible.

A tdlc group G is said to be of type FP_∞ (in the sense of rational discrete cohomology for tdlc groups) if the trivial rational discrete G-module Q admits a resolution by finitely generated projective rational discrete G-modules of every finite length, equivalently, by finitely generated projective rational discrete G-modules in every degree.

A tdlc group G is called soluble if it admits a finite series of closed normal subgroups
{1} = G_0 ◁ G_1 ◁ … ◁ G_n = G
such that each quotient G_{i+1}/G_i is abelian.

It is known that every soluble constructible tdlc group is of type FP_∞.

Question: Conversely, is every soluble tdlc group of type FP_∞ constructible?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a new question in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook compilation. A web search reveals active recent research on finiteness properties of tdlc groups by Castellano, Corob Cook, and collaborators (including 2024 work on the Schlichting completion), but no source establishing or refuting the converse implication for soluble tdlc groups of type FP_∞ was found. The problem appears to be open.

original_question: It is known that there exist residually finite, locally finite, characteristically simple groups with finitely many orbits under automorphisms(A. B. Apps, J. Algebra, 81(1983), 320–339). Are there any locally finite, characteristically simple groups with finitely many orbits under automorphisms that are not residually finite?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called locally finite if every finitely generated subgroup of $G$ is finite. It is called characteristically simple if it has no proper nontrivial subgroup that is invariant under every automorphism of $G$. It is called residually finite if for every nonidentity element $g \in G$ there exists a normal subgroup $N$ of finite index in $G$ with $g \notin N$. The automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ acts on $G$ by $g \mapsto \varphi(g)$; the orbits of this action are called the automorphism orbits of $G$, and one says $G$ has finitely many orbits under automorphisms if this action has only finitely many orbits.

It is known that there exist residually finite, locally finite, characteristically simple groups having only finitely many orbits under automorphisms.

Question: Does there exist a locally finite, characteristically simple group with only finitely many orbits under automorphisms that is not residually finite?

original_question: A group is said to be self-similar if it admits a faithful state-closed representation by automorphisms of a regular one-rooted m-tree for some m. Does there exist a finitely presented group $G$ and a non-trivial group $H$ such that $G \cong G \times H$?

The question is whether the stronger property — being isomorphic to a proper direct product with itself as one factor — can be realized by a finitely presented group.

original_question: An isometric action of a group G on a metric space S is called acylindrical if for every ε > 0 there exist R, N > 0 such that for every two points x, y with d(x, y) ⩾ R, there are at most N elements g ∈ G satisfying d(x, gx) ⩽ ε and d(y, gy) ⩽ ε. A group is said to be acylindrically hyperbolic if it is not virtually cyclic and admits an acylindrical action on a hyperbolic space with unbounded orbits. Is the automorphism group of a finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic group also acylindrically hyperbolic?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. An isometric action of a group $G$ on a metric space $(S,d)$ is called acylindrical if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exist constants $R, N > 0$ such that for any two points $x, y \in S$ with $d(x,y) \geq R$, the number of elements $g \in G$ satisfying both $d(x, gx) \leq \varepsilon$ and $d(y, gy) \leq \varepsilon$ is at most $N$. A group $G$ is called acylindrically hyperbolic if $G$ is not virtually cyclic and admits an acylindrical isometric action on some Gromov-hyperbolic geodesic metric space with unbounded orbits.

Question. Let $G$ be a finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic group. Is the automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ also acylindrically hyperbolic?
status_search_result: The question is known to be answered affirmatively in several important sub-cases: Genevois (2020/2021) proved that the automorphism group of every infinitely-ended finitely generated group is acylindrically hyperbolic, covering Aut(F_n) for n≥2; the automorphism group of any one-ended hyperbolic group is acylindrically hyperbolic (Genevois–Horbez); and the result is known for groups hyperbolic relative to proper finitely generated subgroups. A general answer for all finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic groups does not appear to be established in the literature, so the problem appears to remain open in full generality.

original_question: Let p be a prime, and P a finite p-group. (a) Suppose that P has an abelian subgroup of order pn. For which n does P necessarily have a normal abelian subgroup of order pn? (b) Suppose that P has an elementary abelian subgroup of order pn. For which n does P necessarily have a normal elementary abelian subgroup of order pn? It is easy to see that for p = 2, the answer to(b) is “yes” only for n = 1. The answer to both questions is “yes” for n < (p + 2)/2(G. G. Glauberman, J. Algebra, 319, no. 2(2008), 800–805), as well as for n ⩽ 5 when p ̸= 2(M. Konvisser, D. Jonah, J. Algebra, 34(1975), 309–330). The answer to both questions is “no” for n ⩾ (p+9)/2 when p ⩾ 5(for p ⩾ 7 due to G. Glauberman, Contemp. Math., 524(2010), 61–65; for p = 3, 5 due to Ya. G. Berkovich, J. Algebra, 248, no. 2(2002), 472–553). Thus, the only open cases for p ⩾ 5 are n = 6 for p = 5, and n = (p + 3)/2, (p + 5)/2, (p + 7)/2 for p > 5.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $P$ be a finite $p$-group. Recall that an abelian subgroup is called elementary abelian if every nonidentity element has order $p$.

(a) Determine the positive integers $n$ such that the following holds for every prime $p$ and every finite $p$-group $P$: if $P$ contains an abelian subgroup of order $p^n$, then $P$ contains a normal abelian subgroup of order $p^n$.

(b) Determine the positive integers $n$ such that the following holds for every prime $p$ and every finite $p$-group $P$: if $P$ contains an elementary abelian subgroup of order $p^n$, then $P$ contains a normal elementary abelian subgroup of order $p^n$.

It is known that for $p=2$, statement (b) holds only for $n=1$. For odd primes $p$, both statements are known to hold whenever $n<(p+2)/2$ and (for $p\neq 2$) whenever $n\le 5$, and both statements fail in general whenever $n\ge (p+9)/2$ and $p\ge 5$. The remaining unresolved cases are: $n=6$ when $p=5$, and $n=(p+3)/2,\,(p+5)/2,\,(p+7)/2$ when $p>5$. Resolve (a) and (b) in these remaining cases.
status_search_result: The problem is a classical question on normal abelian/elementary abelian subgroups of finite p-groups. Bounds due to Glauberman, Konvisser–Jonah, and Berkovich settle the cases n < (p+2)/2 and n ≤ 5 (positive) and n ≥ (p+9)/2 for p ≥ 5 (negative). The intermediate cases (n=6 for p=5; n=(p+3)/2,(p+5)/2,(p+7)/2 for p>5) remain open according to the 2026 Kourovka Notebook listing, with no published full resolution found.

original_question: For a finite group G, let χ1(G) denote the totality of the degrees of all irreducible complex characters of G with allowance for their multiplicities. Suppose that H is a finite group with χ1(H) = χ1(G). a) If G is an almost simple group, must H be isomorphic to G? b) If G is a quasisimple group, must H be isomorphic to G? This is true if G is a simple group(see 11.8(a) in Archive).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, let $\chi_1(G)$ denote the multiset of degrees of all irreducible complex characters of $G$ (each degree counted with its multiplicity, i.e. the number of irreducible characters of that degree). Equivalently, $\chi_1(G)$ encodes the isomorphism type of the complex group algebra $\mathbb{C}G$ as a direct sum of matrix algebras.

Recall that a finite group $G$ is called:
- almost simple if there exists a non-abelian finite simple group $S$ with $S \trianglelefteq G \leq \mathrm{Aut}(S)$;
- quasisimple if $G$ is perfect (i.e. $G = [G,G]$) and the quotient $G/Z(G)$ is a non-abelian finite simple group.

It is known that every non-abelian finite simple group $G$ is determined up to isomorphism by $\chi_1(G)$: that is, for every finite group $H$ with $\chi_1(H) = \chi_1(G)$, one has $H \cong G$.

Decide whether the same uniqueness statement holds in each of the following two settings:

(a) If $G$ is a finite almost simple group and $H$ is a finite group with $\chi_1(H) = \chi_1(G)$, must $H \cong G$?

(b) If $G$ is a finite quasisimple group and $H$ is a finite group with $\chi_1(H) = \chi_1(G)$, must $H \cong G$?
status_search_result: The simple-group case (Question 11.8(a) of the Kourovka Notebook) is established: every non-abelian finite simple group is determined up to isomorphism by the multiset of its irreducible complex character degrees. For quasisimple groups, results of Nguyen, Tong-Viet and others show that every quasisimple group except possibly some covers of alternating groups (and a couple of small exceptions like 3·PSL3(4), 6·PSU4(3)) is determined by its complex group algebra, so part (b) is largely but not completely settled. The almost simple case (a) has been verified for many families (e.g. results on almost simple groups of Lie type and on alternating/sporadic groups), but the general statement is still considered open in the Kourovka problem list.

self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, and let $F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ be the polynomial ring in $n$ variables over $F$. Let $\mathrm{Aut}(F[x_1,\dots,x_n])$ denote the group of $F$-algebra automorphisms of $F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. Define the principal congruence subgroup
$$\Gamma = \{\,\varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(F[x_1,\dots,x_n]) : \varphi(x_i) \equiv x_i \pmod{\mathfrak{m}^2}\ \text{for each } i=1,\dots,n\,\},$$
where $\mathfrak{m} = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$, i.e., $\Gamma$ consists of those automorphisms sending each variable $x_i$ to $x_i$ plus terms of degree $\ge 2$. It is known that $\Gamma$ is a residually-$p$ group, so it has a pro-$p$ completion $\widehat{\Gamma}_p$.

A pro-$p$ group $G$ is said to satisfy a pro-$p$ identity if there exists a non-identity element $w$ in the free pro-$p$ group $\widehat{F}_d$ on some finite set of generators such that every continuous homomorphism $\widehat{F}_d \to G$ sends $w$ to the identity.

Question: Does $\Gamma$ (equivalently, its pro-$p$ completion) satisfy a pro-$p$ identity?
status_search_result: The problem was posed by E. Zelmanov as a new entry in the 2026 problem-collection of group theory problems. Related work (e.g., on pro-p identities in linear groups by Zelmanov and others) has shown pro-p identities for GL_n over pro-finite rings under conditions on p, but no published result resolves the specific question for the principal congruence subgroup of Aut(F[x_1,...,x_n]). No source was found settling this question, so it appears to remain open.

original_question: Suppose that φ is an automorphism of a finite soluble group G. Must G contain a subgroup of index bounded in terms of |φ| and |CG(φ)| whose Fitting height is bounded(a) in terms of |φ|? (b) or even in terms of the composition length of ⟨φ⟩? An affirmative answer to part(b) is known when |φ| is a prime power(B. Hartley– V. Turau), or when(|G|, |φ|) = 1(A. Turull, B. Hartley–I. M. Isaacs). Also cf. 19.43.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite soluble group and let $\varphi$ be an automorphism of $G$. Write $|\varphi|$ for the order of $\varphi$, $C_G(\varphi) = \{g \in G : \varphi(g) = g\}$ for the fixed-point subgroup, and let the composition length of the cyclic group $\langle\varphi\rangle$ denote the number of prime factors (with multiplicity) of $|\varphi|$. The Fitting height $h(H)$ of a finite soluble group $H$ is the length of its (shortest) Fitting series, i.e. the least $n$ such that $F_n(H) = H$, where $F_0(H) = 1$ and $F_{i+1}(H)/F_i(H) = F(H/F_i(H))$ is the Fitting subgroup of $H/F_i(H)$.

Decide whether each of the following holds:

(a) Does there exist a function $f$ and a function $h$ such that $G$ contains a subgroup $H \le G$ with $[G:H] \le f(|\varphi|, |C_G(\varphi)|)$ and Fitting height $h(H) \le h(|\varphi|)$?

(b) Does there exist a function $f$ and a function $h$ such that $G$ contains a subgroup $H \le G$ with $[G:H] \le f(|\varphi|, |C_G(\varphi)|)$ and Fitting height $h(H) \le h(c(\varphi))$, where $c(\varphi)$ is the composition length of $\langle\varphi\rangle$?

It is known that an affirmative answer to (b) holds whenever $|\varphi|$ is a prime power, and whenever $\gcd(|G|, |\varphi|) = 1$.
category_tag: Finite soluble groups and Fitting height
status_search_result: The problem appears in the most recent edition of the Kourovka Notebook of unsolved group-theoretic problems. Search results indicate it remains a question with only partial results: affirmative answers are known in the prime-power case (Hartley–Turau) and the coprime case (Turull; Hartley–Isaacs), but the general case is not resolved.

original_question: Suppose that φ is an automorphism of a finite soluble group G, and let r be the(Prüfer) rank of the fixed-point subgroup CG(φ). Is the Fitting height of G bounded terms of |φ| and r? This is known to be true in the case where |φ| is a product of at most two prime powers(B. Hartley, Preprint, 1994, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress. com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/hartley94-prepr-mims.pdf). An affirmative answer to this question would imply an affirmative answer to 13.8(b).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite soluble group and let $\varphi$ be an automorphism of $G$. Denote by $C_G(\varphi) = \{g \in G : \varphi(g) = g\}$ the fixed-point subgroup of $\varphi$, and let $r$ be the Prüfer rank of $C_G(\varphi)$ (that is, the smallest integer such that every finitely generated subgroup of $C_G(\varphi)$ can be generated by $r$ elements). Let $|\varphi|$ denote the order of $\varphi$ as an element of $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$, and let $h(G)$ denote the Fitting height of $G$ (the length of the shortest normal series of $G$ with nilpotent factors).

Question: Does there exist a function $f:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that $h(G) \le f(|\varphi|, r)$ for every finite soluble group $G$ and every automorphism $\varphi$ of $G$?

It is known that the answer is affirmative whenever $|\varphi|$ is a product of at most two prime powers.

The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Is there an algorithm deciding if a given one-relator group is hyperbolic?
self_contained_problem:
A finitely presented group $G = \langle X \mid r \rangle$ given by a finite alphabet $X$ together with a single relator $r$ (a freely reduced word in $X \cup X^{-1}$) is called a one-relator group. A finitely generated group is called (Gromov) hyperbolic if its Cayley graph (with respect to some, equivalently any, finite generating set) is a $\delta$-hyperbolic geodesic metric space for some $\delta \geq 0$; equivalently, every geodesic triangle in the Cayley graph is $\delta$-thin.

Decide: does there exist an algorithm which, on input a finite presentation $\langle X \mid r \rangle$ of a one-relator group $G$, halts and outputs "yes" if $G$ is hyperbolic and "no" otherwise?
status_search_result: The problem of algorithmically deciding hyperbolicity of one-relator groups is widely cited as open. While one-relator groups with torsion are known to be hyperbolic, and there are conjectural characterizations (e.g., a one-relator group is hyperbolic iff it contains no Baumslag–Solitar subgroup), no complete decision algorithm is known in general. Only partial/semi-algorithms exist (e.g., for free-by-cyclic groups).

original_question: For a ring R, we say that a group G is of type FL(R) if the trivial RG-module R admits a finite resolution by finitely generated free modules. If R is a field, we define the Euler characteristic of G over R to be the alternating sum of R-ranks of homology groups Hi(G; R). Does there exist a group of type FL(Fi) for two fields F1 and F2 such that the Euler characteristics of the group over the fields F1 and F2 differ?
self_contained_problem:
Let R be a (unital) ring and let G be a group. Say that G is of type FL(R) if the trivial RG-module R admits a finite resolution by finitely generated free RG-modules. When R is a field and G is of type FL(R), the homology groups H_i(G; R) are finite-dimensional R-vector spaces and vanish for all sufficiently large i; define the Euler characteristic of G over R by

  χ_R(G) = Σ_{i ≥ 0} (−1)^i dim_R H_i(G; R).

Question: Do there exist two fields F_1 and F_2 and a single group G that is simultaneously of type FL(F_1) and of type FL(F_2) such that χ_{F_1}(G) ≠ χ_{F_2}(G)?

original_question: Is the conjugacy problem in CT(Z) algorithmically decidable? See the definition of CT(Z) in 17.57.
self_contained_problem:
Define the group $\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ as follows. For positive integers $m_1, m_2$ and integers $r_1, r_2$ with $0 \le r_i < m_i$, suppose the residue classes $r_1(m_1) := \{r_1 + k m_1 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ and $r_2(m_2) := \{r_2 + k m_2 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ are disjoint. The associated class transposition $\tau_{r_1(m_1),\, r_2(m_2)} \in \mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{Z})$ is the involution that, for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, interchanges $r_1 + k m_1$ with $r_2 + k m_2$ and fixes every integer not lying in $r_1(m_1) \cup r_2(m_2)$. Let
$$\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z}) := \big\langle \tau_{r_1(m_1),\, r_2(m_2)} : r_1(m_1) \cap r_2(m_2) = \emptyset \big\rangle \le \mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{Z}).$$
Each element of $\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ may be specified by a finite word in such generators. The conjugacy problem for $\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ asks for an algorithm that, given two such finite words representing elements $g, h \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$, decides whether there exists $x \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ with $x^{-1} g x = h$.

Question: Is the conjugacy problem in $\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ algorithmically decidable?
category_tag: Conjugacy problem in class transposition groups
status_search_result: The group CT(Z) generated by class transpositions of the integers was introduced and studied by Stefan Kohl in connection with the Collatz conjecture. Available literature on CT(Z) and the RCWA framework discusses algorithms for computing in this group but does not contain a published resolution (positive or negative) of the decidability of its conjugacy problem; the question continues to appear as an open problem in the Kourovka-style problem lists.

original_question: Given two distinct sets P1 and P2 of odd primes none of which is a subset of the other, is it true that ⟨CTP1(Z), CTP2(Z)⟩ ⪇ CTP1 ∪P2(Z)? See the definition of CTP(Z) in 17.60.
self_contained_problem:

\[

\]

original_question: Let d be an integer that is not divisible√by n-th powers of primes, let xn − d be an irreducible polynomial over Q, let θ = n d, and let K = Q(θ) be the radical extension of degree n of the field Q. The multiplicative group K ∗ of the field K is canonically embedded into the group AutQ(K) of all invertible Q-linear mappings of the Q-space K; let T be the image of K ∗ under this embedding. In the natural basis 1, θ, θ2,..., θn−1 of the Q-space K the group AutQ(K) corresponds to G = GL(n, Q), and the subgroup T to a subgroup T(d) (unsplit maximal torus). Every subgroup H of G containing T(d) and some one-dimensional transformation is rich in elementary transvections(V. A. Koibaev, St. Petersbg. Math. J., 21, no. 5(2010), 731–742) and thus defines a net σ = σ(H) (V. A. Koibaev, A. V. Shilov, J. Math. Sci. New York 171, no. 3(2010), 380–385). Let E(σ) denote the subgroup generated by all transvections in the net group G(σ). Is it true that H ⩽ NG(E(σ))? This inclusion was proved in the case n = 2(V. A. Koibaev, Dokl. Math., 41, no. 3(1990), 414–416).
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer and let $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ be such that $d$ is not divisible by the $n$-th power of any prime and the polynomial $x^n - d$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$. Set $\theta = \sqrt[n]{d}$ and let $K = \mathbb{Q}(\theta)$, the radical extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ of degree $n$. The multiplicative group $K^*$ embeds canonically into $\operatorname{Aut}_\mathbb{Q}(K)$, the group of all invertible $\mathbb{Q}$-linear maps of $K$, by sending $a \in K^*$ to multiplication-by-$a$; let $T \subset \operatorname{Aut}_\mathbb{Q}(K)$ denote the image. With respect to the basis $1, \theta, \theta^2, \ldots, \theta^{n-1}$ of the $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $K$, identify $\operatorname{Aut}_\mathbb{Q}(K)$ with $G = \operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{Q})$, and let $T(d) \subset G$ be the subgroup corresponding to $T$ (an unsplit maximal torus). 

A net (carpet) over $\mathbb{Q}$ is a family $\sigma = (\sigma_{ij})_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}$ of additive subgroups of $\mathbb{Q}$ satisfying $\sigma_{ir}\sigma_{rj} \subseteq \sigma_{ij}$ for all $i, r, j$. The net group $G(\sigma)$ is the subgroup of $G$ consisting of matrices $g = (g_{ij})$ with $g_{ij} \in \sigma_{ij}$ for $i \neq j$ (and diagonal entries invertible), and $E(\sigma)$ is the subgroup of $G(\sigma)$ generated by all elementary transvections $t_{ij}(\xi) = e + \xi e_{ij}$ with $\xi \in \sigma_{ij}$, $i \neq j$.

Now let $H$ be any subgroup of $G$ containing $T(d)$ together with at least one one-dimensional transformation (a transvection or a one-dimensional dilation). It is known that such $H$ is rich in elementary transvections, and so it determines a net $\sigma = \sigma(H)$.

Question: Is it true that $H \leq N_G(E(\sigma))$, i.e., every such $H$ normalizes the elementary net subgroup $E(\sigma(H))$?
status_search_result: Subsequent work by Koibaev and collaborators (Journal of Mathematical Sciences, 2015) computes the normalizer $N_G(E(\sigma))$ of the elementary net group associated with a nonsplit maximal torus $T(d)$ in $\operatorname{GL}(n,k)$ over a field of odd characteristic, and there are related results on overgroups of nonsplit tori. However, available sources do not explicitly confirm that the inclusion $H \leq N_G(E(\sigma(H)))$ has been established for arbitrary $n$ in the setting stated; the case $n=2$ is known. The current status thus appears unresolved or unverifiable from public sources.

original_question: Let G be a finitely generated group with a fixed finite generating set S and the corresponding word metric LS(∗). An element g is said to be distorted in G if LS(g n)/n → 0 as n → ∞; this notion is independent of the choice of the generating set S. For any, not necessarily finitely generated, group H, an element g ∈ H is said to be distorted if there is a finitely generated subgroup G of H containing g in which g is distorted. Do there exist finitely generated left-orderable groups in which every nontrivial element is distorted? Note that it is straightforward to construct countable(not finitely generated) left-orderable groups with this property using HN N-extensions and applying results of V. V. Bludov and A. M. W. Glass.
self_contained_problem:
For a finitely generated group $G$ with a fixed finite generating set $S$, let $L_S(\cdot)$ denote the corresponding word length on $G$. An element $g \in G$ is called distorted in $G$ if 
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{L_S(g^n)}{n} = 0.$$
This property does not depend on the choice of finite generating set $S$. For an arbitrary (not necessarily finitely generated) group $H$, an element $g \in H$ is called distorted in $H$ if there exists a finitely generated subgroup $G \le H$ with $g \in G$ such that $g$ is distorted in $G$.

A group $H$ is called left-orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $H$ that is invariant under left multiplication: $a \le b \implies ca \le cb$ for all $a,b,c \in H$.

Question: Does there exist a finitely generated left-orderable group $H$ in which every nontrivial element is distorted?
status_search_result: The problem appears in the current Kourovka Notebook list of open problems in group theory. A web search did not surface any published resolution; related recent work on finitely generated simple left-orderable groups (e.g., Hyde–Lodha and subsequent papers) addresses adjacent properties (uniform perfectness, quasimorphisms) but not the specific distortion question. The status appears to be open.

original_question: (J. Wiegold). Let Γ be a finite simple group and let Nn(Γ) denote the set of normal subgroups of the free group Fn of rank n whose quotient is isomorphic to Γ. Conjecture: Aut(Fn) acts transitively on Nn(Γ) for n ⩾ 3. This is not true for n = 2(B. H. Neumann, H. Neumann, Math. Nachr., 4(1951), 106–125).
self_contained_problem:
Let $F_n$ denote the free group of rank $n$, and let $\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ be its automorphism group. For a finite simple group $\Gamma$, let
$$N_n(\Gamma) = \{\, N \trianglelefteq F_n : F_n/N \cong \Gamma \,\}$$
be the set of normal subgroups of $F_n$ whose quotient is isomorphic to $\Gamma$. The group $\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ acts on $N_n(\Gamma)$ by $\varphi \cdot N := \varphi(N)$.

Prove or disprove: for every $n \geq 3$ and every finite simple group $\Gamma$, the action of $\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ on $N_n(\Gamma)$ is transitive.

(Equivalently, $\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ acts transitively on the set of epimorphisms $F_n \twoheadrightarrow \Gamma$ modulo $\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)$, i.e., $\Gamma$ has a single $T_n$-system. It is known that the analogous statement fails for $n=2$.)
category_tag: Wiegold conjecture / T-systems of finite simple groups
status_search_result: The Wiegold conjecture remains open in general. It is known only in limited cases: results of Garion–Shalev, Avni, and others (using deep input such as Larsen–Pink) establish transitivity for various families of finite simple groups of Lie type, and recent work (e.g., 2025 preprint on small Ree groups) continues to handle further families, indicating the general conjecture is still unresolved.

original_question: The function dn(σ, τ) = (1/n)·|{x ∈ {1,..., n} | σ(x) ̸= τ (x)}| is a distance on the symmetric group Sn. For a finitely generated group G, an almost-homomorphism is a sequence of set-theoretic maps fn: G → Sn satisfying dn(fn(g)fn(h), fn(gh)) → 0 as n → ∞ for all g, h ∈ G. An almost-homomorphism {fn } is said to be close to a homomorphism if there is a sequence of group homomorphisms ρn: G → Sn such that dn(ρn(g), fn(g)) → 0 as n → ∞ for all g ∈ G. The group G is said to be permutation stable if every almost-homomorphism of G is close to a homomorphism. Conjecture: Metabelian groups are permutation-stable.
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer $n$, let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, and define the normalized Hamming distance on $S_n$ by
$$d_n(\sigma,\tau) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{n}\,\bigl|\{x \in \{1,\dots,n\} : \sigma(x) \neq \tau(x)\}\bigr|.$$
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group. A sequence of (set-theoretic) maps $f_n : G \to S_n$ is called an almost-homomorphism if
$$d_n\bigl(f_n(g)\,f_n(h),\, f_n(gh)\bigr) \to 0 \quad\text{as } n\to\infty, \text{ for every } g,h\in G.$$
An almost-homomorphism $\{f_n\}$ is said to be close to a homomorphism if there exists a sequence of group homomorphisms $\rho_n : G \to S_n$ with
$$d_n\bigl(\rho_n(g),\, f_n(g)\bigr) \to 0 \quad\text{as } n\to\infty, \text{ for every } g \in G.$$
The group $G$ is called permutation stable if every almost-homomorphism of $G$ is close to a homomorphism.

A group $G$ is metabelian if it admits an abelian normal subgroup $A \trianglelefteq G$ such that $G/A$ is abelian (equivalently, the commutator subgroup $[G,G]$ is abelian).

Prove or disprove: every finitely generated metabelian group is permutation stable.
status_search_result: The conjecture, attributed to Levit and Lubotzky, remains open in general. Important special cases have been established: Levit–Lubotzky proved permutation stability of permutational wreath products of finitely generated abelian groups; Zheng showed the lamplighter group is permutation stable via co-sofic invariant random subgroups; and a 2023 preprint proves that all finitely generated free metabelian groups are permutation stable. The full conjecture for arbitrary finitely generated metabelian groups has not been resolved.

original_question: Is a flexibly permutation-stable group always permutation-stable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with a fixed finite generating set $S$, and let $F_S$ denote the free group on $S$. For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\mathrm{Sym}(N)$ denote the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,N\}$, equipped with the normalized Hamming distance $d_H(\sigma,\tau) = \frac{1}{N}|\{i : \sigma(i)\neq \tau(i)\}|$. For $M \geq N$, regard $\mathrm{Sym}(N)$ as a subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}(M)$ by fixing the points $N+1,\dots,M$.

A homomorphism $\varphi : F_S \to \mathrm{Sym}(N)$ is called an $\varepsilon$-almost action of $G$ if for every relation $r$ in $G$ (i.e., every $r$ in the kernel of the canonical map $F_S \to G$ from some, equivalently any, presentation), $d_H(\varphi(r), \mathrm{id}) \leq \varepsilon$. (For finitely presented $G$ it suffices to require this for the finitely many defining relations.)

The group $G$ is called permutation-stable (P-stable) if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that whenever $\varphi : F_S \to \mathrm{Sym}(N)$ is a $\delta$-almost action, there is an honest homomorphism $\psi : G \to \mathrm{Sym}(N)$ (i.e., a homomorphism $F_S \to \mathrm{Sym}(N)$ that factors through $G$) with $\max_{s \in S} d_H(\varphi(s), \psi(s)) \leq \varepsilon$.

The group $G$ is called flexibly permutation-stable if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that whenever $\varphi : F_S \to \mathrm{Sym}(N)$ is a $\delta$-almost action, there exist $M \geq N$ and an honest homomorphism $\psi : G \to \mathrm{Sym}(M)$ with
$$\max_{s \in S} \frac{1}{M}\big|\{i \in \{1,\dots,M\} : \varphi(s)(i) \neq \psi(s)(i)\}\big| \leq \varepsilon,$$
where $\varphi(s)$ is viewed in $\mathrm{Sym}(M)$ via the natural embedding above.

Both properties are independent of the choice of finite generating set $S$ (and of presentation) and are thus invariants of the group $G$.

Question: Must every flexibly permutation-stable group be permutation-stable?
status_search_result: The relationship between flexible permutation-stability and (strict) permutation-stability is an active research topic. Surface groups have been shown to be flexibly stable, but no separation between the two notions is known, and the implication "flexibly P-stable implies P-stable" is generally listed as an open problem in the area.

original_question: Assume that a finite group G has a family of d-generator subgroups whose indices have no common divisor. Is it true that G can be generated by d + 1 elements? The answer is positive if G is solvable(L. G. Kovács, H.-S. Sim, Indag. Math., 2(1991), 229–232). For an arbitrary finite group G it is proved that G can be generated by d + 2 elements(A. Lucchini, Commun. Algebra, 28, no. 4(2000), 1875–1880).
self_contained_problem:
Let $d$ be a positive integer and let $G$ be a finite group. Suppose that $G$ has a family $\{H_i\}_{i\in I}$ of subgroups such that:

(i) each $H_i$ can be generated by $d$ elements, and
(ii) the indices $[G:H_i]$, $i\in I$, have no common divisor greater than $1$ (equivalently, $\gcd\{[G:H_i] : i\in I\} = 1$).

Question: Must $G$ be generated by $d+1$ elements?

(Known partial results: the answer is "yes" when $G$ is solvable; for arbitrary finite $G$ it is known that $G$ can be generated by $d+2$ elements. The problem is whether the bound $d+1$ holds for all finite groups.)
status_search_result: The question whether $d+1$ generators suffice for an arbitrary finite group with a family of $d$-generated subgroups of coprime indices appears to remain open. The solvable case was settled by Kovács and Sim (1991), and Lucchini (2000) proved the weaker bound $d+2$ for all finite groups; no later resolution of the gap to $d+1$ in the general case was located in the search.

original_question: (W. Willems). Conjecture: The sum of squares of the degrees of the irreducible p-Brauer characters of a finite group G is at least the p′-part of |G|. This is known to be true for p = 2(G. Malle, Adv. Math., 380(2021), Paper no. 107609, 15 pp.).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a prime. Write $|G| = p^a m$ with $\gcd(m,p)=1$; the integer $m$ is called the $p'$-part of $|G|$. Let $\operatorname{IBr}_p(G)$ denote the set of irreducible $p$-Brauer characters of $G$ (i.e., the irreducible Brauer characters with respect to a $p$-modular system), and for $\varphi \in \operatorname{IBr}_p(G)$ let $\varphi(1)$ be its degree. Prove or disprove the following statement: for every finite group $G$ and every prime $p$,
$$\sum_{\varphi \in \operatorname{IBr}_p(G)} \varphi(1)^2 \;\geq\; |G|_{p'},$$
where $|G|_{p'}$ denotes the $p'$-part of $|G|$.
category_tag: Brauer character degrees of finite groups
status_search_result: Willems' conjecture remains open in general. It is known to hold for p-solvable groups (originally by Willems) and for p = 2 (Malle, Adv. Math. 2021), with a reduction to quasi-simple groups by Tong-Viet. No full proof for all primes has appeared.

original_question: (M. Herzog, J. Schönheim). Let G be a group and let k ⩾ 2. self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be a group and let $k \geq 2$ be an integer. original_question: Is there an almost simple but not simple group which is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph? Note that if a group G is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg– Kegel graph, then G is recognizable by its Gruenberg–Kegel graph, and therefore G is almost simple(P. J. Cameron, N. V. Maslova, J. Algebra, 607(2022), 186–213).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, the Gruenberg–Kegel graph (prime graph) $\Gamma(G)$ is the graph whose vertex set is the set of prime divisors of $|G|$ and in which two distinct primes $r$ and $s$ are adjacent if and only if $G$ contains an element of order $rs$.

Say that a finite group $G$ is recognizable by its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if every finite group $H$ with $\Gamma(H) = \Gamma(G)$ (equality of labeled graphs on the set of prime divisors) is isomorphic to $G$, and that $G$ is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if every finite group $H$ such that $\Gamma(H)$ is isomorphic (as an abstract unlabeled graph) to $\Gamma(G)$ is isomorphic to $G$.

Recall that a finite group $G$ is called almost simple if there exists a non-abelian finite simple group $S$ such that $S \trianglelefteq G \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$; in particular every non-abelian finite simple group is almost simple.

It is known that if $G$ is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph, then $G$ is recognizable by its Gruenberg–Kegel graph, and consequently $G$ is almost simple.

Question: Does there exist a finite almost simple group that is not simple and is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph?
status_search_result: A 2025 preprint on characterization of groups by the isomorphism type of the Gruenberg–Kegel graph explicitly poses this exact question as an open problem, noting that no almost-simple-but-not-simple example has been exhibited; only simple examples (such as certain $E_8(q)$ and ${}^2E_6(2)$) are known to be recognizable by the isomorphism type of the Gruenberg–Kegel graph.

original_question: Which finite almost simple groups are the automorphism groups of regular polytopes of rank 3? In other words, which finite almost simple groups are generated by three involutions two of which commute? This question has been answered for finite simple groups; see 7.30 in Archive. Ya.
self_contained_problem:
A finite group $G$ is called almost simple if there exists a finite non-abelian simple group $S$ such that $S \trianglelefteq G \leq \mathrm{Aut}(S)$ (identifying $S$ with its image of inner automorphisms). An abstract regular polytope of rank $3$ is a regular polytope whose automorphism group is generated by three involutions $\rho_0, \rho_1, \rho_2$ satisfying the commuting condition $(\rho_0 \rho_2)^2 = 1$ (together with the standard intersection condition for string C-groups of rank 3).

Equivalently, the automorphism group of a regular polytope of rank $3$ is a group generated by three involutions, two of which commute.

Classify all finite almost simple groups $G$ that arise as the automorphism group of some abstract regular polytope of rank $3$; equivalently, determine all finite almost simple groups that can be generated by three involutions, two of which commute.
category_tag: finite almost simple groups and regular polytopes
status_search_result: The analogous question for finite simple groups (Kourovka 7.30, Mazurov) has been resolved through a series of works covering alternating, sporadic, and Lie-type cases. For almost simple groups, partial results exist: e.g., results on PSL(2,q) and PGL(2,q) (Leemans–Liebeck and others) show certain almost simple groups are or are not C-groups of rank 3, and atlases of regular polytopes for small almost simple groups have been compiled. A complete classification for all finite almost simple groups does not yet appear in the literature, so the problem appears to be partially solved.

original_question: (V. V. Uspenskii). A Hausdorff topological group G is called minimal if it does not admit a strictly coarser Hausdorff group topology. A topological group is called Raikov complete if its two-sided uniform structure is complete. It is known that a finite direct product of Raikov complete minimal topological groups is again minimal. Is it true that an arbitrary Cartesian product of Raikov complete minimal topological groups remains minimal? It is known that an arbitrary Cartesian product of centre-free minimal topological groups is minimal(M. Megrelishvili, Topology Appl., 62, no. 1(1995), 1–19).
self_contained_problem:
A Hausdorff topological group $G$ is called minimal if it admits no strictly coarser Hausdorff group topology. A topological group is called Raikov complete if it is complete with respect to its two-sided uniform structure (the supremum of the left and right uniformities).

It is known that:
(i) any finite direct product of Raikov complete minimal topological groups is again minimal;
(ii) any Cartesian product of centre-free minimal topological groups is minimal.

Question: Is it true that, for every family $\{G_i : i \in I\}$ of Raikov complete minimal Hausdorff topological groups, the Cartesian product $\prod_{i \in I} G_i$ (endowed with the product topology and the coordinate-wise group operation) is again a minimal topological group?
status_search_result: The problem is a long-standing question of Uspenskij on whether arbitrary products of Raikov complete minimal groups are minimal. Only partial positive results are known, e.g., products of complete totally minimal groups are minimal, and products of centre-free minimal groups are minimal. Recent work (e.g., "Products of locally minimal groups," 2022) continues to give partial answers, indicating the general question remains open.

original_question: (D. Segal). A group word w is said to be concise in a class C of groups if for every group G in C such that the set Gw of word values of w in G is finite, the verbal subgroup w(G) = ⟨Gw ⟩ is also finite(see also Archive 2.45). Is every word concise in the class of residually finite groups? See(D. Segal, Words. Notes on verbal width in groups, Cambridge Univ. Press, 2009) for a partial solution.
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be the free group on countably many generators $x_1, x_2, \ldots$, and let $w \in F$ be a group word. For a group $G$, define the set of $w$-values in $G$ by
$$G_w = \{\, w(g_1, \ldots, g_n)^{\pm 1} : g_1, \ldots, g_n \in G \,\},$$
and the verbal subgroup $w(G) = \langle G_w \rangle$.

The word $w$ is called concise in a class $\mathcal{C}$ of groups if, for every $G \in \mathcal{C}$ such that $G_w$ is finite, the verbal subgroup $w(G)$ is also finite.

A group $G$ is residually finite if for every $1 \neq g \in G$ there exists a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$ of finite index with $g \notin N$.

Question: Is every group word $w$ concise in the class of residually finite groups? Equivalently, does every residually finite group $G$ in which the set $G_w$ of values of a word $w$ is finite necessarily have a finite verbal subgroup $w(G)$?
category_tag: Concise words in residually finite groups
status_search_result: The question of whether every word is concise in the class of residually finite groups (equivalently, in profinite groups) remains open and is regarded as the central conjecture on this topic. Partial results are known: many specific families of words have been shown to be concise in residually finite groups, including Engel words and generalizations, and any word expressible as a commutator of two non-commutator words. An ERC project (GroupConciseness) and several recent papers (2018–2025) explicitly state the problem is still open.

original_question: Conjecture: The derived length of a finite solvable group G does not exceed |Cod(G)| − 1. The Fitting height of G is known to be at most min{|Cod(G)|−1, |Cod(G)|/2+1} (G. Qian, Y. Zeng, J. Group Theory, to appear).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite solvable group. For an irreducible complex character $\chi \in \mathrm{Irr}(G)$, define its codegree by
$$\mathrm{cod}(\chi) = \frac{|G:\ker\chi|}{\chi(1)},$$
and let
$$\mathrm{Cod}(G) = \{\mathrm{cod}(\chi) : \chi \in \mathrm{Irr}(G)\}$$
denote the set of codegrees of $G$. Let $\mathrm{dl}(G)$ denote the derived length of $G$, i.e., the smallest non-negative integer $n$ such that the $n$-th term $G^{(n)}$ of the derived series of $G$ is trivial.

Prove or disprove: for every finite solvable group $G$,
$$\mathrm{dl}(G) \le |\mathrm{Cod}(G)| - 1.$$

original_question: Let S be a finite simple nonabelian group that is not isomorphic to any group 2B2(q). A nonidentity automorphism x of S is called a τ-automorphism if every two conjugates of x in ⟨x, Inn(S)⟩ generate a subgroup of order not divisible by 3. If S admits a τ-automorphism, we call S a τ-group. (a) List all τ-groups up to isomorphism. (b) Do τ-automorphisms of odd order exist?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a finite nonabelian simple group that is not isomorphic to any Suzuki group ${}^2B_2(q)$. Identify $S$ with its inner automorphism group $\mathrm{Inn}(S)$ inside $\mathrm{Aut}(S)$. A nonidentity automorphism $x \in \mathrm{Aut}(S)$ is called a $\tau$-automorphism of $S$ if for every two conjugates $x_1, x_2$ of $x$ in the subgroup $\langle x, \mathrm{Inn}(S)\rangle \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$, the order of the subgroup $\langle x_1, x_2\rangle$ is not divisible by $3$. A finite nonabelian simple group $S$ (not isomorphic to any ${}^2B_2(q)$) is called a $\tau$-group if it admits at least one $\tau$-automorphism.

(a) Determine, up to isomorphism, all $\tau$-groups.

(b) Decide whether there exists a $\tau$-automorphism of odd order (of any $\tau$-group).

original_question: Let G be a finite group and p be a prime. Let Ψp,G be the class function of G which vanishes on all p-singular elements of G and whose value at each p-regular element x of G is the number of p-elements of CG(x). (a) Is it true that Ψp,G is a character of G? (b) If yes, can Ψp,G be afforded by a projective RG-module, where R is a complete discrete valuation ring of characteristic zero such that the field of fractions of R is a splitting field for G and its subgroups, and the residue field R/J(R) is a splitting field of characteristic p for G and its subgroups? It is known that Ψp,G is a character when G ≅ Sn for any positive integer n and any prime p(T. Scharf, J. Algebra, 139, no. 2(1991), 446–457).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $p$ be a prime. An element of $G$ is called a $p$-element if its order is a power of $p$, and a $p$-regular element if its order is coprime to $p$; an element of $G$ is called $p$-singular if it is not $p$-regular. Define the class function $\Psi_{p,G}\colon G\to\mathbb{Z}$ by
$$\Psi_{p,G}(x)=\begin{cases}\#\{y\in C_G(x):y\text{ is a }p\text{-element}\},&\text{if }x\text{ is }p\text{-regular},\\ 0,&\text{if }x\text{ is }p\text{-singular},\end{cases}$$
where $C_G(x)$ denotes the centralizer of $x$ in $G$.

(a) Is $\Psi_{p,G}$ always a character of $G$ (i.e. the character of some finite-dimensional complex representation of $G$)?

(b) If the answer to (a) is yes, let $R$ be a complete discrete valuation ring of characteristic $0$ whose field of fractions $K$ is a splitting field for $G$ and all of its subgroups, and whose residue field $R/J(R)$ has characteristic $p$ and is a splitting field for $G$ and all of its subgroups. Is $\Psi_{p,G}$ afforded by a projective $RG$-module, i.e. does there exist a finitely generated projective $RG$-module $P$ such that the character of the $KG$-module $K\otimes_R P$ equals $\Psi_{p,G}$?

(It is known that $\Psi_{p,G}$ is a character when $G\cong S_n$ for every positive integer $n$ and every prime $p$.)

original_question: Let C1,..., Cn be(left or right) cosets of a finite group G such that U:= C1 ∪ · · · ∪ Cn is not G. Is it always true that |G \ U | ⩾ |G|/2n? Affirmative answers are known in some special cases(B. Sambale, M. Tărnăuceanu, J. Algebraic Combin., 55(2022), 979–987).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $C_1, C_2, \dots, C_n$ be cosets in $G$ (each $C_i$ is either a left coset $g_iH_i$ or a right coset $H_ig_i$ of some subgroup $H_i \le G$, allowed to differ from one $i$ to another). Assume that the union $U := C_1 \cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is a proper subset of $G$, i.e., $U \ne G$. Determine whether the inequality
$$|G \setminus U| \;\ge\; \frac{|G|}{2^n}$$
holds for every such finite group $G$ and every such choice of cosets $C_1, \dots, C_n$.

No general resolution appears to be available in the literature as of 2026; the problem remains posed as an open question in current group-theory problem collections.

original_question: (a) Does there exist a finitely generated simple group that is of exponential growth but not of uniformly exponential growth? (b) Does there exist a finitely generated hereditarily just-infinite group that is of exponential growth but not of uniformly exponential growth?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with a finite generating set $S$ (assumed symmetric, $S=S^{-1}$). Let $B_S(n)=\{g\in G:\ell_S(g)\le n\}$ where $\ell_S$ is the word length, and define the exponential growth rate
$$\omega(G,S)=\lim_{n\to\infty}|B_S(n)|^{1/n}\in[1,\infty).$$
$G$ is said to be of exponential growth if $\omega(G,S)>1$ for some (equivalently every) finite generating set $S$, and of uniformly exponential growth if
$$\omega(G):=\inf_S \omega(G,S)>1,$$
where the infimum is taken over all finite generating sets $S$ of $G$.

Recall that $G$ is simple if it has no proper nontrivial normal subgroup, and $G$ is just-infinite if it is infinite and every proper quotient is finite. $G$ is hereditarily just-infinite if it is residually finite and every finite-index subgroup of $G$ is just-infinite.

Decide each of the following:
(a) Does there exist a finitely generated simple group of exponential growth that is not of uniformly exponential growth?
(b) Does there exist a finitely generated hereditarily just-infinite group of exponential growth that is not of uniformly exponential growth?
status_search_result: A web search returned no evidence that either part has been resolved. The questions are recorded as new problems in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook update, and related work on uniform exponential growth (e.g. for groups acting on hyperbolic spaces) does not address simple or hereditarily just-infinite groups specifically. The general problem of constructing groups of exponential but non-uniformly exponential growth (Wilson's examples) remains active, but no such construction is known to be simple or hereditarily just-infinite.

original_question: Let p be a prime number. A group Γ is called p-Jordan if there exist constants J and e such that any finite subgroup G ⊂ Γ contains a normal abelian subgroup of order coprime to p and of index at most J · |G(p) |e. (For example by the results of Brauer–Feit and Larsen–Pink, for any field K of characteristic p the group GLn(K) is p-Jordan with e = 3.) Let the p-Jordan exponent e(Γ) of the group Γ be the infimum of all constants e for which the above bound holds for some constant J = J(e). a) Is it true that this infimum is always attained? b) Is it true that e(Γ) ⩽ 3 for any p-Jordan group Γ?
self_contained_problem:
Fix a prime number $p$. For a finite group $G$, let $|G_{(p)}|$ denote the order of a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ (equivalently, the largest power of $p$ dividing $|G|$). A group $\Gamma$ is called $p$-Jordan if there exist constants $J \geq 1$ and $e \geq 0$ such that every finite subgroup $G \subseteq \Gamma$ contains a normal abelian subgroup $A 	rianglelefteq G$ whose order is coprime to $p$ and whose index satisfies
$$[G:A] \;\leq\; J\cdot |G_{(p)}|^{e}.$$
(Classical results of Brauer–Feit and Larsen–Pink imply, for instance, that for any field $K$ of characteristic $p$ the group $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ is $p$-Jordan with $e=3$.) Define the $p$-Jordan exponent of a $p$-Jordan group $\Gamma$ by
$$e(\Gamma) \;=\; \inf\{\, e \geq 0 : 	ext{there exists } J=J(e) 	ext{ such that the above bound holds}\,\}.$$

(a) Is the infimum defining $e(\Gamma)$ always attained, i.e. is there always a constant $J$ for which the bound holds with exponent $e(\Gamma)$ itself?

(b) Is it true that $e(\Gamma) \leq 3$ for every $p$-Jordan group $\Gamma$?

original_question: Is it true that the extension of the A. Agrachev–R. Gamkrelidze construction of groups from pre-Lie rings in(J. Soviet Math., 17(1981), 1650–1675) suggested in Definition 66 of(A. Smoktunowicz, J. Pure Appl. Algebra, 229, no. 12(2025), 108128) produces groups from pre-Lie rings? If this extended construction does give a group, then it also gives a brace, and so an affirmative answer to this question would have consequences for the theory of set-theoretic solutions of the Yang–Baxter equation and for the theory of braces.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(A,+,\cdot)$ be a pre-Lie ring; that is, $(A,+)$ is an abelian group equipped with a binary operation $\cdot$ satisfying the left pre-Lie identity
$$(a\cdot b)\cdot c - a\cdot(b\cdot c) = (b\cdot a)\cdot c - b\cdot(a\cdot c)\qquad(a,b,c\in A).$$
The classical construction of A. Agrachev and R. Gamkrelidze associates to a suitable (e.g. nilpotent, or formally completed) pre-Lie ring $A$ a group structure on the underlying set by means of a "group of flows" formula: one defines a binary operation $\ast$ on $A$ via a formal series in the pre-Lie product (a pre-Lie analogue of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula) that turns $(A,\ast)$ into a group whose multiplication can be expressed using only the operation $\cdot$.

Consider the following extension of this construction (the analogue of "Definition 66" in the setting referred to): given a pre-Lie ring $A$ (not assumed to be nilpotent or to lie in a complete topological setting), define a binary operation $\ast$ on $A$ by the same formal pre-Lie BCH-type expression, interpreted via the prescribed extension procedure that allows the formula to be evaluated on arbitrary pre-Lie rings.

Question: Does this extended construction always yield a group $(A,\ast)$ from any pre-Lie ring $A$? 

(If the answer is affirmative, then the resulting structure together with the addition of $A$ also forms a brace, with consequences for the theory of set-theoretic solutions of the Yang–Baxter equation and for the theory of braces. Recall that a left brace is a triple $(B,+,\circ)$ where $(B,+)$ is an abelian group, $(B,\circ)$ is a group, and $a\circ(b+c)+a = a\circ b + a\circ c$ for all $a,b,c\in B$.)
status_search_result: The question appears in the latest collection of new problems in the Kourovka Notebook (2026), suggesting it is currently open. Recent work by Smoktunowicz and collaborators (e.g., arXiv:2410.05924, 2208.02535, 2202.00085) studies the passage between pre-Lie rings and braces beyond the strongly nilpotent / Lazard regime, but no source verifies that the proposed extension of the Agrachev–Gamkrelidze construction yields a group on arbitrary pre-Lie rings.

original_question: (M. Bridson). Let Fm be a free group of rank m and let ϕ ∈ Aut(Fm) be a polynomially growing automorphism of maximal degree m − 1, which means that for some(equivalently, any) free basis {x1,..., xm } of Fm, the sequence maxi |ϕn(xi)| grows at the rate of nm−1, where |g| denotes the minimal length of g in the xi and their inverses. a) Is the free-by-cyclic group Fm ⋊ϕ Z virtually special? b) In particular, are the Hydra groups Gm = Fm ⋊ Z = ⟨a1,..., am, t | t−1 a1 t = a1, t−1 ai t = ai ai−1 for all i > 1⟩ virtually special?
self_contained_problem:
Let $m \geq 2$ be an integer and let $F_m$ denote the free group of rank $m$ with free basis $\{x_1,\dots,x_m\}$. For $g \in F_m$, let $|g|$ denote the minimal length of a word representing $g$ in the letters $x_1^{\pm 1},\dots,x_m^{\pm 1}$.

An automorphism $\varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(F_m)$ is said to be polynomially growing of maximal degree $m-1$ if, for some (equivalently, every) free basis $\{x_1,\dots,x_m\}$ of $F_m$, one has
$$\max_{1 \leq i \leq m} |\varphi^n(x_i)| \asymp n^{m-1} \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$

A group $G$ is called virtually special if it has a finite-index subgroup that embeds as a subgroup of a right-angled Artin group (equivalently, the fundamental group of a special cube complex in the sense of Haglund–Wise).

(a) For every such polynomially growing automorphism $\varphi$ of maximal degree $m-1$, is the free-by-cyclic group $F_m \rtimes_\varphi \mathbb{Z}$ virtually special?

(b) In particular, consider the Hydra groups
$$G_m = \langle a_1,\dots,a_m,\, t \mid t^{-1} a_1 t = a_1,\ t^{-1} a_i t = a_i a_{i-1}\ \text{for all } i>1 \rangle,$$
each of which is a free-by-cyclic group of the form $F_m \rtimes \mathbb{Z}$ with monodromy a polynomially growing automorphism of maximal degree $m-1$. Are the Hydra groups $G_m$ virtually special?

original_question: Let G be a right-angled Artin group. Is the stable commutator length scl(g) a rational number for every g ∈ [G, G]? For free groups this is true by Calegari’s Rationality Theorem. (See 18.40 for the definition of scl(g).)
self_contained_problem:
Let Γ be a finite simple graph with vertex set V and edge set E. The right-angled Artin group associated with Γ is the group
   A(Γ) = ⟨ V | [v, w] = 1 for all {v, w} ∈ E ⟩.
For a group G and an element g in the commutator subgroup [G, G], the commutator length cl_G(g) is the least integer n ≥ 0 such that g can be written as a product of n commutators in G. The stable commutator length of g is defined by
   scl_G(g) = lim_{n → ∞} cl_G(g^n) / n.
(The limit exists since cl_G(g^n) is subadditive in n.)

Question: Let G = A(Γ) be a right-angled Artin group. Is it true that for every g ∈ [G, G], the stable commutator length scl_G(g) is a rational number?
status_search_result: Recent work (Chen–Heuer 2020, "Stable commutator length in right-angled Artin and Coxeter groups") establishes spectral gap results and shows every rational q ≥ 1 arises as scl of some integral chain in a RAAG, but does not resolve whether scl is rational for every element of [G,G] in every RAAG. The rationality question for elements of right-angled Artin groups appears to remain open beyond the free group case (Calegari's Rationality Theorem).

original_question: If two Artin groups of spherical type are quasi-isometric, must they be commensurable? (This is not true for right-angled Artin groups.)
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a finite set and let $M=(m_{st})_{s,t\in S}$ be a Coxeter matrix, i.e. $m_{ss}=1$ and $m_{st}=m_{ts}\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ for $s\neq t$. The associated Artin group is
$$A_M=\langle\, S \mid \underbrace{sts\cdots}_{m_{st}\text{ factors}}=\underbrace{tst\cdots}_{m_{st}\text{ factors}} \text{ for all } s\neq t \text{ with } m_{st}<\infty\,\rangle.$$
The Artin group $A_M$ is said to be of spherical (finite) type if the corresponding Coxeter group (obtained by adjoining the relations $s^2=1$ for all $s\in S$) is finite.

Two finitely generated groups $G_1,G_2$ (each equipped with a word metric for some finite generating set) are quasi-isometric if there exist a map $f\colon G_1\to G_2$ and constants $K\geq 1$, $C\geq 0$ such that
$$\tfrac{1}{K}d(x,y)-C\leq d(f(x),f(y))\leq K\,d(x,y)+C \quad \text{for all } x,y\in G_1,$$
and every point of $G_2$ lies within distance $C$ of the image of $f$. Two groups $G_1,G_2$ are commensurable if they contain finite-index subgroups $H_i\leq G_i$ with $H_1\cong H_2$.

Question: If two Artin groups of spherical type are quasi-isometric, must they be commensurable?
status_search_result: Recent work has established the commensurability classification among irreducible spherical Artin groups (e.g., showing Artin groups of types F₄ and H₄ are not commensurable with type D₄), but the quasi-isometric classification of spherical Artin groups remains incomplete, and no published proof asserts that QI implies commensurability for all spherical Artin groups. The problem appears still open.

original_question: (Well-known problem). Is Thompson’s group F automatic?
self_contained_problem:
Thompson's group $F$ is the group with presentation
$$F = \langle x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots \mid x_n^{-1} x_k x_n = x_{k+1} \text{ for all } k > n \rangle,$$
equivalently the group of orientation-preserving piecewise-linear homeomorphisms of the unit interval $[0,1]$ whose breakpoints lie in the dyadic rationals $\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$ and whose slopes are integer powers of $2$.

A finitely generated group $G$ with finite generating set $A$ is called automatic if there exists a regular language $L \subseteq A^*$ surjecting onto $G$ (i.e. every element of $G$ has at least one representative in $L$) such that:
(i) for each $a \in A \cup \{1\}$, the set
$$\{(u, v) \in L \times L : u\, a =_G v\}$$
is recognized by a synchronous two-tape finite automaton (the "fellow traveller property" expressed via padded pairs of words).

Equivalently, there is a constant $K$ such that for any two words $u, v \in L$ with $u =_G v\,a$ for some $a \in A \cup \{1\}$, the corresponding paths in the Cayley graph $K$-fellow-travel.

Question: Is Thompson's group $F$ automatic?
status_search_result: The question of whether Thompson's group F is automatic appears to remain open as of recent literature. Related progress has been made: F has been shown to be 1-counter graph automatic (Elder–Taback, 2015) and autostackable (Cleary–Hermiller–Stein–Taback), but neither implies the standard automaticity property, and these works explicitly state that automaticity of F is unresolved.

$$	frac{1}{K} d_G(x,y) - C \le d_H(f(x), f(y)) \le K\, d_G(x,y) + C \qquad 	ext{for all } x,y \in G,$$
and such that every point of $H$ lies within distance $C$ of the image of $f$.

(b) Is $F$ quasi-isometric to $F 	imes F$?

original_question: (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev). A subgroup H of a right-orderable group G is said to be right-relatively convex if it is convex under some right ordering on G. Is the lattice of right-relatively convex subgroups of a right-orderable group always a sublattice of the lattice of its subgroups?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a group. A right ordering on G is a total order ≤ on the underlying set of G such that for all x, y, z ∈ G, x ≤ y implies xz ≤ yz. The group G is called right-orderable if it admits at least one right ordering. A subset C ⊆ G is convex with respect to a right ordering ≤ if for all a, b ∈ C and all g ∈ G with a ≤ g ≤ b, one has g ∈ C. A subgroup H ≤ G is called right-relatively convex if there exists some right ordering on G with respect to which H is convex.

Let G be a right-orderable group, and let R(G) denote the family of all right-relatively convex subgroups of G, partially ordered by inclusion. It is known that R(G) forms a lattice under its own meet and join operations. Let L(G) denote the lattice of all subgroups of G (under intersection and the subgroup generated by the union).

Question: Is R(G) always a sublattice of L(G)? Equivalently, for any two right-relatively convex subgroups H₁, H₂ of G:
(a) is the intersection H₁ ∩ H₂ right-relatively convex in G, and
(b) is the subgroup ⟨H₁ ∪ H₂⟩ generated by H₁ ∪ H₂ right-relatively convex in G,
so that the meet and join in R(G) coincide respectively with intersection and subgroup-join in L(G)?

original_question: (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev). Are there order automorphisms of Dlab groups that are not inner automorphisms?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the real line and let $I=[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$ be a closed interval of the extended real line. A Dlab group on $I$ is a group of order-preserving bijections of $I$ defined as follows. Fix an order-preserving bijection $\varphi:I\to I$ that has exactly two fixed points, namely the endpoints $a$ and $b$, and satisfies $\varphi(x)>x$ for all $x\in(a,b)$. The Dlab group $D(I,\varphi)$ is the group of all order-preserving bijections $g:I\to I$ such that $g$ fixes $a$ and $b$ and commutes with some integral power of $\varphi$ on a neighborhood of each interior point; equivalently, $D(I,\varphi)$ consists of those order automorphisms $g$ of $I$ for which there exist integers $m,n$ with $g\varphi^{m}=\varphi^{n}g$ on $I$. The group $D(I,\varphi)$ is a right-ordered (in fact lattice-ordered) group under the pointwise order inherited from $I$.

An order automorphism of a right-ordered group $(G,\le)$ is a group automorphism $\alpha:G\to G$ such that $\alpha(g)\ge e$ if and only if $g\ge e$, i.e.\ $\alpha$ preserves the positive cone. An automorphism is inner if it has the form $g\mapsto h g h^{-1}$ for some $h\in G$.

Question. Does there exist a Dlab group $D(I,\varphi)$ that admits an order automorphism which is not an inner automorphism?

The immersion $x$ (or the surface $M$) is said to be of finite type if its position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_{t_1} + x_{t_2} + \cdots + x_{t_k},$$
where $x_0 \in E^4$ is a constant vector, $k$ is a positive integer, and each $E^4$-valued map $x_{t_i}$ is non-constant and satisfies $\Delta x_{t_i} = \lambda_{t_i} x_{t_i}$ for some real number $\lambda_{t_i}$, with $\lambda_{t_1}, \ldots, \lambda_{t_k}$ pairwise distinct.

Three classes of surfaces in $S^3$ are easily seen to be of finite type:
(a) minimal surfaces of $S^3$ (i.e., surfaces with vanishing mean curvature in $S^3$);
(b) standard 2-spheres (intersections of $S^3$ with affine 3-planes that meet $S^3$ in a 2-sphere of any radius);
(c) products of two plane circles, i.e., flat tori of the form $\{(a\cos u, a\sin u, b\cos v, b\sin v) : u,v \in \mathbb{R}\}$ with $a^2 + b^2 = 1$, $a,b > 0$.

Question: Are these the only finite type surfaces in $S^3 \subset E^4$? Equivalently, prove or disprove that every finite type surface in $S^3$ is either a minimal surface of $S^3$, a standard 2-sphere, or a product of two plane circles.
status_search_result: The classification of finite type surfaces in $S^3 \subset E^4$ is a long-standing conjecture due to B.-Y. Chen. Search results show only partial classifications (e.g., for ruled surfaces, tubes, and surfaces with specific Gauss-map or curvature conditions). No source indicates a complete proof or counterexample, and recent works (e.g., on surfaces of finite Chen-type) continue to address special cases, indicating the conjecture remains open in general.
