paper_title: A single impurity in an ideal atomic Fermi gas: current understanding and some open problems
original_question: For a system consisting of a single impurity interacting with identical fermions through the wide-resonance Hamiltonian, prove or disprove that, for fixed mass ratio m/M and scattering length a, there is an upper limit on the number of fermions that can belong to a stable non-Efimovian bound state with that impurity, either in vacuum or with a Fermi sea present.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a single distinguishable "impurity" particle of mass $M$ interacting with $N$ identical spin-polarized fermions of mass $m$ in three-dimensional space. The impurity-fermion interaction is taken in the zero-range (wide-resonance) limit, parametrized solely by the s-wave scattering length $a$, while fermion-fermion interactions vanish by Pauli exclusion in the s-wave channel. Concretely, the Hamiltonian acts on wave functions on $\mathbb{R}^{3(N+1)}$ that are antisymmetric under exchange of the $N$ fermion coordinates, as the free kinetic operator
$$H_0 = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2M}\Delta_{\mathbf R} - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\sum_{i=1}^N \Delta_{\mathbf r_i},$$
supplemented by the Bethe–Peierls boundary condition
$$\Psi(\mathbf r_1,\dots,\mathbf r_N,\mathbf R) \;\underset{\mathbf r_i\to\mathbf R}{\sim}\; \left(\frac{1}{|\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R|}-\frac{1}{a}\right)A_i(\dots),\qquad i=1,\dots,N,$$
which encodes the contact two-body interaction. A bound state is called "non-Efimovian" if it is normalizable and its existence and energy depend only on $m$, $M$, $\hbar$ and $a$ (no additional three-body or higher short-range parameter is needed).

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every fixed mass ratio $m/M>0$ and every fixed scattering length $a\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$, there exists an integer $N_{\max}(m/M,a)<\infty$ such that no stable non-Efimovian bound state of the impurity with $N>N_{\max}$ identical fermions exists, both
 (a) in vacuum (no background fermions), and
 (b) in the presence of a non-interacting Fermi sea of the same fermion species at finite density.
category_tag: Few-body bound states in Fermi gases
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open theoretical problem: whether an upper bound exists on the number of identical fermions that can form a non-Efimovian bound state with a single impurity at fixed mass ratio and scattering length. A web search did not surface a proof or disproof; the heuristic argument (attractive interaction lowering energy versus Pauli kinetic cost) is suggestive but not conclusive, and no subsequent rigorous result resolving the bound was found.

paper_title: A single impurity in an ideal atomic Fermi gas: current understanding and some open problems
original_question: Explain why the Chevy ansatz, obtained by truncating the impurity wave-function expansion to a single particle-hole pair, remains extremely accurate even for large scattering length where strong particle-hole correlations might be expected. Determine whether the particle-hole-pair expansion has a hidden small parameter, identify when that expansion fails if it does fail, and quantify how the truncation error in observables such as the energy and quasiparticle residue depends on the truncation order, the mass ratio m/M, and the interaction parameter 1/k_F a.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a single impurity of mass M immersed in a non-interacting three-dimensional Fermi sea of identical fermions of mass m at zero temperature, with Fermi momentum k_F. The impurity interacts with the bath fermions via a short-range two-body interaction characterized by the s-wave scattering length a, so that the dimensionless coupling is 1/(k_F a). Define the variational "particle-hole" expansion of the polaron ground state by writing

|Ψ_n⟩ = α_0 c^†_{p=0} |FS⟩ + Σ_{|k|>k_F, |q|<k_F} α_{k q} c^†_{q-k} a^†_k a_q |FS⟩ + (two particle-hole terms) + … + (n particle-hole terms),

where |FS⟩ is the filled Fermi sea, a^†, a are bath-fermion operators, c^† creates the impurity, and the coefficients are determined by minimizing ⟨Ψ_n|H|Ψ_n⟩/⟨Ψ_n|Ψ_n⟩. The case n=1 is the Chevy ansatz (one particle-hole pair).

Numerical evidence indicates that, even at unitarity 1/(k_F a)=0 and on the attractive side, the n=1 truncation reproduces the polaron energy E and quasiparticle residue Z to remarkable accuracy (within a fraction of a percent for E in the equal-mass case).

(a) Provide a rigorous explanation for why the n=1 (Chevy) truncation is so accurate over the entire range of 1/(k_F a), and identify a hidden small parameter (if any) controlling the convergence of the n-particle-hole expansion.

(b) Determine the regime, as a function of the mass ratio m/M and the interaction parameter 1/(k_F a), in which the particle-hole expansion fails to converge or converges only slowly.

(c) Establish quantitative bounds, scaling laws, or asymptotic estimates for the truncation error |E_n − E_∞| and |Z_n − Z_∞| as functions of the truncation order n, the mass ratio m/M, and 1/(k_F a).
status_search_result: Subsequent work has provided partial answers: extending the ansatz to higher particle-hole orders shows destructive interference between higher-order channels, accounting for the basic Chevy ansatz's percent-level accuracy at unitarity; quantitative improvements with two particle-hole excitations have been computed and connections to diagrammatic theory established (variational coefficients = on-shell vertex functions). However, no rigorous identification of a hidden small parameter, no proven error bounds in n, m/M, and 1/(k_F a), and no general criterion for failure of the expansion (e.g. near polaron–molecule transition or extreme mass ratios) has been established. Thus the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: A single impurity in an ideal atomic Fermi gas: current understanding and some open problems
original_question: For composite dressed quasiparticles in this impurity problem, including the dimeron, trimeron, and tetrameron, determine whether there is a stronger general lower bound on the effective mass than positivity alone, namely whether dressing always increases the mass so that M*_b / M_b >= 1, where M_b is the bare mass of the corresponding composite bound state and M*_b is its effective mass in the Fermi gas.
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider a single distinguishable impurity of bare mass $M_{\rm imp}$ immersed in a non-interacting (ideal) gas of identical fermions of mass $m$ at zero temperature in three dimensions. The impurity interacts with the fermions through a short-range two-body interaction characterized by the s-wave scattering length $a$. Depending on $a$ and on the mass ratio $M_{\rm imp}/m$, the impurity together with $b\ge 1$ fermions can form a bound cluster in vacuum (a $b$-mer): $b=1$ gives the bare impurity (polaron sector), $b=2$ the dimer (dimeron sector), $b=3$ the trimer (trimeron sector), $b=4$ the tetramer (tetrameron sector). Let $M_b = M_{\rm imp} + b\,m$ denote the bare total mass of such a $b$-cluster.

When this cluster is placed in the Fermi sea, it becomes a dressed quasiparticle (polaron, dimeron, trimeron, tetrameron, ...) with a well-defined dispersion $E_b(\mathbf{P})$ near zero total momentum $\mathbf{P}=0$. The effective mass $M_b^*$ is defined by
$$E_b(\mathbf{P}) = E_b(0) + \frac{|\mathbf{P}|^2}{2 M_b^*} + o(|\mathbf{P}|^2), \qquad |\mathbf{P}|\to 0.$$

Question. Prove or disprove the following conjecture: for every such composite dressed quasiparticle (in particular for the dimeron, trimeron, and tetrameron) in a polarized ideal Fermi gas, dressing by the medium can only increase the inertia, i.e.
$$\frac{M_b^*}{M_b} \;\ge\; 1.$$
Equivalently, find a general lower bound on $M_b^*/M_b$ that is strictly stronger than the trivial positivity bound $M_b^* > 0$, valid throughout the parameter range (mass ratio and scattering length) in which the corresponding composite bound state exists.
status_search_result: The conjecture that dressing increases the mass of composite quasiparticles (dimerons, trimerons, tetramerons) in a polarized ideal Fermi gas, i.e. $M^*_b/M_b\ge 1$, appears to remain an open problem. Existing literature on Fermi polarons and dimerons reports calculations consistent with the bound, and rigorous lower bounds on effective masses have been established only for related (Fröhlich-type) polaron models, not for these composite few-body dressed states. No proof or counterexample for the stated composite-mass bound was located.

paper_title: Variants of the focusing NLS equation. Derivation, justification and open problems related to filamentation
original_question:
Fix d in {2, 3}, let v_0 in H^1(R^d) be initial data for the cubic focusing NLS that produce a finite-time blow-up solution v at time T > 0, and let v_epsilon be the solution of the regularized equation

 i partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + f(epsilon^r |v|^2)) |v|^2 v = 0

with the same initial data. What is the limiting behavior of v_epsilon(t) as epsilon tends to 0 for times t > T, that is, after the blow-up time of the unregularized cubic NLS has already passed?
self_contained_problem:
Let $d \in \{2,3\}$ and consider the cubic focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation
$$
i\partial_t v + \Delta v + |v|^2 v = 0, \qquad t > 0,\ x \in \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad v(0,\cdot) = v_0 \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^d),
$$
and assume that $v_0$ is chosen so that the corresponding solution $v$ blows up in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$ at some finite time $T > 0$ (such initial data exist in both dimensions $d=2$ and $d=3$).

Fix a real number $r > 0$ and a smooth bounded function $f:[0,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(0)=0$ that saturates the cubic nonlinearity (so that the regularized nonlinearity $(1+f(\varepsilon^r |v|^2))|v|^2 v$ remains bounded enough to yield global-in-time solutions for every $\varepsilon > 0$). For each $\varepsilon > 0$, let $v_\varepsilon$ denote the global solution of the regularized equation
$$
i\partial_t v_\varepsilon + \Delta v_\varepsilon + \bigl(1 + f(\varepsilon^r |v_\varepsilon|^2)\bigr)|v_\varepsilon|^2 v_\varepsilon = 0, \qquad v_\varepsilon(0,\cdot) = v_0.
$$

It is known that on $[0,T)$, $v_\varepsilon \to v$ in a suitable sense as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Describe rigorously the limiting behavior of $v_\varepsilon(t,\cdot)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$ for times $t > T$, i.e., past the blow-up time of the unregularized cubic NLS.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open question regarding the post-blow-up limit of saturated regularizations of the focusing cubic NLS in dimensions 2 and 3. Recent literature on saturated NLS variants and filamentation discusses regularization arresting blow-up but does not provide a rigorous description of the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit beyond the blow-up time; no resolution was located.

paper_title: Variants of the focusing NLS equation. Derivation, justification and open problems related to filamentation
original_question:
For the modified focusing cubic NLS

 i P_2(epsilon nabla) partial_t v + Delta v + |v|^2 v = 0,

assume that the positive self-adjoint operator P_2(epsilon nabla) gives only partial off-axis regularization, meaning it controls derivatives only in some distinguished directions rather than the full H^1 norm. Can one develop both the local and the global well-posedness theory in that partial off-axis case, and in particular decide whether this partial off-axis dependence is enough to prevent finite-time breakdown of solutions that would blow up for the standard focusing cubic NLS?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the modified focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation
  i P_2(ε∇) ∂_t v + Δ v + |v|^2 v = 0,    (t,x) ∈ ℝ × ℝ^d,
where d ∈ {2,3}, ε > 0 is a fixed parameter, and P_2(ε∇) is a positive self-adjoint Fourier multiplier of order two with symbol P_2(εξ) ≥ 0. Assume that P_2 provides only a "partial off-axis" regularization in the sense that there exist unit vectors v_1,…,v_j ∈ ℝ^d (with j = 1 if d = 2, and j ∈ {1,2} if d = 3) and a constant C > 0 such that for every Schwartz function v,
  (P_2(ε∇) v, v)_{L^2} ≥ C ( ‖v‖_{L^2}^2 + ε^2 Σ_{k=1}^{j} ‖v_k · ∇ v‖_{L^2}^2 ),
while the right-hand side does not control the full H^1 norm of v (so derivatives in directions orthogonal to span{v_1,…,v_j} are not controlled by the quadratic form of P_2).

The equation formally conserves the L^2-type quantity (P_2(ε∇) v, v)_{L^2} and the standard energy E(v) = ½‖∇v‖_{L^2}^2 − ¼‖v‖_{L^4}^4.

(a) Develop a local well-posedness theory for the Cauchy problem associated with this equation in a function space adapted to the partial off-axis regularization.

(b) Develop a global well-posedness theory in the same setting.

(c) Decide whether the partial off-axis dependence encoded by P_2(ε∇) is sufficient to prevent the finite-time blow-up phenomena that occur for the standard focusing cubic NLS i ∂_t u + Δ u + |u|^2 u = 0 in dimensions d = 2, 3.
status_search_result: Antonelli, Arbunich, and Sparber, "Regularizing Nonlinear Schrödinger Equations Through Partial Off-axis Variations" (SIAM J. Math. Anal. 51 (2019), 110–130), establish local and global well-posedness for this class of NLS equations with only partial off-axis regularization, including in L^2-supercritical regimes, and show that the partial off-axis term is sufficient to prevent finite-time blow-up. This is explicitly framed as resolving the stated open problem.

paper_title: Variants of the focusing NLS equation. Derivation, justification and open problems related to filamentation
original_question:
For the hyperbolic or non-elliptic cubic NLS

 i partial_t v + (Delta_perp - partial_z^2)v + |v|^2 v = 0

in dimensions 2 and 3, can one prove that every H^1 solution is global, despite the lack of the standard elliptic structure of the usual focusing cubic NLS?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the hyperbolic (non-elliptic) cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation
\[
 i\,\partial_t v + (\Delta_\perp - \partial_z^2)\,v + |v|^2 v = 0,
\]
posed on $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d\in\{2,3\}$, where the spatial coordinate is split as $(x_\perp,z)$ with $x_\perp\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}$ and $z\in\mathbb{R}$, and where $\Delta_\perp$ denotes the Laplacian in the transverse variables $x_\perp$. Equivalently, the spatial operator is the indefinite (Lorentzian-type) operator $\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}\partial_{x_j}^2 - \partial_z^2$ in place of the standard Laplacian. Initial data $v(0,\cdot)=v_0$ are taken in the Sobolev space $H^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$.

Prove or disprove: every solution $v\in C([0,T_{\max});H^1(\mathbb{R}^d))$ extends globally in time, i.e.\ $T_{\max}=+\infty$, despite the absence of the elliptic (positive-definite) structure of the standard focusing cubic NLS and the loss of coercivity of the conserved energy that this entails. In particular, rule out (or exhibit) finite-time blow-up phenomena such as pulse-splitting in dimensions $d=2$ and $d=3$.
status_search_result: Searches on hyperbolic/non-elliptic cubic NLS turn up results on special solutions (radial standing and self-similar waves in 2D), nonexistence of localized travelling waves, and related modulational analysis, but no proof of global $H^1$ existence in dimensions 2 or 3 nor a finite-time blow-up construction. The global existence question for the non-elliptic cubic NLS in dimensions 2 and 3 thus appears to remain open.

paper_title: Variants of the focusing NLS equation. Derivation, justification and open problems related to filamentation
original_question:
When partial off-axis variation of the group velocity and longitudinal self-steepening are both present in the same direction, namely for

 i(1 - epsilon^2 partial_z^2) partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + i epsilon partial_z)(|v|^2 v) = 0,

do solutions still exhibit self-steepening, or does the off-axis regularization suppress or qualitatively change that shock-like steepening effect?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the nonlinear Schrödinger-type equation with mixed partial off-axis dispersion and longitudinal self-steepening, posed for a complex-valued function v = v(t, z, x_⊥), where t ∈ ℝ is time, z ∈ ℝ is the longitudinal spatial variable, x_⊥ ∈ ℝ^{d-1} are the transverse spatial variables, Δ = ∂_z^2 + Δ_{x_⊥} is the full spatial Laplacian, and ε > 0 is a small parameter:

  i(1 − ε² ∂_z²) ∂_t v + Δ v + (1 + i ε ∂_z)(|v|² v) = 0.

The classical focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation (the case ε = 0 with a self-steepening derivative correction) is known to develop the phenomenon of "self-steepening", in which the amplitude profile of the wave forms a steepening front in the longitudinal direction z, leading to shock-like gradient blow-up of |v| or its derivatives along z. The operator (1 − ε² ∂_z²) on the time derivative encodes a partial off-axis variation of the group velocity that is known, in related models, to regularize or prevent certain singular behaviors.

Question: For sufficiently regular initial data, do solutions of the equation above still exhibit the self-steepening phenomenon (i.e., longitudinal shock-like steepening of |v|), or does the partial off-axis regularization provided by the operator (1 − ε² ∂_z²) suppress or qualitatively alter this steepening effect? Provide either a proof that self-steepening (in a precise sense, e.g., blow-up of ‖∂_z v‖_{L^∞} in finite time for some smooth, suitably localized initial data) does occur, or a proof that it is precluded by global-in-time bounds on the relevant longitudinal derivatives.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface any work resolving whether solutions of this specific mixed off-axis / self-steepening NLS variant develop self-steepening, nor any proof that the off-axis term suppresses it. The problem appears to remain open, with related literature only addressing self-steepening in standard or PT-symmetric modified NLS settings, not this off-axis-regularized model.

paper_title: Variants of the focusing NLS equation. Derivation, justification and open problems related to filamentation
original_question: The paper rigorously derives several NLS-type asymptotic models from Maxwell's equations and justifies them on times of order T/epsilon only while the approximating NLS-type solution stays bounded, which in the standard focusing case means times strictly before the focusing time T_foc. Can one rigorously justify at least one of these derived NLS-type models on a time interval [0, T/epsilon] with T greater than or equal to the focusing time T_foc, so that the approximation remains valid in the regime where the different models begin to differ in a physically meaningful way?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Maxwell's equations in a nonlinear isotropic dielectric medium with instantaneous cubic (Kerr) nonlinearity, written in dimensionless form with a small parameter ε > 0 measuring the ratio of the typical wavelength to the typical envelope length scale. For a slowly modulated, monochromatic, polarized wave packet with envelope amplitude of order one, one can formally derive several asymptotic envelope models of nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) type, including:

  (i) the standard focusing cubic NLS equation
        i ∂_t A + (1/2) Δ_⊥ A + (1/2) α ∂_z^2 A + |A|^2 A = 0,
  (ii) variants incorporating self-steepening, space–time focusing, and off-axis (vectorial) corrections of the form
        i ∂_t A + L(∂) A + N(A, ∂A) = 0,
  obtained as O(ε) or O(ε^2) corrections to the standard model.

For each such envelope model, the associated electromagnetic field is reconstructed via the WKB ansatz
        E_app(t,x) = ε A(εt, εx) e^{i(k·x − ω t)/ε} + c.c. + (higher-order corrections),
and the standard rigorous justification result states that there exist constants C, T_* > 0 such that, as long as the model solution A remains bounded on [0, T] in a suitable Sobolev norm, the exact Maxwell solution E exists on the time interval [0, T/ε] and satisfies
        sup_{t ∈ [0, T/ε]} ‖E(t,·) − E_app(t,·)‖_{H^s} ≤ C ε^{1+δ},
for some δ > 0. In the focusing regime in dimension d ≥ 2, the standard cubic NLS solution generically blows up at a finite focusing time T_foc, and the existing justification therefore only applies for T strictly less than T_foc.

Problem. Prove or disprove the following: there exists at least one of the derived NLS-type envelope models (cubic NLS or one of its O(ε), O(ε^2) variants) for which the approximation result above can be rigorously extended to a time interval [0, T/ε] with T ≥ T_foc, i.e., the Maxwell solution exists and remains O(ε^{1+δ})-close to the corresponding asymptotic profile up to and beyond the focusing time of the underlying envelope model.
status_search_result: No published rigorous justification of any NLS-type envelope model derived from Maxwell's equations on a time interval reaching or exceeding the focusing time T_foc appears to exist. Related works (Dumas–Lannes–Szeftel and follow-up surveys) restate the question as a standing open problem: existing error estimates only hold strictly before the focusing time, and extending them past T_foc remains unresolved.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: Given a current set C of coarse variables for bootstrap algebraic multigrid, how should one choose the initial coarse set C0 and then make local additions, removals, or other modifications to C whenever compatible relaxation converges too slowly, so that the updated coarse space improves convergence without introducing unnecessary complexity?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider a sparse linear system $A u = f$ where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is a symmetric positive definite matrix arising, e.g., from the discretization of a partial differential equation on a fine index set $\Omega = \{1,\dots,n\}$. A two-level algebraic multigrid method partitions $\Omega = C \cup F$ into a coarse set $C$ and a fine-only set $F$, and uses an interpolation operator $P$ from $\mathbb{R}^{|C|}$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ together with a smoother $M$ (so that $A = M + M^\top - M^\top D^{-1} M$ for some splitting). 

Compatible relaxation (CR). Given $C \subset \Omega$ with complementary set $F$, let $A_{ff}$ denote the principal submatrix of $A$ on $F$, and let $M_{ff}$ be the corresponding restriction of the smoother. The CR iteration on $F$ is
$$ e^{(k+1)}_F = (I - M_{ff}^{-1} A_{ff})\, e^{(k)}_F, \qquad e^{(k)}_C \equiv 0, $$
and its asymptotic convergence factor is
$$ \rho_{cr}(C) := \rho\bigl(I - M_{ff}^{-1} A_{ff}\bigr). $$
A small $\rho_{cr}(C)$ indicates that $C$ is a good candidate coarse set in the sense that an accurate two-level method can be built on it.

Problem. Design and justify, in a way that is independent of any a priori notion of strength of connection, an algorithm that:

1. Constructs an initial coarse set $C_0 \subset \Omega$ from the matrix $A$ (and possibly a small number of test vectors approximating the algebraically smooth error of $A$), together with a quantitative criterion guaranteeing that $\rho_{cr}(C_0)$ is bounded by a prescribed target $\rho^\star \in (0,1)$ when such a set of bounded size $|C_0| \le \kappa n$ exists.

2. Given a current coarse set $C$ for which $\rho_{cr}(C) > \rho^\star$, prescribes local modifications to $C$ — additions of indices from $F$, removals of indices from $C$, or other local updates — using only locally measurable quantities derived from CR (such as pointwise components of the slowly converging CR error, or local residual quantities), so that the updated set $C'$ satisfies $\rho_{cr}(C') < \rho_{cr}(C)$ while controlling the growth of $|C'|$ and of the resulting operator complexity.

3. Provides a rigorous justification that the local CR-based indicators used in step 2 (e.g., pointwise magnitudes of the slow CR error) actually identify the variables whose addition to $C$ most effectively decreases $\rho_{cr}$, i.e., proves quantitative bounds relating these local indicators to the resulting decrease in the CR convergence rate.
status_search_result: The question of how to choose the initial coarse set and how to perform CR-driven local updates remains an active area. Subsequent works (e.g., Brannick–Falgout's CR-based coarsening, relaxation-corrected bootstrap AMG, and least angle regression coarsening for BAMG) propose heuristic algorithms and partial analyses, but no rigorous justification has been established showing that pointwise CR errors identify the variables whose addition optimally reduces the CR convergence rate. The problem appears still open in its rigorous form.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: For least-squares interpolation in bootstrap algebraic multigrid, how can one define appropriate local weights ωκ, and possibly corresponding local equations for computing test vectors, in a general algebraic setting so that a globally smooth test vector is not overemphasized in local regions where it has large residuals?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider a sparse symmetric positive definite linear system $A x = b$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ on a fine index set $\Omega = \{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $\Omega_c \subset \Omega$ be a chosen set of "coarse" indices and $\Omega_f = \Omega \setminus \Omega_c$ the "fine" indices. For each fine index $i \in \Omega_f$ let $\mathcal{C}_i \subset \Omega_c$ be a prescribed local interpolation neighborhood. A prolongation (interpolation) operator $P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times|\Omega_c|}$ is sought of the form
$$ (P v)_i = v_i \text{ for } i\in\Omega_c, \qquad (P v)_i = \sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} p_{ij}\, v_j \text{ for } i\in\Omega_f. $$

Assume that a finite collection of test vectors $\{x^{(\kappa)}\}_{\kappa=1}^K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ has been generated (e.g.\ by relaxation on $A x = 0$ and bootstrap cycling), each representing an algebraically smooth mode. The least-squares (LS) definition of interpolation chooses the rows $\{p_{ij}\}_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i}$ for each $i\in\Omega_f$ to minimize a weighted residual functional
$$ \mathcal{F}_i(\{p_{ij}\}) \;=\; \sum_{\kappa=1}^K \omega_\kappa^{(i)} \left( x^{(\kappa)}_i - \sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} p_{ij}\, x^{(\kappa)}_j \right)^{\!2}, $$
where $\omega_\kappa^{(i)} \ge 0$ are weights that may depend on the local fine index $i$.

Problem. Provide a purely algebraic prescription, applicable to a general sparse SPD matrix $A$ (not restricted to finite-element discretizations of elliptic boundary value problems), for the local weights $\omega_\kappa^{(i)}$ — and, if needed, a corresponding local linear system whose solutions serve as the test vectors $x^{(\kappa)}$ used in $\mathcal{F}_i$ — with the following property:

If a test vector $x^{(\kappa^*)}$ is globally algebraically smooth (small global Rayleigh quotient $\langle A x^{(\kappa^*)}, x^{(\kappa^*)}\rangle / \langle x^{(\kappa^*)}, x^{(\kappa^*)}\rangle$) but exhibits a large local residual, measured for instance by $\|(A x^{(\kappa^*)})|_{\mathcal{N}_i}\|$ on a local neighborhood $\mathcal{N}_i$ of index $i$, then the weight $\omega_{\kappa^*}^{(i)}$ used at index $i$ is automatically reduced relative to the (possibly large) global weight assigned to $x^{(\kappa^*)}$, so that this mode does not dominate the local LS fit at $i$.

The construction must (a) be defined entirely in terms of the entries of $A$ and the test vectors (no geometric or PDE information), (b) generalize the local-spectral / LSR-type weighting used together with global weights for elliptic finite-element problems, and (c) be compatible, in the sense that the resulting $P$ yields a coarse space on which a two-level method with standard smoothing converges uniformly with respect to $n$ for matrices in a stated algebraic class.

Find such a definition of $\{\omega_\kappa^{(i)}\}$ (and accompanying local equations for the test vectors), or prove that no such definition exists in the stated generality.
status_search_result: The problem of defining purely algebraic local LS weights for bootstrap AMG interpolation is described as unresolved in general algebraic settings, with resolution known only for finite-element discretizations of elliptic problems. Subsequent work, including learning-based local weighted least squares (Wang–Gu–Sun–Xu, J. Comput. Phys. 2023) and rBAMG variants, addresses related sub-optimality of spatially shared weights but does not give a definitive general-purpose algebraic prescription. The problem appears still open.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: When computing the test vectors used by bootstrap algebraic multigrid, what balance between computational work and approximation accuracy should be targeted so that the vectors are accurate enough to define effective interpolation without making setup prohibitively expensive?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an algebraic multigrid (AMG) method for solving large sparse symmetric positive definite linear systems $A x = b$ arising, for example, from discretizations of partial differential equations. In the bootstrap AMG (BAMG) framework, a set of "test vectors" $\{v^{(1)}, \ldots, v^{(k)}\}$ is computed adaptively (typically by applying a small number of relaxation sweeps to the homogeneous problem $A v = 0$, possibly combined with coarse-grid corrections from a tentative multigrid hierarchy) and these test vectors are then used to define the interpolation operator $P$ between fine and coarse grids by requiring that $P$ approximately reproduce each $v^{(i)}$ on the coarse-fine partition. Let $W(\varepsilon)$ denote the computational work (e.g., number of floating-point operations) needed to compute test vectors achieving an accuracy $\varepsilon$ in approximating the slow-to-converge near-kernel components of $A$, and let $\rho(\varepsilon)$ denote the resulting two-grid (or multigrid) convergence factor when interpolation is constructed from these test vectors.

Problem: Determine, in a quantitative and rigorous way, an optimal trade-off between $W(\varepsilon)$ and $\rho(\varepsilon)$. Specifically:

(a) Derive sharp bounds relating the accuracy with which the test vectors approximate the algebraically smooth (near-kernel) modes of $A$ to the convergence factor $\rho$ of the resulting multigrid cycle.

(b) Identify a strategy (number of relaxation sweeps, number of bootstrap cycles, choice of $k$, and use of intermediate coarse-grid information) that minimizes total setup-plus-solve cost while guaranteeing a uniformly bounded $\rho < 1$ independent of the problem size for a prescribed class of operators $A$.

(c) Prove that the proposed strategy achieves the optimal asymptotic balance, in the sense that no strategy with asymptotically less work can yield a uniformly bounded convergence factor on the same class of operators.
status_search_result: The question of optimally balancing test-vector computation cost against interpolation accuracy in bootstrap AMG is a longstanding open methodological problem in algebraic multigrid research. While various heuristics (relaxation count, bootstrap cycling, least-squares interpolation) have been proposed and tested empirically, no rigorous and sharp quantitative theory establishing an optimal work-accuracy trade-off appears in the literature. The status remains open.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: For general Hermitian positive definite problems, how can the compatible-relaxation, algebraic-distance, least-squares-interpolation, and bootstrap test-vector components of bootstrap algebraic multigrid be integrated into an overall algorithm that is practical, easy to tune, and robust as a fast multigrid solver across a diverse set of test problems, including systems of partial differential equations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Hermitian positive definite (HPD) linear systems Ax = b arising from discretizations of partial differential equations, including systems of PDEs. Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid (BAMG) is a multilevel iterative methodology composed of the following principal components:

1. Compatible Relaxation (CR): a relaxation scheme on the fine-degrees-of-freedom subset used to identify a coarse variable set C ⊂ Ω such that the CR convergence rate ρ_CR is small, providing an a posteriori measure of the suitability of the coarse set.
2. Algebraic Distance: a measure d(i,j) between degrees of freedom derived from a small set of smoothed test vectors (typically obtained by relaxing on the homogeneous system Ax = 0 from random initial guesses) that is used to form interpolation sparsity patterns / caliber.
3. Least-Squares Interpolation: given a coarse set C and a set of test vectors {v_k}_{k=1}^K, the interpolation operator P is defined row-wise by minimizing, for each fine point i, the weighted least-squares functional Σ_k ω_k (v_k(i) − Σ_{j∈C_i} P_{ij} v_k(j))^2 over admissible sparsity patterns C_i.
4. Bootstrap Test-Vector Setup: a self-correcting cycle in which a multigrid hierarchy built from current test vectors is itself applied (as a generalized eigensolver / smoother) on the homogeneous problem to produce improved test vectors, which are then fed back to redefine the coarse sets, algebraic distances, and least-squares interpolations.

Problem. Devise an explicit algorithmic specification that integrates all four components above into a single BAMG setup-and-solve algorithm for general HPD problems with the following properties:

(a) Practicality: setup and per-cycle costs are bounded by a modest constant times the cost of a sparse matrix–vector product with A, with provably bounded operator complexity and grid complexity.
(b) Ease of tuning: the algorithm exposes only a small, fixed number of user parameters (e.g., number of test vectors K, number of bootstrap cycles, CR tolerance, interpolation caliber), with default values that perform well across problem classes without per-problem hand tuning.
(c) Robustness: the resulting V-cycle (or W-cycle) yields a uniformly bounded asymptotic convergence factor ρ < 1 independent of problem size and of standard parameters (e.g., mesh size, anisotropy, jumps in coefficients) over a diverse benchmark suite that includes scalar elliptic PDEs with variable/jumping coefficients, anisotropic diffusion, and HPD systems of PDEs (e.g., linear elasticity, Stokes-type HPD reformulations, Maxwell-type HPD problems).

Specify the algorithm, prove (or provide strong empirical evidence supported by analysis) that properties (a)–(c) hold, and demonstrate uniform convergence on a representative diverse test set of HPD problems including PDE systems.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in the BAMG literature: integrating compatible relaxation, algebraic distance, least-squares interpolation, and bootstrap test-vector setup into a single robust, easy-to-tune solver for general HPD problems including PDE systems. Subsequent works (Brandt–Brannick–Kahl–Livshits and follow-ups, including BAMG for nonsymmetric and Markov chain problems) have advanced individual components and partial integrations, but no published result establishes a fully integrated, parameter-light, provably robust BAMG solver across a broad HPD benchmark including PDE systems. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: For non-Hermitian problems, how can restriction R and interpolation P be constructed and tied together locally so that the Galerkin coarse-grid matrix remains suitable for multigrid correction and does not become singular or cause divergence through overcorrection when small singular values or eigenvalues are underestimated on coarse levels?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \in \mathbb{C}^{n 	imes n}$ be a (possibly non-Hermitian) nonsingular matrix associated with a fine grid, and consider a two-level multigrid scheme with a coarse space of dimension $n_c < n$ defined by a restriction operator $R \in \mathbb{C}^{n_c 	imes n}$ and an interpolation operator $P \in \mathbb{C}^{n 	imes n_c}$. The Galerkin coarse-grid operator is defined as
$$A_c = R\,A\,P \in \mathbb{C}^{n_c 	imes n_c}.$$
When $A$ is non-Hermitian, $R$ and $P$ may be chosen independently (typically using approximations to right and left near-kernel modes of $A$). It can happen that $A_c$ is singular or has eigenvalues/singular values whose magnitudes are much smaller than those of the corresponding modes of $A$, and this leads to divergence of the two-level correction step $x \leftarrow x + P A_c^{-1} R\,(b - A x)$ through overcorrection.

Provide a constructive procedure that, given $A$ and given algorithms which separately produce candidate operators $R$ and $P$ from approximations to left and right near-kernel modes of $A$, locally couples these constructions so that the resulting Galerkin coarse operator $A_c = R A P$ is provably nonsingular and the resulting two-level iteration is non-divergent. In particular, derive sufficient local conditions linking the rows of $R$ to the columns of $P$ on each aggregate or coarse degree of freedom which guarantee that small singular values and eigenvalues of $A$ are not underestimated on the coarse level, and prove convergence (or non-divergence) of the resulting multigrid correction.
status_search_result: The problem of robustly constructing coupled R and P for non-Hermitian algebraic multigrid (so that the Galerkin coarse operator remains nonsingular and avoids overcorrection) is a recognized open challenge in bootstrap/adaptive AMG. Subsequent work on non-Hermitian/non-symmetric AMG (e.g., AIR, lAIR, multigrid for Markov chains) provides partial heuristics, but no general procedure with rigorous guarantees has been established.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: How far can bootstrap algebraic multigrid techniques developed for non-elliptic and other challenging sparse systems be extended so that they become genuinely fast solvers for general sparse matrix equations beyond the problem classes where BAMG-like methods have already been implemented?
self_contained_problem:
Algebraic multigrid (AMG) is a class of iterative methods for solving large sparse linear systems $A x = b$, where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is sparse, by building a hierarchy of progressively coarser linear systems together with intergrid transfer operators (interpolation $P$ and restriction $R$) and smoothers (e.g. Gauss–Seidel or weighted Jacobi), without explicit reference to an underlying geometric grid. A solver is called optimal (or a "fast solver") for a family of matrices $\{A_n\}$ of increasing size $n$ if it computes an approximate solution to $A_n x = b$ to a fixed relative accuracy in $O(n)$ arithmetic operations and storage, with convergence rate bounded independently of $n$.

Bootstrap AMG (BAMG) is a variant in which the interpolation operator and the coarse-variable set are constructed adaptively by simultaneously processing several test vectors that are improved by applying the current multigrid hierarchy, combined with a least-squares fitting procedure for the interpolation weights and, when needed, a multilevel eigensolver to expose slow-to-converge modes. BAMG-type methods have been demonstrated as fast solvers for various classes of sparse systems, including certain non-elliptic problems such as discretizations of the Dirac operator in lattice quantum chromodynamics, anisotropic and convection-dominated problems, and graph Laplacians.

Problem. Characterize the largest class $\mathcal{C}$ of families of sparse matrices $\{A_n\}$ for which a bootstrap algebraic multigrid method, in the sense above, can be designed to be a fast solver in the sense that:
(i) the setup cost is $O(n)$;
(ii) each multigrid cycle costs $O(n)$;
(iii) the asymptotic convergence factor is bounded above by some $\rho < 1$ independent of $n$.
In particular, determine whether BAMG techniques can be extended to yield fast solvers for general sparse matrix equations $A x = b$ beyond the problem classes (elliptic PDE discretizations, lattice Dirac systems, graph Laplacians, and related cases) for which they have already been realized, and identify structural conditions on $A$ (e.g. on its sparsity pattern, spectrum, near-null space, or associated bilinear form) that are necessary and/or sufficient for such an extension to exist.
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction concerning the extent of applicability of bootstrap algebraic multigrid. There is no general theorem establishing or refuting the existence of optimal BAMG-type solvers for arbitrary sparse systems; ongoing work continues to extend adaptive/bootstrap AMG to new non-elliptic classes (e.g. lattice QCD, Markov chains, graph problems), but no comprehensive characterization is known. The status is therefore open.

paper_title: Distinct Distances: Open Problems and Current Bounds
original_question: Call a planar n-point set P near-optimal if it determines D(P)=O(n/sqrt(log n)) distinct distances. Characterize the near-optimal point sets.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, let $D(P)$ denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by pairs of points of $P$, i.e., $D(P) = |\{\,\|p-q\| : p,q \in P,\ p \neq q\,\}|$. A family $\{P_n\}_{n\geq 1}$ of planar point sets with $|P_n|=n$ is called near-optimal if $D(P_n) = O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ as $n \to \infty$. Known examples of near-optimal families include the $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ section of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and the triangular lattice. 

Give a structural characterization of all near-optimal planar point sets. In particular, decide whether every near-optimal set must in some precise sense possess "lattice structure", and identify the necessary and sufficient geometric/combinatorial conditions on $P_n$ that force $D(P_n) = O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$.
status_search_result: The problem of characterizing near-optimal point sets for the Erdős distinct distances problem (and Erdős's question of whether every such set has "lattice structure") remains open. Partial results are known—e.g., every near-optimal set must contain a line with Ω(log n) points, and for any 0<α≤1/4 must contain a line or circle with n^α points—but no full characterization has been established.

paper_title: Distinct Distances: Open Problems and Current Bounds
original_question: Let subset(n) be the largest integer with the property that every n-point set in the plane contains a subset of size subset(n) in which each positive distance occurs at most once. Determine the asymptotic order of subset(n).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite point set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, call a subset $P' \subseteq P$ "distance-distinct" if no positive distance is realized by two different unordered pairs of points of $P'$ (equivalently, the pairwise distances among points of $P'$ are all distinct). Define
\[
 \mathrm{sub}(P) = \max\{|P'| : P' \subseteq P \text{ is distance-distinct}\},
\]
and let
\[
 \mathrm{sub}(n) = \min_{\substack{P \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \\ |P| = n}} \mathrm{sub}(P),
\]
so that $\mathrm{sub}(n)$ is the largest integer such that every $n$-point set in the plane contains a distance-distinct subset of size $\mathrm{sub}(n)$.

It is known that
\[
 \mathrm{sub}(n) = O\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{(\log n)^{1/4}}\right),
\]
witnessed by a $\sqrt{n} \times \sqrt{n}$ section of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$, and that $\mathrm{sub}(n) = \Omega(n^{1/3}/(\log n)^{1/3})$.

Determine the asymptotic order of $\mathrm{sub}(n)$ as $n \to \infty$.
status_search_result: The problem, posed by Erdős, asks for the asymptotic order of sub(n). The best published bounds remain Ω(n^{1/3}/(log n)^{1/3}) (Charalambides, 2013) and O(√n/(log n)^{1/4}) (from the √n × √n integer lattice via the Erdős–Guy bound on distinct distances). No sharp asymptotic determination appears in the literature, so the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let L(m,n) be the minimum number of distinct distances between a set of m points and a set of n lines in the plane, where point-line distance is measured in the usual Euclidean way. Determine the asymptotic order of L(m,n).
self_contained_problem:
For positive integers $m$ and $n$, let $P$ be a set of $m$ points in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathcal{L}$ be a set of $n$ lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$. For a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and a line $\ell \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, let $d(p,\ell)$ denote the usual Euclidean (perpendicular) distance from $p$ to $\ell$. Define
$$D(P, \mathcal{L}) = \bigl|\{\, d(p,\ell) : p \in P,\ \ell \in \mathcal{L}\,\}\bigr|,$$
the number of distinct point-line distances determined by $P$ and $\mathcal{L}$, and set
$$L(m,n) = \min_{|P|=m,\ |\mathcal{L}|=n} D(P, \mathcal{L}).$$
Determine the asymptotic order of $L(m,n)$ as $m, n \to \infty$.
status_search_result: The problem appears to remain open. The best known lower bound, due to Sharir, Sheffer, and Smorodinsky, is $L(m,n) = \Omega(m^{1/5}n^{3/5})$ in a certain range of $m,n$, while no matching upper bound is known. Subsequent work (e.g., distinct distances on Pfaffian curves, 2025) treats related variants but does not determine the asymptotic order of $L(m,n)$.

original_question: Let X be a separated locally convex space, and let C and D be convex subsets of X. For a convex set E, define its quasi relative interior by qri E := {x in E | cone(E - x) is a linear space}. Is it possible that the Minkowski sum of the quasi relative interiors, qri C + qri D, is a proper subset of the quasi relative interior of the Minkowski sum, qri(C + D)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a separated locally convex topological vector space. For a convex subset $E\subseteq X$, define its quasi relative interior by
$$\operatorname{qri} E := \{x\in E \mid \operatorname{cone}(E-x)\text{ is a linear subspace of }X\},$$
where $\operatorname{cone}(A) := \{\lambda a : \lambda \ge 0,\ a\in A\}$ and the closure/linearity is considered in $X$. For convex subsets $C,D\subseteq X$, the Minkowski sum is $C+D = \{c+d : c\in C, d\in D\}$.

Question: Do there exist a separated locally convex space $X$ and convex subsets $C,D\subseteq X$ such that
$$\operatorname{qri} C + \operatorname{qri} D \;\subsetneq\; \operatorname{qri}(C+D)\,?$$
category_tag: Quasi relative interior of convex sets
status_search_result: The question, originally posed by Borwein and Goebel (2003), is reported as resolved: an explicit example is provided showing that $\operatorname{qri} C + \operatorname{qri} D$ can be a proper subset of $\operatorname{qri}(C+D)$, answering the question affirmatively.

original_question: Let X be a separated locally convex space, and let C and D be nonempty convex subsets of X. For a convex set E, define its quasi relative interior by qri E := {x in E | cone(E - x) is a linear space}. If qri C intersect qri D is nonempty, can the inclusion qri(C intersect D) subset qri C intersect qri D fail?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a separated locally convex topological vector space over $\mathbb{R}$. For a nonempty convex subset $E \subseteq X$, define the quasi relative interior of $E$ by
$$\operatorname{qri} E := \{ x \in E \mid \operatorname{cone}(E - x) \text{ is a linear subspace of } X \},$$
where $\operatorname{cone}(A) := \{\lambda a : \lambda \geq 0,\ a \in A\}$ is the conic hull of $A \subseteq X$ (and the closure is not taken).

Let $C, D \subseteq X$ be nonempty convex subsets such that $\operatorname{qri} C \cap \operatorname{qri} D \neq \emptyset$. Determine whether the inclusion
$$\operatorname{qri}(C \cap D) \subseteq \operatorname{qri} C \cap \operatorname{qri} D$$
can fail; that is, decide whether there can exist a point $x \in \operatorname{qri}(C \cap D)$ such that $x \notin \operatorname{qri} C \cap \operatorname{qri} D$.
category_tag: quasi relative interior of convex sets
status_search_result: The question, originally posed by Borwein and Goebel, has been answered in the negative: under the assumption $\operatorname{qri} C \cap \operatorname{qri} D \neq \emptyset$, the inclusion $\operatorname{qri}(C\cap D) \subseteq \operatorname{qri} C \cap \operatorname{qri} D$ always holds, so it cannot fail.

original_question: An MSTD subset of the integers has more pairwise sums than pairwise differences. Starting from the minimal 8-element integer example, one can build an MSTD subset of Z^2 by taking its product with a 2-point set. Can one instead construct an MSTD subset of Z^2 directly, without obtaining it from an MSTD subset of Z by such a lifting procedure?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite subset $A$ of an abelian group, define the sumset $A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}$ and the difference set $A-A=\{a-b:a,b\in A\}$. The set $A$ is called MSTD ("more sums than differences") if $|A+A|>|A-A|$.

It is known that there exist MSTD subsets of $\mathbb{Z}$ (the smallest having $8$ elements). From any MSTD set $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ one can produce an MSTD subset of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ by taking the Cartesian product $A\times B$ with any $2$-element set $B\subset\mathbb{Z}$.

Construct an MSTD subset $S\subset\mathbb{Z}^2$ that does not arise from this lifting procedure; that is, exhibit a finite set $S\subset\mathbb{Z}^2$ with $|S+S|>|S-S|$ which is not of the form $\varphi(A\times B)$ for any MSTD set $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$, any finite $B\subset\mathbb{Z}$ with $|B|\ge 2$, and any affine isomorphism $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ (more generally, $S$ should not be obtainable from a one-dimensional MSTD set via such a product/lifting construction).
status_search_result: Subsequent work on MSTD sets in higher dimensions has produced direct constructions of MSTD subsets of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ that are not obtained as products of one-dimensional MSTD sets with a 2-point set. In particular, results in "Constructions of generalized MSTD sets in higher dimensions" (arXiv:2009.02758) and related work give explicit families of MSTD sets in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ for $d\ge 2$ built directly from higher-dimensional fringe constructions, and it is shown that a positive proportion of random subsets of an $n\times n$ grid in $\mathbb{Z}^2$ are MSTD, providing many examples not arising from a one-dimensional lift.

original_question: Define g_0 = 0 and, greedily, let g_i be the least positive integer such that {g_0,...,g_i} has no solutions to 5w + 2x = 5y + 2z. Define a_0 = 0, define a_i by the recurrence given in the paper, and let A be the set of sums of distinct a_i. Is the greedy set G exactly {5x + y : x in A and 0 <= y <= 4}?
self_contained_problem:
Define a sequence of nonnegative integers $g_0, g_1, g_2, \dots$ greedily as follows: set $g_0 = 0$, and for each $i \ge 1$ let $g_i$ be the least positive integer strictly greater than $g_{i-1}$ such that the set $\{g_0, g_1, \dots, g_i\}$ contains no solution to the equation
$$5w + 2x = 5y + 2z$$
other than the trivial solutions $\{w,x\} = \{y,z\}$ (with all four variables drawn from the set, allowing repetition). Let $G = \{g_0, g_1, g_2, \dots\}$ be the resulting greedy set.

Separately, define a sequence $(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$ by $a_0 = 0$ and, for $i \ge 1$,
$$a_i = \left\lfloor \frac{5 + 7\sum_{j=0}^{i-1} a_j}{2} \right\rfloor.$$
Let
$$A = \Bigl\{ \sum_{i \in S} a_i : S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0},\ |S| < \infty \Bigr\}$$
be the set of all finite sums of distinct terms of the sequence $(a_i)$.

Prove or disprove:
$$G \;=\; \{\,5x + y : x \in A,\ 0 \le y \le 4\,\}.$$
status_search_result: The conjecture appears in an ongoing compilation of combinatorial/additive number theory problem sessions, most recently updated in May 2025, and is stated as an open conjecture. No published resolution was found in standard search results.

original_question: For the unrestricted partition generating function product over m >= 1 of (1 + x^m + x^(2m) + ...), can one choose signs in some of the factors so that, after expansion, every coefficient belongs to {0, -1, 1}?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the formal power series identity
$$\prod_{m\ge 1}\bigl(1+x^m+x^{2m}+x^{3m}+\cdots\bigr)=\sum_{n\ge 0}p(n)\,x^n,$$
where $p(n)$ is the number of unrestricted integer partitions of $n$. For each $m\ge 1$ and each $k\ge 1$, let $\varepsilon_{m,k}\in\{+1,-1\}$, and consider the "signed" infinite product
$$F(x)=\prod_{m\ge 1}\Bigl(1+\sum_{k\ge 1}\varepsilon_{m,k}\,x^{km}\Bigr)=\sum_{n\ge 0}b_n\,x^n\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]].$$
(Each coefficient $b_n$ is a finite sum since only finitely many factors contribute to the coefficient of $x^n$.)

Question: Does there exist a choice of signs $\{\varepsilon_{m,k}\}_{m\ge 1,\,k\ge 1}$, with $\varepsilon_{m,k}\in\{+1,-1\}$, such that $b_n\in\{-1,0,+1\}$ for every $n\ge 0$?
status_search_result: A web search did not surface a published resolution of this sign-choice problem for the partition generating function. Related work on sign patterns in infinite products (e.g., the Borwein-type products) addresses different questions, and no source confirming a solution—positive or negative—was located.

original_question: Give an elementary proof that there are infinitely many primes p such that neither p-2 nor p+2 is prime; in other words, prove by elementary means that infinitely many primes are not twin primes.
self_contained_problem: A prime number $p$ is called isolated (or non-twin) if neither $p-2$ nor $p+2$ is prime. Give an elementary proof (i.e., one that does not invoke Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, the prime number theorem, Brun's sieve, or other non-elementary analytic machinery) that there exist infinitely many isolated primes.
status_search_result: Standard non-elementary arguments (Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions such as 15k+7, or Brun's theorem showing almost all primes are isolated) easily yield the result, but these are not elementary. A web search did not reveal an authoritative source confirming or denying the existence of a fully elementary proof of the infinitude of isolated primes; the problem of finding one appears not to be widely cataloged as solved.

original_question: Let x_1,...,x_{n+r} be elements of a finite abelian group. Is it true that either 0 occurs as an n-term subsequence sum, or else the set of n-term subsequence sums has combinatorial dimension at least r+1 in the sense defined in the paper via Davenport's constant and zero-sum-free sequences?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group (written additively). For a finite sequence $S = (x_1, \dots, x_m)$ of elements of $G$ and a positive integer $n \le m$, define the set of $n$-term subsequence sums by
$$\Sigma_n(S) = \Big\{\, x_{i_1} + x_{i_2} + \cdots + x_{i_n} \;:\; 1 \le i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_n \le m \,\Big\} \subseteq G.$$
A sequence over $G$ is called zero-sum-free if no nonempty subsequence of it sums to $0$. The Davenport constant $D(G)$ is the smallest positive integer $d$ such that every sequence over $G$ of length $d$ contains a nonempty zero-sum subsequence; equivalently, $D(G) - 1$ is the maximum length of a zero-sum-free sequence over $G$.

For a subset $T \subseteq G$, define the combinatorial dimension $\dim(T)$ to be the largest integer $k \ge 0$ for which there exist elements $g_1, \dots, g_k \in G$ such that all $2^k$ subset sums $\sum_{i \in I} g_i$ (over $I \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}$) are distinct elements of $T \cup \{0\}$, with the $g_i$ forming a zero-sum-free sequence; equivalently, $\dim(T)$ measures the largest "independent" zero-sum-free configuration whose subset sums lie in $T$ (so that $\dim(G) = D(G) - 1$).

Conjecture: Let $n \ge 1$ and $r \ge 0$ be integers, and let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{n+r}$ be any elements of $G$. Then at least one of the following holds:
(i) $0 \in \Sigma_n(x_1, \dots, x_{n+r})$, i.e., some $n$ of the $x_i$ sum to $0$ in $G$; or
(ii) $\dim\big(\Sigma_n(x_1, \dots, x_{n+r})\big) \ge r + 1.$

Prove or disprove this dichotomy.
status_search_result: Web searches on zero-sum theory, Davenport's constant, and n-term subsequence sums in finite abelian groups did not surface a resolution of this specific dichotomy between containing a zero $n$-sum and the combinatorial dimension of the set of $n$-sums being at least $r+1$. The general area has many open problems (e.g. Davenport's constant for rank $\ge 3$ groups remains open), and no source explicitly confirming or refuting this conjecture was located.

original_question: Let K be a compact subset of R^2 that meets every residue class modulo Z^2, and let A = (K-K) intersect Z^2. Which finite generating sets of Z^2 can arise in this way? In particular, can one realize the axis-cross set {(0,0),(±1,0),(0,±1)}?
self_contained_problem:
Call a compact set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ a 2-dimensional $\mathcal{N}$-set if for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^2$ there exists $y \in K$ with $y - x \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ (equivalently, $K$ meets every residue class modulo $\mathbb{Z}^2$). For such a $K$, define
$$A(K) := (K - K) \cap \mathbb{Z}^2 = \{a - b : a, b \in K\} \cap \mathbb{Z}^2.$$
It is known that $A(K)$ is always a finite generating set of the group $\mathbb{Z}^2$.

Question: Characterize which finite symmetric subsets $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2$ containing $0$ and generating $\mathbb{Z}^2$ can be realized as $A = A(K)$ for some 2-dimensional $\mathcal{N}$-set $K$. In particular:

(a) Does there exist a 2-dimensional $\mathcal{N}$-set $K$ such that $A(K) \subseteq \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z}^2 : xy = 0\}$ (i.e. all integer differences lie on the union of the two coordinate axes)?

(b) More specifically, does there exist a 2-dimensional $\mathcal{N}$-set $K$ with
$$A(K) = \{(0,0),\, (\pm 1, 0),\, (0, \pm 1)\}?$$
category_tag: Difference sets and tilings of Euclidean space
status_search_result: Search results indicate that Renling Jin resolved the problem (with an independent partial solution by Mario Szegedy). Jin's work on 2-dimensional 𝒩-sets shows that any such set must contain distinct points whose integer difference is not purely along a single coordinate axis, ruling out the axis-cross realization.

original_question: Let A be a set of nonnegative integers containing 0 such that each iterated sumset hA has asymptotic density 0, even though A subset 2A subset 3A subset ... is an increasing chain. Must any nontrivial structure nevertheless appear in this sequence of sumsets, and if so, what must happen?
self_contained_problem:
For a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ of nonnegative integers, write $hA = \{a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_h : a_i \in A\}$ for the $h$-fold sumset of $A$, and let $\overline{d}(S) = \limsup_{N \to \infty} |S \cap [0,N]|/(N+1)$ denote the (upper) asymptotic density of $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$.

Suppose $A$ contains $0$, so that $A \subseteq 2A \subseteq 3A \subseteq \cdots$ forms an increasing chain, and assume that $\overline{d}(hA) = 0$ for every integer $h \geq 1$.

Determine what nontrivial structural properties must necessarily appear in the sequence $(hA)_{h \geq 1}$. More precisely, identify and prove a nontrivial mathematical statement that must hold for every such set $A$ — for example, concerning the rate at which the counting functions $|hA \cap [0,N]|$ can grow, the arithmetic structure (such as arithmetic progressions, Sidon-like behavior, or syndeticity properties) that must or cannot appear in the sets $hA$, or rigidity properties of the chain $A \subseteq 2A \subseteq 3A \subseteq \cdots$.
status_search_result: The question originates from a recurring open-problem session on combinatorial and additive number theory and is phrased as a vague exploratory query rather than a precise conjecture. No specific theorem resolving "what nontrivial structure must appear" in iterated sumsets of zero-density sets containing 0 was located. Related work exists on iterated sumsets and Hilbert functions, on densities of sumsets, and on Plünnecke-type results, but none clearly settles the open-ended question as stated.

original_question: For a finite group G, can one always choose a generating set A so that the sequence of sphere sizes S(1), S(2), S(3), ... determined by word length with respect to A is unimodal? The paper notes that computations usually show unimodality but that a general theorem is unknown, even for nonabelian finite groups.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $A \subseteq G$ be a symmetric generating set (i.e., $A = A^{-1}$ and $\langle A \rangle = G$). For each integer $n \geq 0$, let $B(n) = \{g \in G : \ell_A(g) \leq n\}$ be the ball of radius $n$ in the Cayley graph of $G$ with respect to $A$, where $\ell_A(g)$ denotes the word length of $g$ with respect to $A$, and let $S(n) = |B(n)| - |B(n-1)|$ (with $S(0) = 1$) be the corresponding sphere size. The sequence $S(0), S(1), S(2), \ldots$ is called unimodal if there exists an integer $m \geq 0$ such that $S(0) \leq S(1) \leq \cdots \leq S(m) \geq S(m+1) \geq S(m+2) \geq \cdots$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite group $G$, there exists a symmetric generating set $A$ of $G$ such that the sphere-size sequence $S(0), S(1), S(2), \ldots$ associated with $A$ is unimodal.
status_search_result: Web searches did not surface a published proof or disproof of the conjecture that every finite group admits a generating set with a unimodal sphere-size sequence. The question is described in available references as a conjecture for which only computational evidence exists, and no resolution was located in the literature.

original_question: A subset B of the natural numbers is called an essential component if sigma(A+B) > sigma(A) whenever 0 < sigma(A) < 1, and it is extraordinary if the ratio sigma(A+B)/sigma(A) tends to infinity in the liminf sense as sigma(A) tends to 0. Is every essential component necessarily an extraordinary component?
self_contained_problem:
For a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{1,2,3,\dots\}$, define the Schnirelmann density
$$\sigma(A) = \inf_{n \ge 1} \frac{|A \cap \{1,2,\dots,n\}|}{n}.$$
For sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$, denote by $A+B = \{a+b : a \in A,\ b \in B\}$ their sumset.

A set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$ with $0 \in B$ is called an **essential component** if
$$\sigma(A+B) > \sigma(A)$$
for every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ satisfying $0 < \sigma(A) < 1$.

A set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$ with $0 \in B$ is called an **extraordinary component** if
$$\liminf_{\sigma(A) \to 0^{+}} \frac{\sigma(A+B)}{\sigma(A)} = +\infty,$$
where the liminf is taken over all $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $\sigma(A)$ approaching $0$ from above.

Question: Is every essential component necessarily an extraordinary component?
status_search_result: Web searches did not turn up a published resolution of Ruzsa's conjecture that every essential component is an extraordinary component. Standard references discuss Ruzsa's tight bounds on the minimal size of essential components, but no source located states that the essential-vs-extraordinary equivalence has been proved or refuted. Status appears unknown from the available search evidence.

original_question: Fix m >= 0 and let d = ceil(log_3 m). For n >= d, is the maximum number of affine lines contained in a set of m points in F_3^n always equal to the maximum number of lines achievable by m points already lying in F_3^d? Equivalently, when maximizing lines, is it always optimal to compress the configuration into the smallest possible ambient dimension?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_3 = \{0,1,2\}$ denote the field with three elements. An (affine) line in $\mathbb{F}_3^n$ is a set of three distinct points $\{x,y,z\} \subset \mathbb{F}_3^n$ satisfying $x+y+z = 0$ (equivalently, three points in arithmetic progression in $\mathbb{F}_3^n$). For integers $m \ge 0$ and $n \ge 1$, define
$$L(m,n) = \max\{\,\#\{\text{lines } \ell \subset S\} : S \subseteq \mathbb{F}_3^n,\ |S| = m\,\},$$
the maximum number of lines that can be contained in an $m$-point subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^n$.

Set $d = \lceil \log_3 m \rceil$, so $d$ is the smallest nonnegative integer with $3^d \ge m$. Prove or disprove: for every $m \ge 0$ and every $n \ge d$,
$$L(m,n) = L(m,d).$$
In words: when maximizing the number of affine lines among $m$ points, is it always optimal to place the configuration inside the smallest ambient affine space $\mathbb{F}_3^d$ that can hold $m$ points?

original_question: For H_n = {(x,y) in Z x Z : xy congruent to 1 mod n and 1 <= x,y <= n-1}, let v(n) be the number of vertices of the convex hull of H_n. Is v(n) forced to tend to infinity with n, and can one sharpen the lower-density estimate for the error term D(n) = v(n) - 2(tau(n-1)-1) on the set where D(n)=0?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $n \geq 2$, define the modular hyperbola
$$H_n = \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} : xy \equiv 1 \pmod{n},\ 1 \leq x, y \leq n-1\},$$
and let $v(n)$ denote the number of vertices of the convex hull of $H_n$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Let $\tau(\cdot)$ denote the number-of-divisors function, and define
$$D(n) = v(n) - 2(\tau(n-1) - 1).$$
It is known that $\limsup_{n \to \infty} v(n) = \infty$, that $D(n) > 0$ on a set of natural density $1$, and that the set $\{n \leq x : D(n) = 0\}$ has cardinality $\gg x/\log x$.

(a) Prove or disprove that $\lim_{n \to \infty} v(n) = \infty$.

(b) Improve the lower bound $\gg x/\log x$ for the cardinality of $\{n \leq x : D(n) = 0\}$, i.e., establish a stronger lower-density estimate for the set on which $D(n) = 0$.
status_search_result: Searches reveal active work by Konyagin, Shparlinski and others on upper bounds for the number of vertices of convex hulls of modular hyperbolas (e.g. v_a(m) ≤ m^{1/2+o(1)} and m^{5/12+o(1)} for almost squarefree m), and a survey by Shparlinski on modular hyperbolas, but no source establishes that v(n) → ∞ as n → ∞ or improves the x/log x lower-density estimate for {n : D(n)=0}. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Does there exist a subset A of the natural numbers that is simultaneously more-sums-than-differences, meaning |A+A| > |A-A|, and more-products-than-ratios, meaning |A·A| > |A/A|? If such sets exist, can one produce explicit infinite families of them?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite nonempty set $A$ of positive integers, define the sumset, difference set, product set, and quotient set
$$A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\},\quad A-A=\{a-b:a,b\in A\},$$
$$A\cdot A=\{ab:a,b\in A\},\quad A/A=\{a/b:a,b\in A,\ b\neq 0\}\subset\mathbb{Q}.$$
Call $A$ a more-sums-than-differences (MSTD) set if $|A+A|>|A-A|$, and a more-products-than-ratios (MPTR) set if $|A\cdot A|>|A/A|$.

(a) Does there exist a finite subset $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ that is simultaneously MSTD and MPTR, i.e., satisfies both $|A+A|>|A-A|$ and $|A\cdot A|>|A/A|$?

(b) If yes, exhibit an explicit infinite family of such sets.
status_search_result: Searches turned up substantial literature on MSTD sets and on MPTQ (more products than quotients) sets separately, including minimum-cardinality bounds for MPTQ sets and constructions of infinite families of MSTD sets. The MPTQ literature notes the close link to MSTD via logarithmic/exponential transformation, but no source found explicitly produces a single set that is simultaneously MSTD and MPTR/MPTQ, nor an infinite family. The status of the joint question therefore appears unresolved in publicly available sources.

paper_title: On Some Open Problems in Many-Electron Theory
original_question: For Coulomb many-electron systems, is the ionization energy always greater than the electron affinity? Equivalently, if I[M] denotes the ionization energy of the M-electron system, is there a general proof that I[N + 1] < I[N] for Coulomb systems?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a non-relativistic Coulomb many-electron system consisting of N electrons in the field of one or more fixed nuclei (or, more generally, an external potential consisting of a finite sum of attractive Coulomb singularities). The Hamiltonian acting on the antisymmetric subspace of L^2(R^{3N};C^2) is

  H_N = sum_{i=1}^N ( -(1/2) Δ_{x_i} + V_ext(x_i) ) + sum_{1 ≤ i < j ≤ N} 1/|x_i - x_j|,

where V_ext(x) = - sum_{k} Z_k / |x - R_k| with positive nuclear charges Z_k > 0 located at fixed positions R_k in R^3. Let E(N) denote the ground-state energy (infimum of the spectrum) of H_N restricted to fermionic wavefunctions, with E(0) := 0. Define the ionization energy of the M-electron system by

  I[M] := E(M-1) - E(M),    M ≥ 1.

The electron affinity of the N-electron system equals I[N+1] (the energy released when an extra electron is bound to the N-electron system, when binding occurs).

Prove or disprove: for every such Coulomb many-electron system, and for every N ≥ 1 for which E(N+1) is attained as an eigenvalue (i.e. the (N+1)-electron system has a bound ground state),

  I[N+1] < I[N];

equivalently, the ionization energy is strictly greater than the electron affinity.
status_search_result: No general mathematical proof of the inequality I[N+1] < I[N] (ionization energy strictly greater than electron affinity) for arbitrary Coulomb many-electron systems appears to be known. The inequality is empirically observed and can be established for certain restricted Coulomb atoms, while counterexamples exist for non-Coulomb interactions. Standard references in chemistry confirm the inequality empirically without supplying a rigorous proof.

paper_title: Regularity Properties of Sectorial Operators: Counterexamples and Open Problems
context_brief: Angles of R-sectorial operators on L^p
original_question: Let A be an R-sectorial operator on an L^p-space with p in (1, infinity). Must the sectorial angle omega(A) equal the R-sectorial angle omega_R(A)? The same question is asked under stronger semigroup assumptions: if -A generates an analytic C_0-semigroup, does the equality still hold when the semigroup is positive, contractive, or both positive and contractive?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a Banach space. A closed densely defined linear operator $A$ on $X$ is called sectorial if $(-\infty,0)$ is contained in the resolvent set of $A$ and $\sup_{t>0}\|t(t+A)^{-1}\|<\infty$. For a sectorial operator $A$, define the sectorial angle
$$\omega(A)=\inf\{\omega\in(0,\pi):\sigma(A)\subset\overline{\Sigma_\omega}\text{ and }\sup_{\lambda\notin\Sigma_{\omega'}}\|\lambda R(\lambda,A)\|<\infty\text{ for all }\omega'\in(\omega,\pi)\},$$
where $\Sigma_\omega=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}:|\arg z|<\omega\}$.

A family $\mathcal{T}\subset\mathcal{B}(X)$ is called $R$-bounded if there exists $C\ge 0$ such that for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $T_1,\dots,T_n\in\mathcal{T}$ and $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$,
$$\Big\|\sum_{k=1}^n \varepsilon_k T_k x_k\Big\|_{L^2(\Omega;X)}\le C\Big\|\sum_{k=1}^n \varepsilon_k x_k\Big\|_{L^2(\Omega;X)},$$
where $(\varepsilon_k)$ is an i.i.d. sequence of Rademacher random variables. The $R$-bound $\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{T})$ is the smallest such $C$.

A sectorial operator $A$ is called $R$-sectorial if there exists $\omega\in(\omega(A),\pi)$ such that $\mathcal{R}\big(\{\lambda R(\lambda,A):\lambda\notin\Sigma_\omega\}\big)<\infty$. The $R$-sectorial angle $\omega_R(A)$ is the infimum of all such $\omega$. By definition $\omega(A)\le\omega_R(A)$.

Now fix $p\in(1,\infty)$ and let $X=L^p(\mu)$ for some $\sigma$-finite measure space $(\Omega,\mu)$. Let $A$ be an $R$-sectorial operator on $L^p(\mu)$.

(a) Must $\omega(A)=\omega_R(A)$?

(b) Does the equality $\omega(A)=\omega_R(A)$ hold under the additional assumption that $-A$ generates a positive analytic $C_0$-semigroup on $L^p(\mu)$?

(c) Does the equality hold when $-A$ generates a contractive analytic $C_0$-semigroup on $L^p(\mu)$?

(d) Does the equality hold when $-A$ generates an analytic $C_0$-semigroup on $L^p(\mu)$ that is simultaneously positive and contractive?
status_search_result: Web searches did not surface a published proof or counterexample for the equality of sectorial and R-sectorial angles on $L^p$, even under positivity/contractivity assumptions on the generated analytic semigroup. The problem is listed in surveys of regularity properties of sectorial operators as an open question, and no resolution appears in available literature.

paper_title: Regularity Properties of Sectorial Operators: Counterexamples and Open Problems
original_question: Let A be a sectorial operator on an L^p-space with p in (1, infinity), and assume that -A generates a contractive C_0-semigroup. Must A then have a bounded H-infinity calculus, have bounded imaginary powers, or be R-analytic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p\in(1,\infty)$ and let $A$ be a sectorial operator on an $L^p$-space $L^p(\Omega,\mu)$. Recall that a closed densely defined operator $A$ on a Banach space $X$ is called sectorial of angle $\omega\in[0,\pi)$ if its spectrum is contained in the closed sector $\overline{\Sigma_\omega}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}:|\arg z|\le\omega\}\cup\{0\}$ and for every $\sigma\in(\omega,\pi)$ one has $\sup\{\|\lambda(\lambda-A)^{-1}\|:\lambda\notin\overline{\Sigma_\sigma}\}<\infty$; the infimum of such $\omega$ is the sectoriality angle $\omega(A)$.

For $\sigma\in(0,\pi)$ let $H^\infty(\Sigma_\sigma)$ denote the algebra of bounded holomorphic functions on the open sector $\Sigma_\sigma$, and $H^\infty_0(\Sigma_\sigma)$ its subalgebra of functions $f$ satisfying $|f(z)|\le C\min(|z|^s,|z|^{-s})$ for some $s,C>0$. For a sectorial $A$ with $\omega(A)<\sigma$, the holomorphic functional calculus defines $f(A)\in B(X)$ for $f\in H^\infty_0(\Sigma_\sigma)$ via a Cauchy integral. One says that $A$ has a bounded $H^\infty$-calculus if $\|f(A)\|\le C\|f\|_\infty$ for all $f\in H^\infty_0(\Sigma_\sigma)$ for some $\sigma\in(\omega(A),\pi)$.

One says that $A$ has bounded imaginary powers (BIP) if for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$ the operator $A^{it}$ given by the holomorphic functional calculus extends to a bounded operator on $X$.

One says that $A$ is $R$-analytic if $A$ generates a bounded analytic semigroup $(e^{-zA})_{z\in\Sigma_\theta}$ for some $\theta>0$ such that the family $\{e^{-zA}:z\in\Sigma_{\theta'}\}$ is $R$-bounded for every $\theta'\in(0,\theta)$, where a family $\mathcal{T}\subset B(X)$ is $R$-bounded if there exists $C>0$ with
$$\Big\|\sum_{k=1}^n r_k T_k x_k\Big\|_{L^2([0,1];X)}\le C\Big\|\sum_{k=1}^n r_k x_k\Big\|_{L^2([0,1];X)}$$
for all $T_k\in\mathcal{T}$, $x_k\in X$ and Rademacher functions $r_k$.

Assume in addition that $-A$ generates a $C_0$-semigroup of contractions on $L^p(\Omega,\mu)$, i.e. $\|e^{-tA}\|_{B(L^p)}\le 1$ for all $t\ge 0$.

Question: Must $A$ have a bounded $H^\infty$-calculus? Must $A$ have bounded imaginary powers? Must $A$ be $R$-analytic?
status_search_result: The question of whether every negative generator of a contractive $C_0$-semigroup on an $L^p$-space ($p\in(1,\infty)$) has a bounded $H^\infty$-calculus (or BIP, or $R$-analyticity) is a long-standing open problem in the functional-calculus theory of sectorial operators. On Hilbert space ($p=2$) it follows from a result of Le Merdy that contractive semigroups have $H^\infty$-calculus, but for general $p$ no proof or counterexample appears to be known, and recent surveys and lecture notes still list it as open.

paper_title: Regularity Properties of Sectorial Operators: Counterexamples and Open Problems
original_question: Find an analogue, in the borderline case omega_H-infinity(A) = pi/2, of the characterizations known below the critical angle. On Hilbert spaces, if -A generates a contractive analytic C_0-semigroup then A has a bounded H-infinity calculus with omega_H-infinity(A) = omega(A) < pi/2, and conversely operators with bounded H-infinity calculus of angle less than pi/2 are similar to generators of contractive analytic semigroups. On L^p-spaces, if -A generates a contractive positive analytic C_0-semigroup then A has a bounded H-infinity calculus with angle less than pi/2, and conversely such operators admit the structural model described in Theorem 2.11. What is the correct corresponding characterization when the H-infinity angle is exactly pi/2?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. A closed densely defined linear operator $A$ on a Banach space $X$ is called sectorial of angle $\omega\in[0,\pi)$ if its spectrum is contained in the closed sector $\overline{\Sigma_\omega}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}:|\arg z|\le\omega\}\cup\{0\}$ and for every $\theta\in(\omega,\pi)$ one has $\sup\{\|\lambda(\lambda-A)^{-1}\|:\lambda\notin\overline{\Sigma_\theta}\}<\infty$. The sectoriality angle $\omega(A)$ is the infimum of such $\omega$. For $\theta\in(0,\pi)$, let $H^\infty(\Sigma_\theta)$ denote the algebra of bounded holomorphic functions on $\Sigma_\theta$. One says that $A$ has a bounded $H^\infty$-calculus of angle $\theta$ if the natural functional calculus $f\mapsto f(A)$ extends to a bounded algebra homomorphism $H^\infty(\Sigma_\theta)\to\mathcal{B}(X)$; the $H^\infty$-angle $\omega_{H^\infty}(A)$ is the infimum of such $\theta$. The operator $-A$ generates a contractive analytic $C_0$-semigroup if there exists $\delta\in(0,\pi/2]$ such that $z\mapsto e^{-zA}$ is a holomorphic semigroup on $\Sigma_\delta$ with $\|e^{-zA}\|\le 1$ for all $z\in\Sigma_\delta$.

Known characterizations below the critical angle:
(i) On a Hilbert space $H$, if $-A$ generates a contractive analytic $C_0$-semigroup, then $A$ has a bounded $H^\infty$-calculus with $\omega_{H^\infty}(A)=\omega(A)<\pi/2$; conversely, every sectorial operator on a Hilbert space with bounded $H^\infty$-calculus of angle strictly less than $\pi/2$ is similar to (the negative generator of) a contractive analytic $C_0$-semigroup.
(ii) On $L^p(\Omega)$ with $p\in(1,\infty)$, if $-A$ generates a contractive positive analytic $C_0$-semigroup, then $A$ has a bounded $H^\infty$-calculus with $\omega_{H^\infty}(A)=\omega_R(A)<\pi/2$ (where $\omega_R(A)$ denotes the $R$-sectoriality angle), and a converse structural model is available.

Problem. Provide an analogous characterization in the borderline case $\omega_{H^\infty}(A)=\pi/2$. Specifically, identify a class of sectorial operators on Hilbert spaces (respectively on $L^p$-spaces, $1<p<\infty$) that, up to similarity (resp. up to an analogous structural model), coincides exactly with the class of sectorial operators having a bounded $H^\infty$-calculus of angle exactly $\pi/2$.
status_search_result: A web search located surveys and works on $H^\infty$-calculus for sectorial operators (Haase, Le Merdy, and others) which discuss characterizations strictly below the critical angle $\pi/2$, but no source providing the analogous characterization in the borderline case $\omega_{H^\infty}(A)=\pi/2$ was found. The problem appears to remain open.
