original_question: Does every C_0-semigroup of positive contractions on a UMD-Banach lattice admit either a strict dilation or a loose dilation in the class of all UMD-spaces?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let X be a class of Banach spaces. Given a Banach space X ∈ X and a C_0-semigroup (T(t))_{t≥0} of bounded linear operators on X, one says that:

(i) (T(t))_{t≥0} has a strict dilation in the class X if there exist a Banach space Y ∈ X, contractive linear operators J : X → Y and Q : Y → X, and an isometric C_0-group (U(t))_{t∈ℝ} on Y such that
   T(t) = Q U(t) J  for all t ≥ 0;

(ii) (T(t))_{t≥0} has a loose dilation in the class X if there exist a Banach space Y ∈ X, bounded linear operators J : X → Y and Q : Y → X, and a bounded C_0-group (U(t))_{t∈ℝ} on Y such that
   T(t) = Q U(t) J  for all t ≥ 0.

Recall that a Banach space is a UMD-space if martingale differences are unconditional in the corresponding Bochner L^p-spaces (equivalently, the Hilbert transform extends boundedly to L^p(ℝ;X) for some/all p ∈ (1,∞)). A UMD-Banach lattice is a Banach lattice which is a UMD-space.

Question. Let X be a UMD-Banach lattice and let (T(t))_{t≥0} be a C_0-semigroup of positive contractions on X. Does (T(t))_{t≥0} necessarily admit a strict dilation, or at least a loose dilation, in the class of all UMD-spaces?

paper_title: Discrepancy estimates for sequences: new results and open problems
context_brief: Average lower bounds for lattice point sets
original_question: For the d-dimensional lattice point set (({n a1/N}, ..., {n ad/N})) for n=0,1,...,N-1, prove an average-type lower bound showing that for every chi < 1 there is a constant C'_chi > 0 such that, for all N, the discrepancy D_N is at least C'_chi (log N)^(d-1) log log N / N for at least chi N^d choices of the integer vector (a1,...,ad) with 0 <= a1,...,ad < N.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $N\ge 2$ and a vector $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\dots,a_d)\in\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}^d$, consider the $d$-dimensional lattice point set
$$P_N(\mathbf{a})=\Big\{\Big(\Big\{\tfrac{n a_1}{N}\Big\},\dots,\Big\{\tfrac{n a_d}{N}\Big\}\Big):n=0,1,\dots,N-1\Big\}\subset[0,1)^d,$$
where $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$ denotes the fractional part. The (extreme/star) discrepancy of $P_N(\mathbf{a})$ is
$$D_N(\mathbf{a})=\sup_{B}\Big|\frac{\#\{0\le n<N:\,(\{n a_1/N\},\dots,\{n a_d/N\})\in B\}}{N}-\mathrm{vol}(B)\Big|,$$
where the supremum is taken over all axis-aligned boxes $B=\prod_{i=1}^d[\alpha_i,\beta_i)\subset[0,1)^d$.

Prove that for every $\chi<1$ there exists a constant $C'_\chi>0$ such that for every $N\ge 2$,
$$D_N(\mathbf{a})\;\ge\;C'_\chi\,\frac{(\log N)^{d-1}\log\log N}{N}$$
holds for at least $\chi N^d$ choices of $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\dots,a_d)\in\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}^d$.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return any source establishing the stated average-type lower bound $(\log N)^{d-1}\log\log N/N$ holding for a positive proportion $\chi N^d$ of lattice vectors $(a_1,\dots,a_d)$. Related metrical lower bounds for digital Kronecker-sequences and lattice point sets exist, but I could not verify a resolution of this specific quantitative average lower bound, so the status remains unclear.

paper_title: Discrepancy estimates for sequences: new results and open problems
original_question: For digital nets generated by rational functions over finite fields, prove an average-type lower bound for the discrepancy analogous to the lower-bound statement asked for in Open Problem 2 for ordinary digital nets over Z_q.
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be the finite field with $q$ elements. For a positive integer $s$ and dimension $m$, a digital net over $\mathbb{F}_q$ generated by rational functions is constructed as follows. Choose $s$ rational functions $g_1(x),\dots,g_s(x) \in \mathbb{F}_q(x)$. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,s\}$, expand $g_j$ as a formal Laurent series at infinity, $g_j(x) = \sum_{k\ge w_j} a_k^{(j)} x^{-k}$, with coefficients $a_k^{(j)}\in\mathbb{F}_q$. From these expansions one builds $m\times m$ generator matrices $C^{(1)},\dots,C^{(s)}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ (whose entries are taken from the Laurent coefficients), which produce a digital $(t,m,s)$-net $P=\{\mathbf{x}_0,\dots,\mathbf{x}_{q^m-1}\}\subset[0,1)^s$ in the standard digital construction scheme. Let $D_N^*(P)$ denote the star discrepancy of the resulting $N=q^m$ point set,
$$D_N^*(P)=\sup_{\mathbf{a}\in[0,1]^s}\Bigl|\frac{1}{N}\#\{n: \mathbf{x}_n\in[\mathbf{0},\mathbf{a})\}-\prod_{j=1}^s a_j\Bigr|.$$

For comparison, in the classical setting of digital nets over $\mathbb{Z}_q$ generated by $s$-tuples of $m\times m$ matrices, an "average-type" lower bound on the star discrepancy is a statement of the form: there exists a constant $c=c(s,q)>0$ such that, when the generator matrices are chosen uniformly at random from a specified family $\mathcal{G}_{m,s}$ of admissible generators,
$$\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}_{m,s}|}\sum_{C\in\mathcal{G}_{m,s}} D_N^*(P_C) \;\ge\; c\,\frac{(\log N)^{s-1}}{N}\quad\text{(or analogous best-possible order)},$$
together with a matching pointwise lower bound holding for "almost all" choices of generators.

Problem. Establish an average-type lower bound for the star discrepancy of digital nets generated by rational functions over $\mathbb{F}_q$, analogous to the average-type lower bound known/sought for ordinary digital nets over $\mathbb{Z}_q$. More precisely: identify a natural probability measure on the set of admissible $s$-tuples of rational functions $(g_1,\dots,g_s)$ producing digital nets of $N=q^m$ points in $[0,1)^s$, and prove a lower bound of the correct order of magnitude (matching the best known upper bounds, up to constants depending on $s$ and $q$) for the expected star discrepancy, as well as for the star discrepancy of almost every such net.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return specific evidence that an average-type lower bound for the discrepancy of digital nets generated by rational functions over finite fields has been established. General references on digital nets, weighted star discrepancy, and constructions from function fields exist, but none directly resolve this specific average-type lower bound question. Status is therefore reported as unknown.

paper_title: Discrepancy estimates for sequences: new results and open problems
original_question: Given positive integers d1,...,dl with d1+...+dl=d and pairwise coprime bases q1,...,ql, determine functions g(N) as small as possible and f(N) as large as possible such that, for almost all d-dimensional Halton-Niederreiter sequences whose i-th component is a d_i-dimensional digital sequence in base q_i, the discrepancy D_N satisfies D_N = Omega(f(N)) and D_N = O(g(N)).
self_contained_problem:
Let $d, l \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $d_1,\dots,d_l \in \mathbb{N}$ with $d_1+\cdots+d_l = d$. Let $q_1,\dots,q_l$ be pairwise coprime integer bases ($q_i \ge 2$). For each $i$, let $\mathbf{x}^{(i)} = (\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a $d_i$-dimensional digital sequence in base $q_i$ (a digital $(t_i,d_i)$-sequence in the sense of Niederreiter, parameterized by infinite generating matrices over $\mathbb{F}_{q_i}$). The associated Halton–Niederreiter sequence in $[0,1)^d$ is
$$\mathbf{x}_n = (\mathbf{x}^{(1)}_n, \mathbf{x}^{(2)}_n, \dots, \mathbf{x}^{(l)}_n), \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots .$$
For any sequence $(\mathbf{x}_n)_{n\ge 0}$ in $[0,1)^d$ define the star discrepancy of its first $N$ terms by
$$D_N = \sup_{\mathbf{a}\in[0,1]^d}\left| \frac{1}{N} \#\{0\le n < N : \mathbf{x}_n \in [\mathbf{0},\mathbf{a})\} - \prod_{j=1}^d a_j \right|.$$
Equip the space of generating-matrix data parametrizing all such Halton–Niederreiter sequences with the natural product Haar/Lebesgue measure.

Determine functions $f(N)$ as large as possible and $g(N)$ as small as possible such that, for almost every choice of generating data,
$$D_N = \Omega(f(N)) \quad \text{and} \quad D_N = O(g(N)) \quad (N\to\infty).$$
status_search_result: Metrical discrepancy results have been established for related Halton–Kronecker hybrid sequences (analogous to Khintchine and W. M. Schmidt theorems), but no source found in the search provides matching upper and lower metrical bounds for general Halton–Niederreiter hybrids with arbitrary coprime bases and digital components. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Discrepancy estimates for sequences: new results and open problems
original_question: Study the discrepancy of explicit Halton-Kronecker sequences, for example the two-dimensional sequence z_n = (x_n, {n sqrt(2)}) where x_n is the one-dimensional Halton sequence in base 2, that is, the van der Corput sequence. The goal is to understand the discrepancy behavior of concrete, not merely metric-almost-all, Halton-Kronecker examples.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $b\ge 2$, the one-dimensional van der Corput sequence in base $b$ is defined by
$$\phi_b(n)=\sum_{j\ge 0} a_j b^{-j-1},\qquad\text{where } n=\sum_{j\ge 0} a_j b^{j},\ a_j\in\{0,1,\dots,b-1\}.$$
Set $x_n=\phi_2(n)$, the binary van der Corput sequence, and consider the two-dimensional Halton–Kronecker sequence
$$z_n=(x_n,\{n\sqrt{2}\})\in[0,1)^2,\qquad n\ge 0,$$
where $\{t\}$ denotes the fractional part of $t\in\mathbb{R}$. The star-discrepancy of the first $N$ points of a sequence $(z_n)$ in $[0,1)^2$ is
$$D_N^*(z)=\sup_{\substack{B=[0,b_1)\times[0,b_2)\\ 0\le b_1,b_2\le 1}}\left|\frac{\#\{0\le n<N:z_n\in B\}}{N}-b_1 b_2\right|.$$
Determine the asymptotic behavior of $D_N^*(z)$ for this concrete sequence; in particular, find the best possible function $f(N)$ such that
$$N\, D_N^*(z) = O(f(N))\qquad (N\to\infty),$$
and produce matching lower bounds, beyond the metric (almost-all) results known for sequences of the form $(\phi_2(n),\{n\alpha\})$.
status_search_result: Hofer–Larcher and Drmota have proved upper bounds for the discrepancy of concrete Halton–Kronecker sequences: when α has bounded continued-fraction coefficients (e.g. α=√2), one obtains N D_N^* = O(N^{1/2}(log N)^s), and for algebraic α one has N D_N^* = O(N^{ε}) for every ε>0. Matching sharp asymptotics for the specific sequence (φ_2(n),{n√2}) are not established, so the problem is partially solved rather than fully resolved.

paper_title: Discrepancy estimates for sequences: new results and open problems
original_question: Improve Kritzer's discrepancy bound for hybrid point sets obtained by combining a Hammersley point set with a good lattice point set, gaining almost a logarithmic factor over the bound stated in Theorem 3.2.
self_contained_problem:
Let $s_1, s_2 \geq 1$ be integers and set $s = s_1 + s_2$. For an integer $m \geq 1$, let $N = 2^m$. The two-dimensional Hammersley point set in base $2$ with $N$ points is
$$\mathcal{H}_N = \left\{\left(\tfrac{n}{N},\, \phi_2(n)\right) : n = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1\right\} \subset [0,1)^2,$$
where $\phi_2$ is the base-$2$ radical-inverse function. More generally, an $s_1$-dimensional Hammersley-type point set $\mathcal{H}_N^{(s_1)} \subset [0,1)^{s_1}$ is constructed analogously using $s_1 - 1$ pairwise coprime bases together with the coordinate $n/N$.

For a generating vector $\mathbf{g} = (g_1, \ldots, g_{s_2}) \in \mathbb{Z}^{s_2}$ with $\gcd(g_i, N) = 1$, the associated good lattice point set in dimension $s_2$ is
$$\mathcal{L}_N(\mathbf{g}) = \left\{\left(\left\{\tfrac{n g_1}{N}\right\}, \ldots, \left\{\tfrac{n g_{s_2}}{N}\right\}\right) : n = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1\right\} \subset [0,1)^{s_2}.$$

The hybrid (Hammersley–good lattice) point set is
$$\mathcal{P}_N = \left\{(\mathbf{x}_n, \mathbf{y}_n) : n = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1\right\} \subset [0,1)^s,$$
where $\mathbf{x}_n$ is the $n$-th point of $\mathcal{H}_N^{(s_1)}$ and $\mathbf{y}_n$ is the $n$-th point of $\mathcal{L}_N(\mathbf{g})$.

The star discrepancy of a finite point set $\mathcal{P} \subset [0,1)^s$ is
$$D_N^*(\mathcal{P}) = \sup_{\mathbf{t} \in [0,1]^s} \left| \frac{\#\{n : \mathbf{p}_n \in [\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{t})\}}{N} - \prod_{i=1}^s t_i \right|.$$

It is known that there exists a generating vector $\mathbf{g}$ such that
$$N\, D_N^*(\mathcal{P}_N) = O\!\left((\log N)^{s}\right),$$
with an implied constant depending only on $s$.

Problem. Show that there exists a choice of generating vector $\mathbf{g}$ for which the bound can be improved to
$$N\, D_N^*(\mathcal{P}_N) = O\!\left((\log N)^{s-1+\varepsilon}\right) \quad \text{or} \quad O\!\left((\log N)^{s-1} (\log\log N)^{c}\right)$$
for some constant $c > 0$, thereby gaining almost a full factor of $\log N$ over the previously known bound.
status_search_result: A web search surfaces follow-up work on hybrid point sets combining Hammersley/Halton-type and (polynomial) lattice point sets, including component-by-component constructions and existence results, but none of the located references explicitly claim to improve the relevant Kritzer star-discrepancy bound by almost a logarithmic factor. The status of this specific improvement could not be conclusively verified.

context_brief: Metrical lower bound for hybrid sequences
original_question: Let x_n be the van der Corput sequence in base 2. Show that for almost all real alpha there exists a constant C(alpha) > 0 such that the discrepancy of the hybrid sequence z_n = (x_n, {n alpha}) satisfies D_N >= C(alpha) (log N)^2 / N for infinitely many N.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $n \ge 0$ with binary expansion $n = \sum_{j \ge 0} a_j(n) 2^j$ (where each $a_j(n) \in \{0,1\}$ and only finitely many $a_j(n)$ are nonzero), define the $n$-th element of the van der Corput sequence in base $2$ by
$$x_n = \sum_{j \ge 0} a_j(n) 2^{-j-1} \in [0,1).$$
For a real number $\alpha$, let $\{n\alpha\}$ denote the fractional part of $n\alpha$, and consider the two-dimensional hybrid sequence
$$z_n = (x_n, \{n\alpha\}) \in [0,1)^2, \qquad n = 0,1,2,\dots$$
For $N \ge 1$, let $D_N = D_N(z_0, z_1, \dots, z_{N-1})$ denote the (extreme or star) discrepancy of the first $N$ terms, i.e.
$$D_N = \sup_{B} \left| \frac{\#\{0 \le n < N : z_n \in B\}}{N} - \lambda(B) \right|,$$
where the supremum is over all axis-aligned boxes $B \subseteq [0,1)^2$ and $\lambda$ denotes the Lebesgue measure.

Prove that for almost every $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ (with respect to Lebesgue measure) there exists a constant $C(\alpha) > 0$ such that
$$D_N \ge C(\alpha) \, \frac{(\log N)^2}{N}$$
holds for infinitely many positive integers $N$.
status_search_result: Recent work (2024–2025) on digital Kronecker–van der Corput hybrid sequences establishes matching upper bounds of order $(\log N)^{2+\varepsilon}/N$ for almost all $\alpha$, and proves $\Omega((\log N)^2/N)$ lower bounds only for specific $\alpha$ tied to counterexamples of an X-adic Littlewood-type conjecture. The metrical lower bound for almost every $\alpha$ for the classical van der Corput–Kronecker hybrid sequence appears to remain unresolved.

paper_title: Discrepancy estimates for sequences: new results and open problems
original_question: Work out in detail the program sketched in the paper for using hybrid sequences in the J.P. Morgan Credit Metrics credit-risk simulation system: choose a dimension s<d for which an s-dimensional low-discrepancy sequence with N points is preferable to pseudorandom simulation, identify the s credits contributing most to portfolio risk, run the Credit Metrics simulation using quasi-Monte Carlo coordinates for those high-risk credits and pseudorandom coordinates for the remaining credits, and analyze the resulting performance against pure Monte Carlo and pure quasi-Monte Carlo methods.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider the J.P. Morgan Credit Metrics credit-risk simulation framework for a portfolio of d obligors (credits). In a standard Monte Carlo implementation, each simulation trial requires sampling a d-dimensional vector of latent variables (e.g., correlated Gaussian factors driving asset returns) used to determine, for each obligor, whether a credit-rating migration or default occurs over the risk horizon, and to compute the resulting portfolio loss distribution and risk measures such as Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall.

A hybrid sequence in [0,1)^d is a sequence of points whose coordinates are split into two blocks: an s-dimensional block (s < d) taken from a low-discrepancy sequence (a quasi-Monte Carlo sequence such as a Halton, Sobol' or (t,s)-sequence) and a (d−s)-dimensional block taken from a pseudorandom sequence. After applying coordinate-wise transformations (e.g., the inverse Gaussian CDF and a factor decomposition), this yields samples of the d-dimensional latent vector in which s coordinates are quasi-random and d−s coordinates are pseudorandom.

Problem. Carry out in full detail the following program and analyze it quantitatively.

(1) Determine, as a function of N (the number of simulation trials) and d, a threshold dimension s = s(N, d) < d up to which an s-dimensional low-discrepancy point set with N points is provably (or empirically) preferable to N pseudorandom points for integration of the relevant Credit Metrics payoff functionals.

(2) Specify and justify a procedure to identify the s obligors that contribute most to portfolio risk (for instance via marginal risk contributions, exposure-weighted default-probability ranking, or principal-component / factor-loading criteria), so that quasi-Monte Carlo coordinates are assigned to these high-risk credits and pseudorandom coordinates to the remaining d − s credits.

(3) Implement the Credit Metrics simulation with the resulting hybrid sequence and derive rigorous error/discrepancy bounds for the estimated loss-distribution functionals (mean loss, VaR at given confidence level, Expected Shortfall), exploiting available results on the discrepancy of hybrid sequences.

(4) Compare, both theoretically (in terms of asymptotic convergence rates and constants) and empirically (on representative portfolios), the performance of the hybrid method against (a) pure Monte Carlo simulation in dimension d and (b) pure quasi-Monte Carlo simulation in dimension d, identifying regimes of N, d, s and portfolio characteristics in which each method is superior.
category_tag: Hybrid quasi-Monte Carlo methods in credit risk
status_search_result: A 2014 study (Hybrid Monte Carlo-Methods in Credit Risk Management, arXiv:1405.1831, published in Monte Carlo Methods Appl. 2014) carries out the proposed program for Credit Metrics, comparing hybrid sequences against pure Monte Carlo and pure quasi-Monte Carlo, and reports that suitably chosen hybrid sequences in many relevant situations outperform both, and essentially never perform worse. Related work (Ren; Ökten and collaborators) also addresses QMC for credit portfolios. Thus the program is partially carried out, though a complete theoretical analysis covering all parameter regimes appears not fully settled.

paper_title: Discrepancy estimates for sequences: new results and open problems
original_question: Show that every two-dimensional digital sequence in base 2 has discrepancy at least c (log N)^2 / N for infinitely many N for some constant c>0, or at least establish this lower bound for a substantial subclass such as NUT sequences or finite-row sequences.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Fix the base $b=2$ and the field $\mathbb{F}_2$. A digital sequence in base $2$ in dimension $s=2$ is constructed as follows. Choose two infinite matrices $C_1,C_2 \in \mathbb{F}_2^{\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}}$ (each column having only finitely many nonzero entries). For an integer $n\ge 0$ with binary expansion $n=\sum_{j\ge 0} n_j 2^j$, $n_j\in\{0,1\}$, write $\vec n=(n_0,n_1,\dots)^\top$. For $i\in\{1,2\}$ set $(y^{(i)}_{n,1},y^{(i)}_{n,2},\dots)^\top := C_i \vec n \pmod 2$, and define
$$x^{(i)}_n := \sum_{k\ge 1} y^{(i)}_{n,k}\, 2^{-k} \in [0,1).$$
The corresponding two-dimensional digital sequence is $\mathbf{x}_n=(x^{(1)}_n, x^{(2)}_n)$, $n=0,1,2,\dots$.

For $N\ge 1$, the star discrepancy of the first $N$ points is
$$D_N^* \;=\; \sup_{\mathbf{a}\in[0,1)^2} \left| \frac{1}{N}\#\{0\le n<N : \mathbf{x}_n\in [0,a_1)\times[0,a_2)\} \;-\; a_1 a_2 \right|.$$

A NUT (Niederreiter–upper-triangular) digital sequence is one where each generating matrix $C_i$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal. A finite-row digital sequence is one where each row of every $C_i$ contains only finitely many nonzero entries.

Problem. Prove that there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ such that for every two-dimensional digital sequence in base $2$,
$$D_N^* \;\ge\; c\,\frac{(\log N)^2}{N} \qquad \text{for infinitely many } N.$$
If a full proof is out of reach, establish the same lower bound for at least one substantial subclass of two-dimensional digital sequences in base $2$, such as the class of NUT sequences or the class of finite-row sequences.
status_search_result: Although Schmidt's classical lower bound $D_N^* \gg (\log N)/N$ holds for any one-dimensional infinite sequence and there are matching upper bounds of order $(\log N)^2/N$ for two-dimensional digital sequences (Faure, Sobol', Niederreiter), no general lower bound of order $(\log N)^2/N$ for the star discrepancy of two-dimensional digital sequences in base 2 (or even for the NUT or finite-row subclasses) appears in the available literature. Recent surveys and works on digital nets and sequences (e.g., Dick–Pillichshammer's monograph and subsequent papers) continue to list this as an open problem, with progress only on related $L_p$-discrepancy questions. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Discrepancy estimates for sequences: new results and open problems
original_question: Determine the correct order of the best general lower bound for discrepancy that holds for all sequences in the d-dimensional unit cube [0,1)^d.
self_contained_problem:
For an infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in the $d$-dimensional unit cube $[0,1)^d$, define the star discrepancy of its first $N$ terms by
$$D_N^*(x_1,\dots,x_N) \;=\; \sup_{B}\left|\frac{\#\{1\le n\le N : x_n\in B\}}{N} - \mathrm{vol}(B)\right|,$$
where the supremum is taken over all axis-aligned boxes $B=\prod_{i=1}^d[0,a_i)\subseteq[0,1)^d$.

A classical theorem asserts that for every fixed $d\ge 1$ there exists a constant $c_d>0$ such that for every infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $[0,1)^d$,
$$N\,D_N^*(x_1,\dots,x_N) \;\ge\; c_d\,(\log N)^{\alpha(d)} \qquad \text{for infinitely many } N,$$
for some exponent $\alpha(d)$. The known constructions (e.g., Halton, digital $(t,d)$-sequences) show that there exist sequences with
$$N\,D_N^*(x_1,\dots,x_N) \;\le\; C_d\,(\log N)^{d} \qquad \text{for all } N\ge 2,$$
while the best general lower bound currently established is of order $(\log N)^{\beta(d)}$ with $\beta(d)<d$ for $d\ge 3$.

Problem. Determine the correct order of magnitude, as $N\to\infty$, of
$$\inf_{(x_n)_{n\ge 1}\subset[0,1)^d}\;\sup_{N\ge 2}\;\frac{N\,D_N^*(x_1,\dots,x_N)}{(\log N)^{s}},$$
i.e., find the precise exponent $s=s(d)$ such that the star discrepancy of every infinite sequence in $[0,1)^d$ satisfies $N\,D_N^*\gtrsim (\log N)^{s(d)}$ infinitely often, and such that this lower bound is sharp up to constants.
status_search_result: The exact order of the best general star-discrepancy lower bound for infinite sequences in $[0,1)^d$ remains open for $d\ge 3$. The conjectured order is $(\log N)^d$, matching known constructions, but the best known general lower bound (after work of Bilyk–Lacey–Vagharshakyan and others) is only of order $(\log N)^{(d-1)/2+\eta_d}$ for some small $\eta_d>0$. The analogous problem has been resolved for $L_p$-discrepancy ($1<p<\infty$), where the sharp order is $(\log N)^{d/2}$ (Proinov lower bound matched by Dick–Pillichshammer-type constructions), but the star (i.e., $L_\infty$) discrepancy case is still open.

paper_title: Discrepancy estimates for sequences: new results and open problems
original_question: Do there exist real numbers alpha and beta such that the two-dimensional Kronecker sequence ({n alpha}, {n beta}) has low discrepancy, meaning that D_N <= C (log N)^2 / N for all N for some constant C?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite sequence $x_1,\dots,x_N$ in the unit square $[0,1)^2$, the (star) discrepancy is defined by
$$D_N = \sup_{B} \left| \frac{\#\{1 \le n \le N : x_n \in B\}}{N} - \mathrm{vol}(B) \right|,$$
where the supremum is taken over all axis-aligned boxes $B = [0,a_1) \times [0,a_2) \subseteq [0,1)^2$. An infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge 1}$ in $[0,1)^2$ is called a low-discrepancy sequence if there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that
$$D_N \le C \frac{(\log N)^2}{N} \quad \text{for all } N \ge 2.$$
For real numbers $\alpha, \beta$, let $\{t\}$ denote the fractional part of $t$, and consider the two-dimensional Kronecker sequence
$$x_n = (\{n\alpha\}, \{n\beta\}), \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$$
Question: Do there exist real numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that this Kronecker sequence is a low-discrepancy sequence in the sense above?
status_search_result: The problem of whether some pair $(\alpha,\beta)$ makes the 2D Kronecker sequence a low-discrepancy sequence with bound $C(\log N)^2/N$ remains open. Existing results (e.g., on Halton–Kronecker and digital Kronecker–Van der Corput hybrid sequences) sidestep the pure 2D Kronecker case; almost-everywhere bounds of the form $O((\log N)^{2+\varepsilon})$ are known for $N D_N$, but no explicit $(\alpha,\beta)$ achieving the conjectured $(\log N)^2/N$ bound is known, and the optimality of such a bound is itself a major open conjecture.

paper_title: Open questions on prominences from coordinated observations by IRIS, Hinode, SDO/AIA, THEMIS, and the Meudon/MSDP
original_question: For a solar filament, is the associated magnetic flux rope brought upward through the photosphere by a levitation process, or is that flux rope instead created by successive reconnections between magnetic field lines?
self_contained_problem:
A solar filament is a cool, dense plasma structure suspended in the solar corona along a magnetic polarity inversion line, supported against gravity by an underlying magnetic flux rope (a bundle of helically twisted magnetic field lines). Two competing scenarios have been proposed for how this flux rope comes into existence:

(L) Levitation scenario: a pre-formed, coherent twisted flux rope is bodily transported upward across the photosphere from the convection zone into the corona by an emergence/levitation process.

(R) Reconnection scenario: no coherent flux rope crosses the photosphere; instead, an initially sheared magnetic arcade in the corona is gradually transformed into a twisted flux rope through a sequence of magnetic reconnections between neighboring field lines, driven by photospheric shearing and converging flows.

Determine which of (L) or (R) is the correct mechanism by which the magnetic flux rope associated with a solar filament is formed, or characterize the conditions under which each mechanism operates.
status_search_result: Recent solar physics literature (through 2022–2026) continues to treat the origin of filament-supporting flux ropes as an open question, with both photospheric emergence/levitation and coronal reconnection-based formation actively studied. Modern reviews and simulations suggest the two mechanisms may be complementary rather than mutually exclusive, but no consensus single mechanism has been established observationally.

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
context_brief: Fundamental limits in measuring stellar mass and star formation rate
original_question: For galaxies observed over a wide range of redshifts and halo masses, can astronomers reduce the systematic uncertainties involved in converting observed spectra or broadband photometry into stellar mass, meaning the total mass in stars, and star formation rate, meaning the rate at which stellar mass grows through star formation; or are standard methods reaching a fundamental limit in how accurately these quantities can be measured and used to improve galaxy-formation theory?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the inverse problem of estimating two fundamental quantities of a galaxy from observational data:

(i) the stellar mass M⋆, defined as the total mass currently locked in stars in the galaxy, and
(ii) the star formation rate (SFR), defined as the rate (in solar masses per unit time) at which new stellar mass is being produced by ongoing star formation.

The available data consist either of an observed galaxy spectrum or of broadband photometric fluxes in a finite set of bands, observed at a known redshift z. Standard estimators map this data to (M⋆, SFR) via stellar population synthesis: one assumes a stellar initial mass function, a parametric or non-parametric star formation history, a metallicity evolution, a dust attenuation law, and (where relevant) a model of nebular emission and AGN contamination, then fits the predicted spectral energy distribution to the data.

Question: Across a broad range of redshifts z and host halo masses M_h, is it possible in principle to construct estimators of M⋆ and SFR whose systematic uncertainties (arising from the choice of IMF, star formation history parametrization, dust law, metallicity, stellar evolution tracks, and nebular/AGN contributions) can be made arbitrarily small with improved modeling and data, or is there a fundamental floor on the achievable systematic accuracy of these two quantities when inferred from spectra or broadband photometry? Quantify, if possible, this floor, and determine whether it is small enough that the inferred (M⋆, SFR) can meaningfully discriminate between competing theories of galaxy formation and evolution.
category_tag: galaxy stellar mass and SFR estimation
status_search_result: This is an open conceptual/methodological question in extragalactic astrophysics. Recent SED-fitting reviews (e.g., Conroy 2013; Pacifici et al. 2023) and JWST-era studies continue to report systematic uncertainties of order 0.2–0.3 dex in stellar mass and significantly larger in SFR depending on assumptions, with no consensus that a hard fundamental floor has been established or eliminated. The problem remains active and unresolved.

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
context_brief: Star formation and assembly histories of low-mass galaxies
original_question: What are the star formation and assembly histories of galaxies with stellar masses below 10^9 solar masses, including gas-poor dwarf spheroidal galaxies concentrated around more massive galaxies and dwarf irregular galaxies with gas fractions ranging from nearly zero to one that tend to be more isolated?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the population of galaxies whose stellar mass M_* satisfies M_* < 10^9 M_sun, where M_sun denotes the mass of the Sun. This population spans a wide range of physical properties, including:

(a) dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSph), which are gas-poor and tend to be spatially concentrated around more massive host galaxies; and

(b) dwarf irregular galaxies (dIrr), whose gas fraction f_gas = M_gas / (M_gas + M_*) can vary essentially from 0 to 1 and which tend to be found in more isolated environments than dSphs.

For galaxies in this low-mass regime, determine:

1. Their star formation history, i.e. the function SFR(t) giving the star formation rate as a function of cosmic time t, from formation to the present epoch, including its dependence on stellar mass, gas fraction, and environment.

2. Their assembly history, i.e. how their present-day stellar (and dark matter) mass was assembled over cosmic time through in-situ star formation versus mergers/accretion, again as a function of M_*, gas content, and environment (isolated vs. satellite).

In particular, account for the differences between gas-poor satellite dSphs and gas-rich isolated dIrrs, and identify the physical mechanisms (e.g. reionization, supernova feedback, ram-pressure stripping, tidal interactions) that shape these histories across the M_* < 10^9 M_sun regime.
status_search_result: The star formation and assembly histories of galaxies below 10^9 M_sun remain an active area of research with many unresolved questions. Recent observational programs (e.g. resolved stellar population studies of Local Group dwarfs, JWST observations of high-redshift dwarfs) and simulations (FIRE, EDGE, etc.) have provided partial constraints, especially for Local Group dSphs, but a comprehensive understanding across the full dwarf-galaxy regime — particularly for isolated dIrrs and at higher redshifts — is still lacking. The problem is therefore considered open.

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
context_brief: Angular momentum and realistic disk-galaxy formation
original_question: How can fully cosmological simulations form realistic rotationally supported disk galaxies with thin, high-angular-momentum stellar disks, rather than producing overly compact disks and large bulges through excessive early gas cooling and angular-momentum transfer from baryons to dark matter?
self_contained_problem:
In the standard cold dark matter cosmological framework, baryons are assumed to acquire specific angular momentum comparable to that of their host dark matter halos through tidal torques during the early stages of structure formation. After collapse and dissipation, conservation of angular momentum should allow the baryons to settle into rotationally supported, thin stellar disks with exponential surface-density profiles and small central bulges, in agreement with observed late-type spiral galaxies.

In practice, fully cosmological hydrodynamical simulations that follow gas cooling, star formation, and feedback inside evolving dark matter halos have systematically suffered from the so-called "angular momentum catastrophe": excessive early gas cooling concentrates baryons into dense clumps which, via dynamical friction against the surrounding dark matter, transfer a large fraction of their angular momentum to the halo. The resulting galaxies have disks that are too compact (with radial scale lengths up to an order of magnitude smaller than observed), rotation speeds that are too high, and bulge-to-disk ratios that are too large.

Problem. Devise a prescription within fully cosmological hydrodynamical simulations — specifying the treatment of gas cooling, star formation thresholds, and stellar/AGN feedback (and any required numerical resolution and integration scheme) — under which Milky Way-mass halos at redshift zero host realistic rotationally supported spiral galaxies with thin, high-specific-angular-momentum stellar disks, exponential surface-density profiles with realistic scale lengths, small bulge-to-disk ratios, and flat rotation curves, without artificially transferring angular momentum from the baryons to the dark matter. Establish that the resulting disk population reproduces, statistically, the observed distributions of disk size, specific angular momentum, and morphology across a representative sample of halo masses and merger histories.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since 2014. Modern cosmological hydrodynamical simulations (e.g., FIRE-2, EAGLE, IllustrisTNG, Auriga) with improved stellar feedback and resolution now routinely produce Milky Way-mass galaxies with realistic thin, rotationally supported stellar disks, largely mitigating the angular momentum catastrophe. However, fully reproducing the observed statistical distributions of disk sizes, specific angular momentum, and bulge-to-disk ratios across galaxy populations remains an active area of research, and detailed angular momentum transfer mechanisms are still being characterized (e.g., 2024 FIRE study). The problem is best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
original_question: Does dividing galaxies into central galaxies, defined as galaxies located at the centers of the most massive or dominant dark matter halos, and satellite galaxies, defined as galaxies in bound subhalos of more massive halos, provide the right framework for studying galaxy evolution across clusters, compact groups, Local-Group-like systems, and other environments?
self_contained_problem:
In the standard cosmological picture, galaxies form within dark matter halos. Define a central galaxy to be a galaxy located at the center of the most massive (dominant) dark matter halo of a given system, and a satellite galaxy to be a galaxy residing in a gravitationally bound subhalo of a more massive host halo. Consider the full range of environments in which galaxies are found, including rich clusters, compact groups, Local-Group-like systems, loose groups, filaments, and isolated field environments.

Determine whether the binary classification of galaxies into centrals and satellites, as defined above, constitutes an adequate framework for describing and studying galaxy evolution across all such environments. Specifically, address the following:

(a) To what extent can galaxies be unambiguously and accurately identified as either central or satellite, given observational uncertainties in halo membership and the dynamical complexity of group/cluster environments?

(b) Are there environmental processes affecting galaxy evolution (e.g., pre-processing in infalling groups, tidal interactions in compact groups, backsplash galaxies, or dynamics in Local-Group-like pairs) whose effects are not captured by the central/satellite dichotomy?

(c) Provide either a justification that the central/satellite division is sufficient as the organizing framework for galaxy evolution studies, or identify a more refined classification scheme that better captures the dependence of galaxy evolution on environment.
status_search_result: The question is a conceptual open problem in galaxy formation rather than a settled mathematical theorem. Subsequent literature on satellite quenching, pre-processing, splashback/backsplash galaxies, and orphan/fly-by galaxies indicates that the simple central/satellite dichotomy captures much, but not all, environmental influence on galaxy evolution; the framework remains widely used but is acknowledged to be incomplete. No definitive resolution exists.

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
context_brief: Relative roles of environmental galaxy-evolution processes
original_question: How do environmental processes such as ram-pressure stripping, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, and assembly bias combine through interacting actions, back-reactions, and self-regulation to produce the observed detailed trends in satellite galaxy properties, and how can the relative role of each physical process be quantified?
self_contained_problem:
Satellite galaxies in groups and clusters are subject to several environmental physical processes that alter their gas content, star-formation activity, morphology, and structural properties. The principal processes are: (i) ram-pressure stripping, the removal of cold interstellar gas by the hydrodynamic pressure of the hot intracluster/intragroup medium as a galaxy moves through it; (ii) galaxy harassment, the cumulative effect of many high-speed gravitational encounters with other group/cluster members; (iii) strangulation (or starvation), the removal or cutoff of the extended hot gas reservoir that would otherwise cool and replenish the disk, halting future star formation; (iv) tidal stripping, the removal of stars and dark matter from the outer regions of a satellite by the tidal field of the host halo or of nearby galaxies; and (v) assembly bias, the dependence of galaxy properties on the assembly history of the host dark-matter halo at fixed halo mass.

These processes do not act independently: each can trigger, suppress, amplify, or be modified by the others through back-reactions, and the resulting evolution is self-regulating. Provide a quantitative framework that:

(a) Describes how these five processes combine—through their interactions, back-reactions, and self-regulation—to produce the observed statistical trends in satellite galaxy properties (such as quenched fractions, gas fractions, colors, morphologies, sizes, and stellar-to-halo mass relations) as functions of host halo mass, halocentric distance, infall time, and stellar mass.

(b) Quantifies the relative contribution of each individual process to those trends, in such a way that the contributions can be disentangled from observations and from cosmological simulations.

In particular, derive or specify observables and estimators that uniquely separate the signatures of ram-pressure stripping, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, and assembly bias on the satellite population.
status_search_result: This is a broad open question in galaxy formation. Disentangling the relative contributions of ram-pressure stripping, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, and assembly bias on satellite galaxies remains an active topic; recent works (e.g., on quenching timescales and assembly bias signatures with SDSS/DESI and IllustrisTNG/EAGLE simulations) provide partial constraints but no unified quantitative decomposition has been established.

context_brief: Satellite star formation persistence and rapid quenching
original_question: How can satellite galaxies sustain significant star formation for several billion years after being accreted into larger halos and then quench rapidly enough to avoid producing too many galaxies with intermediate specific star formation rates, given that current models with instantaneous or gradual hot-gas stripping still decline too rapidly or fail to match observations?

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
context_brief: Model extensions for upcoming galaxy-evolution data
original_question: How should next-generation galaxy-formation models be extended to exploit upcoming resolved spectroscopy, atomic hydrogen, and molecular-gas observations, including explicit treatment of the transition from atomic to molecular gas, possible modeling of spatially resolved physical properties, and detailed chemical evolution with abundance ratios as constraints?
self_contained_problem:
Develop a next-generation framework for modeling galaxy formation and evolution that can be quantitatively confronted with upcoming observations of resolved optical/near-infrared spectroscopy, atomic hydrogen (HI) 21-cm surveys, and molecular-gas (e.g., CO) surveys. The framework should specify and justify:

1. An explicit prescription for the transition between atomic (HI) and molecular (H2) hydrogen in the interstellar medium, expressed as a function of local physical conditions (gas surface density, metallicity, radiation field, pressure, etc.), and incorporated self-consistently into the star formation law used by the model.

2. A treatment of spatially resolved physical properties of galaxies (gas, stars, star formation rate, metallicity), going beyond global one-zone descriptions, suitable for comparison with integral-field spectroscopic surveys and resolved gas maps.

3. A detailed chemical evolution module tracking individual elemental species (not only total metallicity), including yields from Type II and Type Ia supernovae, AGB stars, and stellar winds, accounting for finite stellar lifetimes, so that abundance ratios (e.g., [α/Fe], [N/O], [C/O]) can be used as observational constraints on star formation histories and feedback.

The problem is to construct such an extended model (analytical, semi-analytical, or hydrodynamical) and to demonstrate that it simultaneously reproduces, within observational uncertainties, the statistical distributions and scaling relations of (i) HI and H2 content of galaxies, (ii) spatially resolved star formation and metallicity profiles, and (iii) stellar abundance ratios across galaxy mass and morphological type.
status_search_result: This is a broad open research program in galaxy formation theory. While individual components (HI/H2 transition prescriptions e.g. Krumholz-McKee-Tumlinson; resolved semi-analytic models; chemical evolution with detailed yields) have been developed and partially integrated in models such as L-Galaxies (Henriques+/Yates+), GAEA (De Lucia+), SHARK, and hydrodynamical simulations (IllustrisTNG, EAGLE, FIRE, SIMBA), no single model fully and consistently reproduces all observational constraints listed. The overarching goal therefore remains open as of 2026.

paper_title: On open problems in polling systems
context_brief: Renewal-arrival polling systems with large deterministic switch-over times
original_question: Consider a cyclic polling system with finitely many queues, deterministic switch-over times between successive queues, and general renewal arrival processes at the queues. The source conjectures that, when the deterministic switch-over times tend to infinity, the polling system converges to a deterministic cyclic system. Provide a rigorous proof of that conjecture.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cyclic polling system defined as follows. There are N ≥ 2 queues Q_1, ..., Q_N served by a single server that visits them in the cyclic order Q_1 → Q_2 → ... → Q_N → Q_1 → .... Customers arrive at queue Q_i according to an independent renewal process with generic inter-arrival time A_i (with finite mean 1/λ_i) and require independent service times with generic distribution B_i (finite mean). Between completing service at Q_i and starting service at Q_{i+1}, the server incurs a deterministic switch-over time s_i ≥ 0. Within each queue, the server uses a fixed work-conserving service discipline (e.g., exhaustive or gated). Assume the total load ρ = Σ_i λ_i E[B_i] < 1 so that the system is stable.

Let S = Σ_i s_i denote the total switch-over time per cycle, and consider the family of such polling systems indexed by S, where the individual switch-over times s_i are scaled so that S → ∞ (e.g., s_i = α_i S for fixed positive weights α_i summing to 1). Let "the deterministic cyclic system" denote the idealized system in which arrivals at each queue occur at deterministic equidistant epochs with rate λ_i and service times equal to their means E[B_i], with the same switch-over structure.

Prove rigorously that, as S → ∞, the stochastic cyclic polling system with general renewal arrivals converges (in an appropriate distributional sense, e.g., for the joint stationary distribution of scaled queue lengths and waiting times at polling instants) to the corresponding deterministic cyclic system.

original_question: Let A be a nonnegative primitive tensor of order m and dimension n, where primitiveness means that there exists a positive integer r such that T_A^r(x) > 0 for every nonnegative nonzero vector x, and let γ(A) be the least such r. The general upper bound proved for primitive tensors is γ(A) <= (n - 1)^2 + 1. Characterize the tensors A for which the primitive degree attains this maximal value γ(A) = (n - 1)^2 + 1.
self_contained_problem:
Let $m \ge 2$ and $n \ge 2$ be integers, and let $\mathcal{A} = (a_{i_1 i_2 \cdots i_m})$ be a nonnegative tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$, i.e. $a_{i_1\cdots i_m} \ge 0$ for all indices $i_j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$. Define the map $T_{\mathcal{A}}: \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^n \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^n$ by
\[ (T_{\mathcal{A}}(x))_i \;=\; \sum_{i_2,\dots,i_m=1}^n a_{i\, i_2 \cdots i_m}\, x_{i_2}\, x_{i_3}\cdots x_{i_m}, \qquad i = 1,\dots,n, \]
and let $T_{\mathcal{A}}^r$ denote the $r$-fold composition of $T_{\mathcal{A}}$ with itself. The tensor $\mathcal{A}$ is called primitive if there exists a positive integer $r$ such that $T_{\mathcal{A}}^r(x) > 0$ (componentwise) for every nonzero vector $x \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^n$. The smallest such $r$ is called the primitive degree of $\mathcal{A}$ and is denoted $\gamma(\mathcal{A})$. It is known that for every nonnegative primitive tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$,
\[ \gamma(\mathcal{A}) \;\le\; (n-1)^2 + 1. \]
Give a complete characterization of all nonnegative primitive tensors $\mathcal{A}$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$ for which equality $\gamma(\mathcal{A}) = (n-1)^2 + 1$ holds.
status_search_result: Web searches surface the foundational works establishing the bound $\gamma(\mathcal{A}) \le (n-1)^2+1$ and the directed-hypergraph characterization of primitivity, but no source explicitly resolves the characterization of tensors attaining $\gamma(\mathcal{A}) = (n-1)^2+1$. Status appears unverified.

original_question: Let A be a nonnegative tensor of order m and dimension n. Define the majorization matrix by M(A)_{ij} = a_{ij...j}. For a fixed j in [n], call A j-primitive if there exists a positive integer k such that (M(A^k))_{u j} > 0 for every u in [n]. Call A irreducible if there is no nonempty proper subset I of {1, ..., n} such that a_{i_1...i_m} = 0 whenever i_1 is in I and i_2, ..., i_m are all outside I. Is it true that A is primitive if and only if A is irreducible and there exists some j in [n] for which A is j-primitive?
self_contained_problem:
Let $m, n \geq 2$ be integers and let $A = (a_{i_1 i_2 \cdots i_m})_{1 \le i_1,\ldots,i_m \le n}$ be a nonnegative tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$ (i.e., all entries $a_{i_1\cdots i_m} \ge 0$).

Define the majorization matrix $M(A)$ of $A$ to be the $n \times n$ nonnegative matrix with entries
$$ M(A)_{ij} = a_{i\, j\, j\, \cdots\, j}, \qquad i,j \in [n] := \{1,\ldots,n\}. $$
Powers $A^k$ of $A$ are defined via the standard tensor product so that each $A^k$ is again a nonnegative tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$.

Definitions:
1. ($j$-primitivity) For a fixed $j \in [n]$, the tensor $A$ is called $j$-primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that
$$ \big(M(A^k)\big)_{u\,j} > 0 \quad \text{for every } u \in [n]. $$
2. (Irreducibility) The tensor $A$ is called reducible if there exists a nonempty proper subset $I \subsetneq [n]$ such that
$$ a_{i_1 i_2 \cdots i_m} = 0 \quad \text{whenever } i_1 \in I \text{ and } i_2,\ldots,i_m \in [n]\setminus I. $$
$A$ is irreducible if it is not reducible.
3. (Primitivity) $A$ is called primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that every entry of the majorization matrix $M(A^k)$ is strictly positive.

Question: Prove or disprove the following statement. A nonnegative tensor $A$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$ is primitive if and only if $A$ is irreducible and there exists some $j \in [n]$ such that $A$ is $j$-primitive.
status_search_result: Web searches for the conjecture characterizing primitivity of a nonnegative tensor as the conjunction of irreducibility and the existence of some j for which the tensor is j-primitive did not return a definitive resolution. Related work characterizes primitivity of nonnegative tensors via cycles in the associated directed hypergraph, and other conjectures on the primitive degree have been confirmed, but a clear published proof or counterexample of this specific equivalence was not located.

context_brief: Gap structure in attainable j-primitive degrees
original_question: Fix integers m >= 2, n >= 2, and j in [n]. Let A be a nonnegative tensor of order m and dimension n, and let M(A) denote its majorization matrix, defined by M(A)_{ij} = a_{ij...j}. Call A j-primitive if there exists a positive integer k such that (M(A^k))_{u j} > 0 for every u in [n], and let γ_j(A) be the least such k. Define R_j(m, n) to be the set of integers k for which there exists a nonnegative tensor A of order m and dimension n that is j-primitive but not primitive, with γ_j(A) = k. Does the set R_j(m, n) have gaps, meaning missing integers between two values that do occur?
self_contained_problem:
Fix integers $m\ge 2$ and $n\ge 2$, and let $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$. A tensor $A=(a_{i_1 i_2\cdots i_m})$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$ is a real array indexed by $(i_1,\dots,i_m)\in[n]^m$, and is called nonnegative if all its entries are nonnegative. The product $A^k$ (in the sense used for nonnegative tensor primitivity) is defined recursively so that for any tensor $B$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$, the entries of $AB$ are $(AB)_{i j_2\cdots j_m}=\sum_{i_2,\dots,i_m\in[n]} a_{i i_2\cdots i_m}\, b_{i_2 j_2\cdots j_m}\cdots$ (the standard tensor power yielding again a tensor of the same format).

The majorization matrix $M(A)$ of $A$ is the $n\times n$ matrix with entries $M(A)_{ij}=a_{i j j\cdots j}$ for $i,j\in[n]$.

The tensor $A$ is called primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that all entries of $M(A^k)$ are positive. For a fixed $j\in[n]$, $A$ is called $j$-primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that $(M(A^k))_{u j}>0$ for every $u\in[n]$; the least such $k$ is the $j$-primitive degree $\gamma_j(A)$.

Define
$$R_j(m,n)=\{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}: \text{ there exists a nonnegative tensor }A\text{ of order }m\text{ and dimension }n\text{ that is }j\text{-primitive but not primitive, with }\gamma_j(A)=k\}.$$

Question: Does $R_j(m,n)$ have gaps? That is, do there exist integers $a<b<c$ with $a,c\in R_j(m,n)$ but $b\notin R_j(m,n)$?
status_search_result: A web search did not surface a paper resolving the gap structure of the set $R_j(m,n)$ of attainable $j$-primitive degrees of nonnegative but non-primitive tensors. Related works on primitive degrees of nonnegative tensors and directed hypergraphs exist, but no conclusive result on the existence or non-existence of gaps in $R_j(m,n)$ was found.

context_brief: Global regularity from smooth initial data
original_question: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, starting from a smooth divergence-free initial velocity field, what are the most general assumptions on that initial field that guarantee the existence of a smooth solution for all times t greater than or equal to 0 rather than the formation of a finite-time singularity? $$\partial_t v + (v\cdot

paper_title: Some open questions in hydrodynamics
original_question: Which properties of the velocity field are sufficient to guarantee the existence of a unique global smooth solution of the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations for all times, assuming the initial conditions are already smooth? This asks for structural conditions on the evolving velocity field that rule out singularity formation and ensure global regularity.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for an unknown velocity field $u(x,t):\mathbb{R}^3	imes[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p(x,t):\mathbb{R}^3	imes[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}$:

$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla) u = -\nabla p + \nu\,\Delta u, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$

with viscosity $\nu>0$ and divergence-free initial data $u(\cdot,0)=u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ that decays sufficiently rapidly at infinity (for instance, Schwartz class).

Determine a structural property $\mathcal{P}$ of the evolving velocity field $u(\cdot,t)$ that is both sharp and verifiable, with the following meaning: if $\mathcal{P}$ holds along the evolution starting from any such smooth initial datum $u_0$, then there exists a unique solution $u\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty))$ that remains smooth for all $t\ge 0$ (i.e., no finite-time singularity forms). Equivalently, identify a quantity or qualitative feature of $u$ — beyond the known classical regularity criteria such as $u\in L^s_t L^q_x$ with $\frac{2}{s}+\frac{3}{q}\le 1$, $q>3$ (Ladyzhenskaya–Prodi–Serrin), the Beale–Kato–Majda condition $\int_0^T \|\omega(\cdot,t)\|_{L^\infty}\,dt<\infty$ on the vorticity $\omega=\nabla\times u$, and Escauriaza–Seregin–Šverák's $u\in L^\infty_t L^3_x$ — whose validity along solutions can be derived from the Navier-Stokes system itself and that suffices to rule out blow-up, thereby yielding global smooth existence.
status_search_result: The question is a refined form of the global regularity problem for the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Clay Millennium Problems, and remains open. Numerous conditional regularity criteria are known (Ladyzhenskaya–Prodi–Serrin, Beale–Kato–Majda, Escauriaza–Seregin–Šverák $L^\infty_t L^3_x$, Constantin–Fefferman vorticity-direction criterion, etc.), but no property derivable a priori from the equations themselves is known to imply global smoothness.

paper_title: Some open questions in hydrodynamics
original_question: How can one define the most plausible initial conditions at the beginning of the hydrodynamic stage in a relativistic heavy-ion collision? The issue is to specify the initial relativistic-fluid state at the start of stage (ii), even though the experimentally observed hadrons are produced only much later and the earlier state cannot be measured directly.
self_contained_problem:
In the standard multi-stage description of an ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collision, the evolution of the produced matter is commonly split into: (i) a pre-equilibrium stage immediately after the collision, in which strongly out-of-equilibrium gluon/parton dynamics dominate; (ii) a relativistic hydrodynamic stage, modeled by the equations of relativistic (viscous) fluid dynamics for an energy-momentum tensor T^{μν}(x) with prescribed equation of state and transport coefficients; (iii) a hadronization / freeze-out stage, after which the resulting hadrons stream freely and are eventually detected.

The hydrodynamic stage (ii) is an initial-value problem: given a space-like (or proper-time) hypersurface Σ_0 at the start of stage (ii), one must specify on Σ_0 the full set of fluid fields—energy density ε(x), flow four-velocity u^μ(x) (with u^μ u_μ = −1), and the dissipative components (e.g. shear-stress tensor π^{μν}, bulk pressure Π, baryon diffusion)—as initial data for the relativistic hydrodynamic evolution equations.

The fundamental difficulty is that the state on Σ_0 cannot be measured directly: only the asymptotic hadrons produced after stage (iii) are experimentally observed, while the matter on Σ_0 is hidden behind subsequent non-trivial dynamics.

Problem. Provide a principled mathematical/physical prescription that determines, from first principles or from a controlled effective description of the pre-equilibrium dynamics in stage (i), the most plausible initial data (ε, u^μ, π^{μν}, Π, …) on the initial hypersurface Σ_0 of the hydrodynamic stage in a relativistic heavy-ion collision, in such a way that the prescription is:

(a) compatible with the underlying microscopic theory (QCD) governing stage (i);
(b) capable of producing initial conditions whose subsequent hydrodynamic evolution and freeze-out yield predictions consistent with the experimentally observed hadronic final state;
(c) able to characterize the event-by-event fluctuations of these initial conditions.

In particular, formulate and justify a definition of "the most plausible initial conditions" at the onset of the hydrodynamic stage.
status_search_result: Recent reviews on relativistic hydrodynamics in heavy-ion collisions explicitly state that the specification of thermal initial conditions on the hydrodynamic hypersurface remains an open problem: it depends on a pre-equilibrium / thermalization dynamics that is not fully understood, and several competing initial-condition models (Glauber, KLN, IP-Glasma, EKRT, dynamical initialization, etc.) are still in use without a first-principles consensus.

original_question: How can one explicitly construct solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations that either blow up in finite time or remain globally regular, so that the possibility of finite-time singularity formation from smooth initial data can be tested directly rather than only indirectly through a priori estimates?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (or on the three-dimensional torus $\mathbb{T}^3$):
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$
with viscosity $\nu>0$, where $u(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^3$ is the velocity field and $p(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}$ the pressure, subject to a smooth, divergence-free initial datum $u_0$ of finite kinetic energy.

Provide an explicit construction (e.g., via a closed-form ansatz, a self-similar profile, a cascade-type iterative scheme, or any other concrete analytic/algorithmic procedure) of solutions of these equations exhibiting either of the following behaviors:

(a) Finite-time singularity: a smooth divergence-free initial datum $u_0$ together with an explicit solution $u(t,x)$ such that there exists $T^*<\infty$ with
$$\limsup_{t\to T^{*-}}\|u(t,\cdot)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty \quad\text{or}\quad \limsup_{t\to T^{*-}}\|\nabla u(t,\cdot)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty;$$

(b) Global regularity: a smooth divergence-free initial datum $u_0$ (not in the small-data perturbative regime) together with an explicit solution $u(t,x)\in C^\infty([0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3)$ remaining smooth for all $t\ge 0$.

The objective is a constructive, explicit answer—rather than one obtained only through a priori estimates—that directly demonstrates whether finite-time singularity formation from smooth initial data is possible.
status_search_result: The problem is a constructive form of the Navier-Stokes global regularity question, one of the Clay Millennium Problems, which remains open as of 2026. While significant recent progress has been made on related questions (e.g., non-uniqueness of weak solutions by Buckmaster–Vicol, finite-time blow-up for Navier-Stokes with forcing by Albritton–Brué–Colombo, and numerical evidence of potential singularities by Hou and collaborators), no explicit construction of either a finite-time singular smooth solution or a globally regular non-perturbative solution to the standard 3D Navier-Stokes equations has been established.

original_question: Find new combinatorial invariants of flat virtual knots, and determine richer algebraic structures that can detect flat virtual-knot phenomena beyond mod 2 linking numbers despite the fact that the flat biquandle algebra is isomorphic to the Weyl algebra and has no non-trivial finite-dimensional representations.
self_contained_problem:
A flat virtual knot (equivalently, a virtual string) is an equivalence class of virtual knot diagrams under the generalized Reidemeister moves together with the relation that identifies each classical crossing with its mirror (i.e., over/under information is forgotten, while virtual crossings remain distinct from flat classical crossings). Two flat virtual knots are known to be distinguished, in part, by mod 2 linking numbers between components and by the flat biquandle algebra, which is the unital associative algebra generated by two invertible elements A and B subject to the single relation
   A^{-1} B^{-1} A B - B^{-1} A B = B A^{-1} B^{-1} A - A.
This algebra is isomorphic to the Weyl algebra and admits no nontrivial finite-dimensional representations.

Problem. Construct new combinatorial invariants of flat virtual knots, and identify richer algebraic structures (for example, modules, quotients, deformations, or representation-theoretic data associated with the flat biquandle algebra / Weyl algebra) capable of distinguishing flat virtual knots that cannot be separated by mod 2 linking numbers, in spite of the absence of nontrivial finite-dimensional representations of the flat biquandle algebra.
status_search_result: The classification and invariant theory of flat virtual knots remains an active and open area. Recent works (e.g., parity biquandle invariants and virtual biquandle cocycle quiver representations from 2016–2025) develop new invariants but do not resolve the broader problem of finding combinatorial invariants of flat virtual knots beyond mod 2 linking numbers, nor extract a complete algebraic invariant from the flat biquandle (Weyl) algebra.

original_question: Clarify the relationship between flat virtual-knot theories and theories of doodles, including doodles with virtual crossings, and determine the resulting structures for cobordism, associated groups, and free-abelian cobordism classes of immersed surfaces without triple points.
self_contained_problem:
A flat virtual knot is an equivalence class of 4-valent planar diagrams whose crossings are of two types — flat (transverse, with no over/under information) and virtual (drawn with a small circle) — modulo the flat versions of the generalized Reidemeister moves: the three classical Reidemeister moves performed with flat crossings, the three virtual Reidemeister moves performed with virtual crossings, and the mixed "detour" move that allows an arc containing only virtual crossings to be replaced by any other such arc with the same endpoints.

A doodle is a collection of closed curves immersed in the 2-sphere (or, more generally, in a closed oriented surface) having only transverse double points and no triple points, considered up to the doodle Reidemeister-type moves that exclude the move corresponding to passing one strand across a double point of two others (so triple points are forbidden during isotopy). A cobordism between two doodles is an immersed orientable surface in (surface)×[0,1] whose singular set consists only of double-point curves, with no triple points; the set of cobordism classes of doodles forms a free abelian group under disjoint union.

Formulate and develop a precise correspondence between flat virtual knot theory and the theory of doodles in the following sense:

(a) Define a category of "virtual doodles" by allowing diagrams to contain both flat (double-point) crossings and virtual crossings, together with appropriate Reidemeister-type and detour moves, and determine the precise relationship (functor, equivalence, or embedding) between this category and the category of flat virtual knots.

(b) Define cobordism of virtual doodles via immersed surfaces without triple points in the appropriate thickened surface, and determine the resulting cobordism group; in particular, decide whether the cobordism classes form a free abelian group as in the classical doodle case, and compute or characterize this group.

original_question: Develop effective invariants and, if possible, a classification theory for welded knots. In particular, determine whether Satoh's map from welded knots or links to ambient-isotopy classes of ribbon torus embeddings in four-space is faithful, and determine whether a welded knot with trivial fundamental group must itself be trivial as a welded knot.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

A virtual knot diagram is an immersed closed curve in the plane whose only singularities are double points, each labelled either as a classical crossing (with over/under information) or as a virtual crossing (drawn as a small circle, with no over/under information). Welded knots are equivalence classes of virtual knot diagrams under planar isotopy and the following local moves:
- the three classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3 (applied to classical crossings);
- the three virtual Reidemeister moves V1, V2, V3 (analogues of R1, R2, R3 in which all crossings involved are virtual);
- the mixed move M (a strand carrying only virtual crossings may be slid past a classical crossing);
- the forbidden overcrossing move F1: an overstrand may pass through a virtual crossing.
(The other "forbidden" move, F2, in which an understrand passes through a virtual crossing, is NOT allowed.)

A ribbon torus-knot is a smooth embedding T : S^1 × S^1 → R^4 (or S^4) which bounds an immersed solid torus B^2 × S^1 → R^4 whose only self-intersections are so-called ribbon singularities (transverse double disks each of whose preimages consists of one disk in the interior of B^2 × S^1 and one disk meeting the boundary in a circle). Ribbon torus-knots are considered up to ambient isotopy of R^4.

Satoh's tube construction associates to every welded knot K a ribbon torus-knot Tube(K) ⊂ R^4, well defined up to ambient isotopy, by tubing the underlying virtual diagram. This induces a well-defined surjective map
   Tube : { welded knots } / equivalence  →  { ribbon torus-knots } / ambient isotopy.

The fundamental group of a welded knot K is the group π_1(K) defined by the Wirtinger presentation read from any virtual diagram representing K (with one generator per classical arc and one Wirtinger relation per classical crossing); this is invariant under welded equivalence, and π_1(unknot) ≅ Z.

Problems.

(a) Construct a complete (or otherwise effective) system of invariants for welded knots that can be used to classify them up to welded equivalence.

(b) Determine whether Satoh's tube map
   Tube : { welded knots } / equivalence  →  { ribbon torus-knots } / ambient isotopy
is injective (faithful). Equivalently: if two welded knots K_1, K_2 satisfy Tube(K_1) ≅ Tube(K_2) as ribbon torus-knots in R^4, must K_1 and K_2 be equivalent as welded knots? The same question is asked for welded links and ribbon torus-links.

(c) Determine whether a welded knot K with π_1(K) ≅ Z is necessarily welded-equivalent to the trivial welded knot.
category_tag: Welded knots and ribbon torus embeddings
status_search_result: The faithfulness of Satoh's tube map and the question of whether a welded knot with infinite cyclic fundamental group must be trivial are still discussed as open problems in recent literature on welded knots and ribbon torus-knots (e.g., 2024 work on non-triviality of welded knots and ribbon torus-knots, and 2021 work on generalizations of Satoh's tube map). No proof of injectivity, nor a counterexample for either question, appears to be established. A full classification of welded knots is also not available.

original_question: Construct explicit presentations of a virtual biquandle that uses the given linear non-commutative representation at classical crossings together with a genuinely informative algebraic structure at virtual crossings.
self_contained_problem:
A virtual biquandle is a set $X$ equipped with four binary operations $\triangleright, \triangleright^{-1}, \blacktriangleright, \blacktriangleright^{-1}: X \times X \to X$ (encoding the labelings at classical crossings) together with an invertible unary operation $f: X \to X$ (encoding the labeling at virtual crossings), such that the operations satisfy the algebraic axioms corresponding to invariance under all generalized Reidemeister moves for virtual link diagrams (the classical Reidemeister moves I, II, III; the virtual Reidemeister moves V1, V2, V3; and the mixed move involving one classical and two virtual crossings).

A linear (non-commutative) representation at classical crossings is a virtual biquandle structure on a module $X$ over an associative (possibly non-commutative) ring $R$ such that the operations $\triangleright$ and $\blacktriangleright$ are given by $R$-linear formulas of the form
$$ a \triangleright b = a\,S + b\,T, \qquad a \blacktriangleright b = a\,U + b\,V $$
for fixed elements $S, T, U, V \in R$ (or, more generally, by linear endomorphisms of $X \oplus X$), so that the resulting set-theoretic Yang–Baxter operator at classical crossings is linear and non-commutative.

Construct an explicit presentation of a virtual biquandle in which:
1. the operations at classical crossings form such a linear non-commutative representation, and
2. the unary operation $f$ at virtual crossings is given by a genuinely non-trivial algebraic structure (i.e., not merely the identity or a scalar map, but a structurally informative operation that interacts non-trivially with the classical operations through the mixed Reidemeister move).

Exhibit the underlying ring $R$, the module $X$, the constants $S, T, U, V$, and the map $f$, and verify that all virtual biquandle axioms are satisfied.
status_search_result: The problem appears in a well-known list of unsolved problems in virtual knot theory. Recent work (2023–2025) on virtual biquandles, group biquandles, and biquandle cocycle quiver representations develops related algebraic structures, but no source explicitly identifies a fully satisfactory construction of a virtual biquandle combining a linear non-commutative representation at classical crossings with a genuinely informative structure at virtual crossings. Status appears unresolved in published literature.

original_question: Does the fundamental biquandle classify virtual links up to mirror images, including the known ambiguity that the biquandle has the same value on the orientation-reversed mirror image obtained by reflection in a plane perpendicular to the diagram plane?
self_contained_problem:
Recall that a virtual link diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose vertices are decorated as either classical crossings (with over/under information) or virtual crossings (drawn as a small circle), considered up to the generalized Reidemeister moves (the three classical Reidemeister moves, the three purely virtual Reidemeister moves, and the mixed move). Virtual links are equivalence classes of such diagrams.

To an oriented virtual link diagram L one associates its fundamental biquandle BQ(L) as follows. The diagram is divided by the classical crossings into "semi-arcs" (an arc is broken at every classical undercrossing as well as at the two strands meeting at every classical crossing, but is not broken at virtual crossings). Assign one generator to each semi-arc. At each classical crossing one imposes two relations expressing the two outgoing labels as biquandle operations of the two incoming labels: if a, b are the under- and over-incoming labels and c, d the corresponding outgoing labels, then c = a^b and d = b_a (with the appropriate sign convention determined by the sign of the crossing). The resulting algebraic structure BQ(L), generated by the semi-arc labels modulo these relations, is an invariant of the oriented virtual link.

The "vertical mirror" of L is the virtual link L* obtained by reflecting the diagram in a plane perpendicular to the diagram plane (equivalently, by switching all classical crossings and reversing the orientation of every component). It is known that BQ(L) ≅ BQ(L*) as biquandles for every oriented virtual link L.

Question. Is the fundamental biquandle a complete invariant of virtual links up to this vertical-mirror ambiguity? That is, does BQ(L₁) ≅ BQ(L₂) (as biquandles) imply that L₂ is equivalent, as a virtual link, to either L₁ or its vertical mirror L₁*?
status_search_result: The completeness of the fundamental biquandle for virtual links (up to the known vertical-mirror ambiguity) is consistently listed as an open conjecture in the virtual knot theory literature. Recent surveys and problem lists on virtual knot theory still record it as unresolved, and current work focuses on biquandle-derived invariants (cocycles, brackets, quivers) rather than a proof of completeness.

original_question: Suppose a non-trivial classical knot K is modified by virtualizing some crossings so that the resulting virtual knot K~ is non-trivial and has unit Jones polynomial. Must K~ be non-classical, or could it still be virtually equivalent to a classical knot? More generally, if a virtual knot has unit Jones polynomial, is it equivalent to a classical diagram after virtual equivalence together with crossing virtualization, and if one classical knot can be obtained from another by crossing virtualization plus virtual Reidemeister moves, must the two classical knots already be classically equivalent?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A virtual knot diagram is a generic immersion of a circle in the plane whose double points are decorated as either classical crossings (with over/under information) or virtual crossings (drawn as a small circle around the double point). Two virtual knot diagrams are virtually equivalent if they are related by a finite sequence of the classical Reidemeister moves and the virtual Reidemeister moves (the "detour moves"). Crossing virtualization is the local operation that replaces a classical crossing by the same crossing flanked on two opposite sides by virtual crossings (equivalently, switching the crossing and surrounding it by virtual crossings). The Jones polynomial V(K) of a virtual knot K is the Kauffman-bracket Jones polynomial extended to virtual diagrams; one says V(K)=1 (unit Jones polynomial) if it equals the Jones polynomial of the unknot. A virtual knot is called classical if it is virtually equivalent to a diagram with no virtual crossings.

Problems.

(a) Let K be a non-trivial classical knot, and let K̃ be a virtual knot obtained from K by virtualizing some non-empty subset of its classical crossings. Assume K̃ is non-trivial and satisfies V(K̃)=1. Must K̃ be non-classical, or is it possible for K̃ to be virtually equivalent to a classical knot diagram?

(b) Let K be any virtual knot with V(K)=1. Must K be equivalent, via virtual equivalence together with applications of crossing virtualization (in either direction), to a classical knot diagram?

(c) Let K and K' be classical knots, viewed as virtual knot diagrams. If K can be obtained from K' by a finite sequence of crossing virtualizations and virtual Reidemeister moves, must K and K' represent the same classical knot (i.e., be classically equivalent)?
category_tag: Virtual knot theory and Jones polynomial
status_search_result: The questions appear in standard lists of unsolved problems in virtual knot theory. Partial results are known: virtual knots produced by virtualizing a single classical crossing of a non-trivial classical knot are known to be non-classical and to have unit Jones polynomial; however, the general questions (arbitrary subsets of virtualized crossings, the converse characterization of unit-Jones virtual knots up to virtual equivalence plus virtualization, and whether crossing virtualization plus virtual Reidemeister moves can identify inequivalent classical knots) remain open as of available sources.
