paper_title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics
original_question: What mechanism explains the surprisingly low proton-to-pion ratio at the LHC despite fits with a reduced chemical freeze-out temperature, and can baryon final-state annihilation or late baryon freeze-out be distinguished from other explanations without creating tension with hyperon abundances and resonance-ratio constraints?
self_contained_problem:
Consider ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions at LHC energies (Pb–Pb at center-of-mass energies of a few TeV per nucleon pair), modeled within the statistical/thermal hadronization framework with chemical freeze-out temperature T_chem and kinetic freeze-out temperature T_kin, possibly followed by a hadronic rescattering phase described by transport models (e.g., URQMD, EPOS).

Empirical observations to be explained simultaneously:
(i) The integrated proton-to-pion yield ratio p/π measured in central Pb–Pb collisions lies well below predictions of standard equilibrium thermal fits, even after lowering T_chem by roughly 10 MeV relative to pre-LHC values.
(ii) Lowering T_chem by this amount creates tension with measured hyperon (Λ, Ξ, Ω) abundances, which prefer a higher T_chem closer to the pre-LHC value.
(iii) Measured short-lived resonance-to-stable-particle yield ratios (e.g., K*/K, ρ/π, Λ*/Λ) are well reproduced by hadronic transport simulations including post-hadronization rescattering, and disfavor scenarios in which chemical and kinetic freeze-out coincide (T_chem = T_kin).

Problem: Identify a hadronic-phase mechanism — for instance, baryon–antibaryon final-state annihilation (BB̄ → multi-meson) producing late effective baryon freeze-out — that quantitatively reproduces the suppressed p/π ratio, while remaining simultaneously consistent with measured hyperon abundances and with the resonance-ratio constraints (i)–(iii). Determine whether such a mechanism can be unambiguously distinguished from alternative explanations (e.g., non-equilibrium chemistry, flavor-dependent freeze-out, or modified hadron spectra) by existing or future observables.
status_search_result: The anomalously low p/π ratio at the LHC remains an actively discussed puzzle. Baryon–antibaryon annihilation in the hadronic phase (as implemented in UrQMD/EPOS afterburners) is a leading but not unique explanation, and tensions with hyperon yields and resonance-ratio constraints persist. Recent LHC measurements (e.g., strange-baryon studies in 2024–2025) continue to probe these issues without delivering a fully unique mechanistic resolution.

paper_title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics
original_question: Does the initial temperature inferred from excess direct photons in heavy-ion collisions increase from RHIC to LHC energies, and can higher-precision photon measurements plus calculations with medium-modified rates and state-of-the-art space-time evolution establish that trend?
self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the transverse-momentum spectrum of "direct photons" (the inclusive photon yield with hadron-decay contributions subtracted) exhibits, in the soft region (roughly 1 ≲ p_T ≲ 4 GeV), an exponential excess above prompt-photon (next-to-leading-order pQCD) baselines. This excess is commonly characterized by an inverse logarithmic slope T_eff defined via fitting dN/(p_T dp_T) ∝ exp(−p_T / T_eff). Through a hydrodynamic / fireball model of the collision evolution, T_eff is related (with corrections from space-time averaging over the fireball history and from blue-shifting due to collective transverse flow) to an inferred initial fireball temperature T_0 at the thermalization time τ_0.

Available measurements give T_eff ≈ 200 MeV at top RHIC energy (Au+Au at √s_NN = 200 GeV) and T_eff ≈ 300 MeV at LHC energies (Pb+Pb at √s_NN = 2.76 TeV), with corresponding model-extracted initial temperatures in the range T_0 ≈ 300–500 MeV, well above the QCD pseudo-critical temperature T_c ≈ 155 MeV.

Question. Establish, using improved direct-photon measurements (reduced statistical and systematic uncertainties) together with theoretical thermal-photon-rate calculations that incorporate medium modifications and a state-of-the-art (3+1)-dimensional viscous relativistic hydrodynamic space-time evolution coupled to a realistic initial-state model, whether the inferred initial temperature T_0(√s_NN) is a strictly increasing function of collision energy between √s_NN = 200 GeV and √s_NN = 2.76 TeV (and at higher LHC energies). Quantify the magnitude of the increase ΔT_0 with statistical significance ≥ 3σ.
status_search_result: As of 2026, while direct-photon measurements at RHIC and LHC continue to indicate higher inferred initial temperatures at LHC than at RHIC (with hydrodynamic extractions reaching ≳500 MeV), the experimental and theoretical uncertainties remain large and the energy dependence of T_0 has not been established with the high precision called for. The question therefore appears still open.

paper_title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics
original_question: What is the precise theoretical connection between the observed broadening or melting of the ρ meson in hot hadronic matter and chiral symmetry restoration in the quark-gluon plasma, and can missing LHC, intermediate-mass, and small-system dilepton data determine whether collective features in small systems accompany hot-matter formation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a strongly interacting medium described by finite-temperature QCD with light quark flavors. In the hadronic phase, the ρ meson has a vector-current spectral function ρ_V(q_0, q; T, μ_B) that, in equilibrium at temperature T and baryon chemical potential μ_B, governs the thermal dilepton emission rate

  dN_{ℓ⁺ℓ⁻}/d⁴q d⁴x = -(α²/(π³ M²)) f_B(q_0; T) Im Π_V(q_0, q; T, μ_B),

where Im Π_V is proportional to ρ_V, M² = q_0² - |q|², and f_B is the Bose distribution. Empirically, ρ_V exhibits a strong broadening ("melting") as T approaches the pseudocritical temperature T_pc ≈ 155 MeV. Chiral symmetry restoration is characterized by the degeneracy of the vector and axial-vector spectral functions, ρ_V(q_0, q; T) → ρ_A(q_0, q; T), as encoded by the Weinberg-type sum rules

  ∫_0^∞ (ds/s) [ρ_V(s; T) - ρ_A(s; T)] = f_π(T)² / something,
  ∫_0^∞ ds [ρ_V(s; T) - ρ_A(s; T)] = f_π(T)²,
  ∫_0^∞ ds · s · [ρ_V(s; T) - ρ_A(s; T)] = -2π α_s ⟨(q̄q)²⟩(T) (up to standard coefficients),

with chiral order parameters such as the quark condensate ⟨q̄q⟩(T) and the pion decay constant f_π(T).

Provide a rigorous theoretical derivation, starting from the QCD Lagrangian (or a controlled effective field theory thereof), establishing a quantitative and model-independent connection between the observed in-medium broadening of ρ_V and the temperature/density evolution of the chiral order parameters that signal chiral symmetry restoration. In particular, determine whether the melting of the ρ as seen in heavy-ion dilepton spectra implies, and is implied by, chiral restoration in the same medium, beyond the level of model-dependent conjectures.

Additionally, formulate and answer the following experimental-theoretical question: assuming forthcoming high-precision dilepton data in the low- and intermediate-mass regions from heavy-ion collisions at the LHC and RHIC, as well as small-system (pp, pA) collisions, can one decide whether the collective behavior observed in small collision systems is accompanied by the formation of a thermalized partonic medium of the same nature as that produced in large systems?
category_tag: QCD chiral symmetry and dilepton spectra
status_search_result: The theoretical connection between ρ-meson melting and chiral symmetry restoration remains an active research topic. Recent works (2021–2025), including studies using Weinberg-type sum rules, chiral effective theories, and inverse QCD sum rules, continue to refine the link but treat it as not yet rigorously derived from first principles. Likewise, the experimental program on intermediate-mass dileptons and small-system collectivity is still ongoing, with definitive determinations awaiting LHC/RHIC detector upgrades and analyses.

paper_title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics
context_brief: Intermediate-pT hydro decoupling and quark scaling
original_question: How does hydrodynamic behavior decouple from hadron production at intermediate transverse momentum between a few and 10 GeV, where hadrons are increasingly poorly described by hydrodynamics but not yet fully described by perturbative-QCD jets, and what physical interpretation, if any, remains for constituent-quark scaling in that transition region?
self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the bulk of low transverse momentum (pT ≲ 2 GeV) hadron production is well described by relativistic viscous hydrodynamics applied to a strongly coupled quark–gluon plasma, while the high-pT region (pT ≳ 10 GeV) is dominated by perturbative-QCD parton energy loss and jet fragmentation. In the intermediate window pT ∈ (a few GeV, 10 GeV), neither description is fully accurate. An empirical regularity known as constituent-quark-number (NCQ) scaling states that the elliptic flow v2 of identified hadrons satisfies, to good approximation,
   v2^h(pT) / n_h ≈ f(pT / n_h),
where n_h is the number of valence (constituent) quarks of hadron h (n_h = 2 for mesons, 3 for baryons), and f is a universal function.

Provide:

(a) A controlled, quantitative dynamical framework that interpolates between the hydrodynamic regime and the perturbative-QCD jet regime across the intermediate-pT window, and that specifies in what precise sense (e.g. for which observables, particle species, system sizes, and pT ranges) hydrodynamic behavior decouples from hadron production as pT increases through this window.

(b) A first-principles physical interpretation of constituent-quark-number scaling in this transition region: identify the underlying microscopic mechanism (for example quark recombination/coalescence at hadronization, or another mechanism) responsible for the approximate scaling relation above, derive the form of f and the expected magnitude and pattern of deviations from exact scaling as functions of pT, hadron species, collision energy, and system size, and explain whether NCQ scaling carries information about partonic degrees of freedom beyond what is captured by hydrodynamics or by pQCD.
status_search_result: The intermediate-pT regime between hydrodynamics and pQCD jets remains an active research area. Hybrid Hydro-Coal-Frag models (viscous hydro at low pT, quark coalescence at intermediate pT, and jet fragmentation at high pT) reproduce approximate NCQ scaling phenomenologically, supporting a coalescence/recombination interpretation, but a controlled first-principles description of the hydro-to-jet transition and a derivation of NCQ scaling beyond approximate scaling relations is not established. Recent (2024–2025) studies at RHIC continue to investigate the onset and breaking of NCQ scaling, indicating the underlying questions remain open.

paper_title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics
original_question: Are the charge-specific multi-particle correlations observed in heavy-ion collisions genuine Chiral Magnetic signals from QCD chiral anomaly effects in strong magnetic fields, or are they backgrounds produced by local charge conservation modulated by elliptic flow, and can proposed parameter-isolating tests such as isobar-beam collisions deliver a decisive limit or answer?
self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the QCD chiral anomaly in the presence of a strong, transient electromagnetic field is predicted to induce charge-dependent multi-particle azimuthal correlations, collectively known as the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME): an electric current along the magnetic field producing a charge separation across the reaction plane. A standard observable is the three-particle correlator γ_{αβ} = ⟨cos(φ_α + φ_β − 2Ψ_RP)⟩, where φ_α, φ_β are the azimuthal angles of charged particles of species α,β ∈ {+,−} and Ψ_RP is the reaction-plane angle, together with related charge-dependent harmonics. A competing, purely conventional explanation attributes the observed signal to local charge conservation (correlated emission of opposite-sign pairs) modulated by elliptic flow v_2.

Setup of the proposed isobar test: collide two nuclei with the same mass number but different atomic numbers (e.g., ⁹⁶₄₄Ru + ⁹⁶₄₄Ru versus ⁹⁶₄₀Zr + ⁹⁶₄₀Zr) at the same √s_{NN} and centrality. Then v_2 (and hence the flow-driven background) is approximately equal between the two systems, while the magnetic-field magnitude |B| differs by a controlled amount. A genuine CME contribution should produce a difference in the charge-dependent correlators (e.g., the ratio of Δγ to v_2) between the two species that scales with the |B|² difference, whereas a purely flow-driven background should not.

Question: Determine whether the charge-dependent multi-particle correlations measured in heavy-ion collisions are dominated by a genuine CME signal arising from the QCD chiral anomaly in strong magnetic fields, or instead by background from local charge conservation modulated by elliptic flow. In particular, decide whether an isobar-collision program of the form above can yield, and does yield, a decisive quantitative limit (or measurement) on the CME fraction of the observed charge-separation signal.
category_tag: Chiral Magnetic Effect in heavy-ion collisions
status_search_result: The STAR Collaboration carried out the proposed isobar test (Ru+Ru vs Zr+Zr at √s_NN = 200 GeV) with a pre-registered blind analysis of ~3.8 billion events, published in Phys. Rev. C 105, 014901 (2022). No CME signature satisfying the predefined criteria was observed, providing a strong upper limit on the CME contribution. Subsequent analyses (Phys. Rev. C 106, L051903) accounting for differences in multiplicity and flow between the isobars are consistent with a small finite CME fraction of order (6.8±2.6)% of the observed Δγ. Thus the isobar program has delivered a decisive constraint, but the question of a nonzero residual CME signal remains under active investigation.

paper_title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics
original_question: What are the temperature, parton-type, parton-energy, and path-length dependences of the jet-quenching stopping power q-hat divided by T cubed, and why do spectral slopes, fragmentation functions, and energy-loss coefficients appear to cancel so that the nuclear-modification factor RAA has nearly invariant magnitude and shape across parton flavours and collision energies?
self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, a strongly coupled quark–gluon plasma (sQGP) is produced with a local temperature T. A high-energy parton (gluon g, light quark u/d/s, charm c, or bottom b) traversing this medium loses energy via interactions characterized by the jet transport coefficient q̂, defined as the mean squared transverse momentum acquired per unit path length. The dimensionless ratio q̂/T^3 is regarded as the medium's stopping power. The nuclear modification factor R_AA(p_T) for a given hadron species is defined as the ratio of the yield in nucleus–nucleus collisions to the yield in proton–proton collisions scaled by the average number of binary nucleon–nucleon collisions, as a function of transverse momentum p_T.

Problem. Determine, from first principles in a controlled QCD-based framework of in-medium parton energy loss:

(a) the functional dependence of q̂/T^3 on the medium temperature T, on the parton flavour (mass), on the parton energy E, and on the in-medium path length L; and

(b) provide a quantitative explanation of why the convolution of (i) the partonic spectral slopes of the initial hard scattering, (ii) the vacuum and medium-modified fragmentation functions, and (iii) the energy-loss kernel produces an R_AA whose magnitude and p_T-shape are nearly invariant across parton flavours (g, u/d/s, c, b, and J/ψ) and across collision energies spanning roughly 0.2, 2.76, and 5 TeV per nucleon pair. In particular, identify the cancellation mechanism (or rule it out) that makes R_AA approximately universal despite the strong dependence of each individual ingredient on flavour and energy.
status_search_result: The temperature, parton-type, energy, and path-length dependences of q̂/T^3 remain active areas of investigation. The JETSCAPE Collaboration's Bayesian extractions (2021–2024) have constrained q̂/T^3 to roughly 30–50% precision and reported mild T- and E-dependence, but the parton-type and path-length dependences and the universality of R_AA remain not fully understood. The problem is generally regarded as open.

paper_title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics
context_brief: AMPT density tomography versus hydrodynamic pressure tomography
original_question: Are pressure tomography from hydrodynamics and density tomography from AMPT-like transport two limits of the same collective physics, or are they distinct mechanisms with experimentally separable consequences such as directed photon flow or nonlinear mode mixing?
self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the azimuthal anisotropy of produced particles can be modeled in (at least) two distinct theoretical frameworks:

1. Relativistic viscous hydrodynamics, in which the azimuthal anisotropy of final-state momentum distributions arises from pressure gradients in the initial spatial geometry of the fireball ("pressure tomography": stronger pressure gradients in directions of larger anisotropy of the energy-density profile push more matter outward in those directions).

2. A parton transport approach of AMPT type ("escape" or "density tomography"), in which a small number of parton–parton scatterings produce an image of the initial-state density distribution: particles preferentially escape in the directions of lower opacity, leading to a depletion in the directions of larger matter density.

Formulate and answer the following question precisely. Let f_hydro and f_transport denote the families of observables (e.g., harmonic flow coefficients v_n{m} for n ≥ 1 and m ≥ 2, nonlinear response coefficients χ_{n,mk} relating higher harmonics to products of lower ones, and directed flow of direct photons v_1^γ) predicted by, respectively, a hydrodynamic evolution and an AMPT-like transport evolution of the same initial-state ensemble.

Determine whether:

(a) Pressure tomography and density tomography are two limits (high opacity / many rescatterings versus low opacity / few rescatterings, respectively) of one and the same underlying collective response, in the sense that f_hydro and f_transport coincide on a common set of observables once the opacity (or mean free path) is varied continuously between the two regimes; or

(b) They are distinct dynamical mechanisms that produce experimentally separable predictions, and in that case, identify at least one observable—such as the directed flow of direct photons v_1^γ(p_T, η) or a nonlinear mode-mixing coefficient (e.g., χ_{4,22}, χ_{5,23}, χ_{6,33}, χ_{6,222})—on which the two frameworks give predictions that differ in sign or in magnitude beyond theoretical and experimental uncertainties.

Provide either a derivation showing equivalence in the appropriate limit, or a concrete observable together with quantitative predictions distinguishing the two mechanisms.
status_search_result: The relationship between hydrodynamic "pressure tomography" and AMPT "escape/density tomography" remains an active research topic. Studies indicate qualitative differences (e.g., escape mechanism does not generate radial flow, while hydro pressure push does; heavy-ion data favor hydro while small-system results lean toward the escape picture), but no consensus derivation establishes them as two limits of one mechanism, nor a single decisive experimental observable separating them. Thus the question is best characterized as still open.

paper_title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics
original_question: Is there an identifiable onset of the strongly coupled quark-gluon plasma as a function of collision time, beam energy, volume, system size, or energy density, and how does collectivity and macroscopic behavior emerge as those conditions are varied?
self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic nuclear collisions, the strongly coupled quark-gluon plasma (sQGP) is a deconfined state of QCD matter believed to be produced when sufficiently high energy densities and temperatures are reached. Collective behavior in such collisions is typically diagnosed via observables such as anisotropic flow coefficients v_n, strangeness enhancement, jet quenching, and hydrodynamic-like azimuthal correlations, measured across systems ranging from proton–proton (pp), proton–nucleus (pA), to nucleus–nucleus (AA) collisions, and across a range of center-of-mass energies √s_NN, system volumes, charged-particle multiplicities, and inferred energy densities.

Determine whether there exists an identifiable onset of the sQGP as a function of (i) collision evolution time, (ii) beam energy √s_NN, (iii) interaction volume, (iv) system size (e.g., pp, pA, light-ion, heavy-ion), or (v) energy density. Specifically:

1. Establish whether collective and macroscopic (hydrodynamic-like) behavior appears at a sharp threshold in any of these variables, or instead emerges as a continuous and gradual crossover.
2. Characterize how collectivity—measured through flow harmonics v_n, their multiparticle cumulants, strangeness enhancement, and energy-loss observables—develops as the above control variables are varied, including in small systems (high-multiplicity pp and pA collisions).
3. Determine whether the onset, if any, occurs at the same value of the control variable for all such observables, or whether different observables turn on at different thresholds.

Provide either a quantitative criterion (with values of √s_NN, multiplicity, volume, or energy density) marking the onset of sQGP formation that is consistent with all relevant observables, or a demonstration that no such common threshold exists and that the transition to sQGP-like behavior is continuous.
status_search_result: The onset of the sQGP and the emergence of collectivity in small systems remain open questions in heavy-ion physics. Recent experimental and theoretical work (LHC, RHIC BES) continues to investigate flow-like signals in pp and pA collisions and the energy/system-size dependence of QGP signatures, without a consensus on a single identifiable onset; many results are consistent with a gradual emergence rather than a sharp threshold.

paper_title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics
original_question: What are the relevant microscopic degrees of freedom in the strongly interacting quark-gluon plasma if they are not quasi-free quarks and gluons, and how can precision measurements of macroscopic properties and transport coefficients identify them?
self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions a strongly interacting deconfined state of QCD matter — the quark–gluon plasma (QGP) — is produced at temperatures above the QCD pseudocritical temperature T_c ≈ 155 MeV. Phenomenology shows that the QGP behaves as a near-perfect fluid with very small specific shear viscosity η/s, and a variety of macroscopic properties and transport coefficients have been measured or inferred, including the equation of state p(ε), the speed of sound c_S, the shear and bulk viscosities η/s and ζ/s, the heavy-quark spatial diffusion coefficient D_s, the jet transport parameter q̂, and the parton energy-loss coefficient ê. There is also evidence for deconfinement (J/ψ regeneration, sequential Υ suppression) and indirect signs of chiral symmetry restoration (ρ-meson modification, strangeness enhancement). These observations are inconsistent with a description in terms of quasi-free quarks and gluons.

Problem. Identify the relevant microscopic degrees of freedom of the strongly coupled QGP at temperatures in the regime roughly T_c ≲ T ≲ a few × T_c. Concretely:

(a) Propose a set of effective constituents (e.g., dressed quasiparticles, hadron-like bound states, semi-classical color fields, holographic/AdS-CFT-inspired excitations, or other) and a corresponding effective theory or kinetic/transport framework that simultaneously reproduces the measured equation of state and speed of sound (including lattice-QCD results), the small η/s near the KSS bound 1/(4π), the bulk viscosity ζ/s peak near T_c, and the heavy-quark and jet transport coefficients D_s, q̂, ê.

(b) Determine which combinations of precision measurements of these macroscopic properties and transport coefficients can discriminate between competing candidate sets of degrees of freedom, and exhibit observables (with quantitative predictions) whose values uniquely fix the microscopic content of the medium.
status_search_result: The identification of the microscopic degrees of freedom of the strongly coupled quark–gluon plasma remains a central open question in high-energy nuclear physics. Subsequent reviews and white papers (e.g., the long-range plans for nuclear physics and EIC/sPHENIX/LHC heavy-ion programs) continue to list this as a key unresolved issue, with no consensus identification of the constituents.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Does ρ has other discontinuity? What are they? Is ρ piece-wise constant?
self_contained_problem:
For a real number α > 1 and a finite word w over the alphabet {0,1}, say that w contains an α-power if there exist a nonempty word x and a prefix y of x such that w has a factor equal to x^k y (for some integer k ≥ 1) with (k|x| + |y|)/|x| = α. A binary word is α-power-free if it contains no β-power with β ≥ α (in the standard "≥-power-free" convention used for fractional exponents). Let L_α ⊆ {0,1}* denote the language of all finite α-power-free binary words, and let s_α(n) = |L_α ∩ {0,1}^n|. Define the binary power-free growth function

  ρ(α) = lim sup_{n → ∞} s_α(n)^{1/n},   for α > 1.

It is known that ρ is non-decreasing, that ρ(α) = 0 for α ≤ 2 (apart from finitely many words there are no binary square-free words), and that ρ is discontinuous at α = 2 (the value jumps to a positive number for α slightly greater than 2). 

(a) Determine whether ρ has any discontinuities other than the one at α = 2, and if so locate and describe all such points of discontinuity.

(b) Determine whether the function ρ : (1, ∞) → [0, 2] is piecewise constant, i.e. whether there exists a (possibly infinite) partition of (1, ∞) into intervals on each of which ρ is constant.
status_search_result: Searches turned up related work by Shur and others on growth rates of power-free languages, including a 2025 proof of Shur's large-alphabet conjecture and recent work on low-complexity binary words avoiding (5/2)+-powers, but no source explicitly resolves whether the binary power-free growth function ρ has discontinuities other than at α = 2 or whether it is piecewise constant. The status appears unresolved in publicly available literature.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Kirby Baker, Georges Mac Nulty and Walter Taylor have shown that the pattern abXbcY caZbaT ac is 4-avoidable, but not 3-avoidable [7]. What is the minimal proportion of the fourth letter needed to avoid that pattern?
self_contained_problem:
An infinite word $w$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$ is said to avoid a pattern $p$ (a word over a separate alphabet of variables) if there is no nonerasing morphism $h$ from the variable alphabet to $\Sigma^+$ such that $h(p)$ occurs as a factor of $w$. A pattern is called $k$-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over a $k$-letter alphabet that avoids it.

Consider the pattern
$$P = abXbcYcaZbaTac,$$
where $a,b,c$ are pattern variables and $X,Y,Z,T$ are pattern variables (each variable to be replaced by a nonempty word). It is known that $P$ is $4$-avoidable but not $3$-avoidable.

For an infinite word $w$ over a $4$-letter alphabet $\{1,2,3,4\}$ that avoids $P$, define the proportion of the letter $4$ in $w$ as
$$\rho_4(w) = \liminf_{n\to\infty} \frac{|w[1..n]|_4}{n},$$
where $|u|_4$ denotes the number of occurrences of the letter $4$ in $u$.

Determine
$$\inf\{\rho_4(w) : w \text{ is an infinite word over } \{1,2,3,4\} \text{ avoiding } P\}.$$
That is, find the minimal proportion of the fourth letter needed to avoid the pattern $abXbcYcaZbaTac$.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Given a pattern p, what is the complexity of deciding whether p is avoidable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $E$ be a (disjoint) finite alphabet of variables. A pattern is a nonempty word $p \in E^+$. Given a pattern $p$ and a word $w \in A^*$, we say that $w$ encounters $p$ if there is a non-erasing morphism $h : E^+ \to A^+$ such that $h(p)$ is a factor (contiguous subword) of $w$; otherwise $w$ avoids $p$. The pattern $p$ is said to be avoidable if there exist a finite alphabet $A$ and an infinite word over $A$ all of whose finite factors avoid $p$ (equivalently, infinitely many finite words over some finite alphabet avoid $p$).

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem:
  Input: a pattern $p \in E^+$.
  Question: is $p$ avoidable?

In particular, decide whether this problem is decidable, and if so locate it in the standard complexity hierarchy (e.g. P, NP, PSPACE, etc.) by establishing matching upper and lower bounds.
status_search_result: The avoidability of patterns is known to be decidable (via the Bean–Ehrenfeucht–McNulty / Zimin reduction characterization of unavoidable patterns), and the related problem of deciding whether a pattern is unavoidable has been shown to be NP-complete (Rampersad–Shallit and follow-up work; cf. "The Complexity of Unavoidable Word Patterns", Theory of Computing Systems, 2022). However, the precise complexity of the avoidability decision problem itself does not appear to be fully pinned down with matching bounds in the surveyed literature, so the question as posed remains open.

original_question: Is aabaacbaab 3-D0L-avoidable (i.e. is there a ternary morphism g such that g ω (a) avoids aabaacbaab)?

A word $w \in \Sigma^*$ is a factor of a word $u$ (finite or infinite) if $u$ can be written as $u = x w y$ for some words $x, y$. 

A pattern over a set of variables $V$ is a non-empty word $p \in V^*$. An occurrence of $p$ in a word $u \in \Sigma^* \cup \Sigma^\omega$ is a non-erasing morphism $h \colon V^* \to \Sigma^*$ such that $h(p)$ is a factor of $u$. The word $u$ avoids $p$ if there is no occurrence of $p$ in $u$.

A morphism $g \colon \Sigma^* \to \Sigma^*$ is prolongable on a letter $a \in \Sigma$ if $g(a) = a w$ for some non-empty word $w$ such that $g^n(w) \neq \varepsilon$ for all $n \geq 0$; in this case the iterates $g^n(a)$ form a sequence of prefixes converging to a unique infinite word $g^\omega(a) \in \Sigma^\omega$.

self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and let E be an alphabet of variables, disjoint from A. A pattern is a nonempty word p ∈ E*. paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: The number of k-power-free binary words of length n grows polynomially with n for k ≤ 7/3, but exponentially for k > 7/3 [24]. Examine analogous results for alphabets of arbitrary size.
self_contained_problem:
Let Σ_q denote a finite alphabet of size q ≥ 2, and let Σ_q^* be the set of all finite words over Σ_q. For a real number k > 1, a word w = w_1 w_2 ... w_n ∈ Σ_q^* is said to contain a k-power if there exist indices i and a positive integer p with i + ⌈kp⌉ - 1 ≤ n such that w_{j+p} = w_j for all 0 ≤ j ≤ ⌈kp⌉ - 1 - p; equivalently, w contains a factor of the form x^k = x x x ... where x has length p and the factor has length ⌈kp⌉. A word is k-power-free if it contains no k-power, and is k^+-power-free if it contains no k'-power for any k' > k. Let L_q(k) ⊆ Σ_q^* denote the language of k-power-free words over Σ_q, and let f_{q,k}(n) = |L_q(k) ∩ Σ_q^n| be the number of such words of length n.

It is known that for q = 2, the function f_{2,k}(n) grows polynomially in n when k ≤ 7/3, but grows exponentially in n when k > 7/3. 

Determine, for every alphabet size q ≥ 3, the threshold value k_q ∈ ℝ (and the behaviour at the threshold, distinguishing k-power-free from k^+-power-free) such that f_{q,k}(n) grows polynomially in n for k ≤ k_q and exponentially in n for k > k_q. In particular, establish whether the analogue of the binary dichotomy holds for arbitrary q, identify the critical exponent k_q, and describe the asymptotic behaviour of the exponential growth rate

   α(q, k) = lim_{n → ∞} f_{q,k}(n)^{1/n}

as q → ∞ for fixed k > 1, and as k decreases to k_q for fixed q.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made. Shur and collaborators studied growth rates of power-free languages over arbitrary alphabets, identifying the critical exponent and proving asymptotic formulas for α(q,k) when k ≥ 2. A 2025 result (MFCS 2025) proves Shur's conjecture on the growth of (n/(n-1))-free and (n/(n-1))^+-free languages over q-letter alphabets up to a correction of order O(1/q²). Threshold-word growth on n letters is also known to be exponential. However, a complete dichotomy theorem characterizing the polynomial-vs-exponential threshold for every alphabet size, analogous to the 7/3 result for q=2, is not fully resolved in general.

original_question: Let Σ be an alphabet and let w ∈ Σ∗ a p-free word. Then w is a factor of a maximal p-free word over Σ.
self_contained_problem:

original_question: Let Σ be an alphabet, k ∈ [1, 2], and w ∈ Σ∗ be a k-power-free word. Then in any case, w is a factor of a maximal k-power-free word over Σ.
self_contained_problem:
Let Σ be a finite alphabet and let Σ* denote the free monoid of finite words over Σ. For a real number k ≥ 1, a finite word u ∈ Σ* is called a k-power if it can be written as u = v^⌊k⌋ v', where v ∈ Σ* is nonempty, v' is a prefix of v, and |u| / |v| ≥ k. A word w ∈ Σ* is k-power-free if no factor (contiguous subword) of w is a k-power. A k-power-free word w ∈ Σ* is said to be maximal if no word obtained by appending a letter on the left or on the right of w is k-power-free; equivalently, w is maximal if it cannot be extended (on either side) to a strictly longer k-power-free word over Σ.

status_search_result: The statement is a form of the Restivo–Salemi extendability property for α-power-free languages. It has been established in several cases (notably for binary alphabets and for α ≥ 5 with k ≥ 3 letters in subsequent work), but a full proof for all alphabets and all exponents in [1,2] does not appear in the literature, so the conjecture remains only partially resolved.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Does a given word generate a finite or infinite subtree?
self_contained_problem:
Fix a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ and a real number $\beta>1$ (or a rational exponent). A word is called $\beta$-power-free if it contains no factor of the form $u^k v$ with $|u^k v|/|u|\ge \beta$ and $v$ a prefix of $u$ (equivalently, no factor that is a $\beta$-power). Let $L\subseteq \Sigma^*$ denote the language of all $\beta$-power-free words over $\Sigma$. Order $L$ by the prefix relation: $u\preceq v$ iff $u$ is a prefix of $v$. The Hasse diagram of $(L,\preceq)$ is a rooted tree $T_L$ (the prefix tree of $L$), whose vertex set is $L$, whose root is the empty word, and where the children of a node $w\in L$ are the words $wa$ ($a\in\Sigma$) that lie in $L$. For $w\in L$, let $T_L(w)$ denote the subtree of $T_L$ rooted at $w$, that is, the set of all words in $L$ having $w$ as a prefix.

Problem. Give an algorithm that, on input a word $w\in L$, decides whether the subtree $T_L(w)$ is finite or infinite. Equivalently, decide whether $w$ can be extended to arbitrarily long words in $L$ (and thus to an infinite $\beta$-power-free word).
status_search_result: A compilation of WORDS-conference open problems lists this question (attributed to Petrova and Shur, WORDS 2011) and notes it is decidable in some particular power-free language cases, but a general resolution does not appear in the search results. No definitive recent solution was found.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Which square-free words u can be shuffled to obtain a square-free word u ▷β u?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. A word $w \in \Sigma^*$ is called a square if $w = xx$ for some nonempty $x \in \Sigma^*$, and $w$ is square-free if no factor (contiguous subword) of $w$ is a square.

Given two words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$, the shuffle set $u \shuffle v$ is the set of all words obtained by interleaving $u$ and $v$ while preserving the relative order of the letters within each: formally, $w \in u \shuffle v$ iff $w = u_1 v_1 u_2 v_2 \cdots u_k v_k$ for some factorizations $u = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$ and $v = v_1 v_2 \cdots v_k$ (where the $u_i, v_i$ may be empty).

Characterize the square-free words $u \in \Sigma^*$ for which there exists at least one square-free word in $u \shuffle u$ (i.e., $u$ can be shuffled with itself to produce a square-free word).
status_search_result: Partial results are known. Currie (2013/2015, "Square-Free Shuffles of Words") showed that for every n ≥ 3 there exists a square-free ternary word u of length n such that u⧢u contains a square-free word, and that there are infinite square-free ternary words u such that u⧢u contains an infinite square-free word. Harju and others studied infinite self-shuffling square-free words. However, a complete characterization of which square-free words u admit a square-free shuffle u⧢u does not appear to have been given, so the underlying classification problem remains open.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Which words w can be obtained in more than one way from a single word u using different conducting sequences?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the set of finite words over $A$. For a word $u=u_1u_2\cdots u_n\in A^*$ of length $n$, a *conducting sequence* is a word $c=c_1c_2\cdots c_{2n}\in\{1,2\}^{2n}$ in which the symbol $1$ occurs exactly $n$ times and the symbol $2$ occurs exactly $n$ times. Given $u$ and a conducting sequence $c$, define the *shuffle of $u$ with itself directed by $c$* to be the word $w=w_1w_2\cdots w_{2n}\in A^{2n}$ obtained as follows: scan $c$ from left to right; the $k$-th occurrence of the symbol $1$ in $c$ contributes $u_k$ to $w$ at that position, and the $k$-th occurrence of the symbol $2$ in $c$ also contributes $u_k$ to $w$ at that position. Equivalently, $w$ is an interleaving of two copies of $u$ in which $c$ records which copy each letter of $w$ comes from.

Characterize all words $w\in A^{2n}$ for which there exists a single word $u\in A^n$ and two distinct conducting sequences $c\neq c'$ in $\{1,2\}^{2n}$ such that the shuffle of $u$ with itself directed by $c$ and the shuffle of $u$ with itself directed by $c'$ both equal $w$. That is, describe precisely those words $w$ that can be obtained as a self-shuffle of some single word $u$ in more than one way via different conducting sequences.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Does there exist an infinite square-free word w such that w = w ▷β w for some infinite β?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^\omega$ denote the set of (right-)infinite words over $\Sigma$. An infinite word $w \in \Sigma^\omega$ is called square-free if there is no nonempty finite word $u$ such that $uu$ occurs as a factor (contiguous block) of $w$.

Given two infinite words $u, v \in \Sigma^\omega$ and an infinite binary word $\beta \in \{0,1\}^\omega$ in which both letters $0$ and $1$ occur infinitely often, the shuffle of $u$ and $v$ directed by $\beta$, denoted $u \triangleright_\beta v$, is the unique infinite word obtained by reading, for $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$, the next unread letter of $u$ when the $n$-th letter of $\beta$ is $0$, and the next unread letter of $v$ when the $n$-th letter of $\beta$ is $1$.

An infinite word $w$ is said to be self-shuffling if there exists an infinite binary word $\beta$ (with both $0$ and $1$ appearing infinitely often) such that
$$w \;=\; w \triangleright_\beta w.$$

Question: Does there exist an infinite word $w$ over some finite alphabet which is simultaneously square-free and self-shuffling?

The result also appeared in The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 22(1) #P55 (2015).

original_question: We have FRT(4) = RT (4) = 7/5. Advances in problem solving The conjecture was solved by Golnaz Badkobeh, Maxime Crochemore and Michaël Rao. In addition they proved that FRT(k) = RT (k) for k ≤ 6 (private communication at WORDS 2015).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite alphabet $A$ of size $k\ge 2$ and a finite or infinite word $w$ over $A$, the exponent of a nonempty factor $u$ of $w$ is $|u|/p$, where $p$ is the smallest period of $u$. The critical exponent of $w$ is the supremum of the exponents of its finite factors. The repetition threshold $\mathrm{RT}(k)$ is the infimum, over all infinite words $w$ over a $k$-letter alphabet, of the critical exponent of $w$ (its values were determined by Dejean's conjecture, now a theorem). The finite repetition threshold $\mathrm{FRT}(k)$ is the smallest rational number $r$ such that there exists an infinite word $w$ over a $k$-letter alphabet whose finite factors all have exponent at most $r$ and which contains only finitely many factors of exponent exactly $\mathrm{RT}(k)$.

Prove or disprove the following: for the four-letter alphabet,
$$\mathrm{FRT}(4)=\mathrm{RT}(4)=\tfrac{7}{5},$$
and, more generally, $\mathrm{FRT}(k)=\mathrm{RT}(k)$ for every alphabet size $k$ (in particular for all $k\le 6$).
status_search_result: Badkobeh, Crochemore and Rao established FRT(4) = RT(4) = 7/5 and, more broadly, proved FRT(k) = RT(k) for all sufficiently large k (specifically for 5 ≤ k ≤ 11 and for k ≥ 6 in their RAIRO 2014 paper "Finite repetition threshold for large alphabets"), with additional cases k ≤ 6 reported at WORDS 2015. The conjecture is therefore considered solved.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: What is the minimum exponent of a repetion which is avoidable by an infinite word constructed by iterated (prefix)-suffix duplication?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $w \in \Sigma^*$ be a finite word. A (prefix-)suffix duplication step applied to $w$ produces a new word $w \cdot u$, where $u$ is either a prefix or a suffix of $w$. Starting from a single letter $a \in \Sigma$ and iterating such duplication steps, one obtains finite words; an infinite word $\mathbf{w} \in \Sigma^{\omega}$ is said to be generated by iterated (prefix-)suffix duplication if it is the limit of an infinite chain of finite words obtained by repeatedly applying these steps.

For a real number $\alpha > 1$, an infinite word $\mathbf{w}$ avoids $\alpha$-powers (or $\alpha^+$-powers) if no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is a repetition of exponent $\geq \alpha$ (resp. $> \alpha$), where the exponent of a nonempty word $u$ is $|u|/p$ with $p$ the smallest period of $u$.

Determine the infimum
$$\alpha^* = \inf\{\alpha : \text{there exists a finite alphabet } \Sigma \text{ and an infinite word } \mathbf{w} \in \Sigma^{\omega} \text{ obtained by iterated (prefix-)suffix duplication that avoids } \alpha\text{-powers}\}.$$

In other words, what is the smallest exponent of repetition that can be avoided by some infinite word constructed by iterated (prefix-)suffix duplication?
status_search_result: Searches show related work on prefix-suffix duplication and prefix-suffix square completion, where it is known that infinite words generated by such operations can avoid repetitions of exponent greater than 2, but no source clearly establishes the minimum (infimum) exponent attainable specifically for iterated (prefix-)suffix duplication. The status appears to remain open or at least not definitively settled in the accessible literature.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Does the language of finite words constructed, starting with a single word, by iterating prefix-suffix square completion remains semi-linear?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$. For a word $w \in \Sigma^*$, define the prefix-suffix square completion relation $\Rightarrow$ as follows: $w \Rightarrow w'$ if either
(i) (suffix square completion) $w' = wx$ for some nonempty $x \in \Sigma^*$ such that $w$ has a suffix of the form $yxy$ for some $y \in \Sigma^*$ with $|x|=|y|$ pattern $yxy$ being a factor with $w$ ending in $yxy$, equivalently $w$ ends in $yx$ and the concatenation $yxyx = (yx)^2$ is a square appended (precisely: $w = uyxy$ and $w' = uyxyx$, so the new word ends with the square $(yx)^2$); or
(ii) (prefix square completion) $w' = xw$, where $w$ begins with $yxy$ and analogously prepending produces a square $(xy)^2$ as a prefix.

Let $\Rightarrow^*$ denote the reflexive transitive closure of $\Rightarrow$. For a word $w_0 \in \Sigma^*$, let
$$L(w_0) = \{ w \in \Sigma^* : w_0 \Rightarrow^* w \}$$
be the language of all words obtainable from $w_0$ by iterated prefix-suffix square completion.

Recall that a language $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ is called semi-linear if its Parikh image $\{(|w|_a)_{a \in \Sigma} : w \in L\} \subseteq \mathbb{N}^{|\Sigma|}$ is a semi-linear subset of $\mathbb{N}^{|\Sigma|}$ (i.e., a finite union of sets of the form $\{v_0 + n_1 v_1 + \cdots + n_k v_k : n_i \in \mathbb{N}\}$).

Question: Is $L(w_0)$ semi-linear for every alphabet $\Sigma$ and every starting word $w_0 \in \Sigma^*$?
status_search_result: A web search reveals related work on prefix-suffix square completion and on the prefix-suffix duplication operation (where iterated duplication languages are known to be semi-linear), but no source directly resolving whether languages obtained by iterated prefix-suffix square completion from a single starting word are semi-linear was found. The status of this specific question is therefore unclear from the available evidence.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Show that the number of abelian cube-free ternary words grows exponentially with length. Given a n-letter alphabet, define the sequence Zn recursively by Z1 = 1, Zn = Zn1 nZn1 , n > 1.
self_contained_problem:
A finite word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_m$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$ is called an *abelian cube* if it can be written as a concatenation $w = uvx$ of three non-empty factors $u, v, x$ of equal length such that $v$ and $x$ are each permutations of $u$ (equivalently, $u$, $v$, and $x$ have identical Parikh vectors, i.e., for every letter $a \in \Sigma$ the number of occurrences of $a$ in $u$, in $v$, and in $x$ are equal). A word is called *abelian cube-free* if none of its factors (contiguous subwords) is an abelian cube. Let $a(n)$ denote the number of abelian cube-free words of length $n$ over the ternary alphabet $\Sigma = \{1,2,3\}$.

Prove that $a(n)$ grows exponentially in $n$; that is, show that there exist constants $C > 0$ and $r > 1$ such that $a(n) \geq C \cdot r^n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

(Auxiliary construction available for use: for each $n \geq 1$, define a sequence $Z_n$ of words over the alphabet $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ recursively by $Z_1 = 1$ and $Z_n = Z_{n-1}\, n\, Z_{n-1}$ for $n > 1$.)
category_tag: Combinatorics on words / abelian pattern avoidance
status_search_result: The problem of showing that the number of abelian cube-free ternary words grows exponentially in length was solved by Carpi (1998) and given a different proof by Aberkane and Currie ("The Number of Ternary Words Avoiding Abelian Cubes Grows Exponentially," Journal of Integer Sequences, 2004), which establishes a lower bound of order $r^n$ with $r = 2^{1/24}$. Subsequent work has improved the lower bound on the growth rate (e.g., to $31/19 \approx 1.0595$).

original_question: Given pattern p and integer n, what is the complexity of deciding whether Zn encounters p in the abelian sense? Define the abelian repetitive threshold function and the dual abelian repetitive threshold function on (1, 2] by: ART(n) = inf{s : y s is avoidable on n letters in the abelian sense} DART(r) = min{n ∈ IN : y r is avoidable in the abelian sense on n letter}.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let A be a finite alphabet. Two finite words u, v over A are abelian equivalent if v is a permutation of u, i.e. each letter of A occurs the same number of times in u and v. For a real number s > 1 with s = k + f where k is a positive integer and 0 ≤ f < 1, an abelian s-power is a word of the form x_1 x_2 … x_k y, where x_1, …, x_k are pairwise abelian equivalent nonempty words of the same length |x_i| = m, and y is an abelian-equivalent prefix-style factor of length ⌊f·m⌋ that is abelian equivalent to a prefix of x_1 of that length. A word w is said to encounter an abelian s-power if some factor of w is an abelian s-power; otherwise w avoids abelian s-powers. More generally, given a pattern p (a word over a set of variables), a word w over A encounters p in the abelian sense if there is a non-erasing morphism h, with the convention that the images of equal variables are abelian equivalent (rather than equal), such that h(p) is a factor of w; otherwise w avoids p in the abelian sense.

Let Z_n denote the set of all infinite words over an n-letter alphabet, and say that Z_n encounters p in the abelian sense if every infinite word over n letters encounters p in the abelian sense.

Define on the interval (1, 2] the abelian repetitive threshold function
  ART(n) = inf { s ∈ (1, 2] : abelian s-powers are avoidable over an n-letter alphabet by some infinite word },
and the dual abelian repetitive threshold function
  DART(r) = min { n ∈ ℕ : abelian r-powers are avoidable over an n-letter alphabet by some infinite word }.

Problems.
(a) Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem: given a pattern p and a positive integer n, decide whether Z_n encounters p in the abelian sense.
(b) Determine the values of ART(n) for every integer n ≥ 2, and determine the values of DART(r) for every r ∈ (1, 2].
status_search_result: The abelian repetition threshold problem remains an active open area: only partial values are known (e.g., bounds on the abelian repetition threshold for small alphabets), and the general values of ART(n) and DART(r), as well as the complexity of deciding abelian encounter of a pattern over an n-letter alphabet, do not appear to be settled. Surveys and follow-up works continue to list these as open.

original_question: How many k-abelian equivalence classes of words of a given length contain an nth power?
self_contained_problem:
Fix integers k ≥ 1 and an alphabet Σ. For two finite words u, v ∈ Σ*, say that u and v are k-abelian equivalent, written u ∼_k v, if for every word w with |w| ≤ k the number of occurrences of w as a factor of u equals the number of occurrences of w as a factor of v. This is an equivalence relation on Σ*, and it preserves length. For an integer n ≥ 2, an n-th power is a word of the form w^n = ww···w (n copies of some word w ∈ Σ*).

Given integers k ≥ 1, n ≥ 2, an alphabet Σ, and a length N ≥ 1, determine the number of k-abelian equivalence classes of words in Σ^N that contain at least one n-th power; that is, compute (or give a closed-form / asymptotic expression for)
   f_{k,n,|Σ|}(N) := #{ [u]_{∼_k} : u ∈ Σ^N and there exists v ∈ [u]_{∼_k} such that v is an n-th power }.

The question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is there a pure morphic binary word avoiding 2-abelian cubes?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$ be the binary alphabet, and let $\Sigma^*$ (resp. $\Sigma^\omega$) denote the set of finite (resp. one-sided infinite) words over $\Sigma$. For a word $w\in\Sigma^*$ and a positive integer $k$, let $|w|_u$ denote the number of occurrences of the factor $u\in\Sigma^*$ in $w$. Two finite words $u,v$ are said to be $k$-abelian equivalent, written $u\sim_k v$, if $|u|_x=|v|_x$ for every $x\in\Sigma^*$ with $|x|\le k$. (Equivalently, $u\sim_k v$ iff $u$ and $v$ have the same prefix and suffix of length $k-1$ and the same multiset of factors of length $k$.) A $2$-abelian cube is a nonempty word of the form $w_1w_2w_3$ with $w_1\sim_2 w_2\sim_2 w_3$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w}\in\Sigma^\omega$ avoids $2$-abelian cubes if no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is a $2$-abelian cube.

A morphism is a map $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ satisfying $h(xy)=h(x)h(y)$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w}\in\Sigma^\omega$ is called pure morphic if there exist a morphism $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ and a letter $a\in\Sigma$ with $h(a)=ax$ for some nonempty $x\in\Sigma^*$ such that $\mathbf{w}=\lim_{n\to\infty} h^n(a)$, the fixed point of $h$ starting with $a$.

Question: Does there exist a pure morphic infinite word $\mathbf{w}\in\Sigma^\omega$ that avoids $2$-abelian cubes?
status_search_result: It is known that 2-abelian cubes are avoidable on a binary alphabet (proved via constructions including morphic images), and that 3-abelian cubes are avoidable on binary alphabets. However, whether such an infinite binary word avoiding 2-abelian cubes can be obtained as a pure morphic word (a fixed point of a single iterated morphism, not merely a morphic image) does not appear to have been resolved in the literature; results on related k-abelian square-freeness suggest pure morphic constructions are often insufficient. Status appears to remain open/unknown.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is there a natural integer p such that 2-abelian-squares of period at least p can be avoided over a binary alphabet?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$ be the binary alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. For a word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n \in \Sigma^*$ and an integer $k \geq 1$, the $k$-abelian equivalence relation $\sim_k$ on $\Sigma^*$ is defined by: $u \sim_k v$ if and only if, for every word $x \in \Sigma^*$ with $|x| \leq k$, the number of occurrences of $x$ as a (contiguous) factor of $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $x$ as a factor of $v$ (in particular, $|u| = |v|$). 

A non-empty word $w$ is called a $k$-abelian square if $w = uv$ with $|u| = |v|$ and $u \sim_k v$. The period of such a $k$-abelian square $w = uv$ is the integer $|u|$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w} \in \Sigma^{\mathbb{N}}$ is said to avoid $2$-abelian squares of period at least $p$ if no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is a $2$-abelian square whose period is $\geq p$.

Question: Does there exist a positive integer $p$ such that there exists an infinite binary word $\mathbf{w} \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ avoiding all $2$-abelian squares of period at least $p$?
status_search_result: The question of whether 2-abelian squares of period at least some integer p can be avoided over a binary alphabet appears in the literature on avoidability of long k-abelian repetitions and is repeatedly cited as an open problem. While related results are known (e.g., 3-abelian cubes and 5-abelian cubes are avoidable on binary alphabets), no construction or impossibility proof for the binary 2-abelian-square version with bounded period appears to have been published.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Are there infinite additive-cube-free words on the following alphabets: {0, 1, 2, 3}, {0, 1, 4} and {0, 2, 5}?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite subset of the integers. A finite word w = a_1 a_2 ... a_n with letters in A is called an additive cube if it can be partitioned into three consecutive nonempty blocks of equal length whose letter-sums coincide; that is, there exist indices 0 = i_0 < i_1 < i_2 < i_3 = n with i_1 - i_0 = i_2 - i_1 = i_3 - i_2 such that
  sum_{j=i_0+1}^{i_1} a_j = sum_{j=i_1+1}^{i_2} a_j = sum_{j=i_2+1}^{i_3} a_j.
An infinite word over A is called additive-cube-free if none of its finite factors is an additive cube.

Determine, for each of the following alphabets A, whether there exists an infinite additive-cube-free word over A:
(a) A = {0, 1, 2, 3};
(b) A = {0, 1, 4};
(c) A = {0, 2, 5}.

original_question: Can we avoid long abelian cubes over two letters?

original_question: Find good heuristics to compute candidates for question 1.6.15.5.

Background. A finite word u over an alphabet A is called an abelian cube if it can be written as a concatenation u = u_1 u_2 u_3 of three nonempty factors that are pairwise permutations of each other (equivalently, the three factors have the same Parikh vector). original_question: What is the minimal k such that one can avoid abelian squares of period at least k over three letters (2 < k < 6)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma_3 = \{0,1,2\}$ be a three-letter alphabet. A finite word $w \in \Sigma_3^*$ is called an abelian square if $w = uv$ where $|u| = |v|$ and $v$ is a permutation of the letters of $u$ (i.e., $u$ and $v$ have the same Parikh vector). The integer $|u|$ is called the period of the abelian square $uv$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w} \in \Sigma_3^{\mathbb{N}}$ is said to avoid abelian squares of period at least $k$ if no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is an abelian square $uv$ with $|u| \geq k$.

It is known that there is no infinite word over $\Sigma_3$ that avoids all abelian squares (i.e., the case $k=1$ is impossible), while for sufficiently large $k$ such infinite words exist (in particular, for $k \geq 6$). 

Determine the minimal integer $k$ with $2 < k < 6$ (that is, $k \in \{3,4,5\}$) such that there exists an infinite word over the three-letter alphabet $\Sigma_3$ avoiding every abelian square of period at least $k$.

However, no source explicitly identifies the exact minimal $k \in \{3,4,5\}$ for which abelian squares of period at least $k$ can be avoided over three letters. original_question: Is there a morphism over 5 letters with two eigenvalues of norm smaller than 1 and an abelian-square-free fixed point?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be an alphabet of 5 letters and let $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ be a morphism. The incidence (or frequency) matrix of $h$ is the $5\times 5$ integer matrix $M_h$ whose $(a,b)$-entry equals the number of occurrences of the letter $a$ in $h(b)$. A right-infinite word $\mathbf{w}\in\Sigma^\omega$ is called a fixed point of $h$ if there exists a letter $a\in\Sigma$ with $h(a)=au$ for some $u\in\Sigma^+$ and $\mathbf{w}=\lim_{n\to\infty}h^n(a)$. Two finite words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$ are called abelian equivalent if, for every letter $c\in\Sigma$, the number of occurrences of $c$ in $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $c$ in $v$. A finite word is an abelian square if it can be written as $uv$ with $u,v$ abelian equivalent and $|u|=|v|\ge 1$. A word $\mathbf{w}$ (finite or infinite) is abelian-square-free if no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is an abelian square.

Question: Does there exist a morphism $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ over a 5-letter alphabet $\Sigma$ such that the incidence matrix $M_h$ has at least two eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity) of complex modulus strictly less than $1$, and such that $h$ admits an abelian-square-free infinite fixed point?

original_question: How to decide if eigenvalues of norm 1 may be allowed in the result stated just above? 2. Complexity issues In the literature, with a word several notions of complexity can be associated, the most famous one being certainly the factor complexity: given a word w, this complexity measures the number pw (n) of different factors of length n occuring in w. The famous characterization of Morse-Hedlund for ultimately periodic words led to introduce the infinite Surmian words whose complexity is pw (n) = n + 1, the best known example of them being certainly the famous Fibonacci word.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $h:A^*\to A^*$ be a morphism. The incidence matrix of $h$ is the $|A|\times|A|$ matrix $M_h$ whose entry $(M_h)_{a,b}$ counts the number of occurrences of the letter $a$ in the image $h(b)$. The morphism $h$ is called primitive if some power $M_h^k$ has all entries strictly positive. For a letter $a\in A$ such that $h(a)$ begins with $a$ and $|h^n(a)|\to\infty$, write $h^{\omega}(a)$ for the (right) infinite fixed point of $h$ obtained as the limit of $h^n(a)$.

Two finite words $u,v\in A^*$ are called abelian-equivalent, written $u\sim_{\mathrm{ab}} v$, if for every letter $c\in A$ the number of occurrences of $c$ in $u$ equals that in $v$. A template over $A$ is a tuple $t=(p,e,v_0,\dots,v_k)$ where $p,e\in A^*$ and each $v_i\in\mathbb{Z}^{|A|}$; a finite word $w$ is said to realize the template $t$ if $w$ admits a factorization $w = p\, u_1\, u_2\cdots u_k\, e$ such that for each $i$, the Parikh vector of $u_{i+1}$ minus the Parikh vector of $u_i$ equals $v_i$ (so that templates uniformly encode the standard notions of abelian $k$-th powers and their generalizations). One says that $h^{\omega}(a)$ realizes the template $t$ if some factor of $h^{\omega}(a)$ realizes $t$.

It is known that there is an algorithm which, given a primitive morphism $h$ whose incidence matrix $M_h$ has no eigenvalue of (complex) absolute value equal to $1$, a letter $a$ as above, and any template $t$, decides whether $h^{\omega}(a)$ realizes $t$.

Problem. Determine whether this decidability result extends to the case where $M_h$ is allowed to have eigenvalues of absolute value $1$: that is, give an algorithm which, on input an arbitrary primitive morphism $h$ (with no restriction on the spectrum of $M_h$), an admissible letter $a$, and a template $t$, decides whether $h^{\omega}(a)$ realizes $t$, or else show that no such algorithm exists.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Draw a study of the recurrence quotients for other families of infinite word that sturmian words, such as words of complexity 2n + 1, or toinfinite words in general.
self_contained_problem:
Let $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ be an infinite word over a finite alphabet $A$. The factor complexity of $w$ is the function $p_w(n)$ counting the number of distinct factors (contiguous finite subwords) of $w$ of length $n$. The word $w$ is uniformly recurrent if for every $n$ there exists an integer $R_w(n)$ such that every factor of $w$ of length $R_w(n)$ contains every factor of $w$ of length $n$ as a factor; the smallest such integer defines the recurrence function $R_w(n)$. The recurrence quotient of $w$ is defined as
$$\rho(w) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{R_w(n)}{n}.$$

For Sturmian words (the aperiodic infinite words of factor complexity $p_w(n) = n + 1$), the recurrence quotient has been studied in detail and is closely related to the continued fraction expansion of the slope.

Carry out an analogous systematic study of the recurrence quotient $\rho(w)$ for other families of infinite words beyond Sturmian words. In particular:
(a) Determine $\rho(w)$, or its possible range of values, for infinite words of factor complexity $p_w(n) = 2n + 1$ (for instance Arnoux–Rauzy words on a three-letter alphabet, or more generally episturmian and ternary words of this complexity).
(b) More broadly, develop a theory of the recurrence quotient for arbitrary uniformly recurrent infinite words, identifying which values of $\rho(w)$ can be attained and how $\rho(w)$ relates to combinatorial parameters such as factor complexity, balance, and frequencies of letters.
status_search_result: Cassaigne and Chekhova explicitly computed the recurrence function for Arnoux–Rauzy sequences (which have factor complexity 2n+1), giving partial answers for that subfamily. However, a comprehensive theory of the recurrence quotient for all infinite words of complexity 2n+1 and for general (uniformly recurrent) infinite words has not been established, so the program described remains only partially addressed.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Give characterizations of Arnoux-Rauzy words with a given balance.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $A$ be a finite alphabet with $|A|\ge 2$. An infinite word $w\in A^{\mathbb N}$ is called an Arnoux–Rauzy word if, for every length $n\ge 0$, $w$ has exactly one left special factor and exactly one right special factor of length $n$, and each of these special factors can be extended (on the appropriate side) by every letter of $A$. (Equivalently, the factor complexity satisfies $p_w(n)=(|A|-1)n+1$ and the bispecial structure is the Arnoux–Rauzy one.)

For an integer $C\ge 1$, an infinite word $w$ over $A$ is said to be $C$-balanced if, for every letter $a\in A$ and for every pair of factors $u,v$ of $w$ with $|u|=|v|$, one has
$$\bigl||u|_a-|v|_a\bigr|\le C,$$
where $|x|_a$ denotes the number of occurrences of the letter $a$ in $x$. The word $w$ is called finitely balanced if it is $C$-balanced for some $C$.

Problem. Provide a characterization of those Arnoux–Rauzy words $w$ over $A$ that are $C$-balanced, for each fixed integer $C\ge 1$. More precisely, for a given $C$, describe in an effective way (for instance via a condition on the directive sequence of $w$) the set of all Arnoux–Rauzy words on $A$ which are $C$-balanced.
status_search_result: Partial results are known. Sufficient conditions for $C$-balancedness of Arnoux–Rauzy words have been obtained, and a characterization is available if one replaces $C$-balance with the stronger notion of strong $C$-balance. However, even the case of 2-balanced ternary Arnoux–Rauzy words is not fully solved: it is shown that the prefixes of directive sequences of such words do not form a rational language, ruling out a rational-language characterization. Thus the general problem of characterizing Arnoux–Rauzy words with a given balance remains only partially resolved.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Find efficient algorithms for the polynomial time solvable problems which were discussed in the paper.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the set of all finite words over $A$. Given a (possibly infinite, but recursively presented) set of words $F \subseteq A^*$, an $F$-factorization of a word $w \in A^*$ is a sequence of words $u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k \in F$ such that $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$. Several decision and enumeration problems are naturally associated with $F$-factorizations, for instance:

(i) Existence: given $w$, decide whether $w$ admits an $F$-factorization.
(ii) Counting: given $w$, compute the number of distinct $F$-factorizations of $w$.
(iii) Optimization: given $w$, find an $F$-factorization minimizing or maximizing the number of factors.
(iv) Uniqueness: decide whether every word over $A$ has at most one $F$-factorization (i.e., whether $F$ is a code).

For natural classes of sets $F$ (such as regular sets, sets defined by avoidance of a finite list of patterns, sets of bifix-free or unbordered words, sets of Lyndon words, etc.) several of the above problems are known to be solvable in polynomial time in $|w|$, but the exponents and constants of the known algorithms are often far from optimal.

Problem. For each of the $F$-factorization problems above that is known to be solvable in polynomial time, design an algorithm whose running time is as efficient as possible — ideally linear or quasi-linear in the length of the input word $w$ — and establish matching lower bounds in a suitable model of computation.
status_search_result: No specific resolution of this open-ended algorithmic question on F-factorizations of words was located. The problem is broad (asking for improved algorithms across several polynomial-time-solvable F-factorization problems), and progress on individual subproblems exists in the combinatorics-on-words literature, but no comprehensive solution was found.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: What is the complexity of the problem of determining whether a regular F -factorization possesses synchronization property if the parameters of the synchronization are not given ? What about this problem for context-free F -factorizations?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $F \subseteq \Sigma^*$ be a language. An $F$-factorization of a word $w \in \Sigma^*$ is a decomposition $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$ with each factor $u_i \in F$. A language $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ is said to admit an $F$-factorization if every $w \in L$ can be written as a concatenation of words from $F$.

Fix integers $m \geq 1$ and $d \geq 0$ (called synchronization parameters). An $F$-factorization $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$ of a word $w$ is said to have the $(m,d)$-synchronization property if, for every position $i \geq m$ in $w$, any two $F$-factorizations of $w$ agree on whether $i$ is a factor boundary, after looking at a window of length $d$ around $i$. More generally, an $F$-factorization scheme has the synchronization property if there exist parameters $(m,d)$ such that the above holds for all words admitting an $F$-factorization.

Question: Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem.
(a) Regular case: Given a regular language $F$ (specified, say, by a finite automaton or regular expression), decide whether the $F$-factorization possesses the synchronization property, where the parameters $(m,d)$ of the synchronization are not given as part of the input but are existentially quantified.
(b) Context-free case: The same decision problem when $F$ is given as a context-free language (e.g., by a context-free grammar).

original_question: Given a morphism f and a letter a such that a is the initial letter of f (a), is it decidable that f ω (a) is quasiperiodic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $A^*$ (resp. $A^\omega$) the set of finite (resp. one-sided infinite) words over $A$. A finite word $q \in A^+$ is said to be a quasiperiod of a (finite or infinite) word $w$ if every position of $w$ lies inside an occurrence of $q$ in $w$; that is, $w$ can be covered by (possibly overlapping) occurrences of $q$. An infinite word $w \in A^\omega$ is called quasiperiodic if it admits at least one quasiperiod.

A morphism is a map $f: A^* \to A^*$ extended to words by concatenation. A letter $a \in A$ is said to be prolongable for $f$ if $a$ is the first letter of $f(a)$ and $|f^n(a)| \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$; in this case the iteration produces a unique infinite fixed point
$$f^\omega(a) = \lim_{n \to \infty} f^n(a) \in A^\omega.$$

Question: Is there an algorithm which, given as input a finite alphabet $A$, a morphism $f: A^* \to A^*$, and a letter $a \in A$ that is the initial letter of $f(a)$ (with $f$ prolongable on $a$), decides whether the infinite word $f^\omega(a)$ is quasiperiodic?

However, no source explicitly announces a decision procedure for quasiperiodicity of an arbitrary morphic word $f^\omega(a)$, nor an undecidability result. The status therefore appears to remain unresolved based on accessible sources.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Let X be a finite set of words, and let w be a non-periodic bi-infinite word. Assume that w possesses k disjoint factorizations, with k ≤ |X|. Is it true that we have r(X) ≤ |X| − k + 1?.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X \subseteq \Sigma^+$ be a finite set of nonempty words over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$. The combinatorial rank $r(X)$ of $X$ is defined as
$$r(X) = \min\{\,|F| : F \subseteq \Sigma^+ \text{ and } X \subseteq F^*\,\}.$$
A bi-infinite word over $\Sigma$ is a sequence $w = \cdots a_{-1}a_0 a_1 \cdots \in \Sigma^{\mathbb{Z}}$, and $w$ is called non-periodic if there is no positive integer $p$ with $a_{i+p}=a_i$ for all $i\in\mathbb{Z}$. An $X$-factorization of $w$ is a factorization of $w$ as a bi-infinite concatenation of elements of $X$, i.e. an increasing bi-infinite sequence of integer cut points $(\ldots < c_{-1} < c_0 < c_1 < \ldots)$ such that for each $i$, the factor $a_{c_i}a_{c_i+1}\cdots a_{c_{i+1}-1}$ belongs to $X$. Two $X$-factorizations are called disjoint if their sets of cut points are disjoint.

Question: Suppose $X$ is a finite set of words and $w$ is a non-periodic bi-infinite word that admits $k$ pairwise disjoint $X$-factorizations, where $k \le |X|$. Is it always true that
$$r(X) \le |X| - k + 1\,?$$
status_search_result: The cumulative defect effect for bi-infinite words is known only in restricted cases (e.g. when X is a finite prefix set with 3 disjoint factorizations, giving rank ≤ |X|−2), and the two-element case has been studied separately. No source found establishes or refutes the general conjecture for arbitrary k disjoint factorizations, so its current status appears unresolved.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Denote by p(w) the smallest period of a word w ∈ Σ+ . Let X ⊆ Σ+ satisfying p(x) < p(w) for all x ∈ X. Is it true that w has at most |X| + 1 − r(X) disjoint X-factorizations?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^+$ the set of nonempty finite words over $\Sigma$. For a word $w \in \Sigma^+$, denote by $p(w)$ the smallest period of $w$, i.e., the least positive integer $p$ such that $w[i] = w[i+p]$ for all valid indices $i$.

For a finite set $X \subseteq \Sigma^+$, the (combinatorial) rank $r(X)$ is defined as the minimum cardinality of a set $Y \subseteq \Sigma^+$ such that $X \subseteq Y^*$, where $Y^*$ denotes the submonoid generated by $Y$.

An $X$-factorization of $w$ is a sequence $(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_k)$ with each $x_i \in X$ and $w = x_1 x_2 \cdots x_k$. Two $X$-factorizations $(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ and $(y_1,\ldots,y_\ell)$ of the same word $w$ are called disjoint if the sets of "cut positions" $\{|x_1\cdots x_i| : 1 \le i \le k-1\}$ and $\{|y_1\cdots y_j| : 1 \le j \le \ell-1\}$ are disjoint.

Suppose $X \subseteq \Sigma^+$ is finite and satisfies $p(x) < p(w)$ for every $x \in X$. Prove or disprove: the number of pairwise disjoint $X$-factorizations of $w$ is at most $|X| + 1 - r(X)$.
status_search_result: Web search did not return any direct evidence of resolution of this specific question on the number of disjoint X-factorizations bounded by |X|+1-r(X) under the period condition p(x) < p(w). Related defect-type results for bi-infinite words and combinatorial rank exist, but no source confirms the conjecture is proved or refuted in the finite-word setting stated here.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is there a positive integer k such that the system (S) is equivalent to one of its subsystems induced by q equations?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the free monoid generated by $\Sigma$. For a finite set of unknowns $X = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$, a word equation is a pair $(u, v) \in (X \cup \Sigma)^* \times (X \cup \Sigma)^*$, usually written $u = v$. A morphism $h : (X \cup \Sigma)^* \to \Sigma^*$ that fixes every letter of $\Sigma$ is called a solution of the equation $u = v$ if $h(u) = h(v)$. A (possibly infinite) system $S$ of word equations on the unknowns $X$ is the conjunction of all its equations, and a solution of $S$ is a morphism that solves every equation in $S$. Two systems are said to be equivalent if they have exactly the same set of solutions. A subsystem of $S$ is any subset $S' \subseteq S$.

By the compactness theorem for free monoids (Ehrenfeucht's conjecture), every system $S$ of word equations on finitely many unknowns over $\Sigma^*$ is equivalent to some finite subsystem of itself. The question is whether this finite bound can be made uniform: 

Does there exist a positive integer $k$, depending only on the number $n$ of unknowns (and possibly on $|\Sigma|$), such that every system $S$ of word equations on $n$ unknowns over $\Sigma^*$ is equivalent to one of its subsystems consisting of at most $k$ equations?
status_search_result: Ehrenfeucht's compactness property (proved by Albert–Lawrence and Guba) guarantees that every infinite system of word equations on finitely many unknowns is equivalent to a finite subsystem, but no uniform bound on the size of such a subsystem in terms of the number of unknowns is known. For three unknowns the best known upper bound is 18 (Saarela, 2018), with the conjectured value being 3, and for $n \geq 4$ unknowns there exist independent systems of size $\Theta(n^4)$ but no finite upper bound is known. The general question therefore remains open.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is PCP decidable for unique equality continuation instances?
self_contained_problem:
An instance of the Post Correspondence Problem (PCP) over a finite alphabet $A$ is a pair of morphisms $g, h : B^* \to A^*$, where $B$ is a finite set of indices. A solution is a nonempty word $w \in B^+$ with $g(w) = h(w)$; the PCP asks, given $(g,h)$, whether such a $w$ exists.

For an instance $(g,h)$ and words $u, v \in A^*$, say that a word $w \in B^*$ is an equality continuation from $(u,v)$ if $u\,g(w) = v\,h(w)$. The instance $(g,h)$ is said to have unique equality continuations if for every pair $(u,v) \in A^* \times A^*$ that is reachable as a prefix pair during the reading of some attempted matching (equivalently, for every $(u,v)$ such that there exists at least one $w \in B^*$ with $u\,g(w) = v\,h(w)$), there is at most one letter $b \in B$ that can extend $(u,v)$ towards equality, in the sense that $u\,g(b)$ is a prefix of $v\,h(b)$ or vice versa.

Question: Is the Post Correspondence Problem decidable when restricted to instances $(g,h)$ that have unique equality continuations? That is, does there exist an algorithm which, given any such instance, decides whether it admits a solution $w \in B^+$ with $g(w) = h(w)$?
status_search_result: The corresponding ω-PCP (infinite-solution) version for unique continuation instances is known to be decidable (Halava, Harju, Karhumäki, Latteux). However, decidability of the (finite) PCP for unique equality continuation instances does not appear in the literature as resolved; it is listed among open questions in surveys on PCP variants and no decidability or undecidability proof was located.
