paper_title: Some open problems of Ramsey minimal graphs.
original_question: Let F, G, and H be non-empty graphs, and write F → (G, H) to mean that every red-blue coloring of the edges of F contains either a red copy of G or a blue copy of H. A graph F is Ramsey (G, H)-minimal if F → (G, H) but, for every edge e of F, the graph F − e fails to satisfy F − e → (G, H). Let ℜ(G, H) denote the set of all Ramsey (G, H)-minimal graphs. For each integer n ≥ 6, classify all graphs in ℜ(2K2, Pn), where 2K2 is the matching consisting of two disjoint edges and Pn is the path graph on n vertices.
self_contained_problem:
Let F, G, and H be non-empty finite simple graphs. Write F → (G, H) to mean that for every red–blue coloring of the edges of F, the graph F contains either a red subgraph isomorphic to G or a blue subgraph isomorphic to H. A graph F is called Ramsey (G, H)-minimal if F → (G, H) and, for every edge e ∈ E(F), the graph F − e satisfies F − e ↛ (G, H). Let ℜ(G, H) denote the class of all Ramsey (G, H)-minimal graphs (up to isomorphism).

Let 2K₂ denote the graph consisting of two disjoint edges (a matching on four vertices), and let Pₙ denote the path on n vertices.

For each integer n ≥ 6, determine (i.e., give a complete classification of, up to isomorphism) all graphs that belong to ℜ(2K₂, Pₙ).
status_search_result: Complete characterizations of ℜ(2K₂, Pₙ) appear in the literature only for small n (notably n = 3, 4, 5), and partial structural results are known for general n (e.g., 2Pₙ is the only disconnected member, and no tree belongs to the class). No complete classification for n ≥ 6 was located, so the problem appears to be open.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: Can gate elimination alone be used to prove a 4n lower bound on the number of gates needed to compute some n-input Boolean function by a Boolean circuit?
self_contained_problem:
A Boolean circuit over the full binary basis B_2 (the set of all Boolean functions {0,1}^2 → {0,1}) is a directed acyclic graph whose sources are labeled by input variables x_1, …, x_n or constants, whose internal nodes (gates) have fan-in 2 and are labeled by functions in B_2, and which has a designated output node; the size of the circuit is the number of gates. The "gate elimination" method is the standard inductive technique for proving circuit-size lower bounds: one identifies a small set of input variables whose restriction (substituting constants 0/1) is guaranteed to eliminate at least k gates from any optimal circuit for the function, yielding by induction a lower bound of the form k·n − O(1) on the circuit size of an explicit family of Boolean functions f_n : {0,1}^n → {0,1}.

Question: Does there exist an explicit family of Boolean functions f_n : {0,1}^n → {0,1} for which a pure gate-elimination argument can prove that every B_2-circuit computing f_n has size at least 4n − O(1)?
category_tag: Boolean circuit lower bounds via gate elimination
status_search_result: Lower bounds of 4n−O(1), 4.5n−o(n) (Lachish–Raz), and 5n−o(n) (Iwama–Morizumi) have been proved using gate-elimination style arguments, but these are over the U_2 basis (B_2 minus parity/its negation), not the full binary basis B_2 considered here. Over B_2 the best known bound is 3.1n−o(n) (Li–Yang, STOC 2022), and works such as "On the Limits of Gate Elimination" (Golovnev et al., MFCS 2016) explicitly establish barriers for the gate-elimination technique over B_2. Whether a 4n lower bound over B_2 is achievable via pure gate elimination appears to remain open.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: Can one prove a 5n lower bound for the Boolean-circuit size of an n-input, n-output Boolean function, that is, for some function in B_{n,n}?
self_contained_problem:
Let $B_{n,n}$ denote the set of all Boolean functions $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n$ with $n$ inputs and $n$ outputs. The (combinational) circuit size of $f$, denoted $C(f)$, is the minimum number of gates in a Boolean circuit over the full binary basis $B_2$ (the set of all binary Boolean operations) that computes $f$. 

Exhibit an explicit family of functions $f_n \in B_{n,n}$ together with a proof that 
$$C(f_n) \ge 5n - o(n)$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.
status_search_result: A 5n − o(n) lower bound (in fact a 7n − o(n) lower bound) for the circuit size of an explicit function in B_{n,n} has been established. Demenkov et al. and later authors give simple proofs of a 5n − o(n) lower bound for functions with few outputs and a 7n − o(n) lower bound for explicit functions with n outputs, so the question of obtaining a 5n bound for some function in B_{n,n} is solved.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: Does there exist a symmetric Boolean function whose circuit size grows superlinearly with n, where symmetric means that the output depends only on the number of 1 bits among the inputs?
self_contained_problem: A Boolean function $f:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is called symmetric if its value depends only on the Hamming weight $|x| = x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n$ of its input. The circuit size $C(f)$ of $f$ is the minimum number of gates in a Boolean circuit over the full binary basis (all two-input Boolean gates allowed) that computes $f$.\n\nQuestion: Does there exist an infinite family $\{f_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ of symmetric Boolean functions $f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ whose circuit size $C(f_n)$ grows superlinearly in $n$, i.e., $C(f_n)/n \to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$?
status_search_result: It is known that every symmetric Boolean function on n variables can be computed by a Boolean circuit of size at most 4.5n + o(n) (Demenkov, Kojevnikov, Kulikov, Yaroslavtsev), so no symmetric Boolean function family has superlinear circuit complexity. Hence the answer to the question is no.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: Can one improve on brute-force search for the satisfiability problem for Boolean circuits of size 4n on n inputs?
self_contained_problem:
A Boolean circuit on n inputs is a directed acyclic graph whose sources are labeled with input variables x_1,...,x_n (or constants), whose internal nodes (gates) are labeled with binary Boolean operations chosen from the full binary basis B_2 (all functions {0,1}^2 -> {0,1}), and which has one designated output node. The size of the circuit is the number of gates. The circuit satisfiability problem (Circuit-SAT) takes as input such a circuit C and asks whether there exists an assignment a in {0,1}^n with C(a) = 1.

Brute-force search solves Circuit-SAT in time 2^n · poly(|C|) by trying every input assignment.

Question: Does there exist a (possibly randomized) algorithm that, given as input a Boolean circuit C over the basis B_2 of size at most 4n on n input variables, decides whether C is satisfiable in time 2^{(1-ε)n} · poly(n) for some absolute constant ε > 0, thereby improving on brute-force search?
status_search_result: Known improved Circuit-SAT algorithms (e.g., Calabro–Impagliazzo–Paturi and follow-ups) beat brute force for circuits of constant depth with cn gates, but these techniques degrade and become no better than 2^n once the circuit size grows to roughly 4n or beyond for general (unrestricted-depth) circuits over B_2. No known algorithm improves on brute-force search for Circuit-SAT on general size-4n circuits; the question is widely cited as open in the circuit complexity literature.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
context_brief: Producing hard families from small hard functions
original_question: Suppose one starts with a Boolean function on a constant number of inputs that already has high circuit complexity. Can one systematically turn it into a family of n-input Boolean functions whose circuit complexity stays high, rather than losing hardness through the mass production effect?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C(f)$ denote the minimum number of gates in a Boolean circuit over the binary basis $B_2$ (the set of all two-input Boolean functions) that computes a Boolean function $f:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}$. It is known by counting that for every $k$ there exists a Boolean function $g:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}$ with $C(g) \ge (2^k/k)(1-o(1))$, but no explicit such $g$ is known for super-constant $k$.

Suppose one is given, as an oracle or fixed combinatorial object, a Boolean function $g:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}$ on a constant number $k$ of inputs whose circuit complexity $C(g)$ is as large as possible (i.e., close to $2^k/k$). The question is whether such a hard "seed" $g$ can be used to construct, in a systematic and uniform way, an explicit family $\{f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\}_{n\ge 1}$ of Boolean functions such that $C(f_n)$ grows superlinearly (or even, ideally, matches the best known existential lower bounds up to constants) as $n\to\infty$.

More precisely: does there exist a polynomial-time (or otherwise effective) procedure that, given the truth table of any Boolean function $g$ on $k$ variables with $C(g)\ge c\cdot 2^k/k$ for some constant $c>0$, outputs a description of an $n$-variable Boolean function $f_n$ (for each $n$) such that $C(f_n) = \omega(n)$, avoiding the "mass production" phenomenon by which natural reductions from a $k$-input hard function only yield circuit lower bounds that vanish in $n$?
status_search_result: No general construction is known that converts a hard constant-arity Boolean function into an explicit family with high circuit complexity; proving superlinear lower bounds against unrestricted $B_2$-circuits remains a longstanding open problem in complexity theory, and the best known explicit lower bound is still of the form $(3+1/86)n - o(n)$ (Find–Golovnev–Hirsch–Kulikov 2016). The "mass production" obstruction described by Valiant remains unresolved.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: Can one prove superlinear lower bounds for Boolean circuits whose depth is logarithmic in the number of inputs, that is, O(log n)?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Boolean circuits over the standard basis (AND, OR, NOT) with bounded fan-in (say fan-in 2), computing Boolean functions $f:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$. The size of a circuit is the number of gates, and its depth is the length of the longest path from an input to the output gate.

Exhibit an explicit family of Boolean functions $\{f_n\}_{n\ge 1}$, with $f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ computable by some uniform algorithm (e.g., in NP, or even just in some explicit complexity class), together with a function $s(n) = \omega(n)$, such that any Boolean circuit of depth $O(\log n)$ computing $f_n$ must have size at least $s(n)$.

Equivalently: prove that there exists an explicit Boolean function family that cannot be computed by Boolean circuits of simultaneously linear size $O(n)$ and logarithmic depth $O(\log n)$, with a superlinear size lower bound holding for all $O(\log n)$-depth circuits computing it.
status_search_result: Proving a superlinear size lower bound for any explicit Boolean function on circuits of depth O(log n) (over the standard unbounded basis) is a well-known and long-standing open problem in circuit complexity. No such lower bound is currently known; even for restricted models such as linear/XOR circuits of logarithmic depth, no superlinear bounds are known. Recent surveys and works (e.g., Golovnev–Kulikov on circuit depth reductions, and standard complexity references) confirm the problem remains open as of 2026.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: Can one prove multiplicative-complexity lower bounds mc(f) ≥ n, or even mc(f) ≥ (1 + ε)n, for explicit Boolean functions f, where mc(f) is the minimum number of AND-type gates needed to compute f when XOR-type gates are treated as free?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Boolean circuits over the De Morgan/XOR basis in which each gate is one of two types:
- XOR-type gates: gates computing an affine function over GF(2), such as XOR, NOT, or constants (these are treated as "free");
- AND-type gates: gates computing a non-affine binary function over GF(2), such as AND.

For a Boolean function f : {0,1}^n → {0,1}, define the multiplicative complexity mc(f) to be the minimum number of AND-type gates appearing in any such circuit that computes f (with no restriction on the number of XOR-type gates).

The problem is to exhibit an explicit family of Boolean functions f_n : {0,1}^n → {0,1} (computable, say, in polynomial time, or otherwise given by an explicit construction) for which one can prove the lower bound
    mc(f_n) ≥ n,
and, more ambitiously, to prove a lower bound of the form
    mc(f_n) ≥ (1 + ε) n
for some absolute constant ε > 0 and all sufficiently large n.
status_search_result: Available literature indicates that the strongest known multiplicative-complexity lower bound for an explicit Boolean function is still essentially n−1 (via the dim(f)/2 bound and similar arguments), and no explicit function is known to satisfy mc(f) ≥ n, let alone mc(f) ≥ (1+ε)n. Recent work focuses on concrete multiplicative complexity of small or symmetric functions and on exact values for low-MC classes, but the asymptotic lower-bound question for explicit functions remains open.

paper_title: PROGRESS IN THE OPEN PROBLEMS IN THEORY OF FUNCTIONS OF BOUNDED INDEX
original_question: Let b_1,b_2 ∈ C^2 be directions, let g(z_1,z_2) be an entire function of bounded L-index in the directions b_1 and b_2, and interpret bounded L^*-index in a direction b^* by the same directional-derivative criterion as above, with L replaced by L^* and b replaced by b^*. Determine a positive continuous function L^* and a direction b^* such that every entire solution F of the mixed-derivative equation ∂^2F/(∂b_1 ∂b_2) = g(z_1,z_2) has bounded L^*-index in the direction b^*.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. For a nonzero direction $b=(b_1,\dots,b_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive continuous function $L:\mathbb{C}^n\to(0,\infty)$, an entire function $F:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{C}$ is said to have bounded $L$-index in the direction $b$ if there exists $m_0\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ such that for every $m\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and every $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$,
$$\frac{|\partial_b^m F(z)|}{m!\,L(z)^m}\le\max_{0\le k\le m_0}\frac{|\partial_b^k F(z)|}{k!\,L(z)^k},$$
where $\partial_b F(z)=\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\,\partial F/\partial z_j$ and $\partial_b^m$ denotes the $m$-fold iterate. The same definition with $L,b$ replaced by $L^*,b^*$ defines bounded $L^*$-index in direction $b^*$.

Problem. Let $n=2$ and let $b_1,b_2\in\mathbb{C}^2\setminus\{0\}$ be two given directions. Suppose $g:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}$ is an entire function having bounded $L$-index in each of the directions $b_1$ and $b_2$ (for some positive continuous $L$). Determine a positive continuous function $L^*:\mathbb{C}^2\to(0,\infty)$ and a direction $b^*\in\mathbb{C}^2\setminus\{0\}$, possibly together with appropriate initial conditions, such that every entire solution $F:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}$ of the mixed-derivative equation
$$\partial_{b_1}\partial_{b_2} F(z_1,z_2)=g(z_1,z_2)$$
has bounded $L^*$-index in the direction $b^*$.
status_search_result: The problem belongs to a program on bounded L-index in direction and PDEs. Related results exist (e.g., for second-order PDEs entire solutions are shown to have bounded L-index in a direction under suitable hypotheses), but a definitive solution to this specific mixed-derivative problem in two prescribed directions was not located in the available sources.

paper_title: PROGRESS IN THE OPEN PROBLEMS IN THEORY OF FUNCTIONS OF BOUNDED INDEX
original_question: Let L ∈ Q_b^n, let F be an entire function on C^n, and for r > 0 define G_r^b(F) as the union over zeros z of F of the discs {z + tb : |t| < r/L(z)} along the direction b. For z_0 ∈ C^n, let n_b(r/L(z_0), z_0, 1/F) count the zeros of the slice t ↦ F(z_0 + tb) in the disc |t| ≤ r/L(z_0), and let F(z_0 + tb) ≡ 0 force this quantity to be -1. Is F of bounded L-index in the direction b exactly when both of the following hold: (1) there exist r > 0 and P(r) > 0 such that for every z outside G_r^b(F), the logarithmic directional derivative satisfies |(1/F(z)) ∂F(z)/∂b| ≤ P(r)L(z); and (2) there exist r > 0 and n_e(r) ∈ Z_+ such that for every z_0 with F(z_0 + tb) not identically zero, and every t_0 ∈ C, one has n_b(r/L(z_0), z_0, 1/F) ≤ n_e(r)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $b\in\mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$ be a fixed direction and let $L:\mathbb{C}^n\to(0,\infty)$ be a continuous positive function belonging to the class $Q_b^n$, i.e. for every $r>0$,
$$\lambda_b(r):=\sup_{z\in\mathbb{C}^n}\sup_{|t_1|,|t_2|\le r/L(z)}\frac{L(z+t_1 b)}{L(z+t_2 b)}<\infty.$$
Let $F:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{C}$ be an entire function. Recall that $F$ is said to be of bounded $L$-index in the direction $b$ if there exists $m_0\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ such that for every $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$ and every $m\in\mathbb{Z}_+$,
$$\frac{|\partial_b^m F(z)|}{m!\,L(z)^m}\le \max_{0\le k\le m_0}\frac{|\partial_b^k F(z)|}{k!\,L(z)^k},$$
where $\partial_b F(z):=\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\partial F/\partial z_j$.

For $r>0$ define the exceptional set
$$G_r^b(F):=\bigcup_{z:\,F(z)=0}\bigl\{z+tb:\,|t|<r/L(z)\bigr\}.$$
For $z_0\in\mathbb{C}^n$, let $n_b(\rho,z_0,1/F)$ denote the number of zeros (counted with multiplicities) of the entire slice function $t\mapsto F(z_0+tb)$ in the disc $\{t\in\mathbb{C}:|t|\le\rho\}$ when this slice is not identically zero, and set $n_b(\rho,z_0,1/F):=-1$ if $F(z_0+tb)\equiv 0$ in $t$.

Assume $\mathbb{C}^n\setminus G_r^b(F)\ne\varnothing$. Decide whether the following equivalence holds:

$F$ is of bounded $L$-index in the direction $b$ if and only if both
\begin{enumerate}
\item there exist $r>0$ and $P(r)>0$ such that
$$\Bigl|\frac{\partial_b F(z)}{F(z)}\Bigr|\le P(r)\,L(z)\quad\text{for all }z\in\mathbb{C}^n\setminus G_r^b(F),$$
\item there exist $r>0$ and $n_e(r)\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ such that for every $z_0\in\mathbb{C}^n$ for which $F(z_0+tb)\not\equiv 0$,
$$n_b\bigl(r/L(z_0),z_0,1/F\bigr)\le n_e(r).$$
\end{enumerate}
status_search_result: The equivalence is known to hold under the additional restriction $2n(r_2)r_1<r_2/\lambda_b(r_2)$, but whether this technical restriction can be removed appears to remain open. Subsequent works by Bandura and Skaskiv on directional logarithmic derivatives and zero distribution provide criteria of boundedness of $L$-index in direction, but a complete unrestricted proof of the stated equivalence has not been clearly established.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Let rho(n) be the limiting minimum density of 1s in binary nth-power-free words and extend rho to real exponents x via binary words avoiding factors of exponent at least x. Does rho have discontinuities other than the known right-discontinuities at 7/3 and the integers n >= 3, and is rho piecewise constant?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite or infinite word w over the alphabet {0,1}, the exponent of a nonempty factor u of w is defined as |u|/p, where p is the smallest period of u (so a factor of exponent ≥ n is exactly an n-th power for integer n, and more generally factors of fractional exponent are considered for real exponents). For a real number x ≥ 2, call an infinite binary word x-power-free if it contains no factor of exponent ≥ x. Define the density of 1s in a finite binary word as the number of occurrences of the letter 1 divided by the length of the word, and define the lower density of 1s in an infinite binary word w as the liminf over n → ∞ of the density of 1s in the length-n prefix of w. Let
   ρ(x) = inf { lower density of 1s in w : w is an infinite x-power-free binary word },
defined for all real x ≥ 2 for which x-power-free infinite binary words exist (in particular for x ≥ 2 since binary 2⁺-power-free words such as the Thue–Morse word exist; ρ is also defined at integer values n ≥ 3 via n-th-power-free words). original_question: Kirby Baker, Georges F. McNulty and Walter Taylor have shown that the pattern abXbcYcaZbaTac is 4-avoidable, but not 3- avoidable [8]. What is the minimal proportion of the fourth letter needed to avoid that pattern?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma_k=\{0,1,\dots,k-1\}$ be a finite alphabet. A pattern is a word $p$ over an alphabet of variables. An infinite word $w\in\Sigma_k^{\mathbb N}$ is said to encounter $p$ if there exists a non-erasing morphism $h$ from the variable alphabet to $\Sigma_k^{+}$ such that $h(p)$ is a factor of $w$; otherwise $w$ avoids $p$. The pattern $p$ is $k$-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over $\Sigma_k$ avoiding $p$.

Consider the pattern 
$$p \;=\; ab\,X\,bc\,Y\,ca\,Z\,ba\,T\,ac,$$
on the variable alphabet $\{a,b,c,X,Y,Z,T\}$. It is known that $p$ is $4$-avoidable but not $3$-avoidable.

For an infinite word $w$ over $\Sigma_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$, let
$$\mathrm{freq}_w(\alpha) \;=\; \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{|w[1..n]|_{\alpha}}{n}$$
denote the (lower) frequency of letter $\alpha$ in $w$.

Determine the value of
$$\mu \;=\; \inf\Bigl\{\,\max_{\alpha\in\Sigma_4}\bigl(1 - 3\,\mathrm{freq}_w(\alpha)\bigr)\,\Bigr\}^{-1}\quad\text{(equivalently)}$$
$$\mu \;=\; \inf_{w}\;\min_{\alpha\in\Sigma_4}\mathrm{freq}_w(\alpha),$$
where the infimum is taken over all infinite words $w\in\Sigma_4^{\mathbb N}$ that avoid the pattern $p$. In other words, what is the minimal possible asymptotic proportion of the least-frequent (fourth) letter in an infinite $4$-letter word avoiding $ab\,X\,bc\,Y\,ca\,Z\,ba\,T\,ac$?

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Given a pattern p, what is the complexity of deciding whether p is avoidable?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet of letters and let E be a disjoint countably infinite alphabet of variables. A pattern is a nonempty word p ∈ E*. An occurrence of p in a word w ∈ A* is the image h(p) of p under a non-erasing morphism h : E* → A* such that h(p) is a factor of w. An infinite word w over A is said to avoid p if no factor of w is an occurrence of p. The pattern p is called avoidable if there exists some finite alphabet A and some infinite word over A that avoids p; otherwise p is called unavoidable.

It is known (Bean–Ehrenfeucht–McNulty, Zimin) that avoidability of patterns is decidable. Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem:

  Input: a pattern p ∈ E*.
  Question: is p avoidable?

That is, determine the precise complexity class (e.g., in P, NP-complete, coNP-complete, PSPACE-complete, etc.) of deciding pattern avoidability.
status_search_result: Deciding whether a pattern is unavoidable is known to be coNP-complete (equivalently, deciding avoidability is NP-complete), as established for the unavoidability problem and reported in recent work on "The Complexity of Unavoidable Word Patterns" (Theory of Computing Systems, 2022). However, fine-grained questions about the complexity of avoidability for restricted classes of patterns and related variants remain active. The general decidability question has long been answered, while the precise complexity classification matching upper and lower bounds appears settled at NP-completeness for the basic version.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Explore the applications of the probabilistic method in the scope of pattern avoidance.
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and let A* denote the set of finite words over A. A pattern is a word p over a separate alphabet of variables E = {e_1, e_2, ...}. A word w in A* is said to encounter the pattern p if there exists a non-erasing morphism h : E* -> A* such that h(p) appears as a factor of w; otherwise w avoids p. The pattern p is said to be k-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over some alphabet of size k that avoids p, and the avoidability index lambda(p) is the smallest such k (infinity if no such k exists).

The probabilistic method, in particular variants of the Lovász Local Local Lemma (including the entropy compression / Moser–Tardos framework), provides a general technique for proving the existence of infinite words avoiding prescribed sets of forbidden factors when each long enough factor has only "few" forbidden extensions.

Develop and exploit applications of the probabilistic method (Lovász Local Lemma, entropy compression, and related tools) to problems of pattern avoidance in words. In particular, for as broad a class of patterns p as possible, obtain new upper bounds on the avoidability index lambda(p), and on the related quantities for avoidance of patterns in the abelian, k-abelian, or additive sense, and for avoidance of patterns by circular (necklace) words. Determine to what extent such probabilistic arguments can match or improve the bounds known from explicit morphic constructions.
status_search_result: The question is a broad research direction rather than a single sharply posed conjecture. Probabilistic techniques (Lovász Local Lemma, entropy compression introduced by Moser–Tardos and applied to non-repetitive sequences by Grytczuk, Kozik, Micek, and to pattern avoidance by Ochem, Pinlou, and others) have produced many partial results since 2013, but as a general program the exploration is ongoing and considered open.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: If p is k-avoidable then there are circular words with length |p| on k letters that avoid p.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let A be a finite alphabet and let E be a separate set of symbols called pattern variables. A pattern is a nonempty word p ∈ E^+; its length |p| is its number of letters as a word over E. A word w ∈ A^* is said to encounter p if there exists a non-erasing morphism h : E^+ → A^+ such that h(p) is a factor of w; otherwise w avoids p. A circular word of length n on A is an equivalence class of words in A^n under cyclic rotation, equivalently a word read on a cycle of n positions; a circular word w avoids p if no factor of w (taken cyclically, i.e., no factor of ww of length at most n) encounters p.

A pattern p is said to be k-avoidable if there exist infinitely many (equivalently, arbitrarily long) words over a k-letter alphabet that avoid p.

Conjecture. Prove or disprove: for every pattern p and every integer k ≥ 1, if p is k-avoidable, then for every sufficiently large integer n there exists a circular word of length n on a k-letter alphabet that avoids p.

The status appears to remain open in the literature consulted.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: The number of k-power-free binary words of length n grows polynomially with n for k<= 7/3, but exponentially for k > 7/3 [39]. Examine analogous results for alphabets of arbitrary size.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma_k = \{0, 1, \ldots, k-1\}$ be an alphabet of size $k \geq 2$. For a real number $\alpha > 1$, a finite word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n \in \Sigma_k^*$ is called an $\alpha$-power if it can be written as $w = u^p v$ where $u$ is a nonempty word, $p \geq 1$ is an integer, $v$ is a (possibly empty) prefix of $u$, and $|w|/|u| = \alpha$. A word is $\alpha$-power-free if none of its factors is a $\beta$-power for any $\beta \geq \alpha$. Let $L_k(\alpha, n)$ denote the number of $\alpha$-power-free words of length $n$ over $\Sigma_k$.

It is known that for $k = 2$ there exists a threshold $\alpha^*_2 = 7/3$ such that $L_2(\alpha, n)$ grows polynomially in $n$ for $\alpha \leq 7/3$ and exponentially in $n$ for $\alpha > 7/3$.

For each integer $k \geq 3$, determine the analogous polynomial-versus-exponential growth threshold $\alpha^*_k$, i.e., find the value $\alpha^*_k$ such that $L_k(\alpha, n)$ grows polynomially in $n$ for $\alpha \leq \alpha^*_k$ and exponentially in $n$ for $\alpha > \alpha^*_k$, and characterize the growth behavior at and around this threshold.
status_search_result: Considerable progress has been made for alphabets of size $k \geq 3$. Shur and others established asymptotic growth rates for $\beta$-power-free languages over $k$-letter alphabets, and a 2025 result (Dagstuhl/MFCS) proves Shur's conjecture on the exponential growth rates of $(k/(k-1))$-free and $(k/(k-1))^+$-free languages over large alphabets, with $O(1/k^2)$ corrections. The "exponential conjecture" (that for $k \geq 3$ all infinite power-free languages over $k$ letters have exponential size at the Dejean threshold) has been confirmed in several regimes. Thus the analogue of the binary 7/3 threshold is partially understood: the threshold is conjecturally the Dejean repetition threshold $k/(k-1)$, with strong supporting results, but a complete characterization for all $k$ matching the binary case is not fully settled.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: In the prefix or suffix tree of a repetition-free language, does a given word generate a finite subtree or an infinite subtree?
self_contained_problem:
Let $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ be a repetition-free (i.e., power-free) language over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, meaning that there is a fixed rational number $\alpha > 1$ (or an integer $k \ge 2$) such that no word in $L$ contains a factor of the form $u^\alpha$ (respectively $u^k$) with $u$ nonempty, and $L$ is closed under taking factors. The prefix tree $T_{\mathrm{pref}}(L)$ of $L$ is the rooted tree whose nodes are the words of $L$, with the empty word as the root, and in which the parent of a nonempty word $w \in L$ is obtained by deleting its last letter; the suffix tree $T_{\mathrm{suf}}(L)$ is defined analogously by deleting the first letter. For a word $w \in L$, the subtree rooted at $w$ in $T_{\mathrm{pref}}(L)$ consists of $w$ together with all of its descendants (i.e., all words in $L$ having $w$ as a prefix), and similarly for $T_{\mathrm{suf}}(L)$.

Problem. Given a repetition-free language $L$ and a word $w \in L$, decide whether the subtree of $T_{\mathrm{pref}}(L)$ (respectively $T_{\mathrm{suf}}(L)$) rooted at $w$ is finite or infinite. Equivalently, determine whether $w$ can be extended to the right (respectively to the left) by arbitrarily long words while remaining in $L$, or whether all such extensions have bounded length.

No source found indicating a complete resolution.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: For a conducting sequence beta in {0,1}*, which words u can be shuffled with themselves to obtain a unique square-free word?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. A word $w \in \Sigma^*$ is called square-free if it contains no nonempty factor of the form $xx$ (i.e., no nonempty word repeated twice consecutively appears as a contiguous block of $w$).

For two words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$ of lengths $m$ and $n$ respectively, and a binary "conducting sequence" $\beta \in \{0,1\}^{m+n}$ containing exactly $m$ zeros and $n$ ones, the shuffle of $u$ and $v$ controlled by $\beta$, denoted $u \shuffle_\beta v$, is the unique word of length $m+n$ obtained by reading the $i$-th letter from $u$ when the $i$-th symbol of $\beta$ is $0$ (in order) and from $v$ when it is $1$ (in order).

Define a self-shuffle of $u$ as any word of the form $u \shuffle_\beta u$ where $\beta \in \{0,1\}^{2|u|}$ has exactly $|u|$ zeros and $|u|$ ones.

Problem: Characterize all words $u \in \Sigma^*$ for which there exists a conducting sequence $\beta$ such that $u \shuffle_\beta u$ is square-free, and moreover such a square-free self-shuffle is unique (i.e., $u \shuffle_\beta u$ is square-free for exactly one $\beta$).

However, no source directly resolves the specific question of characterizing words u admitting a unique square-free self-shuffle u ⧢_β u, so the status appears to be unresolved/unknown.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Which square-free words are themselves shuffles of square-free words?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and A* the free monoid of finite words over A. A word w ∈ A* is square-free if it contains no nonempty factor of the form xx (i.e., there are no nonempty u and words p,s with w = p·uu·s). Given two words u,v ∈ A*, the shuffle set u ⧢ v ⊆ A* consists of all words obtained by interleaving u and v while preserving the relative order of letters within each. A shuffled-square is a word w that lies in u ⧢ u for some nonempty word u.

Characterize the set of square-free words w (over any alphabet) such that w is a shuffled-square, i.e., such that there exists a square-free word u with w ∈ u ⧢ u. In particular, give a structural description (or decision procedure) for finite square-free words w admitting a square-free word u with w ∈ u ⧢ u, and determine for which alphabet sizes there exist infinite square-free words w that arise as a shuffle u ⧢ u of an infinite square-free word u with itself.
status_search_result: The general characterization question appears to remain open. Existence results are known: Harju and Müller showed that for every n ≥ 3 there is a square-free ternary word u of length n with u ⧢ u containing a square-free word, and that there is an infinite square-free word u over three letters whose self-shuffle yields an infinite square-free word. Related questions on shuffled-square-free words (avoiding any factor in u ⧢ u) have been studied by Currie, Müller, Guégan–Ochem, and others, with progress on alphabet size, but no complete structural characterization of square-free words that are self-shuffles of square-free words has been published.

original_question: In the tree T, the size of any minimal subtree of index n is O(log n).
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma=\{0,1,2\}$ and let $L\subseteq\Sigma^{*}$ be the language of all square-free words over $\Sigma$, i.e. words containing no nonempty factor of the form $uu$. Order $L$ by the prefix relation; the resulting Hasse diagram is an infinite tree $T$ whose root is the empty word and whose children of a node $w\in L$ are the words $wa$ ($a\in\Sigma$) that still belong to $L$. For a node $w\in L$, write $T(w)$ for the subtree of $T$ rooted at $w$, and call $T(w)$ a "minimal subtree of index $n$" if $|w|=n$ and $T(w)$ is finite (equivalently, $w$ has no infinite extension in $L$, while every proper prefix of $w$ does). The size $|T(w)|$ is the number of nodes of $T(w)$.

Prove or disprove: there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for every $n\ge 1$ and every minimal subtree $T(w)$ of index $n$ in $T$,
$$|T(w)| \;\le\; C\log n.$$
Equivalently, the size of any minimal subtree of index $n$ in $T$ is $O(\log n)$.
status_search_result: The conjecture concerns the tree of ternary square-free words studied by Petrova and Shur (WORDS 2015), who proved that non-branching paths from a node at level $n$ have length $O(\log n)$. The stronger statement that every minimal (finite) subtree at level $n$ has total size $O(\log n)$ is listed among the open problems compiled from the WORDS conferences (1997–2017), and no published resolution was found in the available search results.

original_question: Does the finite repetition threshold on four letters equal the usual repetition threshold, i.e. is FRT(4) = RT(4) = 7/5?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite alphabet $A$, the exponent of a finite nonempty word $w$ is $|w|/p(w)$, where $p(w)$ is the smallest period of $w$. For an infinite word $\mathbf{w}$, let $E(\mathbf{w})$ denote the supremum of the exponents of its finite factors. The repetition threshold on $k$ letters is
$$\mathrm{RT}(k) = \inf\{ E(\mathbf{w}) : \mathbf{w} \text{ is an infinite word over an alphabet of size } k \}.$$
By Dejean's theorem, $\mathrm{RT}(4) = 7/5$. The finite repetition threshold on $k$ letters, $\mathrm{FRT}(k)$, is defined as the infimum of the real numbers $r$ such that there exists an infinite word $\mathbf{w}$ over an alphabet of size $k$ with $E(\mathbf{w}) \le r$ and such that $\mathbf{w}$ has only finitely many distinct factors of exponent equal to $\mathrm{RT}(k)$.

Determine whether $\mathrm{FRT}(4) = \mathrm{RT}(4) = 7/5$.
status_search_result: The equality FRT(4) = RT(4) = 7/5 is established: there exists an infinite Dejean word over a 4-letter alphabet (avoiding factors of exponent greater than 7/5) containing only finitely many (in fact two) factors of exponent exactly 7/5. This was shown in work on finite-repetition thresholds for large alphabets following the ternary case.

original_question: The asymptotic upper bound of rho(n)/n is never reached.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite string (word) $w$ over a finite alphabet, a run (also called a maximal repetition) is a maximal occurrence of a periodic factor of exponent at least $2$, i.e., a substring $w[i..j]$ with smallest period $p \le (j-i+1)/2$ that cannot be extended to the left or to the right while preserving the period $p$. Let $\rho(n)$ denote the maximum, taken over all strings of length $n$ over any alphabet, of the number of runs occurring in the string. It is known that the limit superior
$$ \alpha := \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{\rho(n)}{n} $$
exists and is finite (in fact $\rho(n)<n$ for all $n\ge 1$). Prove or disprove the following: for every positive integer $n$,
$$ \frac{\rho(n)}{n} < \alpha. $$
That is, the asymptotic upper bound of $\rho(n)/n$ is never attained for any finite $n$.
category_tag: combinatorics on words / runs in strings
status_search_result: While the classical "runs" conjecture ρ(n) < n was resolved affirmatively by Bannai, I, Inenaga, Nakashima, Takeda, and Tsuruta (SIAM J. Comput., 2017), the finer statement that ρ(n)/n never attains its asymptotic limsup α does not appear to have been settled in the literature accessible by search. The exact value of α and the precise behaviour of ρ(n)/n for finite n remain subjects of active investigation, so the status of this specific conjecture is unclear.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: By applying prefix-suffix completion, can we construct words that avoid cubes, and every word containing squares?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$. For words $u,v \in \Sigma^*$, write $u \Rightarrow_{ps} v$ (one step of prefix-suffix square completion) if either:
- there exist $x,y \in \Sigma^*$ with $y$ nonempty such that $u$ has the suffix $yx$ where $u = \alpha y x$ for some $\alpha$, and $v = u\,y$ (so that $v$ ends in the square $yy$); or, symmetrically,
- $u$ has a prefix $xy$ with $y$ nonempty, and $v = y\,u$ (so that $v$ begins with the square $yy$).

Equivalently, the suffix square completion appends a nonempty word $y$ to $u$ whenever $u$ already ends with $y$, producing a new suffix $yy$; and the prefix square completion is its mirror image.

Let $\Rightarrow_{ps}^*$ denote the reflexive transitive closure of this relation. An infinite word $w \in \Sigma^\omega$ is said to be generated by prefix-suffix square completion (from a finite seed $w_0$) if there is an infinite sequence $w_0 \Rightarrow_{ps} w_1 \Rightarrow_{ps} w_2 \Rightarrow_{ps} \cdots$ whose limit is $w$.

A word is cube-free if it contains no factor of the form $xxx$ with $x$ nonempty. Note that, by construction, every word produced by a nontrivial prefix-suffix square completion step contains a square.

Question: Does there exist a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ and a finite seed word $w_0 \in \Sigma^*$ from which prefix-suffix square completion generates an infinite word $w$ such that:
(i) $w$ is cube-free, and
(ii) every finite factor of $w$ contains at least one square?

More generally, characterize the infinite words obtainable by iterated prefix-suffix square completion that simultaneously avoid cubes and have the property that every sufficiently long factor contains a square.
status_search_result: Search results confirm prefix-suffix square completion has been studied (e.g., the original paper by Ito, Leupold, Manea, Mitrana and follow-ups on prefix/suffix-square-free words and prefix-suffix square reduction). It is known that infinite cube-free words can be generated by such operations. However, no source located explicitly resolves the combined requirement of avoiding cubes while ensuring every factor contains a square via prefix-suffix square completion. The status therefore appears unresolved based on the available evidence.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: What are the values of the abelian repetitive threshold ART(n) and the dual abelian repetitive threshold DART(r)?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer alphabet size $n \geq 2$, an abelian $\alpha$-power is a nonempty word $w$ that can be factorized as $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k v$, where $k \geq 2$, the factors $u_1,\dots,u_k$ are pairwise abelian-equivalent (each is a permutation of the letters of the others), $v$ is a (possibly empty) prefix of an abelian-equivalent permutation of $u_1$, and $\alpha = |w|/|u_1|$. An infinite word over an $n$-letter alphabet is said to avoid abelian $\alpha$-powers if it contains no factor that is an abelian $\beta$-power with $\beta \geq \alpha$. Define the abelian repetitive threshold
$$\mathrm{ART}(n) = \inf\{\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}_{\geq 1} : \text{there exists an infinite word over an } n\text{-letter alphabet avoiding abelian powers of exponent} > \alpha\}.$$

Dually, for a real parameter $r \geq 1$, define the dual abelian repetitive threshold $\mathrm{DART}(r)$ as the least integer $n$ (alphabet size) such that there exists an infinite word over an $n$-letter alphabet avoiding all abelian powers of exponent strictly greater than $r$.

Determine the exact value of $\mathrm{ART}(n)$ for every integer $n \geq 2$, and determine the exact value of $\mathrm{DART}(r)$ for every real $r \geq 1$.
status_search_result: The exact values of ART(n) remain unknown. Samsonov and Shur (2012) established lower bounds ART(2) ≥ 11/3, ART(3) ≥ 2, ART(4) ≥ 9/5, and ART(k) ≥ (k-2)/(k-3) for k ≥ 5, conjectured to be tight. A 2021/2022 work ("Abelian Repetition Threshold Revisited") showed these lower bounds are not tight for k ∈ {6,7,8,9,10}, leaving exact values open. No exact determination of DART has been published.

original_question: How many words of a given length are strongly k-abelian nth powers?
self_contained_problem:

original_question: Can one avoid abelian cubes uvw with |u| = |v| = |w| >= 2 over a binary alphabet?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma = \{a,b\}$ be a binary alphabet, and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of all finite words over $\Sigma$. Two words $x,y \in \Sigma^*$ are said to be abelian-equivalent (written $x \sim_{ab} y$) if they have the same length and, for every letter $c \in \Sigma$, the number of occurrences of $c$ in $x$ equals the number of occurrences of $c$ in $y$. A word $w$ is called an abelian cube if $w = uvw'$ for some nonempty words $u, v, w' \in \Sigma^*$ with $|u| = |v| = |w'|$ and $u \sim_{ab} v \sim_{ab} w'$. An infinite word $\mathbf{x} \in \Sigma^{\mathbb{N}}$ is said to avoid abelian cubes of period at least $2$ if $\mathbf{x}$ contains no factor of the form $uvw'$ with $|u| = |v| = |w'| \geq 2$ and $u \sim_{ab} v \sim_{ab} w'$.

Question: Does there exist an infinite word over the binary alphabet $\{a,b\}$ that avoids abelian cubes of period at least $2$?

original_question: Is there an integer k such that abelian cubes of period at least k can be avoided over a binary alphabet?

Let $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$ be the binary alphabet, and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. Two words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$ are said to be abelian equivalent, written $u \sim_a v$, if $|u| = |v|$ and, for every letter $a \in \Sigma$, the number of occurrences of $a$ in $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $a$ in $v$. A (finite or infinite) word $w$ is said to avoid abelian cubes of period at least $k$ if no factor of $w$ is an abelian cube of period $\geq k$.

Question: Does there exist a positive integer $k$ such that there is an infinite word over $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$ avoiding all abelian cubes of period at least $k$?

This answers the question in the negative: no such integer $k$ exists.

original_question: Assume that a word with length n, and containing k many distinct abelian-square factors, exists. Then a binary word of lengthn containing at least k many distinct abelian-square factors exists.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. A word over $\Sigma$ is a finite sequence of letters of $\Sigma$. For a word $w$, the Parikh vector of $w$ is the vector indexing each letter $a \in \Sigma$ by the number of occurrences of $a$ in $w$. An abelian square is a word of the form $uv$ where $u$ and $v$ have the same Parikh vector (equivalently, $v$ is a permutation of $u$). Two abelian squares are considered inequivalent (distinct) if their Parikh vectors differ. A factor of a word $w$ is a contiguous subword of $w$.

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every integer $n \geq 1$ and every $k \geq 0$, if there exists a word of length $n$ over some finite alphabet that contains $k$ distinct abelian-square factors (counted up to equivalence of Parikh vectors), then there also exists a binary word (i.e., a word over a 2-letter alphabet) of length $n$ that contains at least $k$ distinct abelian-square factors.
status_search_result: The statement is the Fici–Mignosi conjecture asserting that binary words maximize the number of distinct abelian-square factors. Subsequent works (e.g., on abelian-square-rich words by Fici, Mignosi, and Shallit) show that binary words attain Θ(n²) distinct abelian squares, which is the right order, but the literature does not indicate that the precise conjecture has been settled. Recent papers in 2026 still refer to the conjecture and only resolve special cases, so it appears to remain open.

original_question: Can we avoid long abelian cubes over two letters?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$ be a binary alphabet. A finite nonempty word $w\in\Sigma^+$ is called an abelian cube if it can be written as $w=xyz$ with $|x|=|y|=|z|\ge 1$ and the three factors $x,y,z$ are pairwise abelian-equivalent, i.e. each letter of $\Sigma$ occurs the same number of times in $x$, in $y$, and in $z$. The common length $|x|$ is called the period of the abelian cube.

An infinite word $\mathbf{w}\in\Sigma^{\mathbb N}$ is said to avoid long abelian cubes if there exists an integer $N\ge 1$ such that no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is an abelian cube of period at least $N$.

Question: Does there exist an integer $N$ and an infinite binary word $\mathbf{w}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ such that $\mathbf{w}$ contains no abelian cube $xyz$ with $|x|\ge N$? Equivalently, can long abelian cubes be avoided over a two-letter alphabet?

original_question: Is there a morphism on 3 letters with one eigenvalue of norm smaller than 1, and an abelian-cube-free ﬁxed point?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma = \{a,b,c\}$ be a three-letter alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$. A morphism is a map $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to \Sigma^*$ satisfying $\varphi(uv) = \varphi(u)\varphi(v)$, determined by its values on letters. Its incidence matrix $M_\varphi \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{3\times 3}$ is defined by $(M_\varphi)_{x,y} = $ the number of occurrences of letter $x$ in $\varphi(y)$. The eigenvalues of $\varphi$ are the eigenvalues of $M_\varphi$ in $\mathbb{C}$.

An (right) infinite word $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots \in \Sigma^\omega$ is a fixed point of $\varphi$ if $\varphi(w) = w$ (interpreted as the limit $\lim_{n\to\infty} \varphi^n(w_0)$ when $\varphi(w_0)$ starts with $w_0$ and $|\varphi^n(w_0)| \to \infty$).

Two finite words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$ are abelian-equivalent, written $u \sim_{ab} v$, if $|u| = |v|$ and each letter occurs the same number of times in $u$ and in $v$. An abelian cube is a nonempty word of the form $u_1 u_2 u_3$ with $u_1 \sim_{ab} u_2 \sim_{ab} u_3$. An infinite word $w$ is abelian-cube-free if no factor of $w$ is an abelian cube.

self_contained_problem:
Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$ be irrational. The Sturmian sequence with slope $\alpha$ is the infinite word $s_\alpha = (s_n)_{n\geq 1} \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ defined by $s_n = \lfloor (n+1)\alpha \rfloor - \lfloor n\alpha \rfloor$. For an infinite word $w$, let $R_w(n)$ denote the smallest integer $N$ such that every factor of $w$ of length $n$ occurs in every factor of $w$ of length $N$ (the recurrence function), and define the recurrence quotient
$$\rho(\alpha) := \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{R_{s_\alpha}(n)}{n}.$$
Let
$$S := \{ \rho(\alpha) : \alpha \in (0,1) \setminus \mathbb{Q} \} \subset \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$$
be the spectrum of recurrence-quotient values for Sturmian slopes.

Determine the Hausdorff dimension of $S$, and more generally, for each integer $a \geq 3$, determine the Hausdorff dimension of $S \cap [a, a+1]$.
status_search_result: Searches surface work on the structure of the set of values of the recurrence quotient of Sturmian sequences (Cassaigne and others) and related Diophantine/spectral dimension results, but no source directly establishing the Hausdorff dimension of S or of its intervals S ∩ [a, a+1] was found. The status appears unresolved in the literature accessible via search.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Transform the preceding characterization into another one which makes use of a finite set of substitutions associated with rules governing their composition (i.e. S -adic system of representation).
self_contained_problem:
Let $w$ be an infinite word over a finite alphabet $A$, and let $p_w(n)$ denote its factor complexity, i.e. the number of distinct factors (contiguous finite subwords) of $w$ of length $n$. Suppose that $w$ belongs to a class $\mathcal{C}$ of infinite words characterized by some prescribed asymptotic or combinatorial behavior of the ratio $p_w(n)/n$ (for instance, words with bounded ratio $p_w(n)/n$, or those for which $p_w(n)/n$ converges, etc.).

Recall that an $S$-adic representation of an infinite word $w$ consists of a finite set $S = \{\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_k\}$ of substitutions $\sigma_i : B_i^* \to B_{i-1}^*$ between finite alphabets, together with an infinite directive sequence $(i_n)_{n\ge 1}$ specifying which substitution is applied at each step, such that
$$w = \lim_{n\to\infty} \sigma_{i_1}\sigma_{i_2}\cdots\sigma_{i_n}(a_n)$$
for suitable letters $a_n$. One may further constrain the admissible directive sequences by combinatorial rules (e.g. encoded by a labeled graph or a sofic shift on the index set) governing how the substitutions in $S$ may be composed.

Problem. Provide a characterization of the class $\mathcal{C}$ in terms of an $S$-adic representation: exhibit a finite set $S$ of substitutions, together with explicit rules governing the admissible compositions of elements of $S$, such that an infinite word $w$ belongs to $\mathcal{C}$ if and only if $w$ admits an $S$-adic representation respecting these rules.
status_search_result: The general problem of giving an S-adic characterization of infinite words/subshifts via the growth rate of factor complexity p(n)/n is the well-known S-adic conjecture, which remains open in full generality. Partial results exist: e.g., an S-adic characterization of minimal subshifts with first difference of complexity satisfying 1 ≤ p(n+1) − p(n) ≤ 2, and improvements of the S-adic conjecture have been obtained, but a complete characterization has not been established.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Give an example of sequence for which the mentioned change of spectrum is really signiﬁcant for the balance properties.
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and let w be an infinite word over A. The balance function of w is defined by
  B_w(n) = max_{a ∈ A} max{ ||u|_a − |v|_a| : u, v are factors of w with |u| = |v| = n },
where |x|_a denotes the number of occurrences of the letter a in the finite word x.

Let σ : A* → A* be a primitive substitution (i.e. some power of its incidence matrix M_σ has all entries strictly positive), and let w be an infinite fixed point of σ. The asymptotic behaviour of B_w is governed, in part, by the spectrum (multiset of eigenvalues) of M_σ. For any integer k ≥ 2, the iterate σ^k is also a primitive substitution fixing w, with incidence matrix M_σ^k; its spectrum consists of the k-th powers of the eigenvalues of M_σ, but the dominant subdominant structure controlling balance estimates may be genuinely different. (For instance, for the Thue–Morse substitution 0 → 01, 1 → 10, the spectrum of σ² strictly differs in its qualitative balance-controlling features from that of σ.)

Problem. Exhibit an explicit primitive substitution σ on a finite alphabet, with fixed point w, such that the change of spectrum when passing from σ to some iterate σ^k (k ≥ 2) yields a significant difference in the asymptotic behaviour of the balance function B_w of w (for example, a different growth rate or a different optimal constant) compared to what is predicted by the spectrum of σ alone.
category_tag: Combinatorics on words / balance of substitutive sequences
status_search_result: The question appears in compilations of open problems from the WORDS conferences, attributed to discussions on the balance function of primitive substitutive sequences (with the Thue–Morse example illustrating that the spectra of σ and σ² may differ). I found no published resolution exhibiting a sequence where this change of spectrum is "really significant" for balance properties; the problem appears to remain open, but verification is inconclusive.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Describe the structure of the Rauzy graphs of words reaching the mentioned supremum.
self_contained_problem:
Let $u$ be a uniformly recurrent infinite word over a finite alphabet. For each integer $n\ge 0$, let $\mathcal L_n(u)$ denote the set of factors of $u$ of length $n$, and define the factor complexity $p(n)=\#\mathcal L_n(u)$ and the palindromic complexity $P(n)=\#\{w\in\mathcal L_n(u):w\text{ is a palindrome}\}$. Set $\Delta p(n)=p(n+1)-p(n)$. It is known that for every uniformly recurrent infinite word $u$ and every $n\ge 0$ one has
$$P(n)+P(n+1)\le \Delta p(n)+2.$$
The Rauzy graph $\Gamma_n(u)$ of order $n$ is the directed graph whose vertex set is $\mathcal L_n(u)$ and whose edge set is $\mathcal L_{n+1}(u)$, where an edge labelled $w\in\mathcal L_{n+1}(u)$ goes from the prefix of $w$ of length $n$ to the suffix of $w$ of length $n$.

Describe the structure of the Rauzy graphs $\Gamma_n(u)$ of those uniformly recurrent infinite words $u$ for which the above inequality is attained with equality (equivalently, for which the supremum $P(n)+P(n+1)=\Delta p(n)+2$ is reached).
status_search_result: The problem comes from a list of open problems posed at the WORDS conferences. Searches reveal active subsequent research on palindromic complexity and Rauzy graphs (e.g., on rich/closed-rich words and palindromic defect), but no source explicitly announces a complete structural description of the Rauzy graphs of uniformly recurrent words attaining equality in the bound $P(n)+P(n+1)\le \Delta p(n)+2$. The status thus appears to be unresolved in general.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: What is the number of rich words of a given length?
self_contained_problem:
A finite word $w$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ is called *rich* (or *full*) if it contains exactly $|w|+1$ distinct palindromic factors (including the empty word), which is the maximum possible number of distinct palindromic factors of a word of length $|w|$. For an integer $q\ge 2$ and an integer $n\ge 0$, let $R_q(n)$ denote the number of rich words of length $n$ over an alphabet of cardinality $q$.

Determine $R_q(n)$ exactly, i.e., give a closed-form expression (or an exact enumeration formula) for the number of rich words of length $n$ over an alphabet of size $q$. In particular, settle the case $q=2$ of binary rich words.
category_tag: Combinatorics on words / rich words enumeration
status_search_result: No exact formula for the number $R_q(n)$ of rich words of length $n$ is known. Only bounds and growth-rate results have been established: it is known that $\lim_{n\to\infty} R_q(n)^{1/n}=1$ (subexponential growth), and a 2025 preprint provides the first explicit subexponential upper bound of the form involving iterated logarithms. A binary upper bound $R_2(n)\le c\cdot 1.605^n$ has also been recorded. The enumeration problem itself remains open.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: If u is a palindromic fixed point of a primitive morphism, must there exist a class P₀ morphism whose fixed point has the same language as u?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and A* the free monoid of finite words over A. A morphism φ: A* → A* is called primitive if there exists an integer n ≥ 1 such that, for every pair of letters a, b ∈ A, the letter b occurs in φ^n(a). An infinite word u ∈ A^ℕ is a fixed point of φ if φ(u) = u. The language L(u) of u is the set of all finite factors (contiguous subwords) of u. A finite word w is a palindrome if it equals its reverse. The infinite word u is called palindromic if L(u) contains infinitely many palindromes.

A morphism φ: A* → A* is said to belong to class P₀ if there exist a palindrome p ∈ A* and palindromes q_a ∈ A* (one for each a ∈ A) such that φ(a) = p q_a for every a ∈ A.

Question: Suppose u is a palindromic infinite word that is a fixed point of some primitive morphism. Must there exist a morphism ψ of class P₀ admitting a fixed point v with L(v) = L(u)?
status_search_result: The conjecture (due to Hof, Knill and Simon) is resolved in the negative: a ternary counterexample to the class-P question was provided by Labbé (2014, Electronic J. Combinatorics; arXiv:1307.1589). The binary case was confirmed earlier (B. Tan, 2007). Subsequent work (Labbé–Pelantová, 2015) shows that, up to conjugacy, primitive palindromic substitutive subshifts are generated by morphisms close to but not always exactly of class P, so the original question has a negative answer in general.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
context_brief: Sets of sequences of a given complexity
original_question: Can one find an analogue of the FC algorithm in dimension d >= 4 that generates S-adic sequences of complexity (d-1)n+1 for almost every vector of letter frequencies?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. For an infinite word $w$ over a finite alphabet $A$, the factor complexity $p_w(n)$ is the number of distinct factors of length $n$ that occur in $w$. An $S$-adic sequence is an infinite word produced by an infinite composition of substitutions $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots$ chosen from a finite or countable set $S$ of substitutions on $A$, in the sense that $w = \lim_{k\to\infty} \sigma_1\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_k(a_k)$ for suitable letters $a_k \in A$. For a word $w$ on a $d$-letter alphabet, the vector of letter frequencies is the vector $(f_1,\ldots,f_d) \in \Delta_{d-1} = \{(x_1,\ldots,x_d) : x_i \ge 0,\ \sum x_i = 1\}$ where $f_i = \lim_{n\to\infty} |w_1\cdots w_n|_i / n$ (when the limits exist), with $|u|_i$ denoting the number of occurrences of letter $i$ in $u$.

A known three-letter construction (often called the FC algorithm), based on a multidimensional continued fraction algorithm, produces, for Lebesgue-almost every frequency vector $(f_1,f_2,f_3)\in\Delta_2$, an $S$-adic sequence on a 3-letter alphabet with factor complexity $p(n) = 2n+1$ for all $n\ge 0$.

Problem. For each integer $d \ge 4$, does there exist an algorithm analogous to the FC algorithm — specifically, a finite set $S$ of substitutions on a $d$-letter alphabet together with a rule (driven by a multidimensional continued fraction-type algorithm) for selecting an infinite sequence of substitutions from $S$ — such that for Lebesgue-almost every letter-frequency vector $(f_1,\ldots,f_d) \in \Delta_{d-1}$, the resulting $S$-adic sequence has letter frequency vector $(f_1,\ldots,f_d)$ and factor complexity $p(n) = (d-1)n + 1$ for all $n \ge 0$?
status_search_result: The d=3 case (complexity 2n+1 for almost every frequency vector via a multidimensional continued fraction algorithm conjugate to Selmer / FC) is established. For d ≥ 4, no analogous construction producing S-adic sequences of complexity (d−1)n+1 for almost every frequency vector appears to be known; existing higher-dimensional algorithms (Arnoux–Rauzy–Poincaré, Brun, Selmer, etc.) do not achieve the minimal complexity (d−1)n+1 almost everywhere. Recent work (e.g. on symbolic codings of generic toral translations) addresses related but distinct questions, suggesting the problem remains open.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Find eﬃcient algorithms for the polynomial time solv- able problems which were discussed in the paper.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $A^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $A$. A factorization of a word $w \in A^*$ is a sequence $(u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k)$ of words in $A^*$ such that $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$. Given a family $\mathcal{F} \subseteq A^*$ of words (called the factor family), an $\mathcal{F}$-factorization of $w$ is a factorization $(u_1, \ldots, u_k)$ in which every factor $u_i$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}$.

For a fixed family $\mathcal{F}$, consider the following decision and optimization problems on input $w \in A^*$:
(i) Decide whether $w$ admits an $\mathcal{F}$-factorization.
(ii) Count the number of distinct $\mathcal{F}$-factorizations of $w$.
(iii) Compute an $\mathcal{F}$-factorization of $w$ that minimizes (respectively maximizes) the number of factors $k$.

Suppose that $\mathcal{F}$ is presented in such a way that membership $u \in \mathcal{F}$ can be decided in polynomial time in $|u|$, and that for the family $\mathcal{F}$ each of the problems (i)–(iii) is known to be solvable in polynomial time in $|w|$.

Problem: For each such family $\mathcal{F}$, design an algorithm for problems (i)–(iii) whose running time is as efficient as possible (e.g., linear or near-linear in $|w|$), improving upon the general polynomial-time bounds. In particular, characterize the families $\mathcal{F}$ for which problems (i)–(iii) admit a linear-time algorithm.
status_search_result: The original prompt is a broad call to find more efficient algorithms for several polynomial-time-solvable factorization problems on words. As such it is an umbrella research direction rather than a single concrete conjecture, and no single source confirms a definitive resolution. Status is therefore recorded as unknown.

original_question: Could better algorithms be designed for the problems discussed in the paper if, in regularF -factorizations, only finite languages are considered?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $A^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $A$. Given a family $F = (L_1, L_2, \dots, L_k)$ of languages over $A$, an $F$-factorization of a word $w \in A^*$ is a decomposition $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_n$ such that each factor $u_i$ belongs to some $L_{j_i} \in F$. The $F$-factorization is called regular when each language $L_j$ in the family $F$ is regular.

Consider the standard algorithmic problems associated with regular $F$-factorizations of words (e.g., deciding the existence of an $F$-factorization of a given word, counting the number of $F$-factorizations, or producing one such factorization).

Question: If one restricts attention to the special case where every language $L_j$ in the family $F$ is finite (rather than merely regular), do there exist algorithms for these problems whose complexity is strictly better than the best known algorithms for the general regular case?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface any publication that specifically resolves whether restricting regular $F$-factorizations to families of finite languages yields strictly better algorithms. Related work on factorization in formal languages and factorization forests exists, but nothing directly addresses this complexity comparison, so the status appears unresolved.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: What is the complexity of the problem of determin- ing whether a regular F -factorization possesses synchronization property, when the parameters of the synchronization are not given? What about this problem for context-freeF -factorizations?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a finite set of words over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$. An $F$-factorization of a word $w \in \Sigma^*$ is a decomposition $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_n$ with each $u_i \in F$. A language $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ is called an $F$-factorization language if every word of $L$ admits an $F$-factorization (where the factors used are recorded by the derivation/recognition device).

Say that an $F$-factorization language $L$ has the synchronization property with parameters $(k, m)$ (where $k, m$ are positive integers) if for every $w \in L$ and every two $F$-factorizations $w = u_1 \cdots u_n = v_1 \cdots v_{n'}$, whenever a prefix $u_1 \cdots u_i$ and a prefix $v_1 \cdots v_j$ have lengths differing by at most $m$, the suffixes of factorizations agree after at most $k$ further factors. (Equivalently, after any local discrepancy of size at most $m$ between two factorizations, the two factorizations re-synchronize within $k$ blocks.)

We say $L$ has the synchronization property (without specified parameters) if there exist some $k, m \geq 1$ such that $L$ has the synchronization property with parameters $(k, m)$.

Determine the computational complexity of each of the following decision problems:

(1) Given a regular $F$-factorization language $L$ (specified by a finite automaton together with the finite set $F$), decide whether $L$ has the synchronization property (with the parameters $k, m$ not given as part of the input, i.e., quantified existentially).

(2) The same problem when $L$ is presented as a context-free $F$-factorization language (specified by a context-free grammar together with $F$).
status_search_result: Web searches on synchronization properties of F-factorizations and on the complexity of related synchronization problems for regular and context-free languages return work on adjacent topics (synchronizing words under regular constraints, synchronized context-free languages, factorization of synchronous CFGs) but no source that resolves the specific complexity question for the synchronization property of regular or context-free F-factorizations with unspecified parameters. No direct evidence of a solution was found.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Given a morphism f and a letter a such that a is the initial letter of f(a), is it decidable whether the fixed point f^ω(a) is quasiperiodic?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet, and let A* (resp. A^ω) denote the set of finite (resp. one-sided infinite) words over A. A morphism f : A* → A* extends to A^ω by concatenation. A letter a ∈ A is called prolongable under f if f(a) starts with a and |f^n(a)| → ∞ as n → ∞; in this case the iterates f^n(a) converge to a unique infinite word f^ω(a) ∈ A^ω, called the pure morphic fixed point of f starting at a, satisfying f(f^ω(a)) = f^ω(a).

A finite nonempty word q ∈ A* is called a quasiperiod of an infinite word w ∈ A^ω if every position of w lies inside at least one occurrence of q in w (equivalently, w can be covered by occurrences of q). The infinite word w is called quasiperiodic if it admits at least one quasiperiod.

Problem. Determine whether the following decision problem is decidable:

  Input: a finite alphabet A, a morphism f : A* → A*, and a letter a ∈ A such that f(a) begins with a (so that the fixed point f^ω(a) is well-defined as an infinite word).
  Question: Is f^ω(a) quasiperiodic?

That is, does there exist an algorithm that, given any such (A, f, a), decides whether the pure morphic fixed point f^ω(a) admits a quasiperiod?
status_search_result: Web search did not turn up an explicit resolution of the decidability of quasiperiodicity for pure morphic fixed points. Related results are known: ultimate periodicity of morphic words is decidable (Harju–Linna; Pansiot), and there exist methods to compute the set of quasiperiods of certain morphic words, but no general decidability result for quasiperiodicity of arbitrary morphic fixed points was located. The problem appears to remain open, though this could not be confirmed conclusively.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Can we decide whether given a morphism, it is weakly quasiperiodic on finite (infinite) words?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ (resp. $A^\omega$) denote the set of finite (resp. infinite) words over $A$. A finite word $q \in A^*$ is said to cover a finite or infinite word $w$ if every position of $w$ lies inside some occurrence of $q$ in $w$; equivalently, $w$ can be written as an overlapping concatenation of copies of $q$ so that each symbol of $w$ belongs to at least one such copy. A finite or infinite word $w$ is called weakly quasiperiodic if there exist infinitely many distinct finite words $q_1, q_2, \ldots \in A^*$ each of which covers $w$ (equivalently, $w$ admits infinitely many quasiperiods).

A morphism is a map $\varphi : A^* \to A^*$ satisfying $\varphi(uv) = \varphi(u)\varphi(v)$. Say that $\varphi$ is weakly quasiperiodic on finite words if for every $w \in A^*$ that is sufficiently long (or, in the strongest reading, for every $w \in A^*$), the image $\varphi(w)$ is weakly quasiperiodic. Say that $\varphi$ is weakly quasiperiodic on infinite words if, whenever $\varphi$ is prolongable on a letter $a \in A$ (i.e. $\varphi(a) = a u$ with $u \neq \varepsilon$ and $\varphi^n(a) \to \infty$), the resulting infinite fixed point $\varphi^\omega(a) \in A^\omega$ is weakly quasiperiodic.

Problem. Determine whether each of the following decision problems is decidable:
(i) Given a morphism $\varphi : A^* \to A^*$, decide whether $\varphi$ is weakly quasiperiodic on finite words.
(ii) Given a morphism $\varphi : A^* \to A^*$, decide whether $\varphi$ is weakly quasiperiodic on infinite words.

Status appears unresolved in the literature accessible by search.

original_question: If X is a code and a bi-infinite word w has k disjoint X-factorizations with k <= |X| and at least one factorization non-periodic, must r(X) <= |X|-k+1?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and let A* denote the free monoid of finite words over A, with A^+ = A* \ {ε}. A subset X ⊆ A^+ is called a code if every word in X^+ admits a unique factorization as a concatenation of elements of X. A bi-infinite word over A is a sequence w = (a_i)_{i ∈ ℤ} with a_i ∈ A. An X-factorization of w is a strictly increasing two-way-infinite sequence of integers (i_n)_{n ∈ ℤ} such that, for every n, the block a_{i_n} a_{i_n+1} … a_{i_{n+1}-1} belongs to X. Two X-factorizations of w are called disjoint if their underlying sets of cut-points {i_n : n ∈ ℤ} are disjoint. A bi-infinite word w is periodic if there exists a nonzero integer p such that a_{i+p} = a_i for all i ∈ ℤ, and non-periodic otherwise.

The combinatorial rank r(X) of a finite set X ⊆ A^+ is defined as r(X) = min{|F| : F ⊆ A^+ and X ⊆ F^+}.

Question: Suppose X is a finite code and w is a bi-infinite word over A admitting k pairwise disjoint X-factorizations with k ≤ |X|, at least one of which corresponds to a non-periodic decomposition. Must one have
    r(X) ≤ |X| − k + 1 ?
status_search_result: The closely related defect theorem for bi-infinite words (Karhumäki–Maňuch–Plandowski, TCS 2003) establishes the case k = 2: if a non-periodic bi-infinite word has two disjoint X-factorizations, then the combinatorial rank of X is at most |X| − 1. The general statement for k ≥ 3 stated above does not appear to be confirmed or refuted in the available literature; its current status could not be verified.

original_question: Does there exist an independent system of three equations in three variables having a non-periodic solution?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^+$ the free semigroup of nonempty words over $\Sigma$. Let $\Xi=\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}$ be a set of three unknowns. A (constant-free) word equation in the unknowns $\Xi$ is a pair $(u,v)\in\Xi^+\times\Xi^+$, written $u=v$. A solution is a morphism $h:\Xi^+\to\Sigma^+$ with $h(u)=h(v)$; the solution is called periodic if there exists $w\in\Sigma^+$ such that $h(x_i)\in w^+$ for all $i=1,2,3$, and non-periodic otherwise.

A system $E=\{u_1=v_1,\ldots,u_k=v_k\}$ of word equations is called independent if no proper subsystem of $E$ has the same set of solutions as $E$ (equivalently, $E$ is not equivalent to any of its proper subsystems).

Question: Does there exist an independent system of three word equations in the three unknowns $x_1,x_2,x_3$ that admits a non-periodic solution $h:\Xi^+\to\Sigma^+$?
status_search_result: Recent surveys and research papers on independent systems of three-unknown constant-free word equations (e.g., the "From Ehrenfeucht to Eighteen" line of work and subsequent papers on solution sets of three-variable word equations) report only upper bounds — at most 18 in general, at most 17 if a non-periodic solution exists — and explicitly state the conjecture that the maximal size is a small constant, with no known construction realizing three independent equations sharing a non-periodic solution. No solution to the existence question has been reported, so the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Is the infinite system of word equations {u_i^1 = v_i^1 v_i^2 ... v_i^n : i >= 0} equivalent to one of its subsystems induced by three equations?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$. A word equation is a pair $(L,R)$ with $L,R$ words in variables (and possibly constants); a morphism $h:\text{Vars}\to\Sigma^*$ is a solution if $h(L)=h(R)$. Two systems of word equations are called equivalent if they have exactly the same set of solutions. Fix an integer $n\ge 1$ and, for each $i\ge 0$, fix words $u_i^1$ and $v_i^1,v_i^2,\dots,v_i^n$ in some common set of unknowns, giving the infinite system
$$S=\{\,u_i^1 = v_i^1 v_i^2 \cdots v_i^n \;:\; i\ge 0\,\}.$$
Determine whether $S$ is necessarily equivalent to a subsystem consisting of (at most) three of its equations; that is, decide whether for every such $S$ there exist indices $i_1,i_2,i_3\ge 0$ such that the three equations $u_{i_k}^1=v_{i_k}^1\cdots v_{i_k}^n$, $k=1,2,3$, have the same set of solutions as the whole system $S$.
category_tag: Word equations and combinatorics on words
status_search_result: Surveys on independent systems of word equations indicate that, although every infinite system is equivalent to a finite subsystem (Ehrenfeucht compactness via Hilbert's basis theorem), the precise bound — conjectured to be three for many natural classes of equations of this shape — remains open in general; only partial results (e.g., bounds like 18 for three-variable systems) are known.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is it decidable whether a given PCP instance has the unique-equality-continuation property?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the free monoid of words over $\Sigma$. An instance of the Post Correspondence Problem (PCP) is a finite list $I=((u_1,v_1),\dots,(u_n,v_n))$ of pairs of words $u_i,v_i\in\Sigma^*$. For a finite index sequence $\sigma=i_1i_2\cdots i_k\in\{1,\dots,n\}^*$ write $u_\sigma=u_{i_1}u_{i_2}\cdots u_{i_k}$ and $v_\sigma=v_{i_1}v_{i_2}\cdots v_{i_k}$. The sequence $\sigma$ is called admissible (an "equality continuation" candidate) if $u_\sigma$ is a prefix of $v_\sigma$ or $v_\sigma$ is a prefix of $u_\sigma$.

Say that the instance $I$ has the unique-equality-continuation property if for every admissible sequence $\sigma$ (including the empty sequence) there is at most one index $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ such that the extended sequence $\sigma j$ is also admissible.

Decide: Is there an algorithm that, given an arbitrary PCP instance $I$ as input, determines whether $I$ has the unique-equality-continuation property?
status_search_result: Web searches turned up related results showing that PCP instances satisfying a uniqueness-of-continuation condition form a known decidable subclass (Halava–Harju–Karhumäki–Latteux, 2007, on instances with unique blocks; and the infinite PCP being decidable for unique-continuation instances), but no source was found that resolves the meta-question of whether the property of having unique equality continuation is itself decidable. The status therefore appears unresolved in publicly available sources.
